It is Meccan, except for eight verses, which are His words: ﴿Ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾ up to His words: ﴿And when We raised the mountain above them﴾ (al-A'raf: 163-171).

It has been established that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite it in the Maghrib prayer, dividing it between the two rak'ahs. Its verses number two hundred and six.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

That is: let there be no narrowness in your breast from conveying it to the people, for fear that they will deny you and harm you; indeed Allah is your Guardian and your Helper.

It is connected to "was sent down": that is, it was sent down to you so that you may warn the people by it. His saying: ﴿and a reminder for the believers.﴾ Dhikra means reminding (al-tadhkir).

The Basrans said: dhikra is in the nominative position by the implied subject (idmar mubtada').

Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the nominative position by coordination with "a Book." It may also be accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "and remind by it as a reminder," as the Basrans also said.

The restriction of the reminder to the believers is because they are the ones in whom it is effective; and in this is an indication that warning is restricted to the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord.﴾ It means the Book, and likewise the Sunnah, by His saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (al-Hashr: 7) and similar verses. It is a command to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and to his community. It is said: it is a command to the community after his command, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, to convey, and it is sent down to them through its being sent down to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. ﴿And do not follow, besides Him, any guardians﴾: a prohibition to the community against following guardians besides Allah, whom they worship and make partners with Allah. On this view the pronoun in "besides Him" refers to "Lord." It is also permissible for it to refer to "what" in "what has been sent down to you": that is, do not follow, besides the Book of Allah, guardians whom you imitate in your religion, as the people of ignorance used to do by obeying leaders in what they make lawful for them and unlawful for them.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you remember.﴾ The accusative of "little" (qalilan) is as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun for the later verb: that is, "a little remembrance." "Ma" is superfluous for emphasis, or "little" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "do not follow," and "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah): that is, do not follow besides Him guardians, whose remembrance is little.

It is read "tadhakkarun" with lightening by omitting one of the two taa's, and it is read with doubling through assimilation (idgham).

His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed?﴾ Kam here is the informative kam, which indicates multiplicity; it is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and "We destroyed it" is the predicate. "From a town" is a specifier (tamyiz). It is said: the destruction befell some of the people of the town, so the meaning is: how many a town have We destroyed some of its people, so Our might came upon it and We destroyed all of them. It is said: the meaning is: how many a town have We decreed its destruction, so Our might came upon it. Al-Qaylulah is the sleep at midday.

It is said: it is merely resting at that time because of the intensity of the heat, without sleep. He specified the two times because they are the times of stillness and tranquility, so the coming of punishment in them is more severe and more dreadful.

Similar is His saying: ﴿And the last of their call (da'wahum)﴾ (Yunus: 10), meaning the last of their supplication. It is said: da'wa here means claim (idda'a), and the meaning is: what they claimed for their religion and adopted was not except their acknowledgment of its falsehood and corruption. The subject of "kana" is "illa an qalu," and its predicate is "da'wahum"; the reverse is also permitted, and the meaning is: their claim was not except their saying: "Indeed we were wrongdoers."

The questioning is of the peoples to whom Allah sent the messengers from the earlier nations, for rebuke and reproach. The "lam" is the lam of oath: that is, We will surely question them about what they answered their messengers when called. The "fa'" indicates the ordering of the otherworldly states upon the worldly states. ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾: that is, the prophets whom Allah sent; We will ask them about what their nations answered them, and about who obeyed among them and who disobeyed. It is said: the meaning of ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom they were sent﴾ is: the prophets; and ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾ is: the angels. This is not contradicted by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the guilty will not be questioned about their sins﴾, because, as we have mentioned more than once, the Hereafter has stations: in one station they are questioned, and in another they are not questioned. Likewise all that appears to be contradictory is to be understood by affirming in one place and negating in another with respect to the Day of Resurrection, for it is to be taken as multiplicity of standing-places together with the great length of that day.

Ibn Jarir transmitted the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, regarding His saying "Alif Lam Mim Sad," that he said: "The Alif is from Allah, the Mim is from al-Rahman, and the Sad is from al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge)."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "Its meaning is: I am Allah, the Truthful." It is not hidden from you that all of this is speech based on conjecture and interpretation by guesswork, and there is no proof in any of it; the truth is what we have mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud: "No people were destroyed until they had been given an excuse from themselves," and then he recited: ﴿So their plea was not...﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Farqad regarding the verse, that he said: "One of them is the prophets, and one of them is the angels."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: "We will ask the people about the statement 'There is no god but Allah,' and we will ask Jibril."

It is read "tadhakkarun" with lightening by omitting one of the two taa's, and it is read with doubling through assimilation (idgham).

The questioning is of the peoples to whom Allah sent the messengers from the earlier nations, for rebuke and reproach. Ibn Jarir transmitted the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, regarding His saying "Alif Lam Mim Sad," that he said: "The Alif is from Allah, the Mim is from al-Rahman, and the Sad is from al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge)."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "Its meaning is: I am Allah, the Truthful." It is not hidden from you that all of this is speech based on conjecture and interpretation by guesswork, and there is no proof in any of it; the truth is what we have mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿So let there be no constriction in your breast concerning it﴾, that he said: "It is doubt." And he said, when asked by a Bedouin, "What is haraj among you?" He said: "Confusion (al-labs)."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted the like from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "Narrowness."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud: "No people were destroyed until they had been given an excuse from themselves," and then he recited: ﴿So their plea was not...﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: "We will ask the people about the statement 'There is no god but Allah,' and we will ask Jibril."

His saying: ﴿So their plea was not, when Our might came upon them, except that they said: Indeed we were wrongdoers.﴾ Da'wa means supplication (du'a'): that is, their supplication to their Lord at the descent of punishment was not except their acknowledgment of wrongdoing against themselves. Similar is His saying: ﴿And the last of their call (da'wahum)﴾ (Yunus: 10), meaning the last of their supplication. It is said: da'wa here means claim (idda'a), and the meaning is: what they claimed for their religion and adopted was not except their acknowledgment of its falsehood and corruption. The subject of "kana" is "illa an qalu," and its predicate is "da'wahum"; the reverse is also permitted, and the meaning is: their claim was not except their saying: "Indeed we were wrongdoers."

His saying, 6: ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾: this is a severe threat. The questioning is of the peoples to whom Allah sent the messengers from the earlier nations, for rebuke and reproach. The "lam" is the lam of oath: that is, We will surely question them about what they answered their messengers when called. The "fa'" indicates the ordering of the otherworldly states upon the worldly states. ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾: that is, the prophets whom Allah sent; We will ask them about what their nations answered them, and about who obeyed among them and who disobeyed. It is said: the meaning of ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom they were sent﴾ is: the prophets; and ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾ is: the angels. This is not contradicted by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the guilty will not be questioned about their sins﴾, because, as we have mentioned more than once, the Hereafter has stations: in one station they are questioned, and in another they are not questioned. Likewise all that appears to be contradictory is to be understood by affirming in one place and negating in another with respect to the Day of Resurrection, for it is to be taken as multiplicity of standing-places together with the great length of that day.

7: ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾: that is, to the messengers and to those to whom they were sent, what occurred between them at the time of the call, with knowledge and not with ignorance; that is, knowing what they conceal and what they disclose, and We were not absent from them in any state, so that anything that occurred between them would be hidden from Us.

Ibn Jarir transmitted the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas that these and similar openings of the surahs are an oath which Allah swore by, and they are among the names of Allah.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, regarding His saying "Alif Lam Mim Sad," that he said: "The Alif is from Allah, the Mim is from al-Rahman, and the Sad is from al-Samad (the Eternal Refuge)."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "Its meaning is: I am Allah, the Truthful." It is not hidden from you that all of this is speech based on conjecture and interpretation by guesswork, and there is no proof in any of it; the truth is what we have mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted the like from Mujahid.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Dahhak, who said: "Narrowness."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud: "No people were destroyed until they had been given an excuse from themselves," and then he recited: ﴿So their plea was not...﴾ to the end of the verse.

Ibn Jarir transmitted it from him as a raised (marfu') report.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿Then We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾, that he said: "We will ask the people about what they answered the messengers, and We will ask the messengers about what they conveyed." ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾, he said: "By the placing of the Book on the Day of Resurrection, and We will speak of what they used to do."

Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Farqad regarding the verse, that he said: "One of them is the prophets, and one of them is the angels."

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid regarding the verse, that he said: "We will ask the people about the statement 'There is no god but Allah,' and we will ask Jibril."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad.﴾ What has preceded at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah suffices, so there is no need to repeat it. This (al-Mas) is either a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is "a Book," meaning: "Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad are the letters of a Book sent down to you"; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being "This is al-Mas," i.e., the one named by it. And if these openings are recited as a mere enumeration, then they have no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu). "A Book" is the predicate of the subject in the first case, or the predicate of an omitted subject in the second, meaning "it is a Book."

Al-Kisa'i said: meaning "This is a Book," and "sent down to you" is a qualifier of it. ﴿So let there be no constriction (haraj) in your breast concerning it.﴾ Haraj means narrowness (diq). That is: let there be no narrowness in your breast from conveying it to the people, for fear that they will deny you and harm you; indeed Allah is your Guardian and your Helper.

It is said that the intended meaning is: let your breast not be constricted because they do not believe in it and do not respond to you, for upon you is only the conveying (of the message).

Mujahid and Qatadah said: haraj here means doubt, because the doubter has a constricted breast. That is: do not doubt that it is sent down from Allah. On this view, the prohibition addressed to him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, is by way of indirect address (ta'rid), and the intended audience is his community: that none of them should doubt that. The pronoun in "concerning it" refers to the Book. On the first view, there is an omitted genitive construction: "from its conveying"; on the second, the estimate is "from its being sent down."

The pronoun in ﴿that you may warn thereby﴾ refers to the Book: that you may warn the people by the Book which We have sent down to you. It is connected to "was sent down": that is, it was sent down to you so that you may warn the people by it. Or it is connected to the prohibition, because the absence of doubt about its being sent down from Allah, or the absence of fear of his people, strengthens him for warning and encourages him, since one who is certain proceeds with insight and acts with strength of soul.

His saying: ﴿and a reminder for the believers.﴾ Dhikra means reminding (al-tadhkir).

The Basrans said: dhikra is in the nominative position by the implied subject (idmar mubtada').

Al-Kisa'i said: it is in the nominative position by coordination with "a Book." It may also be accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "and remind by it as a reminder," as the Basrans also said.

It may be genitive, taken as in agreement with the position of "that you may warn," i.e., "for warning and for reminding." The restriction of the reminder to the believers is because they are the ones in whom it is effective; and in this is an indication that warning is restricted to the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord.﴾ It means the Book, and likewise the Sunnah, by His saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (al-Hashr: 7) and similar verses. It is a command to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, and to his community. It is said: it is a command to the community after his command, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, to convey, and it is sent down to them through its being sent down to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace. ﴿And do not follow, besides Him, any guardians﴾: a prohibition to the community against following guardians besides Allah, whom they worship and make partners with Allah. On this view the pronoun in "besides Him" refers to "Lord." It is also permissible for it to refer to "what" in "what has been sent down to you": that is, do not follow, besides the Book of Allah, guardians whom you imitate in your religion, as the people of ignorance used to do by obeying leaders in what they make lawful for them and unlawful for them.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you remember.﴾ The accusative of "little" (qalilan) is as a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun for the later verb: that is, "a little remembrance." "Ma" is superfluous for emphasis, or "little" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "do not follow," and "ma" is verbal (masdariyyah): that is, do not follow besides Him guardians, whose remembrance is little.

It is read "tadhakkarun" with lightening by omitting one of the two taa's, and it is read with doubling through assimilation (idgham).

His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed?﴾ Kam here is the informative kam, which indicates multiplicity; it is in the nominative position as a subject (mubtada'), and "We destroyed it" is the predicate. "From a town" is a specifier (tamyiz). It may also be in the accusative position by an verb implied after it, not before it, because it has the initial position in the sentence; and were it not for the occupation of "We destroyed it" by the pronoun, kam would be permitted to take the accusative by it. The "qaryah" is the place where people gather: that is, how many a town of the great towns have We destroyed, destroying it by destroying its people; or We destroyed its people. And the intended meaning is that We intended to destroy it.

His saying: ﴿So there came upon them Our might.﴾ It is coordinated with "We destroyed," with the estimate of intention as mentioned, because the ordering of the arrival of might after destruction is valid only with this estimate, since destruction is itself the arrival of might.

Al-Farra' said: the fa' has the meaning of the waw, so no estimate is required, and the meaning is: We destroyed it, and Our might came to it; the waw is for mere joining without ordering.

It is said: the destruction befell some of the people of the town, so the meaning is: how many a town have We destroyed some of its people, so Our might came upon it and We destroyed all of them. It is said: the meaning is: how many a town have We decreed its destruction, so Our might came upon it. It is said: We destroyed it by sending the angels of punishment to it. ﴿So there came upon them Our might﴾; and the might is the punishment.

It is related from al-Farra' that when the meaning of the two verbs is one, or like one, you may put whichever you wish first: so the meaning is "how many a town, Our might came upon it, and We destroyed it," like "it drew near and approached," and "it approached and drew near."

"Bayatan" means by night, because one spends the night in it; it is said: "he spent the night (bata yabitu) batan and bayatan." It is a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial state: that is, while spending the night.

His saying: "or they were resting at noon" is coordinated with "bayatan": that is, spending the night or resting at noon. The circumstantial clause came without a waw, avoiding the heaviness of two waws, the waw of coordination and the waw of circumstance; so said al-Farra'.

Al-Zajjaj objected to him, saying: this is an error; rather the waw is not needed. You say: "Zayd came to me riding, or he is walking," because in the clause there is a pronoun that refers back to the first. And "or" in this place is for detailing, not for doubt.
