**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *al-haqq* (the truth). That is, the weighing on this Day is the just scale in which there is no injustice. Or the predicate is *yawma'idhin* (on that Day), and *al-haqq* is an attribute of the subject, meaning the just weighing exists on this Day. It has also been said that *al-haqq* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

The scholars differed over the manner of this weighing that takes place on this Day. It has been said that what is meant is the weighing of the records of the servants' deeds on the scale, as a literal weighing. This is the correct view, and it is the one supported by the evidences. It has also been said that the deeds themselves are weighed, even though they are accidents (*a'rad*), because God will transform them on the Day of Resurrection into bodies, as in the authentic report: «Indeed, al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shadows, or two flocks of birds spreading their wings.»

Likewise, it is established in the Sahih that «the Qur'an will come in the form of a young man, pale of complexion», and similar reports. It has also been said that the scale (*al-mizan*) is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. It has been said too that *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and that they are mentioned as a figure of speech, as you say: "This statement is in the weight of that one."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is permissible from the standpoint of the language, but it is better for us to follow what has come in the sound chains of narration concerning the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: Al-Zajjaj has spoken well, for if the Path (*al-sirat*) were interpreted as the true religion, and Paradise and Hellfire as what befalls the souls rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as blameworthy character traits, and the angels as praiseworthy faculties… Then he said: The community in the earliest period unanimously agreed to take these apparent meanings without interpretation (*ta'wil*). And when they unanimously agreed to prohibit interpretation, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became texts (*nusus*). End of quote.

The correct view is the first opinion.

As for those who consider it far-fetched to take these apparent meanings in their literal sense, they cite no part of the Sharia to which one can refer in their objection. Rather, the most they rely on is mere rational improbability, and such reasoning is no proof against anyone. If their intellects reject it, then the intellects of people stronger than them, from among the Companions, the Successors, and the Successors' successors, have accepted it. Then innovations came like a dark night, and everyone said what he wished, and they turned their backs on the Sharia. If only they had brought rational rulings upon which sensible people agree and on which they uniformly accept them! Instead, every faction claims that reason supports whatever matches its desires and agrees with what it or its followers hold. Thus their intellects contradict one another just as their doctrines contradict one another. Every fair-minded person knows this, and whoever denies it should purify his understanding and intellect from the impurities of partisanship and sectarianism, for if he does, the morning will shine clearly before his eyes.

The weighing and the scales are mentioned in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And We will set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47). And His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101). And His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding forever in Hell﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 102–103). And His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ (al-Nisa': 40). And His saying: ﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. And as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be the Abyss﴾ (al-Qari'ah: 6–9). The *fa'* in *fa-man thaqulat mawazinuhu* is for detailing (*tafsil*).

*Al-mawazin* is the plural of *mizan*, and its origin is *miwzan*, with the *waw* changed to *ya'* because of the kasra before it. The heaviness of these scales is by the heaviness of what is placed in them of the records of deeds. It has also been said that *al-mawazin* is the plural of *mawzun* (that which is weighed), meaning: whoever's weighed deeds outweigh. The first view is better.

The apparent sense of the plural *al-mawazin*, being attributed to the doer, is that each of the two doers has scales, and each scale weighs a category of his deeds. It has also been said that it is one scale, expressed with the plural form, as one says: "So-and-so went to Mecca on mules." The pointing in His saying *fa-ulā'ika* (those) refers back to *man* (whoever), and the plural is according to its meaning, just as the pronoun referring to *mawazinuhu* (his scales) returns according to its wording. It is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *hum al-muflihun* (they are the successful).

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ is like it. The *ba'* in *bima kanu bi-ayatina yazlimun* (because they used to wrong Our signs) is causal (*sababiyyah*), and *ma* is verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah*).

The meaning of *yazlimun* (they wrong) is *yakdhibun* (they deny).

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning: We made for you a place in it and prepared for you in it the means of livelihood.

*Al-ma'ayish* is the plural of *ma'ishah*, meaning that by which one lives, namely food and drink and whatever life is sustained by. It is said: *'asha ya'ishu 'aysh*, *ma'ash*, and *ma'ish*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-ma'ishah* is what they use to reach a living. According to al-Akhfash and many grammarians, *al-ma'ishah* is of the pattern *maf'ilah*.

Al-A'raj read *ma'a'ish* with a hamzah, and similarly Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated it from Nafi'.

Al-Nahhas said: The hamzah is an error that is not permissible, because the singular is *ma'ishah* and the *ya'* is original, like *madinah* and *madain*, and *sahifah* and *sahaif*.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of what preceded it shortly before, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We formed you﴾. This is a mention of another of God's blessings upon His servants.

The meaning: We created you as drops of semen, then We formed you after that. It has also been said that the meaning is: We created Adam from dust, then We formed you in his loins. It has also been said that *and We certainly created you* refers to Adam, mentioned in the plural because he is the father of mankind, and *then We formed you* refers back to him. This is indicated by *then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam*, for the arrangement of this statement after the creating and forming indicates that the one created and formed is Adam, upon him be peace.

Al-Akhfash said: *Thumma* (then) in *thumma sawwarnakum* means *wa* (and). It has also been said that the meaning is: We created you from the loins of Adam, then We formed you when We took from you the covenant. Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of the views. It has also been said that the meaning is: And We certainly created the spirits first, then We formed the bodies, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, meaning: We commanded them to do so, and they obeyed the command and performed the prostration after the command, except Iblis. It has been said: the exception is contiguous (*muttasil*), by giving precedence to the angels over Iblis, because he was distinct among them. Or, as it has been said, because among the angels there is a kind called the jinn. It has also been said other than this, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

His saying: *lam yakun min al-sajidin* (he was not among those who prostrated) is a sentence explaining what is understood from the meaning of the exception (*istithna'*). Whoever makes the exception disjunctive (*munqati'*) says its meaning is: "But Iblis was not among those who prostrated."

The sentence *qala ma mana'aka an la tasjud* (He said: What prevented you from not prostrating?) is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did God say to him?" The *la* in *an la tasjud* is superfluous for emphasis, as evidenced by His saying in Surah Sad: *ma mana'aka an tasjud* (Sad: 75). It has also been said that *mana'a* here means *qala* (said), and the implied meaning is: who told you not to prostrate. It has also been said that *mana'a* means *da'a* (called), meaning: what called you to not prostrate. It has also been said that there is an omission in the statement, and the implied meaning is: what prevented you from obedience and compelled you not to prostrate when I commanded you, meaning at the time I commanded you. It has been used as evidence that a command requires immediacy (*li-l-fawr*), and the discussion is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). The interrogative in *ma mana'aka* is for reproach and rebuke, since He, glorified is He, already knows that.

The sentence *qala ana khayrun minhu* (He said: I am better than him) is a resumptive sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did Iblis say?" He said in answer "I am better than him," and did not say "what prevented me was such-and-such," because the sentence he brought, being resumptive, contains what indicates the preventing reason, which is his belief that he is superior to him. The superior does not act toward the inferior in that manner, along with what this sentence implies of rejecting that someone like him should be commanded to prostrate to someone like him.

Then he gave a reason for the claim of superiority he asserted, in his saying: ﴿You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾, believing that the element of fire is superior to the element of clay.

The enemy of God erred, for the element of clay is superior to the element of fire in terms of its steadiness, its stillness, and its long endurance. Fire is an agitated substance that quickly perishes. Moreover, clay is present in Paradise but fire is not, fire is a punishment, while clay is in need of fire to be made into a shape, and clay is a place of prostration and purity. Had it not been for the prior decree of his wretchedness and the truth of God's word concerning him, he would have had as an example and a model the angels who obeyed this command. Thus their luminous element is nobler than his fiery element.

The sentence *qala fahbit* (He said: Then go down) is a resumptive sentence like the one before it. The *fa'* is for the ordering of the command to descend upon his disobedience of the command. That is: Go down from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient angels who do not disobey God in what He commands them, to the earth, which is the abode of one who disobeys and obeys. Heaven is not suitable for one who is arrogant and disobeys his Lord, like you. For this reason He said: ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

Among the false interpretations is what has been said: the meaning of *ihbit minha* (go down from it) is: come out of your fiery form, of which you boasted, into a dark, disfigured form. It has also been said: what is meant is his descent from Paradise. It has also been said: from the company of the angels. The sentence *fa-khruj* (then get out) is for emphasis of the command to descend. The sentence *innaka min al-saghirin* (indeed you are among the abased) is a cause for the command, meaning: indeed you are among those of abasement and humiliation before God and before His righteous servants. Thus, everyone who clothes himself in the garment of arrogance is punished by being clothed in the garment of humiliation and abasement, and whoever clothes himself in the garment of humility, God clothes him in the garment of exaltation.

The sentence *qala anzirni ila yawm yub'athun* (He said: Reprieve me until the Day they are raised) is a resumptive sentence, as was mentioned in the previous sentences. That is: give me respite until the Day of Resurrection. It seems he asked not to die, because there is no death after the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun in *yub'athun* refers to Adam and his descendants.

God answered him with His saying: ﴿Indeed you are among the reprieved﴾, meaning: among those given respite until that Day. Then you will be punished with what God has decreed for you, and He will bring you down into the depths of Hellfire.

It has been said: the wisdom in granting him respite is to test the servants, to know who obeys him and who disobeys him.

The sentence (16): *qala fa-bima aghwaytani* (He said: Because You have led me astray) is a resumptive sentence like the preceding sentences, coming as an answer to an assumed question. The *ba'* in *fa-bima* is causal and the *fa'* is for the ordering of the sentence upon what precedes it. It has been said that the *ba'* is for swearing an oath, like His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾, meaning: by Your misguiding me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾. *Al-ighwa'* (misguidance) is causing someone to fall into error. It has been said that the *ba'* means *al-lam* (for), and it has been said that it means *ma'a* (with). The meaning is: with Your misguiding me. It has been said that *ma* in *fa-bima aghwaytani* is interrogative, and the meaning is: "By what did You lead me astray?" The first view is better.

What he intends by this misguidance, which he made the cause of what he would do with the servants, is his abandonment of prostration, and that this was by God's misguidance of him, until he chose error over guidance. It has been said that he meant the curse with which God cursed him, meaning: because You cursed me and destroyed me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾. From this is His saying: ﴿So they will meet error﴾ (Maryam: 59), meaning destruction.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: It is said: *ghawa al-rajulu yaghwi ghayyan* when his affair became corrupt for him, or he himself became corrupt. From this is His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred﴾ (Ta-Ha: 121), meaning his life in Paradise was corrupted. *La-aq'udanna lahum* (I will surely sit in wait for them), meaning: I will surely exert myself in misleading them, until they become corrupt because of me, just as I was corrupted because of my abandonment of prostration to their father.

The *al-sirat al-mustaqim* (straight path) is the road that leads to Paradise. Its accusative case is adverbial of place (*zarfiyyah*), meaning: on Your straight path, as Sibawayh related: "Zayd struck the back and the belly." The *lam* in *la-aq'udanna* is the *lam* of oath, and the *ba'* in *bima aghwaytani* is connected to the omitted verb of oath, meaning: by Your misguiding me, I swear that I will surely sit in wait.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 2 of 2)**

His words: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾. He mentioned the four directions because they are the directions from which an enemy attacks his foe. For this reason he omitted mention of above and below. The verb is followed by *min* (from) with the first two directions and by *ʿan* (away from, concerning) with the other two, because the one who comes from in front or behind usually faces what is coming to him with his whole body, whereas the one who comes from the right or the left is usually turned aside. So it was appropriate to use the preposition of origin (*min*) with the first two and the preposition of passing beyond (*ʿan*) with the other two. This is a figurative depiction of his whispering and his enticement, as though they come from someone who actually approaches. It was also said that what is meant by "from before them" is from their worldly life, "from behind them" is from their Hereafter, "from their right" is from the direction of their good deeds, and "from their left" is from the direction of their bad deeds. Al-Nahhas (an-Nahhas, the grammarian and exegete) preferred this view.

His words: ﴿Nor will You find most of them thankful﴾. That is, "And when I do that, You will not find most of them thankful, because of the effect of my whispering on them and my seducing them." He said this on the basis of assumption, as in His words: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them﴾ (Saba, 20). It was also said that he heard this from the angels and then said it. Here "thankful" is used to mean obedience, or it may be taken literally, meaning that they did not thank Allah because of being led astray.

The clause ﴿He said, "Get out of it"﴾ is a resumptive sentence, like the sentences that precede it. That is, out of the heaven, or the Garden, or from among the angels, as was mentioned earlier.

*Madhʾūman*: that is, *madhmūman* (blameworthy), from *dhaʾamahu*, meaning he blamed him. It is said: *dhaʾamtuhu* and *dhammamtuhu* have the same meaning.

Al-Aʿmash read *madhmūman*. Al-Zuhri read *madhūman* without the hamzah. It was also said: *al-madhʾūm* means one who is expelled, and *al-madhḥūr* means one who is driven away.

His words: ﴿Whoever follows you among them﴾. Most readers read the *lam* with a fatha, taking it as the *lam* of oath, and its answer is ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾. It was also said that the *lam* in *la-man tabiʿaka* is for emphasis, and the *lam* in *la-amla'anna* is the *lam* of oath. The first is preferable. The answer of the oath takes the place of the answer of the conditional, because *man* is a conditional particle. In this answer there is a threat beyond measure.

ʿĀṣim, in one transmission from him, read *liman tabiʿaka* with a kasra on the *lam*, and some grammarians rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: its estimate, and Allah knows best, is "for the sake of those who followed you," as one says, "I honoured so-and-so for your sake." It was also said that it is a cause for *uqhruj* (get out), and the pronoun in *minkum* refers to him and to those who follow him. The pronoun of address was given precedence over the pronoun of the third person, and the original form would be *minka wa-minhum*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, that he said: it is justice. "Whoever's scales are heavy" means his good deeds, and "whoever's scales are light" means his good deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi: "The deeds will be weighed."

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the manner of the scale, the weighing, and what is weighed.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man from my community will be called out before the heads of all creation on the Day of Resurrection. Ninety-nine registers will be unfolded for him, each register extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked: 'Do you deny any of this? Have my recording angels, the guardians, wronged you?' He will say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be asked: 'Do you have an excuse, or a good deed?' The man will be overcome with fear and say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be told: 'Yes, indeed, you have a good deed with Us, and no wrong will be done to you today.' Then a small card will be brought out for him, on which is written: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' He will say: 'My Lord, what is this card alongside these registers?' He will be told: 'Indeed, you will not be wronged.' The registers will be placed on one pan and the card on the other pan. The registers will be light, and the card will be heavy." Al-Tirmidhi also graded it sound, and its chain in Ahmad is good (*hasan*).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾, that he said: "They were created in the loins of men and fashioned in the wombs of women."

al-Firyabi reported from him that he said: "They were created in the back of Adam, then they were fashioned in the wombs."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also that he said: "As for 'We created you,' it refers to Adam; and as for 'then We fashioned you,' it refers to his offspring."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿIkrimah concerning the verse that Iblis was created from the fire of might.

It is established in the *Sahih* from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, Iblis was created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan, who said: "The first to use analogy (*qiyas*) was Iblis, in his words: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾." Its chain to al-Hasan is sound.

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and al-Daylami reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to apply analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion was Iblis. Allah said to him: 'Prostrate to Adam.' He said: 'I am better than him. You created me from fire and You created him from clay.'"

Jaʿfar said: Whoever applies analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion, Allah will join him on the Day of Resurrection with Iblis, because he followed him by analogy.

The chain of this hadith should be examined, for I do not think its attribution to the Prophet is sound, and it does not resemble the speech of prophethood.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "*Fa-bimā aghwaytanī* means: 'Since You led me astray (*aḍlaltanī*).'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from him concerning His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, that he said: "The road to Makkah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Ibn Masʿud.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "I will cast doubt upon them regarding the affairs of their Hereafter. And from behind them: I will make them desire their worldly life. And from their right: I will confuse them about the matter of their religion. And from their left: I will make sins attractive to them and make falsehood seem true to them. And ﴿nor will You find most of them thankful﴾: that is, monotheists (*muwahhidīn*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "He says: from where they can see; and from behind them: from where they cannot see; and from their right: from where they can see; and from their left: from where they cannot see."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "He was not able to say 'from above them.'" In another wording: "He knew that mercy descends from above them."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His words *madhʾūman* that he said: "Blamed." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Despised."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning *madhʾūman*, that he said: "Banished." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Driven away."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *al-haqq* (the truth). That is, the weighing on this Day is the just scale in which there is no injustice. Or the predicate is *yawma'idhin* (on that Day), and *al-haqq* is an attribute of the subject, meaning the just weighing exists on this Day. It has also been said that *al-haqq* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

The scholars differed over the manner of this weighing that takes place on this Day. It has been said that what is meant is the weighing of the records of the servants' deeds on the scale, as a literal weighing. This is the correct view, and it is the one supported by the evidences. It has also been said that the deeds themselves are weighed, even though they are accidents (*a'rad*), because God will transform them on the Day of Resurrection into bodies, as in the authentic report: «Indeed, al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shadows, or two flocks of birds spreading their wings.»

Likewise, it is established in the Sahih that «the Qur'an will come in the form of a young man, pale of complexion», and similar reports. It has also been said that the scale (*al-mizan*) is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. It has been said too that *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and that they are mentioned as a figure of speech, as you say: "This statement is in the weight of that one."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is permissible from the standpoint of the language, but it is better for us to follow what has come in the sound chains of narration concerning the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: Al-Zajjaj has spoken well, for if the Path (*al-sirat*) were interpreted as the true religion, and Paradise and Hellfire as what befalls the souls rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as blameworthy character traits, and the angels as praiseworthy faculties… Then he said: The community in the earliest period unanimously agreed to take these apparent meanings without interpretation (*ta'wil*). And when they unanimously agreed to prohibit interpretation, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became texts (*nusus*). End of quote.

The correct view is the first opinion.

As for those who consider it far-fetched to take these apparent meanings in their literal sense, they cite no part of the Sharia to which one can refer in their objection. Rather, the most they rely on is mere rational improbability, and such reasoning is no proof against anyone. If their intellects reject it, then the intellects of people stronger than them, from among the Companions, the Successors, and the Successors' successors, have accepted it. Then innovations came like a dark night, and everyone said what he wished, and they turned their backs on the Sharia. If only they had brought rational rulings upon which sensible people agree and on which they uniformly accept them! Instead, every faction claims that reason supports whatever matches its desires and agrees with what it or its followers hold. Thus their intellects contradict one another just as their doctrines contradict one another. Every fair-minded person knows this, and whoever denies it should purify his understanding and intellect from the impurities of partisanship and sectarianism, for if he does, the morning will shine clearly before his eyes.

The weighing and the scales are mentioned in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And We will set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47). And His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101). And His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding forever in Hell﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 102–103). And His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ (al-Nisa': 40). And His saying: ﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. And as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be the Abyss﴾ (al-Qari'ah: 6–9). The *fa'* in *fa-man thaqulat mawazinuhu* is for detailing (*tafsil*).

*Al-mawazin* is the plural of *mizan*, and its origin is *miwzan*, with the *waw* changed to *ya'* because of the kasra before it. The heaviness of these scales is by the heaviness of what is placed in them of the records of deeds. It has also been said that *al-mawazin* is the plural of *mawzun* (that which is weighed), meaning: whoever's weighed deeds outweigh. The first view is better.

The apparent sense of the plural *al-mawazin*, being attributed to the doer, is that each of the two doers has scales, and each scale weighs a category of his deeds. It has also been said that it is one scale, expressed with the plural form, as one says: "So-and-so went to Mecca on mules." The pointing in His saying *fa-ulā'ika* (those) refers back to *man* (whoever), and the plural is according to its meaning, just as the pronoun referring to *mawazinuhu* (his scales) returns according to its wording. It is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *hum al-muflihun* (they are the successful).

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ is like it. The *ba'* in *bima kanu bi-ayatina yazlimun* (because they used to wrong Our signs) is causal (*sababiyyah*), and *ma* is verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah*).

The meaning of *yazlimun* (they wrong) is *yakdhibun* (they deny).

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning: We made for you a place in it and prepared for you in it the means of livelihood.

*Al-ma'ayish* is the plural of *ma'ishah*, meaning that by which one lives, namely food and drink and whatever life is sustained by. It is said: *'asha ya'ishu 'aysh*, *ma'ash*, and *ma'ish*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-ma'ishah* is what they use to reach a living. According to al-Akhfash and many grammarians, *al-ma'ishah* is of the pattern *maf'ilah*.

Al-A'raj read *ma'a'ish* with a hamzah, and similarly Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated it from Nafi'.

Al-Nahhas said: The hamzah is an error that is not permissible, because the singular is *ma'ishah* and the *ya'* is original, like *madinah* and *madain*, and *sahifah* and *sahaif*.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of what preceded it shortly before, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We formed you﴾. This is a mention of another of God's blessings upon His servants.

The meaning: We created you as drops of semen, then We formed you after that. It has also been said that the meaning is: We created Adam from dust, then We formed you in his loins. It has also been said that *and We certainly created you* refers to Adam, mentioned in the plural because he is the father of mankind, and *then We formed you* refers back to him. This is indicated by *then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam*, for the arrangement of this statement after the creating and forming indicates that the one created and formed is Adam, upon him be peace.

Al-Akhfash said: *Thumma* (then) in *thumma sawwarnakum* means *wa* (and). It has also been said that the meaning is: We created you from the loins of Adam, then We formed you when We took from you the covenant. Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of the views. It has also been said that the meaning is: And We certainly created the spirits first, then We formed the bodies, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, meaning: We commanded them to do so, and they obeyed the command and performed the prostration after the command, except Iblis. It has been said: the exception is contiguous (*muttasil*), by giving precedence to the angels over Iblis, because he was distinct among them. Or, as it has been said, because among the angels there is a kind called the jinn. It has also been said other than this, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

His saying: *lam yakun min al-sajidin* (he was not among those who prostrated) is a sentence explaining what is understood from the meaning of the exception (*istithna'*). Whoever makes the exception disjunctive (*munqati'*) says its meaning is: "But Iblis was not among those who prostrated."

The sentence *qala ma mana'aka an la tasjud* (He said: What prevented you from not prostrating?) is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did God say to him?" The *la* in *an la tasjud* is superfluous for emphasis, as evidenced by His saying in Surah Sad: *ma mana'aka an tasjud* (Sad: 75). It has also been said that *mana'a* here means *qala* (said), and the implied meaning is: who told you not to prostrate. It has also been said that *mana'a* means *da'a* (called), meaning: what called you to not prostrate. It has also been said that there is an omission in the statement, and the implied meaning is: what prevented you from obedience and compelled you not to prostrate when I commanded you, meaning at the time I commanded you. It has been used as evidence that a command requires immediacy (*li-l-fawr*), and the discussion is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). The interrogative in *ma mana'aka* is for reproach and rebuke, since He, glorified is He, already knows that.

The sentence *qala ana khayrun minhu* (He said: I am better than him) is a resumptive sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did Iblis say?" He said in answer "I am better than him," and did not say "what prevented me was such-and-such," because the sentence he brought, being resumptive, contains what indicates the preventing reason, which is his belief that he is superior to him. The superior does not act toward the inferior in that manner, along with what this sentence implies of rejecting that someone like him should be commanded to prostrate to someone like him.

Then he gave a reason for the claim of superiority he asserted, in his saying: ﴿You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾, believing that the element of fire is superior to the element of clay.

The enemy of God erred, for the element of clay is superior to the element of fire in terms of its steadiness, its stillness, and its long endurance. Fire is an agitated substance that quickly perishes. Moreover, clay is present in Paradise but fire is not, fire is a punishment, while clay is in need of fire to be made into a shape, and clay is a place of prostration and purity. Had it not been for the prior decree of his wretchedness and the truth of God's word concerning him, he would have had as an example and a model the angels who obeyed this command. Thus their luminous element is nobler than his fiery element.

The sentence *qala fahbit* (He said: Then go down) is a resumptive sentence like the one before it. The *fa'* is for the ordering of the command to descend upon his disobedience of the command. That is: Go down from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient angels who do not disobey God in what He commands them, to the earth, which is the abode of one who disobeys and obeys. Heaven is not suitable for one who is arrogant and disobeys his Lord, like you. For this reason He said: ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

Among the false interpretations is what has been said: the meaning of *ihbit minha* (go down from it) is: come out of your fiery form, of which you boasted, into a dark, disfigured form. It has also been said: what is meant is his descent from Paradise. It has also been said: from the company of the angels. The sentence *fa-khruj* (then get out) is for emphasis of the command to descend. The sentence *innaka min al-saghirin* (indeed you are among the abased) is a cause for the command, meaning: indeed you are among those of abasement and humiliation before God and before His righteous servants. Thus, everyone who clothes himself in the garment of arrogance is punished by being clothed in the garment of humiliation and abasement, and whoever clothes himself in the garment of humility, God clothes him in the garment of exaltation.

The sentence *qala anzirni ila yawm yub'athun* (He said: Reprieve me until the Day they are raised) is a resumptive sentence, as was mentioned in the previous sentences. That is: give me respite until the Day of Resurrection. It seems he asked not to die, because there is no death after the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun in *yub'athun* refers to Adam and his descendants.

God answered him with His saying: ﴿Indeed you are among the reprieved﴾, meaning: among those given respite until that Day. Then you will be punished with what God has decreed for you, and He will bring you down into the depths of Hellfire.

It has been said: the wisdom in granting him respite is to test the servants, to know who obeys him and who disobeys him.

The sentence (16): *qala fa-bima aghwaytani* (He said: Because You have led me astray) is a resumptive sentence like the preceding sentences, coming as an answer to an assumed question. The *ba'* in *fa-bima* is causal and the *fa'* is for the ordering of the sentence upon what precedes it. It has been said that the *ba'* is for swearing an oath, like His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾, meaning: by Your misguiding me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾. *Al-ighwa'* (misguidance) is causing someone to fall into error. It has been said that the *ba'* means *al-lam* (for), and it has been said that it means *ma'a* (with). The meaning is: with Your misguiding me. It has been said that *ma* in *fa-bima aghwaytani* is interrogative, and the meaning is: "By what did You lead me astray?" The first view is better.

What he intends by this misguidance, which he made the cause of what he would do with the servants, is his abandonment of prostration, and that this was by God's misguidance of him, until he chose error over guidance. It has been said that he meant the curse with which God cursed him, meaning: because You cursed me and destroyed me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾. From this is His saying: ﴿So they will meet error﴾ (Maryam: 59), meaning destruction.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: It is said: *ghawa al-rajulu yaghwi ghayyan* when his affair became corrupt for him, or he himself became corrupt. From this is His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred﴾ (Ta-Ha: 121), meaning his life in Paradise was corrupted. *La-aq'udanna lahum* (I will surely sit in wait for them), meaning: I will surely exert myself in misleading them, until they become corrupt because of me, just as I was corrupted because of my abandonment of prostration to their father.

The *al-sirat al-mustaqim* (straight path) is the road that leads to Paradise. Its accusative case is adverbial of place (*zarfiyyah*), meaning: on Your straight path, as Sibawayh related: "Zayd struck the back and the belly." The *lam* in *la-aq'udanna* is the *lam* of oath, and the *ba'* in *bima aghwaytani* is connected to the omitted verb of oath, meaning: by Your misguiding me, I swear that I will surely sit in wait.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 2 of 2)**

His words: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾. He mentioned the four directions because they are the directions from which an enemy attacks his foe. For this reason he omitted mention of above and below. The verb is followed by *min* (from) with the first two directions and by *ʿan* (away from, concerning) with the other two, because the one who comes from in front or behind usually faces what is coming to him with his whole body, whereas the one who comes from the right or the left is usually turned aside. So it was appropriate to use the preposition of origin (*min*) with the first two and the preposition of passing beyond (*ʿan*) with the other two. This is a figurative depiction of his whispering and his enticement, as though they come from someone who actually approaches. It was also said that what is meant by "from before them" is from their worldly life, "from behind them" is from their Hereafter, "from their right" is from the direction of their good deeds, and "from their left" is from the direction of their bad deeds. Al-Nahhas (an-Nahhas, the grammarian and exegete) preferred this view.

His words: ﴿Nor will You find most of them thankful﴾. That is, "And when I do that, You will not find most of them thankful, because of the effect of my whispering on them and my seducing them." He said this on the basis of assumption, as in His words: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them﴾ (Saba, 20). It was also said that he heard this from the angels and then said it. Here "thankful" is used to mean obedience, or it may be taken literally, meaning that they did not thank Allah because of being led astray.

The clause ﴿He said, "Get out of it"﴾ is a resumptive sentence, like the sentences that precede it. That is, out of the heaven, or the Garden, or from among the angels, as was mentioned earlier.

*Madhʾūman*: that is, *madhmūman* (blameworthy), from *dhaʾamahu*, meaning he blamed him. It is said: *dhaʾamtuhu* and *dhammamtuhu* have the same meaning.

Al-Aʿmash read *madhmūman*. Al-Zuhri read *madhūman* without the hamzah. It was also said: *al-madhʾūm* means one who is expelled, and *al-madhḥūr* means one who is driven away.

His words: ﴿Whoever follows you among them﴾. Most readers read the *lam* with a fatha, taking it as the *lam* of oath, and its answer is ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾. It was also said that the *lam* in *la-man tabiʿaka* is for emphasis, and the *lam* in *la-amla'anna* is the *lam* of oath. The first is preferable. The answer of the oath takes the place of the answer of the conditional, because *man* is a conditional particle. In this answer there is a threat beyond measure.

ʿĀṣim, in one transmission from him, read *liman tabiʿaka* with a kasra on the *lam*, and some grammarians rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: its estimate, and Allah knows best, is "for the sake of those who followed you," as one says, "I honoured so-and-so for your sake." It was also said that it is a cause for *uqhruj* (get out), and the pronoun in *minkum* refers to him and to those who follow him. The pronoun of address was given precedence over the pronoun of the third person, and the original form would be *minka wa-minhum*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, that he said: it is justice. "Whoever's scales are heavy" means his good deeds, and "whoever's scales are light" means his good deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi: "The deeds will be weighed."

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the manner of the scale, the weighing, and what is weighed.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man from my community will be called out before the heads of all creation on the Day of Resurrection. Ninety-nine registers will be unfolded for him, each register extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked: 'Do you deny any of this? Have my recording angels, the guardians, wronged you?' He will say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be asked: 'Do you have an excuse, or a good deed?' The man will be overcome with fear and say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be told: 'Yes, indeed, you have a good deed with Us, and no wrong will be done to you today.' Then a small card will be brought out for him, on which is written: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' He will say: 'My Lord, what is this card alongside these registers?' He will be told: 'Indeed, you will not be wronged.' The registers will be placed on one pan and the card on the other pan. The registers will be light, and the card will be heavy." Al-Tirmidhi also graded it sound, and its chain in Ahmad is good (*hasan*).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾, that he said: "They were created in the loins of men and fashioned in the wombs of women."

al-Firyabi reported from him that he said: "They were created in the back of Adam, then they were fashioned in the wombs."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also that he said: "As for 'We created you,' it refers to Adam; and as for 'then We fashioned you,' it refers to his offspring."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿIkrimah concerning the verse that Iblis was created from the fire of might.

It is established in the *Sahih* from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, Iblis was created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan, who said: "The first to use analogy (*qiyas*) was Iblis, in his words: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾." Its chain to al-Hasan is sound.

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and al-Daylami reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to apply analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion was Iblis. Allah said to him: 'Prostrate to Adam.' He said: 'I am better than him. You created me from fire and You created him from clay.'"

Jaʿfar said: Whoever applies analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion, Allah will join him on the Day of Resurrection with Iblis, because he followed him by analogy.

The chain of this hadith should be examined, for I do not think its attribution to the Prophet is sound, and it does not resemble the speech of prophethood.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "*Fa-bimā aghwaytanī* means: 'Since You led me astray (*aḍlaltanī*).'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from him concerning His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, that he said: "The road to Makkah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Ibn Masʿud.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "I will cast doubt upon them regarding the affairs of their Hereafter. And from behind them: I will make them desire their worldly life. And from their right: I will confuse them about the matter of their religion. And from their left: I will make sins attractive to them and make falsehood seem true to them. And ﴿nor will You find most of them thankful﴾: that is, monotheists (*muwahhidīn*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "He says: from where they can see; and from behind them: from where they cannot see; and from their right: from where they can see; and from their left: from where they cannot see."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "He was not able to say 'from above them.'" In another wording: "He knew that mercy descends from above them."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His words *madhʾūman* that he said: "Blamed." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Despised."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning *madhʾūman*, that he said: "Banished." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Driven away."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *al-haqq* (the truth). That is, the weighing on this Day is the just scale in which there is no injustice. Or the predicate is *yawma'idhin* (on that Day), and *al-haqq* is an attribute of the subject, meaning the just weighing exists on this Day. It has also been said that *al-haqq* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

The scholars differed over the manner of this weighing that takes place on this Day. It has been said that what is meant is the weighing of the records of the servants' deeds on the scale, as a literal weighing. This is the correct view, and it is the one supported by the evidences. It has also been said that the deeds themselves are weighed, even though they are accidents (*a'rad*), because God will transform them on the Day of Resurrection into bodies, as in the authentic report: «Indeed, al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shadows, or two flocks of birds spreading their wings.»

Likewise, it is established in the Sahih that «the Qur'an will come in the form of a young man, pale of complexion», and similar reports. It has also been said that the scale (*al-mizan*) is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. It has been said too that *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and that they are mentioned as a figure of speech, as you say: "This statement is in the weight of that one."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is permissible from the standpoint of the language, but it is better for us to follow what has come in the sound chains of narration concerning the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: Al-Zajjaj has spoken well, for if the Path (*al-sirat*) were interpreted as the true religion, and Paradise and Hellfire as what befalls the souls rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as blameworthy character traits, and the angels as praiseworthy faculties… Then he said: The community in the earliest period unanimously agreed to take these apparent meanings without interpretation (*ta'wil*). And when they unanimously agreed to prohibit interpretation, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became texts (*nusus*). End of quote.

The correct view is the first opinion.

As for those who consider it far-fetched to take these apparent meanings in their literal sense, they cite no part of the Sharia to which one can refer in their objection. Rather, the most they rely on is mere rational improbability, and such reasoning is no proof against anyone. If their intellects reject it, then the intellects of people stronger than them, from among the Companions, the Successors, and the Successors' successors, have accepted it. Then innovations came like a dark night, and everyone said what he wished, and they turned their backs on the Sharia. If only they had brought rational rulings upon which sensible people agree and on which they uniformly accept them! Instead, every faction claims that reason supports whatever matches its desires and agrees with what it or its followers hold. Thus their intellects contradict one another just as their doctrines contradict one another. Every fair-minded person knows this, and whoever denies it should purify his understanding and intellect from the impurities of partisanship and sectarianism, for if he does, the morning will shine clearly before his eyes.

The weighing and the scales are mentioned in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And We will set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47). And His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101). And His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding forever in Hell﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 102–103). And His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ (al-Nisa': 40). And His saying: ﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. And as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be the Abyss﴾ (al-Qari'ah: 6–9). The *fa'* in *fa-man thaqulat mawazinuhu* is for detailing (*tafsil*).

*Al-mawazin* is the plural of *mizan*, and its origin is *miwzan*, with the *waw* changed to *ya'* because of the kasra before it. The heaviness of these scales is by the heaviness of what is placed in them of the records of deeds. It has also been said that *al-mawazin* is the plural of *mawzun* (that which is weighed), meaning: whoever's weighed deeds outweigh. The first view is better.

The apparent sense of the plural *al-mawazin*, being attributed to the doer, is that each of the two doers has scales, and each scale weighs a category of his deeds. It has also been said that it is one scale, expressed with the plural form, as one says: "So-and-so went to Mecca on mules." The pointing in His saying *fa-ulā'ika* (those) refers back to *man* (whoever), and the plural is according to its meaning, just as the pronoun referring to *mawazinuhu* (his scales) returns according to its wording. It is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *hum al-muflihun* (they are the successful).

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ is like it. The *ba'* in *bima kanu bi-ayatina yazlimun* (because they used to wrong Our signs) is causal (*sababiyyah*), and *ma* is verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah*).

The meaning of *yazlimun* (they wrong) is *yakdhibun* (they deny).

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning: We made for you a place in it and prepared for you in it the means of livelihood.

*Al-ma'ayish* is the plural of *ma'ishah*, meaning that by which one lives, namely food and drink and whatever life is sustained by. It is said: *'asha ya'ishu 'aysh*, *ma'ash*, and *ma'ish*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-ma'ishah* is what they use to reach a living. According to al-Akhfash and many grammarians, *al-ma'ishah* is of the pattern *maf'ilah*.

Al-A'raj read *ma'a'ish* with a hamzah, and similarly Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated it from Nafi'.

Al-Nahhas said: The hamzah is an error that is not permissible, because the singular is *ma'ishah* and the *ya'* is original, like *madinah* and *madain*, and *sahifah* and *sahaif*.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of what preceded it shortly before, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We formed you﴾. This is a mention of another of God's blessings upon His servants.

The meaning: We created you as drops of semen, then We formed you after that. It has also been said that the meaning is: We created Adam from dust, then We formed you in his loins. It has also been said that *and We certainly created you* refers to Adam, mentioned in the plural because he is the father of mankind, and *then We formed you* refers back to him. This is indicated by *then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam*, for the arrangement of this statement after the creating and forming indicates that the one created and formed is Adam, upon him be peace.

Al-Akhfash said: *Thumma* (then) in *thumma sawwarnakum* means *wa* (and). It has also been said that the meaning is: We created you from the loins of Adam, then We formed you when We took from you the covenant. Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of the views. It has also been said that the meaning is: And We certainly created the spirits first, then We formed the bodies, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, meaning: We commanded them to do so, and they obeyed the command and performed the prostration after the command, except Iblis. It has been said: the exception is contiguous (*muttasil*), by giving precedence to the angels over Iblis, because he was distinct among them. Or, as it has been said, because among the angels there is a kind called the jinn. It has also been said other than this, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

His saying: *lam yakun min al-sajidin* (he was not among those who prostrated) is a sentence explaining what is understood from the meaning of the exception (*istithna'*). Whoever makes the exception disjunctive (*munqati'*) says its meaning is: "But Iblis was not among those who prostrated."

The sentence *qala ma mana'aka an la tasjud* (He said: What prevented you from not prostrating?) is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did God say to him?" The *la* in *an la tasjud* is superfluous for emphasis, as evidenced by His saying in Surah Sad: *ma mana'aka an tasjud* (Sad: 75). It has also been said that *mana'a* here means *qala* (said), and the implied meaning is: who told you not to prostrate. It has also been said that *mana'a* means *da'a* (called), meaning: what called you to not prostrate. It has also been said that there is an omission in the statement, and the implied meaning is: what prevented you from obedience and compelled you not to prostrate when I commanded you, meaning at the time I commanded you. It has been used as evidence that a command requires immediacy (*li-l-fawr*), and the discussion is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). The interrogative in *ma mana'aka* is for reproach and rebuke, since He, glorified is He, already knows that.

The sentence *qala ana khayrun minhu* (He said: I am better than him) is a resumptive sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did Iblis say?" He said in answer "I am better than him," and did not say "what prevented me was such-and-such," because the sentence he brought, being resumptive, contains what indicates the preventing reason, which is his belief that he is superior to him. The superior does not act toward the inferior in that manner, along with what this sentence implies of rejecting that someone like him should be commanded to prostrate to someone like him.

Then he gave a reason for the claim of superiority he asserted, in his saying: ﴿You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾, believing that the element of fire is superior to the element of clay.

The enemy of God erred, for the element of clay is superior to the element of fire in terms of its steadiness, its stillness, and its long endurance. Fire is an agitated substance that quickly perishes. Moreover, clay is present in Paradise but fire is not, fire is a punishment, while clay is in need of fire to be made into a shape, and clay is a place of prostration and purity. Had it not been for the prior decree of his wretchedness and the truth of God's word concerning him, he would have had as an example and a model the angels who obeyed this command. Thus their luminous element is nobler than his fiery element.

The sentence *qala fahbit* (He said: Then go down) is a resumptive sentence like the one before it. The *fa'* is for the ordering of the command to descend upon his disobedience of the command. That is: Go down from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient angels who do not disobey God in what He commands them, to the earth, which is the abode of one who disobeys and obeys. Heaven is not suitable for one who is arrogant and disobeys his Lord, like you. For this reason He said: ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

Among the false interpretations is what has been said: the meaning of *ihbit minha* (go down from it) is: come out of your fiery form, of which you boasted, into a dark, disfigured form. It has also been said: what is meant is his descent from Paradise. It has also been said: from the company of the angels. The sentence *fa-khruj* (then get out) is for emphasis of the command to descend. The sentence *innaka min al-saghirin* (indeed you are among the abased) is a cause for the command, meaning: indeed you are among those of abasement and humiliation before God and before His righteous servants. Thus, everyone who clothes himself in the garment of arrogance is punished by being clothed in the garment of humiliation and abasement, and whoever clothes himself in the garment of humility, God clothes him in the garment of exaltation.

The sentence *qala anzirni ila yawm yub'athun* (He said: Reprieve me until the Day they are raised) is a resumptive sentence, as was mentioned in the previous sentences. That is: give me respite until the Day of Resurrection. It seems he asked not to die, because there is no death after the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun in *yub'athun* refers to Adam and his descendants.

God answered him with His saying: ﴿Indeed you are among the reprieved﴾, meaning: among those given respite until that Day. Then you will be punished with what God has decreed for you, and He will bring you down into the depths of Hellfire.

It has been said: the wisdom in granting him respite is to test the servants, to know who obeys him and who disobeys him.

The sentence (16): *qala fa-bima aghwaytani* (He said: Because You have led me astray) is a resumptive sentence like the preceding sentences, coming as an answer to an assumed question. The *ba'* in *fa-bima* is causal and the *fa'* is for the ordering of the sentence upon what precedes it. It has been said that the *ba'* is for swearing an oath, like His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾, meaning: by Your misguiding me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾. *Al-ighwa'* (misguidance) is causing someone to fall into error. It has been said that the *ba'* means *al-lam* (for), and it has been said that it means *ma'a* (with). The meaning is: with Your misguiding me. It has been said that *ma* in *fa-bima aghwaytani* is interrogative, and the meaning is: "By what did You lead me astray?" The first view is better.

What he intends by this misguidance, which he made the cause of what he would do with the servants, is his abandonment of prostration, and that this was by God's misguidance of him, until he chose error over guidance. It has been said that he meant the curse with which God cursed him, meaning: because You cursed me and destroyed me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾. From this is His saying: ﴿So they will meet error﴾ (Maryam: 59), meaning destruction.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: It is said: *ghawa al-rajulu yaghwi ghayyan* when his affair became corrupt for him, or he himself became corrupt. From this is His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred﴾ (Ta-Ha: 121), meaning his life in Paradise was corrupted. *La-aq'udanna lahum* (I will surely sit in wait for them), meaning: I will surely exert myself in misleading them, until they become corrupt because of me, just as I was corrupted because of my abandonment of prostration to their father.

The *al-sirat al-mustaqim* (straight path) is the road that leads to Paradise. Its accusative case is adverbial of place (*zarfiyyah*), meaning: on Your straight path, as Sibawayh related: "Zayd struck the back and the belly." The *lam* in *la-aq'udanna* is the *lam* of oath, and the *ba'* in *bima aghwaytani* is connected to the omitted verb of oath, meaning: by Your misguiding me, I swear that I will surely sit in wait.

The clause ﴿He said, "Get out of it"﴾ is a resumptive sentence, like the sentences that precede it. That is, out of the heaven, or the Garden, or from among the angels, as was mentioned earlier.

*Madhʾūman*: that is, *madhmūman* (blameworthy), from *dhaʾamahu*, meaning he blamed him. It is said: *dhaʾamtuhu* and *dhammamtuhu* have the same meaning.

The answer of the oath takes the place of the answer of the conditional, because *man* is a conditional particle. In this answer there is a threat beyond measure.

ʿĀṣim, in one transmission from him, read *liman tabiʿaka* with a kasra on the *lam*, and some grammarians rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: its estimate, and Allah knows best, is "for the sake of those who followed you," as one says, "I honoured so-and-so for your sake." Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi: "The deeds will be weighed."

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the manner of the scale, the weighing, and what is weighed.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man from my community will be called out before the heads of all creation on the Day of Resurrection. Ninety-nine registers will be unfolded for him, each register extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked: 'Do you deny any of this? Have my recording angels, the guardians, wronged you?' He will say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be asked: 'Do you have an excuse, or a good deed?' The man will be overcome with fear and say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be told: 'Yes, indeed, you have a good deed with Us, and no wrong will be done to you today.' Then a small card will be brought out for him, on which is written: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' He will say: 'My Lord, what is this card alongside these registers?' He will be told: 'Indeed, you will not be wronged.' The registers will be placed on one pan and the card on the other pan. The registers will be light, and the card will be heavy." Al-Tirmidhi also graded it sound, and its chain in Ahmad is good (*hasan*).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾, that he said: "They were created in the loins of men and fashioned in the wombs of women."

al-Firyabi reported from him that he said: "They were created in the back of Adam, then they were fashioned in the wombs."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also that he said: "As for 'We created you,' it refers to Adam; and as for 'then We fashioned you,' it refers to his offspring."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿIkrimah concerning the verse that Iblis was created from the fire of might.

It is established in the *Sahih* from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, Iblis was created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan, who said: "The first to use analogy (*qiyas*) was Iblis, in his words: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾." Its chain to al-Hasan is sound.

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and al-Daylami reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to apply analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion was Iblis. Allah said to him: 'Prostrate to Adam.' He said: 'I am better than him. You created me from fire and You created him from clay.'"

Jaʿfar said: Whoever applies analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion, Allah will join him on the Day of Resurrection with Iblis, because he followed him by analogy.

The chain of this hadith should be examined, for I do not think its attribution to the Prophet is sound, and it does not resemble the speech of prophethood.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "*Fa-bimā aghwaytanī* means: 'Since You led me astray (*aḍlaltanī*).'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from him concerning His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, that he said: "The road to Makkah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Ibn Masʿud.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "I will cast doubt upon them regarding the affairs of their Hereafter. And from behind them: I will make them desire their worldly life. And from their right: I will confuse them about the matter of their religion. And from their left: I will make sins attractive to them and make falsehood seem true to them. And ﴿nor will You find most of them thankful﴾: that is, monotheists (*muwahhidīn*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "He says: from where they can see; and from behind them: from where they cannot see; and from their right: from where they can see; and from their left: from where they cannot see."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "He was not able to say 'from above them.'" In another wording: "He knew that mercy descends from above them."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His words *madhʾūman* that he said: "Blamed." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Despised."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning *madhʾūman*, that he said: "Banished." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Driven away."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *al-haqq* (the truth). That is, the weighing on this Day is the just scale in which there is no injustice. Or the predicate is *yawma'idhin* (on that Day), and *al-haqq* is an attribute of the subject, meaning the just weighing exists on this Day. It has also been said that *al-haqq* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

The scholars differed over the manner of this weighing that takes place on this Day. It has been said that what is meant is the weighing of the records of the servants' deeds on the scale, as a literal weighing. This is the correct view, and it is the one supported by the evidences. It has also been said that the deeds themselves are weighed, even though they are accidents (*a'rad*), because God will transform them on the Day of Resurrection into bodies, as in the authentic report: «Indeed, al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shadows, or two flocks of birds spreading their wings.»

Likewise, it is established in the Sahih that «the Qur'an will come in the form of a young man, pale of complexion», and similar reports. It has also been said that the scale (*al-mizan*) is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. It has been said too that *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and that they are mentioned as a figure of speech, as you say: "This statement is in the weight of that one."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is permissible from the standpoint of the language, but it is better for us to follow what has come in the sound chains of narration concerning the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: Al-Zajjaj has spoken well, for if the Path (*al-sirat*) were interpreted as the true religion, and Paradise and Hellfire as what befalls the souls rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as blameworthy character traits, and the angels as praiseworthy faculties… Then he said: The community in the earliest period unanimously agreed to take these apparent meanings without interpretation (*ta'wil*). And when they unanimously agreed to prohibit interpretation, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became texts (*nusus*). End of quote.

The correct view is the first opinion.

As for those who consider it far-fetched to take these apparent meanings in their literal sense, they cite no part of the Sharia to which one can refer in their objection. Rather, the most they rely on is mere rational improbability, and such reasoning is no proof against anyone. If their intellects reject it, then the intellects of people stronger than them, from among the Companions, the Successors, and the Successors' successors, have accepted it. Then innovations came like a dark night, and everyone said what he wished, and they turned their backs on the Sharia. If only they had brought rational rulings upon which sensible people agree and on which they uniformly accept them! Instead, every faction claims that reason supports whatever matches its desires and agrees with what it or its followers hold. Thus their intellects contradict one another just as their doctrines contradict one another. Every fair-minded person knows this, and whoever denies it should purify his understanding and intellect from the impurities of partisanship and sectarianism, for if he does, the morning will shine clearly before his eyes.

The weighing and the scales are mentioned in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And We will set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47). And His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101). And His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding forever in Hell﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 102–103). And His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ (al-Nisa': 40). And His saying: ﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. And as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be the Abyss﴾ (al-Qari'ah: 6–9). The *fa'* in *fa-man thaqulat mawazinuhu* is for detailing (*tafsil*).

*Al-mawazin* is the plural of *mizan*, and its origin is *miwzan*, with the *waw* changed to *ya'* because of the kasra before it. The heaviness of these scales is by the heaviness of what is placed in them of the records of deeds. It has also been said that *al-mawazin* is the plural of *mawzun* (that which is weighed), meaning: whoever's weighed deeds outweigh. The first view is better.

The apparent sense of the plural *al-mawazin*, being attributed to the doer, is that each of the two doers has scales, and each scale weighs a category of his deeds. It has also been said that it is one scale, expressed with the plural form, as one says: "So-and-so went to Mecca on mules." The pointing in His saying *fa-ulā'ika* (those) refers back to *man* (whoever), and the plural is according to its meaning, just as the pronoun referring to *mawazinuhu* (his scales) returns according to its wording. It is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *hum al-muflihun* (they are the successful).

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ is like it. The *ba'* in *bima kanu bi-ayatina yazlimun* (because they used to wrong Our signs) is causal (*sababiyyah*), and *ma* is verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah*).

The meaning of *yazlimun* (they wrong) is *yakdhibun* (they deny).

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning: We made for you a place in it and prepared for you in it the means of livelihood.

*Al-ma'ayish* is the plural of *ma'ishah*, meaning that by which one lives, namely food and drink and whatever life is sustained by. It is said: *'asha ya'ishu 'aysh*, *ma'ash*, and *ma'ish*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-ma'ishah* is what they use to reach a living. According to al-Akhfash and many grammarians, *al-ma'ishah* is of the pattern *maf'ilah*.

Al-A'raj read *ma'a'ish* with a hamzah, and similarly Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated it from Nafi'.

Al-Nahhas said: The hamzah is an error that is not permissible, because the singular is *ma'ishah* and the *ya'* is original, like *madinah* and *madain*, and *sahifah* and *sahaif*.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of what preceded it shortly before, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We formed you﴾. This is a mention of another of God's blessings upon His servants.

The meaning: We created you as drops of semen, then We formed you after that. It has also been said that the meaning is: We created Adam from dust, then We formed you in his loins. It has also been said that *and We certainly created you* refers to Adam, mentioned in the plural because he is the father of mankind, and *then We formed you* refers back to him. This is indicated by *then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam*, for the arrangement of this statement after the creating and forming indicates that the one created and formed is Adam, upon him be peace.

Al-Akhfash said: *Thumma* (then) in *thumma sawwarnakum* means *wa* (and). It has also been said that the meaning is: We created you from the loins of Adam, then We formed you when We took from you the covenant. Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of the views. It has also been said that the meaning is: And We certainly created the spirits first, then We formed the bodies, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, meaning: We commanded them to do so, and they obeyed the command and performed the prostration after the command, except Iblis. It has been said: the exception is contiguous (*muttasil*), by giving precedence to the angels over Iblis, because he was distinct among them. Or, as it has been said, because among the angels there is a kind called the jinn. It has also been said other than this, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

His saying: *lam yakun min al-sajidin* (he was not among those who prostrated) is a sentence explaining what is understood from the meaning of the exception (*istithna'*). Whoever makes the exception disjunctive (*munqati'*) says its meaning is: "But Iblis was not among those who prostrated."

The sentence *qala ma mana'aka an la tasjud* (He said: What prevented you from not prostrating?) is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did God say to him?" The *la* in *an la tasjud* is superfluous for emphasis, as evidenced by His saying in Surah Sad: *ma mana'aka an tasjud* (Sad: 75). It has also been said that *mana'a* here means *qala* (said), and the implied meaning is: who told you not to prostrate. It has also been said that *mana'a* means *da'a* (called), meaning: what called you to not prostrate. It has also been said that there is an omission in the statement, and the implied meaning is: what prevented you from obedience and compelled you not to prostrate when I commanded you, meaning at the time I commanded you. It has been used as evidence that a command requires immediacy (*li-l-fawr*), and the discussion is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). The interrogative in *ma mana'aka* is for reproach and rebuke, since He, glorified is He, already knows that.

The sentence *qala ana khayrun minhu* (He said: I am better than him) is a resumptive sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did Iblis say?"
