**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾. *Al-wazn* (the weighing) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is *al-haqq* (the truth). That is, the weighing on this Day is the just scale in which there is no injustice. Or the predicate is *yawma'idhin* (on that Day), and *al-haqq* is an attribute of the subject, meaning the just weighing exists on this Day. It has also been said that *al-haqq* is the predicate of an omitted subject.

The scholars differed over the manner of this weighing that takes place on this Day. It has been said that what is meant is the weighing of the records of the servants' deeds on the scale, as a literal weighing. This is the correct view, and it is the one supported by the evidences. It has also been said that the deeds themselves are weighed, even though they are accidents (*a'rad*), because God will transform them on the Day of Resurrection into bodies, as in the authentic report: «Indeed, al-Baqarah and Ali 'Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shadows, or two flocks of birds spreading their wings.»

Likewise, it is established in the Sahih that «the Qur'an will come in the form of a young man, pale of complexion», and similar reports. It has also been said that the scale (*al-mizan*) is the book in which the deeds of creation are recorded. It has been said too that *al-wazn* and *al-mizan* mean justice and judgment, and that they are mentioned as a figure of speech, as you say: "This statement is in the weight of that one."

Al-Zajjaj said: This is permissible from the standpoint of the language, but it is better for us to follow what has come in the sound chains of narration concerning the scale.

Al-Qushayri said: Al-Zajjaj has spoken well, for if the Path (*al-sirat*) were interpreted as the true religion, and Paradise and Hellfire as what befalls the souls rather than the bodies, and the devils and jinn as blameworthy character traits, and the angels as praiseworthy faculties… Then he said: The community in the earliest period unanimously agreed to take these apparent meanings without interpretation (*ta'wil*). And when they unanimously agreed to prohibit interpretation, it became obligatory to take the apparent meaning, and these apparent meanings became texts (*nusus*). End of quote.

The correct view is the first opinion.

As for those who consider it far-fetched to take these apparent meanings in their literal sense, they cite no part of the Sharia to which one can refer in their objection. Rather, the most they rely on is mere rational improbability, and such reasoning is no proof against anyone. If their intellects reject it, then the intellects of people stronger than them, from among the Companions, the Successors, and the Successors' successors, have accepted it. Then innovations came like a dark night, and everyone said what he wished, and they turned their backs on the Sharia. If only they had brought rational rulings upon which sensible people agree and on which they uniformly accept them! Instead, every faction claims that reason supports whatever matches its desires and agrees with what it or its followers hold. Thus their intellects contradict one another just as their doctrines contradict one another. Every fair-minded person knows this, and whoever denies it should purify his understanding and intellect from the impurities of partisanship and sectarianism, for if he does, the morning will shine clearly before his eyes.

The weighing and the scales are mentioned in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And We will set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47). And His saying: ﴿When the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101). And His saying: ﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful. And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, abiding forever in Hell﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 102–103). And His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong even the weight of an atom﴾ (al-Nisa': 40). And His saying: ﴿As for one whose scales are heavy, he will be in a pleasant life. And as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be the Abyss﴾ (al-Qari'ah: 6–9). The *fa'* in *fa-man thaqulat mawazinuhu* is for detailing (*tafsil*).

*Al-mawazin* is the plural of *mizan*, and its origin is *miwzan*, with the *waw* changed to *ya'* because of the kasra before it. The heaviness of these scales is by the heaviness of what is placed in them of the records of deeds. It has also been said that *al-mawazin* is the plural of *mawzun* (that which is weighed), meaning: whoever's weighed deeds outweigh. The first view is better.

The apparent sense of the plural *al-mawazin*, being attributed to the doer, is that each of the two doers has scales, and each scale weighs a category of his deeds. It has also been said that it is one scale, expressed with the plural form, as one says: "So-and-so went to Mecca on mules." The pointing in His saying *fa-ulā'ika* (those) refers back to *man* (whoever), and the plural is according to its meaning, just as the pronoun referring to *mawazinuhu* (his scales) returns according to its wording. It is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *hum al-muflihun* (they are the successful).

The discussion of His saying: ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ is like it. The *ba'* in *bima kanu bi-ayatina yazlimun* (because they used to wrong Our signs) is causal (*sababiyyah*), and *ma* is verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah*).

The meaning of *yazlimun* (they wrong) is *yakdhibun* (they deny).

His saying: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾, meaning: We made for you a place in it and prepared for you in it the means of livelihood.

*Al-ma'ayish* is the plural of *ma'ishah*, meaning that by which one lives, namely food and drink and whatever life is sustained by. It is said: *'asha ya'ishu 'aysh*, *ma'ash*, and *ma'ish*.

Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-ma'ishah* is what they use to reach a living. According to al-Akhfash and many grammarians, *al-ma'ishah* is of the pattern *maf'ilah*.

Al-A'raj read *ma'a'ish* with a hamzah, and similarly Kharijah ibn Mus'ab narrated it from Nafi'.

Al-Nahhas said: The hamzah is an error that is not permissible, because the singular is *ma'ishah* and the *ya'* is original, like *madinah* and *madain*, and *sahifah* and *sahaif*.

His saying: ﴿Little is it that you give thanks﴾. The discussion of it is like the discussion of what preceded it shortly before, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We certainly created you, then We formed you﴾. This is a mention of another of God's blessings upon His servants.

The meaning: We created you as drops of semen, then We formed you after that. It has also been said that the meaning is: We created Adam from dust, then We formed you in his loins. It has also been said that *and We certainly created you* refers to Adam, mentioned in the plural because he is the father of mankind, and *then We formed you* refers back to him. This is indicated by *then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam*, for the arrangement of this statement after the creating and forming indicates that the one created and formed is Adam, upon him be peace.

Al-Akhfash said: *Thumma* (then) in *thumma sawwarnakum* means *wa* (and). It has also been said that the meaning is: We created you from the loins of Adam, then We formed you when We took from you the covenant. Al-Nahhas said: This is the best of the views. It has also been said that the meaning is: And We certainly created the spirits first, then We formed the bodies, then We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, meaning: We commanded them to do so, and they obeyed the command and performed the prostration after the command, except Iblis. It has been said: the exception is contiguous (*muttasil*), by giving precedence to the angels over Iblis, because he was distinct among them. Or, as it has been said, because among the angels there is a kind called the jinn. It has also been said other than this, and its verification has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

His saying: *lam yakun min al-sajidin* (he was not among those who prostrated) is a sentence explaining what is understood from the meaning of the exception (*istithna'*). Whoever makes the exception disjunctive (*munqati'*) says its meaning is: "But Iblis was not among those who prostrated."

The sentence *qala ma mana'aka an la tasjud* (He said: What prevented you from not prostrating?) is a resumptive sentence (*isti'nafiyyah*), answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did God say to him?" The *la* in *an la tasjud* is superfluous for emphasis, as evidenced by His saying in Surah Sad: *ma mana'aka an tasjud* (Sad: 75). It has also been said that *mana'a* here means *qala* (said), and the implied meaning is: who told you not to prostrate. It has also been said that *mana'a* means *da'a* (called), meaning: what called you to not prostrate. It has also been said that there is an omission in the statement, and the implied meaning is: what prevented you from obedience and compelled you not to prostrate when I commanded you, meaning at the time I commanded you. It has been used as evidence that a command requires immediacy (*li-l-fawr*), and the discussion is established in the science of the foundations of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*). The interrogative in *ma mana'aka* is for reproach and rebuke, since He, glorified is He, already knows that.

The sentence *qala ana khayrun minhu* (He said: I am better than him) is a resumptive sentence answering an assumed question, as if it were said: "What did Iblis say?" He said in answer "I am better than him," and did not say "what prevented me was such-and-such," because the sentence he brought, being resumptive, contains what indicates the preventing reason, which is his belief that he is superior to him. The superior does not act toward the inferior in that manner, along with what this sentence implies of rejecting that someone like him should be commanded to prostrate to someone like him.

Then he gave a reason for the claim of superiority he asserted, in his saying: ﴿You created me from fire, and You created him from clay﴾, believing that the element of fire is superior to the element of clay.

The enemy of God erred, for the element of clay is superior to the element of fire in terms of its steadiness, its stillness, and its long endurance. Fire is an agitated substance that quickly perishes. Moreover, clay is present in Paradise but fire is not, fire is a punishment, while clay is in need of fire to be made into a shape, and clay is a place of prostration and purity. Had it not been for the prior decree of his wretchedness and the truth of God's word concerning him, he would have had as an example and a model the angels who obeyed this command. Thus their luminous element is nobler than his fiery element.

The sentence *qala fahbit* (He said: Then go down) is a resumptive sentence like the one before it. The *fa'* is for the ordering of the command to descend upon his disobedience of the command. That is: Go down from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient angels who do not disobey God in what He commands them, to the earth, which is the abode of one who disobeys and obeys. Heaven is not suitable for one who is arrogant and disobeys his Lord, like you. For this reason He said: ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾.

Among the false interpretations is what has been said: the meaning of *ihbit minha* (go down from it) is: come out of your fiery form, of which you boasted, into a dark, disfigured form. It has also been said: what is meant is his descent from Paradise. It has also been said: from the company of the angels. The sentence *fa-khruj* (then get out) is for emphasis of the command to descend. The sentence *innaka min al-saghirin* (indeed you are among the abased) is a cause for the command, meaning: indeed you are among those of abasement and humiliation before God and before His righteous servants. Thus, everyone who clothes himself in the garment of arrogance is punished by being clothed in the garment of humiliation and abasement, and whoever clothes himself in the garment of humility, God clothes him in the garment of exaltation.

The sentence *qala anzirni ila yawm yub'athun* (He said: Reprieve me until the Day they are raised) is a resumptive sentence, as was mentioned in the previous sentences. That is: give me respite until the Day of Resurrection. It seems he asked not to die, because there is no death after the Day of Resurrection. The pronoun in *yub'athun* refers to Adam and his descendants.

God answered him with His saying: ﴿Indeed you are among the reprieved﴾, meaning: among those given respite until that Day. Then you will be punished with what God has decreed for you, and He will bring you down into the depths of Hellfire.

It has been said: the wisdom in granting him respite is to test the servants, to know who obeys him and who disobeys him.

The sentence (16): *qala fa-bima aghwaytani* (He said: Because You have led me astray) is a resumptive sentence like the preceding sentences, coming as an answer to an assumed question. The *ba'* in *fa-bima* is causal and the *fa'* is for the ordering of the sentence upon what precedes it. It has been said that the *ba'* is for swearing an oath, like His saying: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾, meaning: by Your misguiding me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾. *Al-ighwa'* (misguidance) is causing someone to fall into error. It has been said that the *ba'* means *al-lam* (for), and it has been said that it means *ma'a* (with). The meaning is: with Your misguiding me. It has been said that *ma* in *fa-bima aghwaytani* is interrogative, and the meaning is: "By what did You lead me astray?" The first view is better.

What he intends by this misguidance, which he made the cause of what he would do with the servants, is his abandonment of prostration, and that this was by God's misguidance of him, until he chose error over guidance. It has been said that he meant the curse with which God cursed him, meaning: because You cursed me and destroyed me, ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾. From this is His saying: ﴿So they will meet error﴾ (Maryam: 59), meaning destruction.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: It is said: *ghawa al-rajulu yaghwi ghayyan* when his affair became corrupt for him, or he himself became corrupt. From this is His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, so he erred﴾ (Ta-Ha: 121), meaning his life in Paradise was corrupted. *La-aq'udanna lahum* (I will surely sit in wait for them), meaning: I will surely exert myself in misleading them, until they become corrupt because of me, just as I was corrupted because of my abandonment of prostration to their father.

The *al-sirat al-mustaqim* (straight path) is the road that leads to Paradise. Its accusative case is adverbial of place (*zarfiyyah*), meaning: on Your straight path, as Sibawayh related: "Zayd struck the back and the belly." The *lam* in *la-aq'udanna* is the *lam* of oath, and the *ba'* in *bima aghwaytani* is connected to the omitted verb of oath, meaning: by Your misguiding me, I swear that I will surely sit in wait.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 8–18 (part 2 of 2)**

His words: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾. He mentioned the four directions because they are the directions from which an enemy attacks his foe. For this reason he omitted mention of above and below. The verb is followed by *min* (from) with the first two directions and by *ʿan* (away from, concerning) with the other two, because the one who comes from in front or behind usually faces what is coming to him with his whole body, whereas the one who comes from the right or the left is usually turned aside. So it was appropriate to use the preposition of origin (*min*) with the first two and the preposition of passing beyond (*ʿan*) with the other two. This is a figurative depiction of his whispering and his enticement, as though they come from someone who actually approaches. It was also said that what is meant by "from before them" is from their worldly life, "from behind them" is from their Hereafter, "from their right" is from the direction of their good deeds, and "from their left" is from the direction of their bad deeds. Al-Nahhas (an-Nahhas, the grammarian and exegete) preferred this view.

His words: ﴿Nor will You find most of them thankful﴾. That is, "And when I do that, You will not find most of them thankful, because of the effect of my whispering on them and my seducing them." He said this on the basis of assumption, as in His words: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them﴾ (Saba, 20). It was also said that he heard this from the angels and then said it. Here "thankful" is used to mean obedience, or it may be taken literally, meaning that they did not thank Allah because of being led astray.

The clause ﴿He said, "Get out of it"﴾ is a resumptive sentence, like the sentences that precede it. That is, out of the heaven, or the Garden, or from among the angels, as was mentioned earlier.

*Madhʾūman*: that is, *madhmūman* (blameworthy), from *dhaʾamahu*, meaning he blamed him. It is said: *dhaʾamtuhu* and *dhammamtuhu* have the same meaning.

Al-Aʿmash read *madhmūman*. Al-Zuhri read *madhūman* without the hamzah. It was also said: *al-madhʾūm* means one who is expelled, and *al-madhḥūr* means one who is driven away.

His words: ﴿Whoever follows you among them﴾. Most readers read the *lam* with a fatha, taking it as the *lam* of oath, and its answer is ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾. It was also said that the *lam* in *la-man tabiʿaka* is for emphasis, and the *lam* in *la-amla'anna* is the *lam* of oath. The first is preferable. The answer of the oath takes the place of the answer of the conditional, because *man* is a conditional particle. In this answer there is a threat beyond measure.

ʿĀṣim, in one transmission from him, read *liman tabiʿaka* with a kasra on the *lam*, and some grammarians rejected this. Al-Nahhas said: its estimate, and Allah knows best, is "for the sake of those who followed you," as one says, "I honoured so-and-so for your sake." It was also said that it is a cause for *uqhruj* (get out), and the pronoun in *minkum* refers to him and to those who follow him. The pronoun of address was given precedence over the pronoun of the third person, and the original form would be *minka wa-minhum*.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾, that he said: it is justice. "Whoever's scales are heavy" means his good deeds, and "whoever's scales are light" means his good deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi: "The deeds will be weighed."

Many hadiths have been reported concerning the manner of the scale, the weighing, and what is weighed.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man from my community will be called out before the heads of all creation on the Day of Resurrection. Ninety-nine registers will be unfolded for him, each register extending as far as the eye can see. He will be asked: 'Do you deny any of this? Have my recording angels, the guardians, wronged you?' He will say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be asked: 'Do you have an excuse, or a good deed?' The man will be overcome with fear and say: 'No, my Lord.' He will be told: 'Yes, indeed, you have a good deed with Us, and no wrong will be done to you today.' Then a small card will be brought out for him, on which is written: 'I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger.' He will say: 'My Lord, what is this card alongside these registers?' He will be told: 'Indeed, you will not be wronged.' The registers will be placed on one pan and the card on the other pan. The registers will be light, and the card will be heavy." Al-Tirmidhi also graded it sound, and its chain in Ahmad is good (*hasan*).

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾, that he said: "They were created in the loins of men and fashioned in the wombs of women."

al-Firyabi reported from him that he said: "They were created in the back of Adam, then they were fashioned in the wombs."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him also that he said: "As for 'We created you,' it refers to Adam; and as for 'then We fashioned you,' it refers to his offspring."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from ʿIkrimah concerning the verse that Iblis was created from the fire of might.

It is established in the *Sahih* from the hadith of ʿAʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, Iblis was created from fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you."

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan, who said: "The first to use analogy (*qiyas*) was Iblis, in his words: ﴿You created me from fire and You created him from clay﴾." Its chain to al-Hasan is sound.

Abu Nuʿaym in *al-Hilya* and al-Daylami reported from Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The first to apply analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion was Iblis. Allah said to him: 'Prostrate to Adam.' He said: 'I am better than him. You created me from fire and You created him from clay.'"

Jaʿfar said: Whoever applies analogy to the matter of religion by his own opinion, Allah will join him on the Day of Resurrection with Iblis, because he followed him by analogy.

The chain of this hadith should be examined, for I do not think its attribution to the Prophet is sound, and it does not resemble the speech of prophethood.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "*Fa-bimā aghwaytanī* means: 'Since You led me astray (*aḍlaltanī*).'"

ʿAbd ibn Humayd reported from him concerning His words: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, that he said: "The road to Makkah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported similarly from Ibn Masʿud.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "I will cast doubt upon them regarding the affairs of their Hereafter. And from behind them: I will make them desire their worldly life. And from their right: I will confuse them about the matter of their religion. And from their left: I will make sins attractive to them and make falsehood seem true to them. And ﴿nor will You find most of them thankful﴾: that is, monotheists (*muwahhidīn*)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾: "He says: from where they can see; and from behind them: from where they cannot see; and from their right: from where they can see; and from their left: from where they cannot see."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir reported from him also concerning the verse, that he said: "He was not able to say 'from above them.'" In another wording: "He knew that mercy descends from above them."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him concerning His words *madhʾūman* that he said: "Blamed." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Despised."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid concerning *madhʾūman*, that he said: "Banished." *Madḥūran*: he said, "Driven away."

"And (We said), 'O Adam!' This is with the implied verb of saying: that is, 'and We said, O Adam!'

He said this to him after the expulsion of Iblis from the Garden, or from the heaven, or from among the angels, as has already been mentioned.

The meaning of 'settling' (al-iskan) and of 'Do not approach this tree' has already been discussed in al-Baqarah.

The meaning of 'from wherever you wish' is: from whatever kind of the Garden's fruits you wish to eat. A similar statement was made earlier in His words, ﴿And eat from it in abundance, wherever you wish﴾ (al-Baqarah: 35). The deletion of the nun in ﴿fa-takUnA﴾ is because it is conjoined to a jussive verb, or because it is in the subjunctive mood as a response to the prohibition.

His words ﴿Then Satan whispered to them﴾: al-waswasah (whispering) is a faint sound; al-waswasah also means inner speech of the soul. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from 'Ikrimah, who said: the clothing of every animal is from it, and the clothing of man is the nail; repentance reached Adam at his nail.

It is also said that the hissing of the hunter and the dogs, and the sounds of ornaments, are waswas.

Al-waswas is also a name of Satan.

The meaning of 'waswasa lahu' is 'waswasa ilayhi' or 'did the whispering for his sake.'

Satan intended to distress them by exposing what had been hidden from them of their nakedness, for they did not see the nakedness of themselves, nor did one of them see it of the other. The waw in 'wuriya' was not changed to a hamzah because the second is a long vowel. It is said: their nakedness appeared only to them, not to others, and there was a light upon them that prevented its being seen.

He said, that is Satan said to them: ﴿What your Lord forbade you from this tree except that you become angels or become of the immortals.﴾ 'An' is in the accusative position, and in the speech there is an elided genitive construction; its estimate is: 'and no dislike that you become angels.' This is what the Basrans said.

The Kufans said: the estimate is 'lest you become angels,' or 'you become of the immortals in the Garden,' or 'of those who do not die.'

al-Nahhas said: God preferred the angels over all creation in more than one place in the Qur'an. Among them is this verse; among them is ﴿I do not say that I am an angel﴾ (Hud: 31); and among them is ﴿nor the favoured angels﴾ (al-Nisa': 172).

Ibn Furak said: there is no proof in this verse, because it is possible that he meant 'two angels' in the sense that they would have no desire for food.

People have differed greatly on this question and have prolonged the discussion to no purpose. This question is not one with which God has charged us to have knowledge, so discussion of it does not concern us.

Those who read with the kasra argued with His words: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾

Abu 'Ubayd said: this is a clear proof for the reading with the kasra, but people have abandoned it, so we have left it.

al-Nahhas said: it is an irregular reading. He denied Abu 'Ubayd's statement and considered it a gross error.

He said: Is it possible to imagine that Adam (peace be upon him) would reach more than the kingdom of the Garden, which is the ultimate goal of seekers? The meaning of 'a kingdom that does not decay' is only staying in the kingdom of the Garden and eternity in it.

We have already discussed the verification of this in al-Ma'idah, and what is meant here is intensification of the oaths issued to them from Iblis. It is also said that they swore to him by acceptance just as he swore to them of counsel.

Nafṭawayh recited:

"If you wish to deceive the noble, you deceive him, but you see the base one experienced and not deceived."

It is also said that the meaning of 'dallahuma' is 'dallalahuma,' from ad-dalah, which is boldness: that is, he emboldened them to disobedience, so they came out of the Garden.

His words, ﴿And they began to stitch over themselves from the leaves of the Garden﴾: tafiqa yaf'alu kadha means shara'a yaf'alu kadha, began to do such a thing.

The meaning is that they began to cut the leaves and stick them to their private parts in order to cover them, from khasafa the sandal, when one makes it layer upon layer.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on surah 7, verses 26–27:

He (glory be to Him) expressed the creation of clothing as "sending down" (*inzal*). That is, "We created for you clothing (*libas*) that covers your private parts (*sawat*) which Iblis exposed from your two parents." *Sawah* means *'awrah* (the parts that must be covered), as has already passed. The discussion of its extent and of what must be covered of it is explained in the books of *furu'* (the branches of jurisprudence).

His saying: ﴿*wa-riyshan*﴾ (and as finery). Al-Hasan, 'Asim (according to the transmission of al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi), and Abu 'Amr (according to the transmission of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Ju'fi) read *wa-riyashan* (رِياشًا). The rest read *wa-rishan* (رِيشًا). *Riyash* is the plural of *rish*, which means clothing.

Al-Farra' said: *rish* and *riyash* are like *libs* and *libas*, as one says *libs* and *libas*. The *rish* of a bird is what God has covered it with.

It was also said that *rish* here means abundance and comfort of living.

Al-Qurtubi said: What most of the lexicographers hold is that *rish* is whatever covers, whether of clothing or of livelihood.

Abu Hatim transmitted, from Abu 'Ubayda: "I gave him a riding animal and its *rish*," meaning what is upon it of equipment.

It was also said that *rish* here means the clothing of adornment, because it is mentioned after His saying ﴿We have sent down upon you clothing﴾ and is conjoined to it.

His saying: ﴿*wa-libasu al-taqwa*﴾ (and the clothing of God-consciousness). The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read *libasa* with a *fatha* (نَصْبٍ). The rest read it with a *damma* (بِالرَّفْعِ). The *nasb* is on the basis that it is conjoined to the first *libas*, and the *raf'* is on the basis that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), with the phrase ﴿*dhalika khayr*﴾ (that is best) as its predicate.

By "the clothing of God-consciousness" is meant the clothing of scrupulousness (*wara'*) and guarding oneself against the disobedience of God. This is scrupulousness itself and fear of God. That is the best clothing and the finest adornment. It was also said: the clothing of God-consciousness is modesty (*haya'*). It was said: it is righteous deeds. It was said: it is the wool garments and coarse clothing, because of the humility before God that is in them. It was said: it is the coat of mail and the helmet worn by one who fights in the way of God. The first view is the better.

It applies to everything in which there is God-consciousness, so all the views mentioned fall under it. Such metaphor is very common in the speech of the Arabs. Among it is the poet's saying:

*When a man does not wear garments of piety, he goes about naked even if he is clothed.*

And similar to it is the saying:

*Cover yourself with the garments of generosity, for I see every fault, and generosity is its covering.*

The reference in His saying ﴿*dhalika*﴾ (that) is to the clothing of God-consciousness: that is, it is the best clothing. Al-A'mash read: ﴿And the clothing of God-consciousness, that is best﴾. The reference in His saying ﴿*dhalika min ayat Allah*﴾ (that is among the signs of God) is to the sending down implied by *anzalna* (We sent down). That is, that sending down is among the signs of God which indicate that it has a Creator.

Then God, glory be to Him, repeated the address to the children of Adam as a warning against Satan. He said: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you﴾, that is, let him not cause you to fall into temptation. So although the prohibition is addressed to Satan, in reality it is addressed to the children of Adam: that they should not be tempted by his temptation and be affected by it. The *kaf* in ﴿*kama akhraja*﴾ (as he brought out) describes an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*): that is, "let him not tempt you with a temptation like the bringing out of your parents from the Garden." The clause ﴿*yanzi'u 'anhuma libasahuma*﴾ (stripping them of their clothing) is in the position of an accusative of circumstance (*hal*), and its explanation has already passed. The *lam* in ﴿*liyuriyahuma sawatihima*﴾ (to show them their private parts) is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*): that is, in order that he might show them. Its explanation has also already passed.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them﴾. This sentence is a reason for what precedes it, together with the exaggeration it contains in warning them against him. For whoever is in this position, seeing the children of Adam from where they cannot see him, is of great cunning, and is worthy of being guarded against with the utmost caution. "His tribe" means his helpers among the devils and his troops.

A group of the scholars have used this verse to argue that seeing the jinn is impossible. But there is nothing in the verse that indicates this. At most it says that he sees us from where we do not see him. It does not say that we never see him. For the absence of our seeing him at the time he sees us does not entail its absence absolutely.

Then God, glory be to Him, informed that He has made the devils allies (*awliya'*) of those who do not believe among His servants, and they are the disbelievers.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning His saying ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down upon you clothing that covers your private parts﴾ that he said: Some people of the Arabs used to circumambulate the House naked. And concerning His saying ﴿*wa-riyshan*﴾ he said: It is wealth.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr concerning His saying ﴿clothing that covers your private parts﴾ that he said: The garments. And ﴿*wa-riyshan*﴾ he said: Wealth. And ﴿the clothing of God-consciousness﴾ he said: The fear of God.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Zayd ibn 'Ali concerning His saying ﴿clothing that covers your private parts﴾ that he said: The clothing of the common people. And ﴿*wa-riyshan*﴾ he said: The clothing of adornment. And ﴿the clothing of God-consciousness﴾ he said: Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿*wa-riyshan*﴾ that he said: Wealth, clothing, living, and blessings. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him concerning His saying "*wa-riyashan*" that he said: It is wealth.

That is, "We created for you clothing (*libas*) that covers your private parts (*sawat*) which Iblis exposed from your two parents." *Sawah* means *'awrah* (the parts that must be covered), as has already passed. The discussion of its extent and of what must be covered of it is explained in the books of *furu'* (the branches of jurisprudence).

His saying: ﴿*wa-riyshan*﴾ (and as finery). Al-Hasan, 'Asim (according to the transmission of al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi), and Abu 'Amr (according to the transmission of al-Hasan ibn 'Ali al-Ju'fi) read *wa-riyashan* (رِياشًا). The rest read *wa-rishan* (رِيشًا). *Riyash* is the plural of *rish*, which means clothing.

Al-Farra' said: *rish* and *riyash* are like *libs* and *libas*, as one says *libs* and *libas*. The *rish* of a bird is what God has covered it with.

It was also said that *rish* here means abundance and comfort of living.

Al-Qurtubi said: What most of the lexicographers hold is that *rish* is whatever covers, whether of clothing or of livelihood.

Abu Hatim transmitted, from Abu 'Ubayda: "I gave him a riding animal and its *rish*," meaning what is upon it of equipment.

It was also said that *rish* here means the clothing of adornment, because it is mentioned after His saying ﴿We have sent down upon you clothing﴾ and is conjoined to it.

His saying: ﴿*wa-libasu al-taqwa*﴾ (and the clothing of God-consciousness). The people of Medina, Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read *libasa* with a *fatha* (نَصْبٍ). The rest read it with a *damma* (بِالرَّفْعِ). The *nasb* is on the basis that it is conjoined to the first *libas*, and the *raf'* is on the basis that it is a subject (*mubtada'*), with the phrase ﴿*dhalika khayr*﴾ (that is best) as its predicate.

By "the clothing of God-consciousness" is meant the clothing of scrupulousness (*wara'*) and guarding oneself against the disobedience of God. This is scrupulousness itself and fear of God. That is the best clothing and the finest adornment. It was also said: the clothing of God-consciousness is modesty (*haya'*). It was said: it is righteous deeds. It was said: it is the wool garments and coarse clothing, because of the humility before God that is in them. It was said: it is the coat of mail and the helmet worn by one who fights in the way of God. The first view is the better.

It applies to everything in which there is God-consciousness, so all the views mentioned fall under it. Such metaphor is very common in the speech of the Arabs. Among it is the poet's saying:

*When a man does not wear garments of piety, he goes about naked even if he is clothed.*

And similar to it is the saying:

*Cover yourself with the garments of generosity, for I see every fault, and generosity is its covering.*

That is, that sending down is among the signs of God which indicate that it has a Creator.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verse 28–30:

al-Fāḥishah (the grave sin): whatever sins one exaggerates in their foulness and ugliness.

Most of the exegetes said: it is the circling of the polytheists around the House (the Ka'bah) naked.

It was also said: it is shirk (associating partners with God). The apparent meaning is that it applies to what is more general than both matters together. The meaning is: when they committed a sinful act that was extremely ugly, they offered two excuses for it. The first: that they did it in imitation of their fathers, since they found them persisting in committing that foul act. The second: that they were commanded to do it by God, glorified is He.

Both excuses are utterly false and corrupt. The fact that their fathers were upon the ugliness does not make it permissible for them to do it. And the command of God, glorified is He, was not for foulness; rather, He commanded them to follow the prophets and to act upon the revealed Books, and He forbade them from opposing them. Among what He forbade them was committing foul deeds. For this reason God, glorified is He, refuted them by commanding His Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, to say to them: ﴿Indeed, God does not command foulness.﴾ So how do you claim that about Him, glorified is He? Then He denounced what they attributed to Him, saying: ﴿Do you say about God what you do not know?﴾ This is part of what the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, was commanded to say to them, and in it there is a great degree of rebuke and reproach. For speaking in ignorance is ugly in every matter; how much more so when it is fabrication against God? Indeed, in this noble verse there is the greatest deterrent and most eloquent admonition for the blind followers (al-muqallidah) who follow their fathers in doctrines that oppose the truth. For that is imitation of the people of disbelief, not of the people of truth, for they are the ones who say: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are following in their footsteps﴾ (az-Zukhruf: 23), and those who say: ﴿We found our fathers upon it, and God commanded us with it.﴾ The blind follower, were it not for his being deceived by the fact that he found his father upon that doctrine, while believing that it is what God commanded and that it is the truth, would not remain upon it. This trait is what kept the Jew upon Judaism, the Christian upon Christianity, and the innovator upon his innovation. Nothing kept them upon these misguidances except that they found their fathers in Judaism, Christianity, or innovation, and they assumed well that what they were upon was the truth that God commanded, and they did not look into their own selves, nor did they seek the truth as it ought to be sought, nor did they investigate the religion of God as it should be investigated. This is pure taqlid (blind imitation) and utter deficiency. So, O you who grew up upon one of these Islamic doctrines: I am a warner to you, exaggerating in warning you against saying this saying and persisting in error, for evil has become mixed with good, the sound with the sickly, and corrupt opinion with sound transmission.

God did not send to this nation except one Prophet, whom He commanded them to follow and forbade them from opposing. He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (al-Hashr: 7). Had the bare opinion of the imams of the doctrines and their followers been a proof upon the servants, this nation would have had many messengers, multiplied according to the number of people of opinion who impose upon people what God did not impose upon them.

Indeed, among the most wondrous heedlessness and the greatest distraction from the truth is the choice of the blind followers for the opinions of men, despite the existence of the Book of God, the existence of the sunnah of His Messenger, the existence of those who take both from him, and the existence among them of the instrument of understanding and the faculty of reason.

His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord commands justice (al-qist)﴾. Al-qist: justice. In it is that God, glorified is He, commands justice, (p-471) not as they claimed, that God commanded them with foulness. It was also said: al-qist here is "there is no god but God." In the speech there is an ellipsis: that is, say: My Lord commands justice, so obey Him.

His saying: ﴿And set your faces upright at every place of prostration﴾ is conjoined to the omitted implied element: that is, turn toward it in your prayer toward the qiblah, in whatever mosque you are, or at every time of prostration, or at every place of prostration, with the meaning that by prostration is meant prayer. And call upon Him, making the religion sincerely His, i.e., call upon Him or worship Him while being sincere in supplication or worship to Him. It was also said: affirm His oneness and do not associate anything with Him.

His saying: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾. The kaf (as) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is connected to what precedes it.

The meaning: just as He brought you into being at the beginning of creation, He will restore you. The intent is then argument against those who deny resurrection, so that He recompenses the good-doer for his goodness and the evildoer for his evil. It was also said: just as He brought you out from your mothers' bellies, you will return to Him in that same state, with nothing with you, and this is like His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ (al-An'am: 94). It was also said: just as He originated you from dust, you will return to dust.

﴿A party He guided﴾ is in the accusative by a verb that is explained by what follows it. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "you will return," meaning: you will return as two parties, happy and wretched. And this is strengthened by the reading of Ubayy: "two parties, a party He guided." The party whom God guided are the believers in God who follow His prophets, and the party upon whom error has been decreed are the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as protectors apart from God﴾ is a causal explanation of His saying: ﴿and a party upon whom error has been decreed﴾, that is: that is because they obeyed the devils in disobedience to God. Yet they think they are guided, and they did not acknowledge their own error, and this is more severe in their rebellion and obstinacy.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency﴾, he said: they used to circumambulate the House naked, so they were forbidden from that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatadah, regarding the verse, he said: By God, God has never honored a servant upon his disobedience, nor was He pleased with it for him, nor did He command it; rather He was pleased for you with obedience to Him and forbade you from disobeying Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying: "My Lord commands justice," he said: with justice; and "set your faces upright at every place of prostration," he said: toward the Ka'bah, wherever you pray, in a church or elsewhere; "as He originated you, you will return," he said: wretched and happy.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: "As He originated you, you will return," etc., he said: God originated the creation of the children of Adam as believer and disbeliever, as He said: ﴿He it is who created you; among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ (al-Taghabun: 2), then He will restore them on the Day of Resurrection as He originated their creation, believer and disbeliever.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Jabir regarding the verse, he said: they will be raised upon what they were upon: the believer upon his faith and the hypocrite upon his hypocrisy.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he mentioned the Qadariyyah and said: May God fight them! Has God not said: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ ﴿A party He guided and a party upon whom error has been decreed﴾?

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, regarding the verse: he said: it means, as We created you the first time, so you will return.

This trait is what kept the Jew upon Judaism, the Christian upon Christianity, and the innovator upon his innovation. Nothing kept them upon these misguidances except that they found their fathers in Judaism, Christianity, or innovation, and they assumed well that what they were upon was the truth that God commanded, and they did not look into their own selves, nor did they seek the truth as it ought to be sought, nor did they investigate the religion of God as it should be investigated. This is pure taqlid (blind imitation) and utter deficiency. So, O you who grew up upon one of these Islamic doctrines: I am a warner to you, exaggerating in warning you against saying this saying and persisting in error, for evil has become mixed with good, the sound with the sickly, and corrupt opinion with sound transmission.

God did not send to this nation except one Prophet, whom He commanded them to follow and forbade them from opposing. He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ (al-Hashr: 7). Had the bare opinion of the imams of the doctrines and their followers been a proof upon the servants, this nation would have had many messengers, multiplied according to the number of people of opinion who impose upon people what God did not impose upon them.

Indeed, among the most wondrous heedlessness and the greatest distraction from the truth is the choice of the blind followers for the opinions of men, despite the existence of the Book of God, the existence of the sunnah of His Messenger, the existence of those who take both from him, and the existence among them of the instrument of understanding and the faculty of reason.

His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord commands justice (al-qist)﴾. Al-qist: justice. In it is that God, glorified is He, commands justice, (p-471) not as they claimed, that God commanded them with foulness. It was also said: al-qist here is "there is no god but God." In the speech there is an ellipsis: that is, say: My Lord commands justice, so obey Him.

His saying: ﴿And set your faces upright at every place of prostration﴾ is conjoined to the omitted implied element: that is, turn toward it in your prayer toward the qiblah, in whatever mosque you are, or at every time of prostration, or at every place of prostration, with the meaning that by prostration is meant prayer. And call upon Him, making the religion sincerely His, i.e., call upon Him or worship Him while being sincere in supplication or worship to Him. It was also said: affirm His oneness and do not associate anything with Him.

His saying: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾. The kaf (as) is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar).

Al-Zajjaj said: it is connected to what precedes it.

The meaning: just as He brought you into being at the beginning of creation, He will restore you. The intent is then argument against those who deny resurrection, so that He recompenses the good-doer for his goodness and the evildoer for his evil. It was also said: just as He brought you out from your mothers' bellies, you will return to Him in that same state, with nothing with you, and this is like His saying: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, as We created you the first time﴾ (al-An'am: 94). It was also said: just as He originated you from dust, you will return to dust.

﴿A party He guided﴾ is in the accusative by a verb that is explained by what follows it. It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "you will return," meaning: you will return as two parties, happy and wretched. And this is strengthened by the reading of Ubayy: "two parties, a party He guided." The party whom God guided are the believers in God who follow His prophets, and the party upon whom error has been decreed are the disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, they took the devils as protectors apart from God﴾ is a causal explanation of His saying: ﴿and a party upon whom error has been decreed﴾, that is: that is because they obeyed the devils in disobedience to God. Yet they think they are guided, and they did not acknowledge their own error, and this is more severe in their rebellion and obstinacy.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And those who, when they commit an indecency﴾, he said: they used to circumambulate the House naked, so they were forbidden from that.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi, the like of it.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, something similar.

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatadah, regarding the verse, he said: By God, God has never honored a servant upon his disobedience, nor was He pleased with it for him, nor did He command it; rather He was pleased for you with obedience to Him and forbade you from disobeying Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid regarding His saying: "My Lord commands justice," he said: with justice; and "set your faces upright at every place of prostration," he said: toward the Ka'bah, wherever you pray, in a church or elsewhere; "as He originated you, you will return," he said: wretched and happy.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: "As He originated you, you will return," etc., he said: God originated the creation of the children of Adam as believer and disbeliever, as He said: ﴿He it is who created you; among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer﴾ (al-Taghabun: 2), then He will restore them on the Day of Resurrection as He originated their creation, believer and disbeliever.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Jabir regarding the verse, he said: they will be raised upon what they were upon: the believer upon his faith and the hypocrite upon his hypocrisy.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from him that he mentioned the Qadariyyah and said: May God fight them! Has God not said: ﴿As He originated you, you will return﴾ ﴿A party He guided and a party upon whom error has been decreed﴾?

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted from him, regarding the verse: he said: it means, as We created you the first time, so you will return.

This is a discourse addressed to all the children of Adam, even though it was revealed on a specific occasion. What counts is the generality of the wording, not the particularity of the occasion. Zeenah (adornment) is what people beautify themselves with of clothing. They were commanded to adorn themselves when coming to the mosques for prayer and circumambulation.

The verse has been used as evidence for the obligation of covering the 'awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered) in prayer, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. Rather, covering it is obligatory in every state, even when a man is alone, as the authentic hadiths indicate. The discussion of the 'awrah and what must be covered of it is detailed in the books of furu' (derivative jurisprudence).

His saying: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be extravagant﴾. God, glorified is He, commanded His servants to eat and drink, and forbade them extravagance. There is no asceticism in abandoning food or drink. One who abandons them entirely is a killer of himself and is among the people of the Fire, as is established in the authentic hadiths. One who reduces them to a degree by which his body becomes weak and unable to perform what is obligatory upon him, whether acts of worship or earning for himself and those he supports, opposes what God has commanded and guided to. One who is extravagant in spending in a manner that only the foolish and wasteful do opposes what God has prescribed for His servants and falls under the Qur'anic prohibition. Likewise, one who prohibits what is lawful or permits what is unlawful enters among the extravagant and leaves the moderate.

Among extravagance is eating without need, and at a time of being full.

His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has brought forth for His servants?﴾ Zeenah is what a person adorns himself with, whether clothing or other permissible things, such as metals about which no prohibition has come concerning adorning oneself with them, jewels, and the like. It has been said that it refers only to clothing, but there is no basis for this. Rather, it is among what the verse includes. There is no blame on one who wears fine, expensive clothing so long as it is not something God has forbidden, and no blame on one who adorns himself with any of the things that have a place in adornment and which no legal impediment prevents. Whoever claims that this contradicts asceticism has clearly erred.

We have already presented in this what is sufficient. Likewise the good things (al-tayyibat) of foods, drinks, and the like that people eat: there is no asceticism in abandoning the good of them. For this reason the verse came framed by a question that implies denunciation of those who forbid that for themselves or for others.

How excellent is what Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: "He has erred greatly who prefers wearing hair and wool over wearing cotton and linen, when the way to them is lawful and available; and who eats herbs and lentils and chooses them over wheat bread; and who abandons eating meat out of fear of the onset of desire." We have already quoted something similar from him at length.

The good things (al-tayyibat) are the enjoyable foods. It has been said that it is a general term for what is good in earnings and in food.

His saying: ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾, meaning that they belong to them originally, even if the disbelievers share them with them as long as they are in this life. ﴿Exclusively on the Day of Resurrection﴾, meaning specifically for them on the Day of Resurrection, with the disbelievers not sharing them.

Nafi' read khalisatan (exclusively) with the raf' (nominative), which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, as a predicate after a predicate. The rest read it with the nasb (accusative), as a circumstantial state (hal).

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: "It is not permissible to pause at al-dunya (the world), because what follows it is connected to His saying ﴿for those who believed﴾, and khalisatan is a circumstantial state from it, with the sense: Say, it is established for those who believed in the life of this world, while it is pure for them on the Day of Resurrection."

His saying: ﴿Thus do We detail the verses for a people who know﴾, meaning, in this manner of detail, We detail the verses containing what is lawful and what is forbidden.

His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies﴾. Fawahish is the plural of fahishah, and its explanation has already been given: ﴿what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾, meaning what is openly done and what is secretly done. It has been said that it is specific to the indecencies of adultery, but there is no basis for this. Ithm (sin) encompasses every disobedience that causes sin. It has been said that it refers specifically to wine. From this is the poet's saying:

"I drank sin until my reason was lost; so sin takes away the intellects."

Similar is the saying of another:

"He drinks sin openly from the cup."

A group of scholars have denied the view of those who restricted ithm to wine. Al-Nahhas said: "As for ithm being wine, this is not known. Its reality is that it encompasses all acts of disobedience, as the poet said:

'I found that the best course is the fear of God, and its worst is sin.'"

Al-Farra' said: "Ithm is what falls short of the truth, and domineering over people." End.

There is nothing in applying the word ithm to wine that indicates it is restricted to it. Rather, it is one of the acts of disobedience to which it truly applies.

In al-Sihah it is said: "Wine is sometimes called ithm," and he recited:

"I drank the sin, the verse..."

Al-Harawi also recited it before him in his Gharibah.

His saying: ﴿and transgression without right﴾. Al-baghy is the injustice that exceeds its limit. He singled it out for mention after its inclusion in what preceded because it is a grave sin, as in His saying: ﴿He forbids indecency, wrongdoing, and transgression﴾ (al-Nahl: 90). ﴿And that you associate with God that for which He has sent down no authority﴾, meaning that you make for God a partner for whom He has not sent down any proof upon you. The intent is to mock the polytheists, because God does not send down evidence that another is a partner to Him. ﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾, of its reality and that God said it. This is like what they used to attribute to God, glorified is He, of permissions and prohibitions that He had not authorized.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the women used to circumambulate the House naked, except that a woman would place a rag over her private part, and say:

"Today some of it, or all of it, will appear; and what appears of it, I will not make lawful."

So God revealed: ﴿Take your adornment at every mosque﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning the verse that he said: "The men used to circumambulate the House naked, so God commanded them to adorn themselves."

Zeenah is clothing, what conceals the private parts, and what else there is of good wheat and goods.

Ibn 'Adi, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Take the adornment of prayer." They said: "And what is the adornment of prayer?" He said: "Wear your sandals and pray in them."

al-'Uqayli, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning God's saying: ﴿Take your adornment at every mosque﴾, that he said: "Pray in your sandals."

The hadiths on the legitimacy of praying in sandals are very numerous. As for whether that is the interpretation of the verse, as is narrated in these two hadiths, I do not know the status of their chains.

It has been reported that the prohibition applies to a man praying in a single garment with nothing of it on his shoulders, and this is in the two Sahihs and elsewhere, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: God permitted eating and drinking as long as it is not extravagance or self-conceit.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the extravagant﴾ that he said: "In food and drink."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated through 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Eat, drink, give charity, and dress without self-conceit or extravagance, for God, glorified is He, loves to see the effect of His blessing upon His servant."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Quraysh used to circumambulate the House while naked, whistling and clapping. So God revealed: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God﴾, and they were commanded to wear clothing. ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world, exclusively on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ He said: "They benefit from them in this world, and no sin will follow them concerning them on the Day of Resurrection."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Dahhak concerning ﴿Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾ that he said: "The polytheists share with the believers the splendor of this world, and it is exclusively for the believers on the Day of Resurrection, not for the polytheists."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿and the good things of provision﴾ that he said: "Fat, meat, and clarified butter."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him who said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah used to forbid things that God had made lawful, of clothing and other things, and this is God's saying: ﴿Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it what is forbidden and what is lawful?﴾ (Yunus: 59). And this is this. So God revealed: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He has brought forth for His servants and the good things of provision? Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world﴾, meaning, the Muslims shared with the disbelievers in the good things in the life of this world, so they ate from the good foods of it, wore from the fine clothing of it, and married from its righteous women. Then God will make the good things pure in the Hereafter for those who believed, and the disbelievers will have no share in them."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "What appeared of them is nakedness, and what was concealed is fornication. They used to circumambulate the House naked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning the verse, who said: "What appeared of them is the circumambulation of the Jahiliyyah while naked, and what was concealed is fornication."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His saying: "And sin," he said: "Disobedience." "And transgression," he said: "That he transgresses against people without right."
