Al-A'mash, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *nashran* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a sukun on the *shin*, as a verbal noun; it is also permissible that it be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). The meaning of these readings returns to *an-nashr* (spreading), which is the opposite of *at-tayy* (folding). It is as if the wind, while still, was folded, and then released from its folds so that it becomes as if opened.

Abu 'Ubayda said: its meaning is scattered in its directions, according to the sense of "we spread them here and there."

'Asim recited *bushran* with a *ba'* (single dot) and a sukun on the *shin*, as the plural of *bashir* (bearer of good news): that is, the winds bring good news of rain. A similar verse is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He sends the winds as bearers of glad tidings﴾ (ar-Rum: 46).

His words: ﴿before His mercy﴾. By *ar-rahmah* here he meant rain: that is, in front of His mercy. The meaning is that He, Glorified is He, sends the winds spreading or bringing glad tidings before the rain.

His words: ﴿until when they carry heavy clouds﴾. "Aqalla fulan ash-shay'" means he carried it and lifted it. *As-sahab* (the cloud) may be masculine or feminine. The meaning is: until the winds carry heavy clouds laden with the water that they are carrying, "We drive it," that is, the cloud, "to a dead land," that is, a barren land with no vegetation. It is said: "I drove it to the land of such-and-such," and "to the land of such-and-such." It was also said: the *lam* here is the *lam* of cause: that is, for the sake of a dead land. *Al-baladu* is the inhabited place on the earth. ﴿Then We sent down water thereby﴾: that is, with the land to which We drove it; or with the cloud: that is, We sent down with the cloud the water which it carries; or with the wind: that is, We sent down with the wind sent before the rain the water. It was also said: the *ba'* here means *min* (from): that is, "We sent down from it water, then We brought forth thereby," that is, with the water, "from all the fruits," that is, from all their kinds.

His words: ﴿Thus We bring forth the dead﴾: that is, like that bringing forth, which is the bringing forth of fruits, We will bring forth the dead from the graves on the day of their gathering ﴿that you may remember﴾: that is, that you may remember, so that you know the greatness of God's power, the wondrousness of His craftsmanship, and that He is capable of resurrecting you just as He was capable of bringing forth the fruits that you witness.

His words: ﴿And the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾.

That is, the good soil, its vegetation comes forth by the permission and facilitation of God, a good, complete and full emergence. ﴿And that which is corrupt comes forth only sparsely﴾: that is, and the corrupt soil does not bring forth its vegetation except sparsely: that is, there is no good in it.

Talhah ibn Musarrif recited *nakdan* with a sukun on the *kaf*.

Ibn al-Qa'qa' recited *nakadan* with a *fatha* on the *kaf*: that is, possessing scarcity.

The rest recited *nakidan* with a *fatha* on the *nun* and a *kasra* on the *kaf*.

It was recited *yukhriju* (with a *damma* on the *ya'*), that is, the land brings it forth. It was said: the meaning of the verse is a comparison: God, Exalted is He, likened the quick of understanding to the good land, and the dull to the corrupt land, as mentioned by an-Nahhas. It was also said: this is a parable for hearts, so He likened the heart receptive to admonition to the good land, and the one far from it to the corrupt land, as said by al-Hasan. It was also said: it is a parable for the heart of the believer and the hypocrite, as said by Qatadah. It was also said: it is a parable for the good and the bad among the children of Adam, as said by Mujahid.

﴿Thus We vary the signs﴾: that is, like that variation ﴿for a people who give thanks﴾ to God and acknowledge His blessing.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu ash-Shaykh have related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, that he said: "secretly" means privately. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ in supplication or in anything else.

Abu ash-Shaykh has related from Qatadah, who said: "humbly" is openly, and "secretly" is privately.

Ibn Abi Hatim has related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His words ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, that he meant "submissively," and "secretly": meaning in a low voice and calm in your needs of the matters of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾: he said: do not invoke evil upon a believing man or woman, such as saying, "O God, disgrace him and curse him" and the like, for that is transgression.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Abu Mijlaz, concerning His words ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, that he said: do not ask for the ranks of the prophets.

Ibn al-Mubarak, Ibn Jarir and Abu ash-Shaykh have related from al-Hasan, who said: The Muslims used to strive greatly in supplication, and no voice of theirs could be heard, except a murmur between them and their Lord. That is because God says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, and because God mentioned a righteous servant and approved his words, so He said: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ (Maryam: 3).

Ibn Abi Hatim has related from Ibn Salih, concerning His words ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾, that he said: after the prophets and their companions had reformed it.

Abu ash-Shaykh has related from Abu Sinan concerning the verse, that he said: I have made lawful what is lawful for Me, forbidden what is forbidden for Me, and set the limits of My bounds, so do not corrupt them.

Abu ash-Shaykh has related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And supplicate Him in fear and hope﴾, that he said: fear of Him and hope for what is with Him. ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the doers of good﴾: meaning the believers; and whoever does not believe in God is among the corrupters.

Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh have related from as-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds﴾, that he said: God sends the wind, and it brings the cloud from between the two horizons, the edge of the sky and the earth, from where they meet, and it brings it out from there; then it spreads it, spreading it through the sky as He wills; then He opens the gates of the sky, and the water flows upon the cloud; then the cloud rains after that.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh have related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿glad tidings before His mercy﴾, that he said: people rejoice in them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from as-Suddi, concerning His words ﴿before His mercy﴾, that he said: it is the rain. And concerning His words ﴿Thus We bring forth the dead﴾, he said: thus you will come forth, and thus is the resurrection, just as the crop comes forth by water.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu ash-Shaykh have related from Mujahid, concerning His words ﴿Thus We bring forth the dead﴾, that he said: when God wills to bring forth the dead, He sends rain upon the sky until it splits the earth open for them; then He sends the spirits, and each spirit descends to its body. Thus God gives life to the dead through the rain, just as He gives life to the earth.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words ﴿And the good land﴾ up to the end of the verse, that he said: it is a parable God struck for the believer. He says: he is good and his deed is good, just as the good land its fruit is good. ﴿And that which is corrupt﴾ is struck as a parable for the disbeliever, like a salt-laden, barren land from which no blessing comes forth. So the disbeliever is the corrupt one and his deed is corrupt. Something similar has been related from a group of the Successors.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 59–64:

When Allah, glorified is He, had made clear the perfection of His power and the wonder of His craftsmanship in the preceding verses, He here mentions the stories of the nations and what they contain of warning and threat to the disbelievers, in order to alert this community to what is right, and that it should not follow those of the earlier nations who opposed the truth.

The lam (la) is the answer to an omitted oath.

He (Nuh) was the first messenger to the people of the earth after Adam. The mention of Nuh has already occurred in Al 'Imran, so it is sufficient to not repeat it here. As for what has been said, that Idris was before Nuh, Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is a delusion."

Al-Mazari said: "If what the historians mention is sound, it is to be understood that Idris was a prophet but not a messenger."

The clause "He said: 'O my people, worship Allah'" is a resumptive clause (isti'nafiyyah), an answer to an assumed question.

His saying "You have no god other than Him" is in the position of a cause (for) his saying "worship": i.e., worship Him, because there is no god for you other than Him that would deserve to be worshipped by you.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read ghayrihi with a raised vowel (raf'), taking it as an attributive adjective (na't) of ilah according to its position (al-mawdi') (i.e., ghayru is in the nominative as a modifier of the place of the noun).

Al-Kisa'i read it with a lowered vowel (khafd) throughout the Qur'an, taking it as an attributive adjective according to the wording (al-lafz).

Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative (nasb) as an exception: meaning, "You have no god except Him."

Abu 'Amr said: "I do not know the genitive nor the accusative." This is refuted by the fact that some of Bani Asad put ghayr in the accusative in all circumstances, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing prevented them from drinking except that a dove cooed in branches of arqal (tamarisk)."

The clause "Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day" includes a justification for the command to worship: i.e., if you do not worship Him, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, or the punishment of the Day of the Flood.

His saying "The eminent ones of his people said" is a resumptive clause, an answer to an assumed question. Al-mala' (the eminent ones) are the nobles and leaders of a people; it has been said they are the men. Its explanation has already occurred in al-Baqarah. Al-dalal (error) is deviating from the path of truth and departing from it: i.e., "Indeed we see you, in your calling to the worship of Allah alone, in error away from the path of truth."

The clause "He said: 'O my people'" is also a resumptive clause, an answer to an assumed question: "There is no error in me" as you claim, "but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds." He was sent to them to bring good to them and to repel evil from them. He negated error from himself and affirmed for himself what is higher in rank and more honourable in station, namely that he is the messenger of Allah to them.

The clause "I convey to you the messages of my Lord" is in the position of a nominative (raf') as a description of "a messenger," or it is a separate clause clarifying the state of the messenger.

Al-Risalat (the messages) are what Allah sent him with to them of what He revealed to him. "And I advise you" is conjoined to "I convey to you," and it is said: nasahtuhu and nasahtu lahu. The addition of the lam indicates emphasis in purifying the advice.

Al-Asma'i said: al-nasih is one who is pure of malice, and everything that is pure has become sincere (nasaha). So the meaning of "I advise" here is: I purify my intention for you from the admixtures of corruption. The noun is al-nasihah.

The clause "And I know from Allah what you do not know" is conjoined to the preceding clause, confirming his messengership and clarifying the increase of his knowledge, and that he is specially endowed with knowledge of things they do not know through Allah's informing him of them.

His saying "Are you amazed" — the waw was given a fatha because it is the conjunctive waw, and the interrogative hamzah entered upon it for denunciation of them.

The conjoined element is omitted: as if it were said: "Do you deem it unlikely and are amazed, or do you deny and are amazed, that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord," i.e., revelation and admonition, "through a man from among you," i.e., through the tongue of a man from among you whom you know, and it was not through the tongue of someone you do not know or whose language you do not understand. It has been said: 'ala here means ma'a (with): i.e., with a man from among you, so that he may warn you thereby, and that you may guard against what opposes it. "And that perhaps you may receive mercy" through what the warning brings you and through your piety, by which you become exposed to the mercy of Allah, glorified is He, toward you and to His good pleasure with you.

"So they denied him": i.e., after that they denied him and did not act upon what he brought of warning. "So We saved him and those with him" from the believers in him who were with him "in the ark, and We drowned those who denied Our signs" and persisted in that and did not return to repentance. The clause "Indeed they were a blind people" is a cause for His saying "and We drowned": i.e., We drowned the deniers because they were blind of heart, in whom admonition has no effect and reminder benefits them not.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first prophet to be sent was Nuh."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Yazid al-Raqashi who said: Nuh (peace be upon him) was named Nuh only because of how much he lamented (naha) over himself.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Between Adam and Nuh there were ten generations, all upon a law of truth.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Malik who said: al-mala' means the nobles of the people.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi regarding "that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord": it means an explanation from your Lord.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "Indeed they were a blind people": he said: disbelievers.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding "Indeed they were a blind people": he said: blind to the truth.

He (Nuh) was the first messenger to the people of the earth after Adam. The mention of Nuh has already occurred in Al 'Imran, so it is sufficient to not repeat it here. As for what has been said, that Idris was before Nuh, Ibn al-'Arabi said: "It is a delusion."

Al-Mazari said: "If what the historians mention is sound, it is to be understood that Idris was a prophet but not a messenger."

The clause "He said: 'O my people, worship Allah'" is a resumptive clause (isti'nafiyyah), an answer to an assumed question.

His saying "You have no god other than Him" is in the position of a cause (for) his saying "worship": i.e., worship Him, because there is no god for you other than Him that would deserve to be worshipped by you.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read ghayrihi with a raised vowel (raf'), taking it as an attributive adjective (na't) of ilah according to its position (al-mawdi') (i.e., ghayru is in the nominative as a modifier of the place of the noun).

Al-Kisa'i read it with a lowered vowel (khafd) throughout the Qur'an, taking it as an attributive adjective according to the wording (al-lafz).

Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i permitted the accusative (nasb) as an exception: meaning, "You have no god except Him."

Abu 'Amr said: "I do not know the genitive nor the accusative." This is refuted by the fact that some of Bani Asad put ghayr in the accusative in all circumstances, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Nothing prevented them from drinking except that a dove cooed in branches of arqal (tamarisk)."

The clause "Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day" includes a justification for the command to worship: i.e., if you do not worship Him, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, or the punishment of the Day of the Flood.

His saying "The eminent ones of his people said" is a resumptive clause, an answer to an assumed question. Al-mala' (the eminent ones) are the nobles and leaders of a people; it has been said they are the men. Its explanation has already occurred in al-Baqarah. Al-dalal (error) is deviating from the path of truth and departing from it: i.e., "Indeed we see you, in your calling to the worship of Allah alone, in error away from the path of truth."

The clause "He said: 'O my people'" is also a resumptive clause, an answer to an assumed question: "There is no error in me" as you claim, "but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds." He was sent to them to bring good to them and to repel evil from them. He negated error from himself and affirmed for himself what is higher in rank and more honourable in station, namely that he is the messenger of Allah to them.

The clause "I convey to you the messages of my Lord" is in the position of a nominative (raf') as a description of "a messenger," or it is a separate clause clarifying the state of the messenger.

Al-Risalat (the messages) are what Allah sent him with to them of what He revealed to him. "And I advise you" is conjoined to "I convey to you," and it is said: nasahtuhu and nasahtu lahu. The addition of the lam indicates emphasis in purifying the advice.

Al-Asma'i said: al-nasih is one who is pure of malice, and everything that is pure has become sincere (nasaha). So the meaning of "I advise" here is: I purify my intention for you from the admixtures of corruption. The noun is al-nasihah.

The clause "And I know from Allah what you do not know" is conjoined to the preceding clause, confirming his messengership and clarifying the increase of his knowledge, and that he is specially endowed with knowledge of things they do not know through Allah's informing him of them.

His saying "Are you amazed" — the waw was given a fatha because it is the conjunctive waw, and the interrogative hamzah entered upon it for denunciation of them.

The conjoined element is omitted: as if it were said: "Do you deem it unlikely and are amazed, or do you deny and are amazed, that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord," i.e., revelation and admonition, "through a man from among you," i.e., through the tongue of a man from among you whom you know, and it was not through the tongue of someone you do not know or whose language you do not understand. It has been said: 'ala here means ma'a (with): i.e., with a man from among you, so that he may warn you thereby, and that you may guard against what opposes it. "And that perhaps you may receive mercy" through what the warning brings you and through your piety, by which you become exposed to the mercy of Allah, glorified is He, toward you and to His good pleasure with you.

"So they denied him": i.e., after that they denied him and did not act upon what he brought of warning. "So We saved him and those with him" from the believers in him who were with him "in the ark, and We drowned those who denied Our signs" and persisted in that and did not return to repentance. The clause "Indeed they were a blind people" is a cause for His saying "and We drowned": i.e., We drowned the deniers because they were blind of heart, in whom admonition has no effect and reminder benefits them not.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first prophet to be sent was Nuh."

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Abu Nu'aym and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Yazid al-Raqashi who said: Nuh (peace be upon him) was named Nuh only because of how much he lamented (naha) over himself.

Ibn al-Mundhir reported similarly from 'Ikrimah.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn 'Abbas who said: Between Adam and Nuh there were ten generations, all upon a law of truth.

Abu al-Shaykh reported from al-Suddi regarding "that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord": it means an explanation from your Lord.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "Indeed they were a blind people": he said: disbelievers.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mujahid regarding "Indeed they were a blind people": he said: blind to the truth.

And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. That is, We sent to the people of 'Ad their brother, meaning one of their own tribe, or their companion. He was called their brother because he was a son of Adam like them. 'Ad was a descendant of Sam ibn Nuh.

It is said: he was 'Ad ibn 'Ws ibn Iram ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and Hud was the son of 'Abd Allah ibn Rabah ibn al-Khulud ibn 'Aws ibn Iram ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. [Hud] is in apposition (ʿatf bayan, explanatory apposition) [to "their brother"]. ﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him."﴾

The explanation of this has already been given shortly before. The interrogative in ﴿Will you not then fear [Allah]?﴾ is for disapproval.

The explanation of "the chiefs" (al-mala'") has also already been given. Safahah (foolishness) means lightness and stupidity.

Its explanation has been given in Surat al-Baqarah. They attributed to him lightness and levity, and they did not stop at that, but said: ﴿Indeed, we think you are among the liars,﴾ emphasizing their belief in his lying about what he claimed of prophethood. Then he answered them by negating foolishness from himself, and he corrected [their claim] by saying that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds. The meaning of this has been explained shortly before.

Likewise, the explanation of ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord﴾ has already been given, and the meaning of "the adviser" (al-nasih) has been mentioned. Al-amin is one known for trustworthiness.

The explanation of ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you?﴾ has also already been given in the story of Nuh that preceded this story.

[Allah says]: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Nuh.﴾ He reminded them of one of Allah's blessings upon them, namely that He made them successors after the people of Nuh, that is, He made them the inhabitants of the land in which they were, or He made them kings. ("Idh") is in the accusative governed by "udhkuru" (remember), and the remembrance is linked to a time.

What is meant is the succession over the earth that they had, for the purpose of emphasis, because when a matter's time deserves to be remembered, it is more deserving of remembrance. ﴿And He increased you in stature, expansion.﴾ That is, height in physique and greatness of body, in addition to what their forefathers had in bodies.

Reports have come from the early generations (al-salaf) about the great size of the bodies of the people of 'Ad.

[Allah says]: ﴿So remember the favours of Allah.﴾ "Al-ala'" is the plural of "ili'" (a favour), and among them is the blessing of succession on the earth, the expansion in stature, and other things with which He bestowed favour upon them. He repeated the reminder to increase the affirmation. "Al-ala'" means blessings. ﴿That perhaps you may prosper﴾ if you remember that, because remembering a blessing is a cause that moves one to give thanks for it, and whoever gives thanks has prospered.

[Allah says]: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone?"﴾ This is their denunciation of his calling them to worship Allah alone, to the exclusion of their deities, which they had made partners of Allah. This was denounced by them only because they found their forefathers following something other than what he called them to. ﴿And abandon what our fathers used to worship.﴾ That is, we abandon what they used to worship, and this falls within what they denounced.

[Allah says]: ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful.﴾ This is their urging for the punishment with which Hud threatened them, due to the severity of their rebellion against Allah, their turning away from the path of truth, and their distance from following what is right.

He answered them with His words: ﴿There has already fallen upon you from your Lord an abomination and wrath.﴾ He made what was expected as if it had already happened, as an alert to the certainty of its occurrence, as the scholars of ma'ani and bayan (rhetoric) have mentioned. It is said that the meaning of "waqa'" (fell) is "wajaba" (became due). "Rijs" means punishment. It is also said that here it means a veil over the heart through increased disbelief.

Then He denounced them for their disputing, saying: ﴿Do you dispute with me over names﴾, meaning the names of the idols they worshipped. He called them names because their named referents have no reality; rather, calling them gods is false, so they are as if non-existent, and only their names exist. ﴿That you have named, you and your fathers﴾, that is, you named your worshipped objects from your own side, you and your fathers, and there is no reality to that. ﴿Allah has not sent down for them any authority.﴾ That is, no proof that you could rely on for your claims that they deserve these false assertions.

Then He threatened them with the most severe threat, saying: ﴿So wait, I am with you among those who wait.﴾ That is, wait for what you have demanded of punishment, for I am with you among those awaiting it, and it will surely befall you and descend upon you without doubt.

Then Allah, glorified is He, informed that He saved Hud and those who believed in him from the punishment that descended upon those who disbelieved in him and did not accept his message, and that He cut off the root of the people who denied, that is, He completely uprooted them all.

The explanation of its meaning has already been verified. The clause ﴿And they were not believers﴾ is conjoined to "they denied": that is, We uprooted these people who combined denial of Our signs with not believing.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud﴾, that he said: "He was not their brother in religion, but their brother in lineage, since he was one of them, and therefore he was called their brother."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, who said: "'Ad were, from Yemen to Syria, like ants."

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Wahb, who said: "A man of 'Ad was sixty cubits by their cubit. His head was like a great dome, and a man's eye would have birds of prey nesting in it, and likewise their nostrils."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, who said: "It was mentioned to us that they were twelve cubits in height."

al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi narrated in Nawadir al-Usul from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "A man among them was eighty fathoms, and a grain of wheat among them was like a kidney of a cow, and one pomegranate could have ten men sitting in its peel."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him regarding ﴿And He increased you in stature, expansion﴾, that he said: "Strength."

'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad, in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "A man of the people of 'Ad would take a stone door-leaf; if five hundred of this nation gathered upon it, they would not be able to lift it. And one of them would put his foot into the earth and it would sink into it."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿the favours of Allah﴾, that he said: "The blessings of Allah." And regarding "rijs", he said: "Wrath."

Ibn 'Asakir narrated, saying: "When Allah sent the wind upon 'Ad, Hud and those who were with him among the believers withdrew into an enclosure, and the wind did not reach them except in a way that softened their skins and pleased their souls. The wind would pass by an 'Adi man, lift him between heaven and earth, and smash him with stones."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, regarding His words ﴿And We cut off the root of those who denied﴾, that he said: "We uprooted them."

al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn Jarir and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "Hud was buried in Hadramawt, in a red sand dune, and at his head is a lote tree."

Ibn 'Asakir narrated from 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'Atikah, who said: "On the qibla side of the Mosque of Damascus, Hud is buried."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The age of Hud was four hundred and seventy-two years."

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 73–79:**

His saying: ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih﴾ is coordinated with what preceded it: that is, "And We sent to Thamud their brother." Thamud is a tribe named after their father, who was Thamud ibn Aad ibn Iram ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Salih is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan), and he is Salih ibn Ubayd ibn Asaf ibn Mashih ibn Ubayd ibn Hadhir ibn Thamud. The diptote form of Thamud (its not taking tanwin) is because it was made the name of a tribe.

Abu Hatim said: it is not diptote because it is non-Arabic (aʿjami).

al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because it derives from al-thamd, which is little water. The reciters have read ﴿Indeed, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord﴾ (Hud 11:68) as the name of a tribe. The dwellings of Thamud were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, up to Wadi al-Qura.

His saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him."﴾ Its explanation has already preceded in the story of Nuh. ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾: that is, a manifest miracle, and it is the bringing forth of the she-camel from the hard rock. The diptote form of Thamud (its not taking tanwin) is because it was made the name of a tribe.

Abu Hatim said: it is not diptote because it is non-Arabic (aʿjami).

al-Nahhas said: this is an error, because it derives from al-thamd, which is little water. The reciters have read ﴿Indeed, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord﴾ (Hud 11:68) as the name of a tribe. The dwellings of Thamud were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, up to Wadi al-Qura.

His saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him."﴾ Its explanation has already preceded in the story of Nuh. ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾: that is, a manifest miracle, and it is the bringing forth of the she-camel from the hard rock. The clause ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾ explains the evidence mentioned, and "a sign" (ayah) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), with the governing element being the sense of pointing (al-ishara). Attributing the she-camel to Allah is an honouring and ennobling of her.

His saying: ﴿So leave her to eat within the land of Allah﴾: that is, let her eat in the land of Allah, for she is the she-camel of Allah and the land is His land, so do not prevent her from what is not yours and you do not own. ﴿And do not touch her﴾ with any harm: that is, do not confront her in any way that would harm her.

His saying: ﴿Lest there seize you a painful punishment﴾ is the answer to the prohibition: that is, if you do not refrain from touching her with any harm, a painful punishment will seize you, meaning severe in pain.

His saying: ﴿And remember when He made you successors after ʿAd﴾: that is, He made you successors in the land, or made you kings in it, as has preceded in the story of Hud. ﴿And settled you in the land﴾: that is, He gave you a dwelling (mubaʾah) in it, which is the abode you inhabit. ﴿You take from its plains palaces﴾: that is, you take from the flatness of the land palaces; or this clause explains the clause ﴿and settled you in the land﴾. Because of their strength and the hardness of their bodies, they used to hew out the mountains and make caves in them to live in, since buildings and roofs would perish before their lifetimes ended. The accusative of "houses" is either as a delimited circumstantial state (hal muqaddarah) or as a second object of "you hew," with the verb being construed to include the sense of "you take" (tattakhidhun).

His saying: ﴿So remember the favours of Allah﴾: its explanation has preceded in the story before this.

His saying: ﴿And do not commit corruption in the land, spreading mischief﴾: al-ʿathy and al-ʿathw are two dialectal forms, and its verification has preceded in al-Baqarah in a way that suffices without repetition.

﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant among his people said﴾: that is, the arrogant leaders of the people of Salih said to the oppressed, those whom the arrogant had oppressed, and ﴿to those of them who believed﴾ is a substitute for "those who were oppressed," with the repetition of the preposition, a substitution of part for whole, since among the oppressed there were some who were not believers. This is on the basis that the pronoun in "of them" refers to "those who were oppressed." If it refers to "his people," it is a substitution of the whole for the oppressed. The content of the saying is: ﴿Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?﴾ They said this by way of mockery and derision.

His saying: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are believers in that with which he has been sent."﴾ They answered them that they believe in his message, although the arrogant's question to them was only about knowledge from them, whether they know of his message or not, hastening to display what faith they had, and drawing attention to the fact that his being a messenger is a clear and evident matter that does not need to be asked about.

It is said: "the horse was hamstrung" when its legs were struck with a sword. It is also said: the origin of ʿaqr is breaking the hock of a camel, then "ʿaqr" was applied to slaughtering, because hamstringing is generally the cause of slaughter. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 80–84:

His saying: "Lut" is coordinated with what preceded it, i.e., "And We sent Lut," or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, i.e., "And mention Lut, when he said to his people."

Al-Farra' said: Lut is derived from their saying: "This was attached (ulīṭa) to my heart," i.e., was joined (ulṣiqa).

Al-Zajjaj said: Some grammarians claimed that Lut may be derived from "I smeared (lṭtu) the basin" when I plastered it with clay, but this is an error, because foreign names are not derived.

Sibawayh said: Nuh and Lut are foreign names, except that they are light, and therefore they are declined. Lut is the son of Haran ibn Tarikh, so he is the nephew of Ibrahim. God sent him to a nation called Sodom.

"Do you commit the indecency (al-fāḥisha)?" That is, the abominable trait that persists in grave obscenity and ugliness. He said this as a denunciation of them and a rebuke to them: "No one in the worlds has done it before you" — i.e., no one did it before you, for sodomy did not exist among any nation before this nation. The "min" is extra, for emphasis, to make the negation general, and it encompasses everything it governs. The sentence is brought to strengthen the censure against them and the rebuke to them.

His saying: "Indeed you come to men with desire" — Nafi' and Hafs read it as a statement with a single broken hamza. The rest read it with two hamzas as an interrogative, which implies rebuke and reproach. Abu 'Ubayd, al-Kisa'i and others preferred the first reading, while al-Khalil and Sibawayh preferred the second. On the first reading this sentence explains His saying "Do you commit the indecency?" and likewise on the second reading, with the added interrogation and its repetition, which conveys intensification in reproach and rebuke. "Shahwatan" is in the accusative as a verbal noun: i.e., you desire them with desire. It may also be a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial state: i.e., desiring. It may also be an object of purpose: i.e., for the sake of desire. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 85–93 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what preceded it, i.e., "and We sent."

Madyan is the name of a tribe, though it is said to be the name of a town; the first view is preferable. The tribe was named after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim, just as it is said Bakr and Tamim (names of tribes).

﴿Their brother Shu'ayb﴾: Shu'ayb is an appositive (‘atf bayan, an explanatory apposition). He was Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjub ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, as stated by 'Ata' and Ibn Ishaq, and others.

Al-Sharafi ibn al-Qatami said that he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

Ibn Sam'an claimed that he was Shu'ayb ibn Hurra ibn Yashjub ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

Qatada said: he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

﴿He said: "O my people!"﴾ up to ﴿"a clear proof from your Lord"﴾ has already been explained in the story of Nuh.

﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: He commanded them to give full measure and weight, because they were people who dealt in measuring and weighing, and they did not give them in full. He mentioned the measure (al-kayl), which is a verbal noun (masdar), and conjoined to it the balance (al-mizan), which is a noun denoting an instrument.

There is disagreement about the reason for this. It is said that by "measure" is meant the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), so that the conjunction of "balance" to it is appropriate. It is also said that by "balance" is meant weighing (al-wazn), which corresponds to "measure." The fa' in ﴿fa-awfu﴾ is for conjunction with "worship" (u'budu) [in the earlier command].

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: al-bakhs (diminishing) means reduction. It may occur by defaming the goods, by making them undesirable, or by deceiving their owner and cheating him. All of this is among the consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. The apparent meaning of ﴿their things﴾ is that they diminished people's goods in all things. It is said that they were tax collectors (makkasin), who levied a tax on everything that entered their markets. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Is there in all the markets of Iraq a levy, and on everything a man sells a dirham's worth of tax?"

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right﴾: Its explanation has already been given shortly before. It includes small and large corruption, subtle and grave. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to acting upon what He commanded them and abandoning what He forbade them. By "better" here is meant absolute benefit, since there is no good at all in not giving full measure and weight, in diminishing people's goods, or in corruption on the earth.

﴿And do not sit on every path threatening [people]﴾: al-sirat is the road, i.e., do not sit on every road threatening people with punishment. It is said that they used to sit on the roads leading to Shu'ayb and threaten anyone who wanted to come to him, saying, "He is a liar, so do not go to him," just as the Quraysh used to do with the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. It is also said that what is meant is sitting on the paths of religion and preventing whoever wants to travel them, and it does not mean sitting on the roads literally. This is supported by ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾. It is also said that the verse means the prohibition of highway robbery and seizing plunder, which was among their practices. It is said that they were tax collectors who took levies on the roads from people's wealth, so they were forbidden from this.

The first view is the closest of them to correctness, although there is no obstacle to applying the prohibition to all of these views mentioned.

The clause ﴿threatening﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and so is what is conjoined to it: i.e., do not sit on every road threatening its people, barring from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked.

By "barring from the way of Allah" is meant preventing people from the road on which they sat, and stopping them from reaching Shu'ayb, for people's travelling on that path to reach the prophet of Allah is travelling the way of Allah. ﴿Those who believe in Him﴾ is the object of ﴿barring﴾. The pronoun in ﴿believe in Him﴾ refers to Allah, or to the way of Allah, or to every road, or to Shu'ayb.

﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: i.e., you seek that the way of Allah be bent and not straight. The discussion of crookedness (al-'iwaj) has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the vowelling of the 'ayn in al-'iwaj (crookedness) is with kasra in its meanings, and with fatha in its physical sense (al-ihram).

﴿And remember when you were﴾: i.e., remember the time when you were few in number, and He multiplied you through offspring. It is said: you were poor, and He enriched you.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾: among the earlier nations, for Allah destroyed them and sent down upon them punishments that took them away and erased their traces.

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the rulings which Allah has legislated for you, and a group among you ﴿who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾ This is in the mode of threat and severe warning to them, and it is not in the mode of commanding patience upon disbelief.

The judgment of Allah between the two parties is the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ (al-Tawba: 52). Or it is a command to the believers to be patient with what befalls them of harm from the disbelievers, until Allah gives them victory over them.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: i.e., the nobles who were arrogant said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you"﴾. They were not satisfied with refusing belief and rebelling against answering what he called them to, but went beyond that, out of transgression, insolence, and wickedness, to threatening their prophet and those who believed in him with expulsion from their town, or with their return, he and those with him, to their disbelieving religion. That is: one of the two matters must happen, either expulsion or return.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) means "beginning," as in the saying: "a hardship returned to me from so-and-so," meaning it befell me, even if no hardship had preceded it. So there is no objection by those who say: how could Shu'ayb be upon their disbelieving religion before Allah sent him as a messenger? The answer is that the address is in the form of the return to their religion by way of giving precedence to his people who followed him.

The clause ﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), an answer to an assumed question. The hamza is for denying the occurrence of what they demanded, namely expulsion or return. The waw is for the circumstantial (hal): i.e., will you return us to your religion while we are unwilling to return to it, or will you expel us from your town while we are unwilling to leave it, or while we are unwilling to both of these matters together? The meaning is: you have no right to compel us to either of the two matters, and it is not valid for you to do so, for the one who is compelled has no choice, and his agreement is not considered agreement, nor is his return to your religion under compulsion considered a return. By this explanation, the difficulty which many exegetes found in this context is resolved, to the point that this led to lengthy digressions.

﴿We have indeed invented against Allah a lie if we return to your religion﴾, which is shirk, ﴿after Allah has saved us from it﴾ through faith. So there will be no return to it on our part at all. ﴿And it is not for us﴾, i.e., it is not valid for us nor proper ﴿to return to it﴾ in any state ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., except in the state of His exalted will, for whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox community). The meaning is that a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It is said that the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾ (Hud: 88). It is also said that it is like their saying: "I will not speak to you until the crow lays eggs," and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle," while the crow does not lay eggs and the camel does not pass through, so it is of the category of conditioning upon the impossible.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge has encircled all known things, so nothing escapes it. ''Knowledge'' (‘ilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It is said that the meaning is: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the town, after you have disliked our living alongside you, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ our return to it. ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., upon Him we have relied, that He may keep us firm in faith, prevent between us and disbelief and its people, complete His blessing upon us, and protect us from His punishment.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. al-futaha (deciding) is judgment. I.e., judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to judge between them, and His judgment is nothing but the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers, as He informed us in more than one place of His Book. So they were in effect asking for the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the befalling of Allah's vengeance upon them.

It is possible that these are those same people, and it is possible that they are others than them, from the various groups of disbelievers to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The lam in ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the answer of an omitted oath: i.e., you have entered his religion and abandoned your religion. ﴿Indeed you would then be losers﴾: the answer of the oath stands in place of the answer of the condition. Their loss is either their destruction, or what they would lose because of giving full measure and weight, and abandoning the cheating with which they used to deal with people.

His saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as though they had never prospered therein﴾: this clause is a resumed sentence, explaining what the vengeance that befell them was. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ''as though they had never prospered therein'' is its predicate. It is said: "ghanaytu bil-makan" when I dwelt in the place, and "ghani al-qawm fi darihim" meaning the people stayed long in their home. Al-maghan means the dwelling, and its plural is al-maghani.

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, and time gave each of them to drink from its two cups.
It did not increase us in rebellion against a relative, nor did poverty diminish our kindness with our wealth."

The meaning of the verse: those who denied Shu'ayb were as though they had not dwelt in their homes, because Allah, exalted is He, uprooted them with punishment. The relative pronoun in ﴿those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿they were the losers﴾. This clause is a resumed sentence like the first, containing an explanation of the loss of the denying people.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾: i.e., Shu'ayb, when he witnessed the descent of punishment upon them, ﴿and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ with which He sent me to you, ﴿and advised you﴾ by explaining what is in the welfare of your religion and your worldly life, ﴿so how could I grieve (asa) over a disbelieving people?﴾ i.e., how could I grieve, persisting in their disbelief in Allah and refusing to answer. Or, asa is intense sorrow: I grieve over that, so I am one who grieves.

Shu'ayb said this statement out of regret over the lack of faith of his people, then he consoled himself, saying: how could grief befall him over a people who are not deserving of grief for them, because of their disbelief in Allah and their refusal to accept what their messenger brought.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn 'Asakir reported from 'Ikrima and al-Suddi, who said: Allah did not send a prophet twice except Shu'ayb: once to Madyan, and the shout seized them; and once to the People of the Thicket (al-Ayka), and Allah seized them with the punishment of the Day of the Canopy (al-Zulla).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong them. ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, he said: they used to threaten whoever came to Shu'ayb and visited him and wished to embrace Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, that he said: they used to sit on the road and tell whoever came past them that Shu'ayb is a liar, "so let him not seduce you from your religion."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding ﴿on every path threatening﴾, that he said: on every path of truth. ﴿And barring from the way of Allah﴾, he said: barring its people. ﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾, he said: seeking to find deviation in it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi regarding ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾ that he said: "It is the tenth (tax post)." Regarding ﴿and to bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾ he said: "You bar [people] from Islam, and seek to make it crooked," [and regarding ﴿seek to make it crooked﴾] he said: "ruin."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They are the ushar (tax collectors)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or someone else (Abu al-Aliyah was uncertain), that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came on the night of the Isra' (night journey) upon a piece of wood on the road. No garment passed by it without it tearing it, and nothing passed by it without it piercing it. He said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is the likeness of people from your community who sit on the road and cut it off.'" Then he recited ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, that he said: "It is not fitting for us to return to your shirk after Allah has saved us." [He continued:] "﴿unless Allah, our Lord, should will﴾. Allah does not will shirk, but [the verse] means: unless Allah has known something, for He has encompassed all things in knowledge."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (pausing and starting, a branch of Qur'anic recitation concerned with where to pause and begin) narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I did not know what [the phrase] ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾ meant until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say: 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you,' meaning: 'I will judge between you.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿Our Lord, open﴾ that he said: "Judge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "Al-fath means al-qada' (judgment). It is a Yemeni dialect: when one of them says, 'Come, I will judge between you,' he says, 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein (lam yaghnaw fiha)﴾ that he said: "They did not live therein."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿So how should I grieve (fa-kayfa aasa)﴾ that he said: "How should I be sorrowful."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In the Masjid al-Haram there are two graves and none other: the grave of Isma'il and the grave of Shu'ayb. The grave of Isma'il is in al-Hijr, and the grave of Shu'ayb is opposite the Black Stone."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Shu'ayb died in Makkah, and those of the believers who were with him; their graves are on the western side of the Ka'bah, between Dar al-Nadwah and the Gate of the Banu Sahm.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "Ya'qub ibn Abi Maslamah related to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when he mentioned Shu'ayb: 'That was the orator of the prophets (khatib al-anbiya'), because of the excellence of his dialogue with his people concerning what he wanted for them. When they denied him and threatened him with stoning and with expulsion from their lands, and they transgressed against Allah, the punishment of the Day of the Shade (yawm al-zullah) seized them.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, that he said: they used to sit on the road and tell whoever came past them that Shu'ayb is a liar, "so let him not seduce you from your religion."

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what preceded it, i.e., "and We sent."

Madyan is the name of a tribe, though it is said to be the name of a town; the first view is preferable. The tribe was named after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim, just as it is said Bakr and Tamim (names of tribes).

﴿Their brother Shu'ayb﴾: Shu'ayb is an appositive (‘atf bayan, an explanatory apposition). He was Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjub ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, as stated by 'Ata' and Ibn Ishaq, and others.

Al-Sharafi ibn al-Qatami said that he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

Ibn Sam'an claimed that he was Shu'ayb ibn Hurra ibn Yashjub ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

Qatada said: he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

﴿He said: "O my people!"﴾ up to ﴿"a clear proof from your Lord"﴾ has already been explained in the story of Nuh.

﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: He commanded them to give full measure and weight, because they were people who dealt in measuring and weighing, and they did not give them in full. He mentioned the measure (al-kayl), which is a verbal noun (masdar), and conjoined to it the balance (al-mizan), which is a noun denoting an instrument.

There is disagreement about the reason for this. It is said that by "measure" is meant the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), so that the conjunction of "balance" to it is appropriate. It is also said that by "balance" is meant weighing (al-wazn), which corresponds to "measure." The fa' in ﴿fa-awfu﴾ is for conjunction with "worship" (u'budu) [in the earlier command].

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: al-bakhs (diminishing) means reduction. It may occur by defaming the goods, by making them undesirable, or by deceiving their owner and cheating him. All of this is among the consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. The apparent meaning of ﴿their things﴾ is that they diminished people's goods in all things. It is said that they were tax collectors (makkasin), who levied a tax on everything that entered their markets. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Is there in all the markets of Iraq a levy, and on everything a man sells a dirham's worth of tax?"

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right﴾: Its explanation has already been given shortly before. It includes small and large corruption, subtle and grave. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to acting upon what He commanded them and abandoning what He forbade them. By "better" here is meant absolute benefit, since there is no good at all in not giving full measure and weight, in diminishing people's goods, or in corruption on the earth.

﴿And do not sit on every path threatening [people]﴾: al-sirat is the road, i.e., do not sit on every road threatening people with punishment. It is said that they used to sit on the roads leading to Shu'ayb and threaten anyone who wanted to come to him, saying, "He is a liar, so do not go to him," just as the Quraysh used to do with the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. It is also said that what is meant is sitting on the paths of religion and preventing whoever wants to travel them, and it does not mean sitting on the roads literally. This is supported by ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾. It is also said that the verse means the prohibition of highway robbery and seizing plunder, which was among their practices. It is said that they were tax collectors who took levies on the roads from people's wealth, so they were forbidden from this.

The first view is the closest of them to correctness, although there is no obstacle to applying the prohibition to all of these views mentioned.

The clause ﴿threatening﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and so is what is conjoined to it: i.e., do not sit on every road threatening its people, barring from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked.

By "barring from the way of Allah" is meant preventing people from the road on which they sat, and stopping them from reaching Shu'ayb, for people's travelling on that path to reach the prophet of Allah is travelling the way of Allah. ﴿Those who believe in Him﴾ is the object of ﴿barring﴾. The pronoun in ﴿believe in Him﴾ refers to Allah, or to the way of Allah, or to every road, or to Shu'ayb.

﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: i.e., you seek that the way of Allah be bent and not straight. The discussion of crookedness (al-'iwaj) has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the vowelling of the 'ayn in al-'iwaj (crookedness) is with kasra in its meanings, and with fatha in its physical sense (al-ihram).

﴿And remember when you were﴾: i.e., remember the time when you were few in number, and He multiplied you through offspring. It is said: you were poor, and He enriched you.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾: among the earlier nations, for Allah destroyed them and sent down upon them punishments that took them away and erased their traces.

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the rulings which Allah has legislated for you, and a group among you ﴿who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾ This is in the mode of threat and severe warning to them, and it is not in the mode of commanding patience upon disbelief.

The judgment of Allah between the two parties is the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ (al-Tawba: 52). Or it is a command to the believers to be patient with what befalls them of harm from the disbelievers, until Allah gives them victory over them.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: i.e., the nobles who were arrogant said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you"﴾. They were not satisfied with refusing belief and rebelling against answering what he called them to, but went beyond that, out of transgression, insolence, and wickedness, to threatening their prophet and those who believed in him with expulsion from their town, or with their return, he and those with him, to their disbelieving religion. That is: one of the two matters must happen, either expulsion or return.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) means "beginning," as in the saying: "a hardship returned to me from so-and-so," meaning it befell me, even if no hardship had preceded it. So there is no objection by those who say: how could Shu'ayb be upon their disbelieving religion before Allah sent him as a messenger? The answer is that the address is in the form of the return to their religion by way of giving precedence to his people who followed him.

The clause ﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), an answer to an assumed question. The hamza is for denying the occurrence of what they demanded, namely expulsion or return. The waw is for the circumstantial (hal): i.e., will you return us to your religion while we are unwilling to return to it, or will you expel us from your town while we are unwilling to leave it, or while we are unwilling to both of these matters together? The meaning is: you have no right to compel us to either of the two matters, and it is not valid for you to do so, for the one who is compelled has no choice, and his agreement is not considered agreement, nor is his return to your religion under compulsion considered a return. By this explanation, the difficulty which many exegetes found in this context is resolved, to the point that this led to lengthy digressions.

﴿We have indeed invented against Allah a lie if we return to your religion﴾, which is shirk, ﴿after Allah has saved us from it﴾ through faith. So there will be no return to it on our part at all. ﴿And it is not for us﴾, i.e., it is not valid for us nor proper ﴿to return to it﴾ in any state ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., except in the state of His exalted will, for whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox community). The meaning is that a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It is said that the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾ (Hud: 88). It is also said that it is like their saying: "I will not speak to you until the crow lays eggs," and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle," while the crow does not lay eggs and the camel does not pass through, so it is of the category of conditioning upon the impossible.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge has encircled all known things, so nothing escapes it. ''Knowledge'' (‘ilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It is said that the meaning is: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the town, after you have disliked our living alongside you, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ our return to it. ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., upon Him we have relied, that He may keep us firm in faith, prevent between us and disbelief and its people, complete His blessing upon us, and protect us from His punishment.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. al-futaha (deciding) is judgment. I.e., judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to judge between them, and His judgment is nothing but the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers, as He informed us in more than one place of His Book. So they were in effect asking for the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the befalling of Allah's vengeance upon them.

﴿And the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved said﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿the eminent ones who were arrogant said﴾. It is possible that these are those same people, and it is possible that they are others than them, from the various groups of disbelievers to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The lam in ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the answer of an omitted oath: i.e., you have entered his religion and abandoned your religion. ﴿Indeed you would then be losers﴾: the answer of the oath stands in place of the answer of the condition. Their loss is either their destruction, or what they would lose because of giving full measure and weight, and abandoning the cheating with which they used to deal with people.

91. ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾: i.e., the shaking (al-zalzala). It is said it was the shout (al-sayha), as in His saying: ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the shout, so they became in their homes prostrate﴾ (Hud: 94). Its explanation has already been given in the story of Salih.

His saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as though they had never prospered therein﴾: this clause is a resumed sentence, explaining what the vengeance that befell them was. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ''as though they had never prospered therein'' is its predicate. It is said: "ghanaytu bil-makan" when I dwelt in the place, and "ghani al-qawm fi darihim" meaning the people stayed long in their home. Al-maghan means the dwelling, and its plural is al-maghani.

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, and time gave each of them to drink from its two cups.
It did not increase us in rebellion against a relative, nor did poverty diminish our kindness with our wealth."

The meaning of the verse: those who denied Shu'ayb were as though they had not dwelt in their homes, because Allah, exalted is He, uprooted them with punishment. The relative pronoun in ﴿those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿they were the losers﴾. This clause is a resumed sentence like the first, containing an explanation of the loss of the denying people.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾: i.e., Shu'ayb, when he witnessed the descent of punishment upon them, ﴿and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ with which He sent me to you, ﴿and advised you﴾ by explaining what is in the welfare of your religion and your worldly life, ﴿so how could I grieve (asa) over a disbelieving people?﴾ i.e., how could I grieve, persisting in their disbelief in Allah and refusing to answer. It is said that they were tax collectors who took levies on the roads from people's wealth, so they were forbidden from this.

The first view is the closest of them to correctness, although there is no obstacle to applying the prohibition to all of these views mentioned.

The clause ﴿threatening﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and so is what is conjoined to it: i.e., do not sit on every road threatening its people, barring from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked.

By "barring from the way of Allah" is meant preventing people from the road on which they sat, and stopping them from reaching Shu'ayb, for people's travelling on that path to reach the prophet of Allah is travelling the way of Allah. ﴿Those who believe in Him﴾ is the object of ﴿barring﴾. The pronoun in ﴿believe in Him﴾ refers to Allah, or to the way of Allah, or to every road, or to Shu'ayb.

﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: i.e., you seek that the way of Allah be bent and not straight. The discussion of crookedness (al-'iwaj) has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the vowelling of the 'ayn in al-'iwaj (crookedness) is with kasra in its meanings, and with fatha in its physical sense (al-ihram).

﴿And remember when you were﴾: i.e., remember the time when you were few in number, and He multiplied you through offspring. It is said: you were poor, and He enriched you.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾: among the earlier nations, for Allah destroyed them and sent down upon them punishments that took them away and erased their traces.

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the rulings which Allah has legislated for you, and a group among you ﴿who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾ This is in the mode of threat and severe warning to them, and it is not in the mode of commanding patience upon disbelief.

The judgment of Allah between the two parties is the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ (al-Tawba: 52). Or it is a command to the believers to be patient with what befalls them of harm from the disbelievers, until Allah gives them victory over them.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: i.e., the nobles who were arrogant said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you"﴾. They were not satisfied with refusing belief and rebelling against answering what he called them to, but went beyond that, out of transgression, insolence, and wickedness, to threatening their prophet and those who believed in him with expulsion from their town, or with their return, he and those with him, to their disbelieving religion. That is: one of the two matters must happen, either expulsion or return.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) means "beginning," as in the saying: "a hardship returned to me from so-and-so," meaning it befell me, even if no hardship had preceded it. So there is no objection by those who say: how could Shu'ayb be upon their disbelieving religion before Allah sent him as a messenger? The answer is that the address is in the form of the return to their religion by way of giving precedence to his people who followed him.

The clause ﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), an answer to an assumed question. The hamza is for denying the occurrence of what they demanded, namely expulsion or return. The waw is for the circumstantial (hal): i.e., will you return us to your religion while we are unwilling to return to it, or will you expel us from your town while we are unwilling to leave it, or while we are unwilling to both of these matters together? The meaning is: you have no right to compel us to either of the two matters, and it is not valid for you to do so, for the one who is compelled has no choice, and his agreement is not considered agreement, nor is his return to your religion under compulsion considered a return. By this explanation, the difficulty which many exegetes found in this context is resolved, to the point that this led to lengthy digressions.

﴿We have indeed invented against Allah a lie if we return to your religion﴾, which is shirk, ﴿after Allah has saved us from it﴾ through faith. So there will be no return to it on our part at all. ﴿And it is not for us﴾, i.e., it is not valid for us nor proper ﴿to return to it﴾ in any state ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., except in the state of His exalted will, for whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox community). The meaning is that a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It is said that the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾ (Hud: 88). It is also said that it is like their saying: "I will not speak to you until the crow lays eggs," and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle," while the crow does not lay eggs and the camel does not pass through, so it is of the category of conditioning upon the impossible.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge has encircled all known things, so nothing escapes it. ''Knowledge'' (‘ilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It is said that the meaning is: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the town, after you have disliked our living alongside you, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ our return to it. ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., upon Him we have relied, that He may keep us firm in faith, prevent between us and disbelief and its people, complete His blessing upon us, and protect us from His punishment.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. al-futaha (deciding) is judgment. I.e., judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to judge between them, and His judgment is nothing but the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers, as He informed us in more than one place of His Book. So they were in effect asking for the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the befalling of Allah's vengeance upon them.

It is possible that these are those same people, and it is possible that they are others than them, from the various groups of disbelievers to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The lam in ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the answer of an omitted oath: i.e., you have entered his religion and abandoned your religion. ﴿Indeed you would then be losers﴾: the answer of the oath stands in place of the answer of the condition. Their loss is either their destruction, or what they would lose because of giving full measure and weight, and abandoning the cheating with which they used to deal with people.

His saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as though they had never prospered therein﴾: this clause is a resumed sentence, explaining what the vengeance that befell them was. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ''as though they had never prospered therein'' is its predicate. It is said: "ghanaytu bil-makan" when I dwelt in the place, and "ghani al-qawm fi darihim" meaning the people stayed long in their home. Al-maghan means the dwelling, and its plural is al-maghani.

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, and time gave each of them to drink from its two cups.
It did not increase us in rebellion against a relative, nor did poverty diminish our kindness with our wealth."

The meaning of the verse: those who denied Shu'ayb were as though they had not dwelt in their homes, because Allah, exalted is He, uprooted them with punishment. The relative pronoun in ﴿those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿they were the losers﴾. This clause is a resumed sentence like the first, containing an explanation of the loss of the denying people.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾: i.e., Shu'ayb, when he witnessed the descent of punishment upon them, ﴿and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ with which He sent me to you, ﴿and advised you﴾ by explaining what is in the welfare of your religion and your worldly life, ﴿so how could I grieve (asa) over a disbelieving people?﴾ i.e., how could I grieve, persisting in their disbelief in Allah and refusing to answer. Or, asa is intense sorrow: I grieve over that, so I am one who grieves.

Shu'ayb said this statement out of regret over the lack of faith of his people, then he consoled himself, saying: how could grief befall him over a people who are not deserving of grief for them, because of their disbelief in Allah and their refusal to accept what their messenger brought.
