Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong them. ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, he said: they used to threaten whoever came to Shu'ayb and visited him and wished to embrace Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, that he said: they used to sit on the road and tell whoever came past them that Shu'ayb is a liar, "so let him not seduce you from your religion."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding ﴿on every path threatening﴾, that he said: on every path of truth. ﴿And barring from the way of Allah﴾, he said: barring its people. ﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾, he said: seeking to find deviation in it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi regarding ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾ that he said: "It is the tenth (tax post)." Regarding ﴿and to bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾ he said: "You bar [people] from Islam, and seek to make it crooked," [and regarding ﴿seek to make it crooked﴾] he said: "ruin."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They are the ushar (tax collectors)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or someone else (Abu al-Aliyah was uncertain), that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came on the night of the Isra' (night journey) upon a piece of wood on the road. No garment passed by it without it tearing it, and nothing passed by it without it piercing it. He said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is the likeness of people from your community who sit on the road and cut it off.'" Then he recited ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, that he said: "It is not fitting for us to return to your shirk after Allah has saved us." [He continued:] "﴿unless Allah, our Lord, should will﴾. Allah does not will shirk, but [the verse] means: unless Allah has known something, for He has encompassed all things in knowledge."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (pausing and starting, a branch of Qur'anic recitation concerned with where to pause and begin) narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I did not know what [the phrase] ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾ meant until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say: 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you,' meaning: 'I will judge between you.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿Our Lord, open﴾ that he said: "Judge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "Al-fath means al-qada' (judgment). It is a Yemeni dialect: when one of them says, 'Come, I will judge between you,' he says, 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein (lam yaghnaw fiha)﴾ that he said: "They did not live therein."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿So how should I grieve (fa-kayfa aasa)﴾ that he said: "How should I be sorrowful."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In the Masjid al-Haram there are two graves and none other: the grave of Isma'il and the grave of Shu'ayb. The grave of Isma'il is in al-Hijr, and the grave of Shu'ayb is opposite the Black Stone."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Shu'ayb died in Makkah, and those of the believers who were with him; their graves are on the western side of the Ka'bah, between Dar al-Nadwah and the Gate of the Banu Sahm.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "Ya'qub ibn Abi Maslamah related to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when he mentioned Shu'ayb: 'That was the orator of the prophets (khatib al-anbiya'), because of the excellence of his dialogue with his people concerning what he wanted for them. When they denied him and threatened him with stoning and with expulsion from their lands, and they transgressed against Allah, the punishment of the Day of the Shade (yawm al-zullah) seized them.'"

﴿Their brother Shu'ayb﴾: Shu'ayb is an appositive (‘atf bayan, an explanatory apposition). He was Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjub ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, as stated by 'Ata' and Ibn Ishaq, and others.

Al-Sharafi ibn al-Qatami said that he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

Ibn Sam'an claimed that he was Shu'ayb ibn Hurra ibn Yashjub ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

Qatada said: he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

﴿He said: "O my people!"﴾ up to ﴿"a clear proof from your Lord"﴾ has already been explained in the story of Nuh.

He mentioned the measure (al-kayl), which is a verbal noun (masdar), and conjoined to it the balance (al-mizan), which is a noun denoting an instrument.

There is disagreement about the reason for this. It is said that by "measure" is meant the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), so that the conjunction of "balance" to it is appropriate. It is also said that by "balance" is meant weighing (al-wazn), which corresponds to "measure." The fa' in ﴿fa-awfu﴾ is for conjunction with "worship" (u'budu) [in the earlier command].

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: al-bakhs (diminishing) means reduction. It may occur by defaming the goods, by making them undesirable, or by deceiving their owner and cheating him. It is said that they were tax collectors (makkasin), who levied a tax on everything that entered their markets. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 85–93 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what preceded it, i.e., "and We sent."

Madyan is the name of a tribe, though it is said to be the name of a town; the first view is preferable. The tribe was named after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim, just as it is said Bakr and Tamim (names of tribes).

﴿Their brother Shu'ayb﴾: Shu'ayb is an appositive (‘atf bayan, an explanatory apposition). He was Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjub ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, as stated by 'Ata' and Ibn Ishaq, and others.

Al-Sharafi ibn al-Qatami said that he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

Ibn Sam'an claimed that he was Shu'ayb ibn Hurra ibn Yashjub ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

Qatada said: he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

﴿He said: "O my people!"﴾ up to ﴿"a clear proof from your Lord"﴾ has already been explained in the story of Nuh.

﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: He commanded them to give full measure and weight, because they were people who dealt in measuring and weighing, and they did not give them in full. He mentioned the measure (al-kayl), which is a verbal noun (masdar), and conjoined to it the balance (al-mizan), which is a noun denoting an instrument.

There is disagreement about the reason for this. It is said that by "measure" is meant the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), so that the conjunction of "balance" to it is appropriate. It is also said that by "balance" is meant weighing (al-wazn), which corresponds to "measure." The fa' in ﴿fa-awfu﴾ is for conjunction with "worship" (u'budu) [in the earlier command].

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: al-bakhs (diminishing) means reduction. It may occur by defaming the goods, by making them undesirable, or by deceiving their owner and cheating him. All of this is among the consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. The apparent meaning of ﴿their things﴾ is that they diminished people's goods in all things. It is said that they were tax collectors (makkasin), who levied a tax on everything that entered their markets. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Is there in all the markets of Iraq a levy, and on everything a man sells a dirham's worth of tax?"

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right﴾: Its explanation has already been given shortly before. It includes small and large corruption, subtle and grave. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to acting upon what He commanded them and abandoning what He forbade them. By "better" here is meant absolute benefit, since there is no good at all in not giving full measure and weight, in diminishing people's goods, or in corruption on the earth.

﴿And do not sit on every path threatening [people]﴾: al-sirat is the road, i.e., do not sit on every road threatening people with punishment. It is said that they used to sit on the roads leading to Shu'ayb and threaten anyone who wanted to come to him, saying, "He is a liar, so do not go to him," just as the Quraysh used to do with the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. It is also said that what is meant is sitting on the paths of religion and preventing whoever wants to travel them, and it does not mean sitting on the roads literally. This is supported by ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾. It is also said that the verse means the prohibition of highway robbery and seizing plunder, which was among their practices. It is said that they were tax collectors who took levies on the roads from people's wealth, so they were forbidden from this.

The first view is the closest of them to correctness, although there is no obstacle to applying the prohibition to all of these views mentioned.

The clause ﴿threatening﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and so is what is conjoined to it: i.e., do not sit on every road threatening its people, barring from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked.

By "barring from the way of Allah" is meant preventing people from the road on which they sat, and stopping them from reaching Shu'ayb, for people's travelling on that path to reach the prophet of Allah is travelling the way of Allah. ﴿Those who believe in Him﴾ is the object of ﴿barring﴾. The pronoun in ﴿believe in Him﴾ refers to Allah, or to the way of Allah, or to every road, or to Shu'ayb.

﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: i.e., you seek that the way of Allah be bent and not straight. The discussion of crookedness (al-'iwaj) has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the vowelling of the 'ayn in al-'iwaj (crookedness) is with kasra in its meanings, and with fatha in its physical sense (al-ihram).

﴿And remember when you were﴾: i.e., remember the time when you were few in number, and He multiplied you through offspring. It is said: you were poor, and He enriched you.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾: among the earlier nations, for Allah destroyed them and sent down upon them punishments that took them away and erased their traces.

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the rulings which Allah has legislated for you, and a group among you ﴿who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾ This is in the mode of threat and severe warning to them, and it is not in the mode of commanding patience upon disbelief.

The judgment of Allah between the two parties is the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ (al-Tawba: 52). Or it is a command to the believers to be patient with what befalls them of harm from the disbelievers, until Allah gives them victory over them.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: i.e., the nobles who were arrogant said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you"﴾. They were not satisfied with refusing belief and rebelling against answering what he called them to, but went beyond that, out of transgression, insolence, and wickedness, to threatening their prophet and those who believed in him with expulsion from their town, or with their return, he and those with him, to their disbelieving religion. That is: one of the two matters must happen, either expulsion or return.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) means "beginning," as in the saying: "a hardship returned to me from so-and-so," meaning it befell me, even if no hardship had preceded it. So there is no objection by those who say: how could Shu'ayb be upon their disbelieving religion before Allah sent him as a messenger? The answer is that the address is in the form of the return to their religion by way of giving precedence to his people who followed him.

The clause ﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), an answer to an assumed question. The hamza is for denying the occurrence of what they demanded, namely expulsion or return. The waw is for the circumstantial (hal): i.e., will you return us to your religion while we are unwilling to return to it, or will you expel us from your town while we are unwilling to leave it, or while we are unwilling to both of these matters together? The meaning is: you have no right to compel us to either of the two matters, and it is not valid for you to do so, for the one who is compelled has no choice, and his agreement is not considered agreement, nor is his return to your religion under compulsion considered a return. By this explanation, the difficulty which many exegetes found in this context is resolved, to the point that this led to lengthy digressions.

﴿We have indeed invented against Allah a lie if we return to your religion﴾, which is shirk, ﴿after Allah has saved us from it﴾ through faith. So there will be no return to it on our part at all. ﴿And it is not for us﴾, i.e., it is not valid for us nor proper ﴿to return to it﴾ in any state ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., except in the state of His exalted will, for whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox community). The meaning is that a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It is said that the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾ (Hud: 88). It is also said that it is like their saying: "I will not speak to you until the crow lays eggs," and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle," while the crow does not lay eggs and the camel does not pass through, so it is of the category of conditioning upon the impossible.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge has encircled all known things, so nothing escapes it. ''Knowledge'' (‘ilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It is said that the meaning is: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the town, after you have disliked our living alongside you, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ our return to it. ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., upon Him we have relied, that He may keep us firm in faith, prevent between us and disbelief and its people, complete His blessing upon us, and protect us from His punishment.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. al-futaha (deciding) is judgment. I.e., judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to judge between them, and His judgment is nothing but the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers, as He informed us in more than one place of His Book. So they were in effect asking for the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the befalling of Allah's vengeance upon them.

﴿And the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved said﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿the eminent ones who were arrogant said﴾. It is possible that these are those same people, and it is possible that they are others than them, from the various groups of disbelievers to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The lam in ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the answer of an omitted oath: i.e., you have entered his religion and abandoned your religion. ﴿Indeed you would then be losers﴾: the answer of the oath stands in place of the answer of the condition. Their loss is either their destruction, or what they would lose because of giving full measure and weight, and abandoning the cheating with which they used to deal with people.

91. ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾: i.e., the shaking (al-zalzala). It is said it was the shout (al-sayha), as in His saying: ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the shout, so they became in their homes prostrate﴾ (Hud: 94). Its explanation has already been given in the story of Salih.

His saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as though they had never prospered therein﴾: this clause is a resumed sentence, explaining what the vengeance that befell them was. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ''as though they had never prospered therein'' is its predicate. It is said: "ghanaytu bil-makan" when I dwelt in the place, and "ghani al-qawm fi darihim" meaning the people stayed long in their home. Al-maghan means the dwelling, and its plural is al-maghani.

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, and time gave each of them to drink from its two cups.
It did not increase us in rebellion against a relative, nor did poverty diminish our kindness with our wealth."

The meaning of the verse: those who denied Shu'ayb were as though they had not dwelt in their homes, because Allah, exalted is He, uprooted them with punishment. The relative pronoun in ﴿those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿they were the losers﴾. This clause is a resumed sentence like the first, containing an explanation of the loss of the denying people.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾: i.e., Shu'ayb, when he witnessed the descent of punishment upon them, ﴿and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ with which He sent me to you, ﴿and advised you﴾ by explaining what is in the welfare of your religion and your worldly life, ﴿so how could I grieve (asa) over a disbelieving people?﴾ i.e., how could I grieve, persisting in their disbelief in Allah and refusing to answer. Or, asa is intense sorrow: I grieve over that, so I am one who grieves.

Shu'ayb said this statement out of regret over the lack of faith of his people, then he consoled himself, saying: how could grief befall him over a people who are not deserving of grief for them, because of their disbelief in Allah and their refusal to accept what their messenger brought.

Al-Zajjaj said: the vowelling of the 'ayn in al-'iwaj (crookedness) is with kasra in its meanings, and with fatha in its physical sense (al-ihram).

﴿And remember when you were﴾: i.e., remember the time when you were few in number, and He multiplied you through offspring. It is said: you were poor, and He enriched you.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾: among the earlier nations, for Allah destroyed them and sent down upon them punishments that took them away and erased their traces.

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the rulings which Allah has legislated for you, and a group among you ﴿who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾ This is in the mode of threat and severe warning to them, and it is not in the mode of commanding patience upon disbelief.

The judgment of Allah between the two parties is the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ (al-Tawba: 52). Or it is a command to the believers to be patient with what befalls them of harm from the disbelievers, until Allah gives them victory over them.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: i.e., the nobles who were arrogant said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you"﴾. They were not satisfied with refusing belief and rebelling against answering what he called them to, but went beyond that, out of transgression, insolence, and wickedness, to threatening their prophet and those who believed in him with expulsion from their town, or with their return, he and those with him, to their disbelieving religion. That is: one of the two matters must happen, either expulsion or return.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) means "beginning," as in the saying: "a hardship returned to me from so-and-so," meaning it befell me, even if no hardship had preceded it. So there is no objection by those who say: how could Shu'ayb be upon their disbelieving religion before Allah sent him as a messenger? The answer is that the address is in the form of the return to their religion by way of giving precedence to his people who followed him.

The clause ﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), an answer to an assumed question. The hamza is for denying the occurrence of what they demanded, namely expulsion or return. The waw is for the circumstantial (hal): i.e., will you return us to your religion while we are unwilling to return to it, or will you expel us from your town while we are unwilling to leave it, or while we are unwilling to both of these matters together? The meaning is: you have no right to compel us to either of the two matters, and it is not valid for you to do so, for the one who is compelled has no choice, and his agreement is not considered agreement, nor is his return to your religion under compulsion considered a return. By this explanation, the difficulty which many exegetes found in this context is resolved, to the point that this led to lengthy digressions.

﴿We have indeed invented against Allah a lie if we return to your religion﴾, which is shirk, ﴿after Allah has saved us from it﴾ through faith. So there will be no return to it on our part at all. ﴿And it is not for us﴾, i.e., it is not valid for us nor proper ﴿to return to it﴾ in any state ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., except in the state of His exalted will, for whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox community). The meaning is that a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It is said that the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾ (Hud: 88). It is also said that it is like their saying: "I will not speak to you until the crow lays eggs," and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle," while the crow does not lay eggs and the camel does not pass through, so it is of the category of conditioning upon the impossible.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge has encircled all known things, so nothing escapes it. ''Knowledge'' (‘ilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It is said that the meaning is: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the town, after you have disliked our living alongside you, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ our return to it. ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., upon Him we have relied, that He may keep us firm in faith, prevent between us and disbelief and its people, complete His blessing upon us, and protect us from His punishment.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. al-futaha (deciding) is judgment. I.e., judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to judge between them, and His judgment is nothing but the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers, as He informed us in more than one place of His Book. So they were in effect asking for the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the befalling of Allah's vengeance upon them.

﴿And the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved said﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿the eminent ones who were arrogant said﴾. It is possible that these are those same people, and it is possible that they are others than them, from the various groups of disbelievers to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The lam in ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the answer of an omitted oath: i.e., you have entered his religion and abandoned your religion. ﴿Indeed you would then be losers﴾: the answer of the oath stands in place of the answer of the condition. Their loss is either their destruction, or what they would lose because of giving full measure and weight, and abandoning the cheating with which they used to deal with people.

91. ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾: i.e., the shaking (al-zalzala). It is said it was the shout (al-sayha), as in His saying: ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the shout, so they became in their homes prostrate﴾ (Hud: 94). Its explanation has already been given in the story of Salih.

His saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as though they had never prospered therein﴾: this clause is a resumed sentence, explaining what the vengeance that befell them was. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ''as though they had never prospered therein'' is its predicate. It is said: "ghanaytu bil-makan" when I dwelt in the place, and "ghani al-qawm fi darihim" meaning the people stayed long in their home. Al-maghan means the dwelling, and its plural is al-maghani.

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, and time gave each of them to drink from its two cups.
It did not increase us in rebellion against a relative, nor did poverty diminish our kindness with our wealth."

The meaning of the verse: those who denied Shu'ayb were as though they had not dwelt in their homes, because Allah, exalted is He, uprooted them with punishment. The relative pronoun in ﴿those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿they were the losers﴾. This clause is a resumed sentence like the first, containing an explanation of the loss of the denying people.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾: i.e., Shu'ayb, when he witnessed the descent of punishment upon them, ﴿and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ with which He sent me to you, ﴿and advised you﴾ by explaining what is in the welfare of your religion and your worldly life, ﴿so how could I grieve (asa) over a disbelieving people?﴾ i.e., how could I grieve, persisting in their disbelief in Allah and refusing to answer. Or, asa is intense sorrow: I grieve over that, so I am one who grieves.

Shu'ayb said this statement out of regret over the lack of faith of his people, then he consoled himself, saying: how could grief befall him over a people who are not deserving of grief for them, because of their disbelief in Allah and their refusal to accept what their messenger brought.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn 'Asakir reported from 'Ikrima and al-Suddi, who said: Allah did not send a prophet twice except Shu'ayb: once to Madyan, and the shout seized them; and once to the People of the Thicket (al-Ayka), and Allah seized them with the punishment of the Day of the Canopy (al-Zulla).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong them. ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, he said: they used to threaten whoever came to Shu'ayb and visited him and wished to embrace Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, that he said: they used to sit on the road and tell whoever came past them that Shu'ayb is a liar, "so let him not seduce you from your religion."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding ﴿on every path threatening﴾, that he said: on every path of truth. ﴿And barring from the way of Allah﴾, he said: barring its people. ﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾, he said: seeking to find deviation in it.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi regarding ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾ that he said: "It is the tenth (tax post)." Regarding ﴿and to bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾ he said: "You bar [people] from Islam, and seek to make it crooked," [and regarding ﴿seek to make it crooked﴾] he said: "ruin."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They are the ushar (tax collectors)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or someone else (Abu al-Aliyah was uncertain), that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came on the night of the Isra' (night journey) upon a piece of wood on the road. No garment passed by it without it tearing it, and nothing passed by it without it piercing it. He said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is the likeness of people from your community who sit on the road and cut it off.'" Then he recited ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, that he said: "It is not fitting for us to return to your shirk after Allah has saved us." [He continued:] "﴿unless Allah, our Lord, should will﴾. Allah does not will shirk, but [the verse] means: unless Allah has known something, for He has encompassed all things in knowledge."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (pausing and starting, a branch of Qur'anic recitation concerned with where to pause and begin) narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I did not know what [the phrase] ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾ meant until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say: 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you,' meaning: 'I will judge between you.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿Our Lord, open﴾ that he said: "Judge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "Al-fath means al-qada' (judgment). It is a Yemeni dialect: when one of them says, 'Come, I will judge between you,' he says, 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein (lam yaghnaw fiha)﴾ that he said: "They did not live therein."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿So how should I grieve (fa-kayfa aasa)﴾ that he said: "How should I be sorrowful."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In the Masjid al-Haram there are two graves and none other: the grave of Isma'il and the grave of Shu'ayb. The grave of Isma'il is in al-Hijr, and the grave of Shu'ayb is opposite the Black Stone."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Shu'ayb died in Makkah, and those of the believers who were with him; their graves are on the western side of the Ka'bah, between Dar al-Nadwah and the Gate of the Banu Sahm.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "Ya'qub ibn Abi Maslamah related to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when he mentioned Shu'ayb: 'That was the orator of the prophets (khatib al-anbiya'), because of the excellence of his dialogue with his people concerning what he wanted for them. When they denied him and threatened him with stoning and with expulsion from their lands, and they transgressed against Allah, the punishment of the Day of the Shade (yawm al-zullah) seized them.'"

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what preceded it, i.e., "and We sent."

Madyan is the name of a tribe, though it is said to be the name of a town; the first view is preferable. The tribe was named after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim, just as it is said Bakr and Tamim (names of tribes).

﴿Their brother Shu'ayb﴾: Shu'ayb is an appositive (‘atf bayan, an explanatory apposition). He was Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjub ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, as stated by 'Ata' and Ibn Ishaq, and others.

Al-Sharafi ibn al-Qatami said that he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

Ibn Sam'an claimed that he was Shu'ayb ibn Hurra ibn Yashjub ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

Qatada said: he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

﴿He said: "O my people!"﴾ up to ﴿"a clear proof from your Lord"﴾ has already been explained in the story of Nuh.

﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: He commanded them to give full measure and weight, because they were people who dealt in measuring and weighing, and they did not give them in full. He mentioned the measure (al-kayl), which is a verbal noun (masdar), and conjoined to it the balance (al-mizan), which is a noun denoting an instrument.

There is disagreement about the reason for this. It is said that by "measure" is meant the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), so that the conjunction of "balance" to it is appropriate. It is also said that by "balance" is meant weighing (al-wazn), which corresponds to "measure." The fa' in ﴿fa-awfu﴾ is for conjunction with "worship" (u'budu) [in the earlier command].

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: al-bakhs (diminishing) means reduction. It may occur by defaming the goods, by making them undesirable, or by deceiving their owner and cheating him. All of this is among the consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. The apparent meaning of ﴿their things﴾ is that they diminished people's goods in all things. It is said that they were tax collectors (makkasin), who levied a tax on everything that entered their markets. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Is there in all the markets of Iraq a levy, and on everything a man sells a dirham's worth of tax?"

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right﴾: Its explanation has already been given shortly before. It includes small and large corruption, subtle and grave. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to acting upon what He commanded them and abandoning what He forbade them. By "better" here is meant absolute benefit, since there is no good at all in not giving full measure and weight, in diminishing people's goods, or in corruption on the earth.

﴿And do not sit on every path threatening [people]﴾: al-sirat is the road, i.e., do not sit on every road threatening people with punishment. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. It is also said that what is meant is sitting on the paths of religion and preventing whoever wants to travel them, and it does not mean sitting on the roads literally. This is supported by ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾. It is also said that the verse means the prohibition of highway robbery and seizing plunder, which was among their practices. It is said that they were tax collectors who took levies on the roads from people's wealth, so they were forbidden from this.

The first view is the closest of them to correctness, although there is no obstacle to applying the prohibition to all of these views mentioned.

The clause ﴿threatening﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and so is what is conjoined to it: i.e., do not sit on every road threatening its people, barring from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked.

Regarding ﴿and to bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾ he said: "You bar [people] from Islam, and seek to make it crooked," [and regarding ﴿seek to make it crooked﴾] he said: "ruin."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They are the ushar (tax collectors)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or someone else (Abu al-Aliyah was uncertain), that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came on the night of the Isra' (night journey) upon a piece of wood on the road. No garment passed by it without it tearing it, and nothing passed by it without it piercing it. He said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is the likeness of people from your community who sit on the road and cut it off.'" Then he recited ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His saying ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, that he said: "It is not fitting for us to return to your shirk after Allah has saved us." [He continued:] "﴿unless Allah, our Lord, should will﴾. Allah does not will shirk, but [the verse] means: unless Allah has known something, for He has encompassed all things in knowledge."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (pausing and starting, a branch of Qur'anic recitation concerned with where to pause and begin) narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I did not know what [the phrase] ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾ meant until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say: 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you,' meaning: 'I will judge between you.'"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying ﴿Our Lord, open﴾ that he said: "Judge."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi that he said: "Al-fath means al-qada' (judgment). It is a Yemeni dialect: when one of them says, 'Come, I will judge between you,' he says, 'Come, I will fatah (open) between you.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿as if they had never dwelt therein (lam yaghnaw fiha)﴾ that he said: "They did not live therein."

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated the same from Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿So how should I grieve (fa-kayfa aasa)﴾ that he said: "How should I be sorrowful."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "In the Masjid al-Haram there are two graves and none other: the grave of Isma'il and the grave of Shu'ayb. The grave of Isma'il is in al-Hijr, and the grave of Shu'ayb is opposite the Black Stone."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih that Shu'ayb died in Makkah, and those of the believers who were with him; their graves are on the western side of the Ka'bah, between Dar al-Nadwah and the Gate of the Banu Sahm.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "Ya'qub ibn Abi Maslamah related to me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say, when he mentioned Shu'ayb: 'That was the orator of the prophets (khatib al-anbiya'), because of the excellence of his dialogue with his people concerning what he wanted for them. When they denied him and threatened him with stoning and with expulsion from their lands, and they transgressed against Allah, the punishment of the Day of the Shade (yawm al-zullah) seized them.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 85–93 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what preceded it, i.e., "and We sent."

Madyan is the name of a tribe, though it is said to be the name of a town; the first view is preferable. The tribe was named after their father, who was Madyan ibn Ibrahim, just as it is said Bakr and Tamim (names of tribes).

﴿Their brother Shu'ayb﴾: Shu'ayb is an appositive (‘atf bayan, an explanatory apposition). He was Shu'ayb ibn Mika'il ibn Yashjub ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, as stated by 'Ata' and Ibn Ishaq, and others.

Al-Sharafi ibn al-Qatami said that he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

Ibn Sam'an claimed that he was Shu'ayb ibn Hurra ibn Yashjub ibn Lawi ibn Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim.

Qatada said: he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Ayfa' ibn Thabit ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim.

﴿He said: "O my people!"﴾ up to ﴿"a clear proof from your Lord"﴾ has already been explained in the story of Nuh.

﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: He commanded them to give full measure and weight, because they were people who dealt in measuring and weighing, and they did not give them in full. He mentioned the measure (al-kayl), which is a verbal noun (masdar), and conjoined to it the balance (al-mizan), which is a noun denoting an instrument.

There is disagreement about the reason for this. It is said that by "measure" is meant the measuring vessel (al-mikyal), so that the conjunction of "balance" to it is appropriate. It is also said that by "balance" is meant weighing (al-wazn), which corresponds to "measure." The fa' in ﴿fa-awfu﴾ is for conjunction with "worship" (u'budu) [in the earlier command].

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: al-bakhs (diminishing) means reduction. It may occur by defaming the goods, by making them undesirable, or by deceiving their owner and cheating him. All of this is among the consuming of people's wealth by falsehood. The apparent meaning of ﴿their things﴾ is that they diminished people's goods in all things. It is said that they were tax collectors (makkasin), who levied a tax on everything that entered their markets. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Is there in all the markets of Iraq a levy, and on everything a man sells a dirham's worth of tax?"

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right﴾: Its explanation has already been given shortly before. It includes small and large corruption, subtle and grave. The reference in His saying ﴿that﴾ is to acting upon what He commanded them and abandoning what He forbade them. By "better" here is meant absolute benefit, since there is no good at all in not giving full measure and weight, in diminishing people's goods, or in corruption on the earth.

﴿And do not sit on every path threatening [people]﴾: al-sirat is the road, i.e., do not sit on every road threatening people with punishment. It is said that they used to sit on the roads leading to Shu'ayb and threaten anyone who wanted to come to him, saying, "He is a liar, so do not go to him," just as the Quraysh used to do with the Prophet (ﷺ). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Suddi, and others. It is also said that what is meant is sitting on the paths of religion and preventing whoever wants to travel them, and it does not mean sitting on the roads literally. This is supported by ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾. It is also said that the verse means the prohibition of highway robbery and seizing plunder, which was among their practices. It is said that they were tax collectors who took levies on the roads from people's wealth, so they were forbidden from this.

The first view is the closest of them to correctness, although there is no obstacle to applying the prohibition to all of these views mentioned.

The clause ﴿threatening﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), and so is what is conjoined to it: i.e., do not sit on every road threatening its people, barring from the way of Allah, seeking to make it crooked.

By "barring from the way of Allah" is meant preventing people from the road on which they sat, and stopping them from reaching Shu'ayb, for people's travelling on that path to reach the prophet of Allah is travelling the way of Allah. ﴿Those who believe in Him﴾ is the object of ﴿barring﴾. The pronoun in ﴿believe in Him﴾ refers to Allah, or to the way of Allah, or to every road, or to Shu'ayb.

﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾: i.e., you seek that the way of Allah be bent and not straight. The discussion of crookedness (al-'iwaj) has already preceded.

Al-Zajjaj said: the vowelling of the 'ayn in al-'iwaj (crookedness) is with kasra in its meanings, and with fatha in its physical sense (al-ihram).

﴿And remember when you were﴾: i.e., remember the time when you were few in number, and He multiplied you through offspring. It is said: you were poor, and He enriched you.

﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾: among the earlier nations, for Allah destroyed them and sent down upon them punishments that took them away and erased their traces.

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾ of the rulings which Allah has legislated for you, and a group among you ﴿who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us, and He is the best of judges.﴾ This is in the mode of threat and severe warning to them, and it is not in the mode of commanding patience upon disbelief.

The judgment of Allah between the two parties is the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers. Similar to it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ (al-Tawba: 52). Or it is a command to the believers to be patient with what befalls them of harm from the disbelievers, until Allah gives them victory over them.

﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said﴾: i.e., the nobles who were arrogant said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you"﴾. They were not satisfied with refusing belief and rebelling against answering what he called them to, but went beyond that, out of transgression, insolence, and wickedness, to threatening their prophet and those who believed in him with expulsion from their town, or with their return, he and those with him, to their disbelieving religion. That is: one of the two matters must happen, either expulsion or return.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that "return" (al-'awd) means "beginning," as in the saying: "a hardship returned to me from so-and-so," meaning it befell me, even if no hardship had preceded it. So there is no objection by those who say: how could Shu'ayb be upon their disbelieving religion before Allah sent him as a messenger? The answer is that the address is in the form of the return to their religion by way of giving precedence to his people who followed him.

The clause ﴿He said: "Even if we were unwilling?"﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), an answer to an assumed question. The hamza is for denying the occurrence of what they demanded, namely expulsion or return. The waw is for the circumstantial (hal): i.e., will you return us to your religion while we are unwilling to return to it, or will you expel us from your town while we are unwilling to leave it, or while we are unwilling to both of these matters together? The meaning is: you have no right to compel us to either of the two matters, and it is not valid for you to do so, for the one who is compelled has no choice, and his agreement is not considered agreement, nor is his return to your religion under compulsion considered a return. By this explanation, the difficulty which many exegetes found in this context is resolved, to the point that this led to lengthy digressions.

﴿We have indeed invented against Allah a lie if we return to your religion﴾, which is shirk, ﴿after Allah has saved us from it﴾ through faith. So there will be no return to it on our part at all. ﴿And it is not for us﴾, i.e., it is not valid for us nor proper ﴿to return to it﴾ in any state ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, i.e., except in the state of His exalted will, for whatever He wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be.

Al-Zajjaj said: i.e., except by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. He said: this is the view of the people of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna, the orthodox community). The meaning is that a return to disbelief will not occur from us unless Allah wills it. So the exception is disjunctive (munqati'). It is said that the exception here is by way of submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, as in His saying: ﴿And my success is not but through Allah﴾ (Hud: 88). It is also said that it is like their saying: "I will not speak to you until the crow lays eggs," and "until the camel passes through the eye of the needle," while the crow does not lay eggs and the camel does not pass through, so it is of the category of conditioning upon the impossible.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾: i.e., His knowledge has encircled all known things, so nothing escapes it. ''Knowledge'' (‘ilman) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). It is said that the meaning is: ﴿And it is not for us to return to it﴾, i.e., to the town, after you have disliked our living alongside you, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ our return to it. ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾, i.e., upon Him we have relied, that He may keep us firm in faith, prevent between us and disbelief and its people, complete His blessing upon us, and protect us from His punishment.

His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. al-futaha (deciding) is judgment. I.e., judge between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of judges. They asked Allah, exalted is He, to judge between them, and His judgment is nothing but the victory of the righteous over the falsifiers, as He informed us in more than one place of His Book. So they were in effect asking for the descent of punishment upon the disbelievers and the befalling of Allah's vengeance upon them.

﴿And the eminent ones of his people who disbelieved said﴾: it is conjoined to ﴿the eminent ones who were arrogant said﴾. It is possible that these are those same people, and it is possible that they are others than them, from the various groups of disbelievers to whom Shu'ayb was sent. The lam in ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾ is a preparatory lam (muwatti'a) for the answer of an omitted oath: i.e., you have entered his religion and abandoned your religion. ﴿Indeed you would then be losers﴾: the answer of the oath stands in place of the answer of the condition. Their loss is either their destruction, or what they would lose because of giving full measure and weight, and abandoning the cheating with which they used to deal with people.

91. ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾: i.e., the shaking (al-zalzala). It is said it was the shout (al-sayha), as in His saying: ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the shout, so they became in their homes prostrate﴾ (Hud: 94). Its explanation has already been given in the story of Salih.

His saying: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as though they had never prospered therein﴾: this clause is a resumed sentence, explaining what the vengeance that befell them was. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ''as though they had never prospered therein'' is its predicate. It is said: "ghanaytu bil-makan" when I dwelt in the place, and "ghani al-qawm fi darihim" meaning the people stayed long in their home. Al-maghan means the dwelling, and its plural is al-maghani.

Hatim al-Ta'i said:

"We were rich for a time through poverty and wealth, and time gave each of them to drink from its two cups.
It did not increase us in rebellion against a relative, nor did poverty diminish our kindness with our wealth."

The meaning of the verse: those who denied Shu'ayb were as though they had not dwelt in their homes, because Allah, exalted is He, uprooted them with punishment. The relative pronoun in ﴿those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ is the subject, whose predicate is ﴿they were the losers﴾. This clause is a resumed sentence like the first, containing an explanation of the loss of the denying people.

﴿So he turned away from them﴾: i.e., Shu'ayb, when he witnessed the descent of punishment upon them, ﴿and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ with which He sent me to you, ﴿and advised you﴾ by explaining what is in the welfare of your religion and your worldly life, ﴿so how could I grieve (asa) over a disbelieving people?﴾ i.e., how could I grieve, persisting in their disbelief in Allah and refusing to answer. Or, asa is intense sorrow: I grieve over that, so I am one who grieves.

Shu'ayb said this statement out of regret over the lack of faith of his people, then he consoled himself, saying: how could grief befall him over a people who are not deserving of grief for them, because of their disbelief in Allah and their refusal to accept what their messenger brought.

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn 'Asakir reported from 'Ikrima and al-Suddi, who said: Allah did not send a prophet twice except Shu'ayb: once to Madyan, and the shout seized them; and once to the People of the Thicket (al-Ayka), and Allah seized them with the punishment of the Day of the Canopy (al-Zulla).

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong people.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Qatada regarding ﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾, that he said: do not wrong them. ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, he said: they used to threaten whoever came to Shu'ayb and visited him and wished to embrace Islam.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding ﴿And do not sit on every path threatening﴾, that he said: they used to sit on the road and tell whoever came past them that Shu'ayb is a liar, "so let him not seduce you from your religion."

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Mujahid, regarding ﴿on every path threatening﴾, that he said: on every path of truth. ﴿And barring from the way of Allah﴾, he said: barring its people. ﴿And seeking to make it crooked﴾, he said: seeking to find deviation in it.

Regarding ﴿and to bar [people] from the way of Allah﴾ he said: "You bar [people] from Islam, and seek to make it crooked," [and regarding ﴿seek to make it crooked﴾] he said: "ruin."

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid that he said: "They are the ushar (tax collectors)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu al-Aliyah, from Abu Hurayrah or someone else (Abu al-Aliyah was uncertain), that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came on the night of the Isra' (night journey) upon a piece of wood on the road. No garment passed by it without it tearing it, and nothing passed by it without it piercing it. He said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is the likeness of people from your community who sit on the road and cut it off.'" Then he recited ﴿and do not sit on every path, threatening [people]﴾.

[He continued:] "﴿unless Allah, our Lord, should will﴾. Allah does not will shirk, but [the verse] means: unless Allah has known something, for He has encompassed all things in knowledge."

When they denied him and threatened him with stoning and with expulsion from their lands, and they transgressed against Allah, the punishment of the Day of the Shade (yawm al-zullah) seized them.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 94–100:

His saying: ﴿And We did not send to any town a prophet⁠—﴾ When Allah, glory be to Him, detailed the circumstances of some of the prophets with their communities, who were mentioned earlier, He summarized the situation of all the other communities to which messengers were sent. That is: and We did not send to any town of the towns a prophet from among the prophets. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: so its people denied, except that We seized them. The exception is an incomplete (mufarragh) exception: that is, We did not send in any state except in the state of Our seizing its people. Thus the position of "akhadhna" (We seized) is accusative. Al-ba'sa' (adversity) means misery and poverty, and al-darra' (hardship) means harm. The explanation of the meaning of al-ba'sa' and al-darra' has already been given. ﴿So that they might humble themselves﴾ means in order that they might supplicate humbly and submit, so that they would abandon the arrogance they were upon and their denial of the prophets.

His saying: ﴿Then We replaced﴾ is conjoined to "akhadhna": that is, then, after seizing the people of the towns, We replaced them ﴿in place of the evil﴾ with which We had afflicted them of trial and testing, the good, that is, the good quality, so they came to abundance, ease and security. ﴿Until they multiplied (ʿafaw)⁠—﴾ It is said: "ʿafa" means increased, and "ʿafa" also means became obliterated (darasa); so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (asma' al-adhdad). What is intended here is that they increased in their persons and their wealth: that is, We gave them good in place of evil until they multiplied. ﴿And they said: "Adversity and ease have already touched our fathers."⁠﴾ That is, they uttered this statement when they came to good after evil. That is: what has touched us of misery and hardship, and then of ease and plenty afterward, is a matter that befell our fathers before us in the same way, so misery and hardship touched them as it touched us, and blessing and good came to them as it came to us. Their meaning is that this is a custom current among the earlier and later generations, and that this is not from Allah, glory be to Him, as a trial for them and a test of what is in them. In this there is, of their great obstinacy, strength of rebelliousness and insolence, what is not hidden. For this reason Allah hastened to punish them and did not give them respite, so He said: ﴿Then We seized them suddenly⁠﴾: that is, abruptly, immediately after they uttered this statement, without delay or respite, while they were not aware of it and did not anticipate it.

The "al" in "al-qura" (the towns) is for specific reference: that is, ﴿And if the people of the towns⁠﴾ to whom We sent Our messengers had believed in the messengers sent to them and had been mindful of what they were determined upon of disbelief, and had not persisted in the vile acts they committed, ﴿We would have opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth⁠﴾: that is, We would have made easy for them the good of heaven and earth, just as ease comes to closed doors when their doors are opened. It has been said: what is meant by the good of heaven is rain, and the good of earth is vegetation; but it is better to take what is in the verse as applying to what is more general than that. It is permissible that the "al" in "al-qura" be for the category (lil-jins), and what is meant is: if the people of the towns, wherever they were and in whatever lands they dwelt, had believed and been mindful, to the end of the verse. ﴿But they denied⁠﴾ the signs and the prophets, and did not believe nor were mindful, so We seized them with punishment because of what they earned of sins that necessitated their punishment.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do the people of the towns feel secure⁠—﴾ is for rebuke and reproach. The people of the towns are the people of the towns mentioned before it. The "fa" is for coordination, and it is like ﴿Do they seek the judgment of ignorance?⁠﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 50). It has been said: what is meant by "the towns" is Makkah and what surrounds it, because of their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ); but taking it in its generality is better.

His saying: ﴿That Our punishment should come upon them by night⁠﴾: that is, at a time of night, which is the night, being in the accusative as an adverbial of time. It is permissible that it be a verbal noun meaning "tabyitan" (a night attack), or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal): that is, while they are spending the night. The clause ﴿while they are asleep⁠﴾ is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

The interrogative in ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment should come upon them in the forenoon while they are playing?⁠﴾ is like the interrogative before it. "Ad-duha" is the late morning of the day, and it is originally a name for the light of the sun when it rises and rises high.

Ibn ʿAmir and the two Haramis read "aw-amina" with the waw sukun (aw-amina), and the rest read it with a fatha on it. The clause ﴿while they are playing⁠﴾ is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: that is, they occupy themselves with what brings them no benefit.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?⁠﴾ is for rebuke, reproach, and denunciation of what they are upon of feeling safe from what is not to be felt safe from, the plan of Allah against them and His punishment of them. In repeating this interrogative there is an added confirmation of the denunciation He made against them. Then He explained the state of one who feels secure from the plan of Allah, saying: ﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people⁠﴾: that is, those who went to excess in loss and fell into His severe threat. It has been said: the plan of Allah here is His gradual leading on through blessing and health; but it is better to take it in its generality.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 94–100:

That is: and We did not send to any town of the towns a prophet from among the prophets. In the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: so its people denied, except that We seized them. The exception is an incomplete (mufarragh) exception: that is, We did not send in any state except in the state of Our seizing its people. Thus the position of "akhadhna" (We seized) is accusative. Al-ba'sa' (adversity) means misery and poverty, and al-darra' (hardship) means harm. The explanation of the meaning of al-ba'sa' and al-darra' has already been given. ﴿So that they might humble themselves﴾ means in order that they might supplicate humbly and submit, so that they would abandon the arrogance they were upon and their denial of the prophets.

His saying: ﴿Then We replaced﴾ is conjoined to "akhadhna": that is, then, after seizing the people of the towns, We replaced them ﴿in place of the evil﴾ with which We had afflicted them of trial and testing, the good, that is, the good quality, so they came to abundance, ease and security. ﴿Until they multiplied (ʿafaw)⁠—﴾ It is said: "ʿafa" means increased, and "ʿafa" also means became obliterated (darasa); so it is one of the words with opposite meanings (asma' al-adhdad). What is intended here is that they increased in their persons and their wealth: that is, We gave them good in place of evil until they multiplied. ﴿And they said: "Adversity and ease have already touched our fathers."⁠﴾ That is, they uttered this statement when they came to good after evil. That is: what has touched us of misery and hardship, and then of ease and plenty afterward, is a matter that befell our fathers before us in the same way, so misery and hardship touched them as it touched us, and blessing and good came to them as it came to us. Their meaning is that this is a custom current among the earlier and later generations, and that this is not from Allah, glory be to Him, as a trial for them and a test of what is in them. In this there is, of their great obstinacy, strength of rebelliousness and insolence, what is not hidden. For this reason Allah hastened to punish them and did not give them respite, so He said: ﴿Then We seized them suddenly⁠﴾: that is, abruptly, immediately after they uttered this statement, without delay or respite, while they were not aware of it and did not anticipate it.

The "al" in "al-qura" (the towns) is for specific reference: that is, ﴿And if the people of the towns⁠﴾ to whom We sent Our messengers had believed in the messengers sent to them and had been mindful of what they were determined upon of disbelief, and had not persisted in the vile acts they committed, ﴿We would have opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth⁠﴾: that is, We would have made easy for them the good of heaven and earth, just as ease comes to closed doors when their doors are opened. It has been said: what is meant by the good of heaven is rain, and the good of earth is vegetation; but it is better to take what is in the verse as applying to what is more general than that. It is permissible that the "al" in "al-qura" be for the category (lil-jins), and what is meant is: if the people of the towns, wherever they were and in whatever lands they dwelt, had believed and been mindful, to the end of the verse. ﴿But they denied⁠﴾ the signs and the prophets, and did not believe nor were mindful, so We seized them with punishment because of what they earned of sins that necessitated their punishment.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do the people of the towns feel secure⁠—﴾ is for rebuke and reproach. The people of the towns are the people of the towns mentioned before it. The "fa" is for coordination, and it is like ﴿Do they seek the judgment of ignorance?⁠﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 50). It has been said: what is meant by "the towns" is Makkah and what surrounds it, because of their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ); but taking it in its generality is better.

His saying: ﴿That Our punishment should come upon them by night⁠﴾: that is, at a time of night, which is the night, being in the accusative as an adverbial of time. It is permissible that it be a verbal noun meaning "tabyitan" (a night attack), or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal): that is, while they are spending the night. The clause ﴿while they are asleep⁠﴾ is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

"Ad-duha" is the late morning of the day, and it is originally a name for the light of the sun when it rises and rises high.

It is permissible that the "al" in "al-qura" be for the category (lil-jins), and what is meant is: if the people of the towns, wherever they were and in whatever lands they dwelt, had believed and been mindful, to the end of the verse. ﴿But they denied⁠﴾ the signs and the prophets, and did not believe nor were mindful, so We seized them with punishment because of what they earned of sins that necessitated their punishment.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do the people of the towns feel secure⁠—﴾ is for rebuke and reproach. The people of the towns are the people of the towns mentioned before it. The "fa" is for coordination, and it is like ﴿Do they seek the judgment of ignorance?⁠﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 50). It has been said: what is meant by "the towns" is Makkah and what surrounds it, because of their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ); but taking it in its generality is better.

His saying: ﴿That Our punishment should come upon them by night⁠﴾: that is, at a time of night, which is the night, being in the accusative as an adverbial of time. It is permissible that it be a verbal noun meaning "tabyitan" (a night attack), or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal): that is, while they are spending the night. The clause ﴿while they are asleep⁠﴾ is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier.

The interrogative in ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment should come upon them in the forenoon while they are playing?⁠﴾ is like the interrogative before it. "Ad-duha" is the late morning of the day, and it is originally a name for the light of the sun when it rises and rises high.

Ibn ʿAmir and the two Haramis read "aw-amina" with the waw sukun (aw-amina), and the rest read it with a fatha on it. The clause ﴿while they are playing⁠﴾ is in the position of an accusative as a circumstantial qualifier: that is, they occupy themselves with what brings them no benefit.

The interrogative in ﴿Then do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?⁠﴾ is for rebuke, reproach, and denunciation of what they are upon of feeling safe from what is not to be felt safe from, the plan of Allah against them and His punishment of them. In repeating this interrogative there is an added confirmation of the denunciation He made against them. Then He explained the state of one who feels secure from the plan of Allah, saying: ﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people⁠﴾: that is, those who went to excess in loss and fell into His severe threat. It has been said: the plan of Allah here is His gradual leading on through blessing and health; but it is better to take it in its generality.

His saying: ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the earth after its former people⁠—﴾ "Nahdi" (We guide/make clear) has been read with a nun and with a yā' (yahdi). On the reading with the nun, the subject of the verb is Allah, glory be to Him, and the object of the verb is ﴿that if We willed, We would strike them for their sins⁠﴾: that is, the matter is this. On the reading with the yā', the subject of "yahdi" is ﴿that if We willed, We would strike them for their sins⁠﴾: that is, We would seize them for their disbelief and denial. The guidance here means clarification, and for this reason it is construed with "li" (to).

His saying: ﴿And We seal upon their hearts⁠﴾: that is, and We seal upon their hearts, as a new independent clause, and it is not correct to conjoin it to "asabna" (We struck), because they are among those whose hearts Allah has sealed for their not accepting faith. It has been said: it is conjoined to a suppressed verb indicated by the speech, as though it were said: they are heedless of guidance, and We seal. It has been said: it is conjoined to "yarithun" (inherit). His saying: ﴿So they do not hear⁠﴾ is the answer to "law" (if): that is, they became, by Our striking them for their sins and sealing upon their hearts, unable to hear what is recited to them by the one whom Allah sent to them of admonition, warning and caution.

Al-Tabari, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Then We replaced the evil with good⁠﴾, that he said: in place of hardship, ease. ﴿Until they multiplied⁠﴾: he said: they increased, and their wealth increased.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿until they multiplied⁠﴾, that he said: they became numerous (jammu).

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Adversity and ease have already touched our fathers⁠﴾, that he said: they said: such a thing has already come upon our fathers, and it amounted to nothing. ﴿So We seized them suddenly while they were not aware⁠﴾.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from him, regarding His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed⁠﴾, that he said: in what Allah revealed, ﴿and been mindful⁠﴾, he said: of what Allah prohibited. ﴿We would have opened to them blessings from the heaven and the earth⁠﴾: he says: heaven gave them its blessing and the earth its vegetation.

Ibn Abi Hatim has related, by way of Muʿadh ibn Rifa'ah from Musa al-Ta'ifi, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Honour bread, for Allah sent it down from the blessings of heaven and brought it forth from the blessings of the earth."

Al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani related, and al-Suyuti said: with a weak chain, from ʿAbdullah ibn Umm Haram, who said: I prayed toward both qiblahs with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Honour bread, for Allah sent it down from the blessings of heaven and subjected to it the blessings of the earth; and whoever gathers what falls from the tablecloth will be forgiven."

Ibn Abi Shaybah has related from al-Hasan, who said: there was a town upon whom Allah had bestowed abundance, to the point that they would clean themselves with bread; so Allah sent hunger upon them.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh have related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Has it not become clear⁠﴾, that he said: has We not made clear?

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from Mujahid something similar.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim have related from al-Suddi, regarding His saying: ﴿those who inherit the earth after its former people⁠﴾, that he said: the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 101–102:

His saying: ﴿Those were the towns﴾, i.e., those which We destroyed, and they are the towns of Noah, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb, whose mention has preceded. ﴿We relate to you﴾, i.e., We recite to you, ﴿some of their tidings﴾, i.e., some of their news. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and for the believers. "We relate" may be in a position of accusative (naṣb) as a ḥāl (circumstantial clause); and ﴿Those were the towns﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), or it may be in a position of nominative (raf') as the khabar, with "the towns" being a ṣifah (adjective) of "those". The min in ﴿some of their tidings﴾ is for partiality (tab'īḍ): i.e., We relate to you some of their tidings. The lam in ﴿Indeed, their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾ is the jawab (response) of the oath.

The meaning: among their news is that the messengers of Allah came to them with His clear proofs, as has been explained in the stories of the prophets mentioned before this. ﴿So they were not going to believe﴾ upon the coming of the messengers ﴿in what they had denied﴾ before their coming. Or: "So they were not going to believe in what their messengers brought them in any state or at any time, in what they had denied before their coming. Rather, they persisted in disbelief, clinging to the skirts of transgression always, and the coming of the messengers did not benefit them nor was any effect of it seen; rather their condition upon its coming was like their condition before it." It was also said: the meaning is: they would not have believed after their destruction in what they had denied, even if We had brought them back to life, like His saying: ﴿And had they been returned, they would have gone back﴾ (al-An'am: 28). It was also said: they asked for miracles, and when they saw them they did not believe in what they had denied before seeing them.

The first is more preferable. The meaning of their denial before the coming of the messengers is that they used to deny everything they heard about the sending of messengers and the revelation of books during the Jahiliyyah.

His saying: ﴿Thus does Allah seal the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, i.e., like that severe sealing, Allah seals the hearts of the disbelievers, so that after that no admonition, reminder, encouragement or warning benefits them.

His saying: ﴿And We did not find in most of them any covenant﴾. The pronoun refers to the people of the towns mentioned earlier: i.e., We did not find in most of the people of these towns any covenant, i.e., a covenant they would observe and adhere to; rather their habit was breaking covenants in every state. It was also said: the pronoun refers to people in general: i.e., We did not find in most people any covenant. It was also said: the intended covenant is that taken from them in the world of the particles (ʿālam al-dharr). It was also said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers in general without restriction to the people of the towns: i.e., most of them have no covenant and no fulfilment, while a few of them may fulfil their covenant and observe it. The "in" in ﴿And indeed, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqīlah), with the pronoun of the matter omitted: i.e., indeed the matter is that We found most of them defiantly disobedient. Or it is the negating "in", and the lam in ﴿defiantly disobedient﴾ carries the meaning of "illa": i.e., none but those who were defiantly disobedient, departing from obedience with a severe departure.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, regarding His saying: ﴿So they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, that he said: It was in Allah's knowledge, on the day they acknowledged Him with the covenant, who among them would deny Him from among those who would affirm Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿So they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, that he said: like His saying: ﴿And had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden﴾ (al-An'am: 28).

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan, regarding His saying: ﴿And We did not find in most of them any covenant﴾, that he said: fulfilment.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning the verse, that he said: it is that covenant of the day the covenant was taken.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And indeed, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾, that he said: That is because Allah only destroyed the towns because they had not preserved what He had enjoined upon them.
