His saying: ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾. There is an omission (ṭayy) in the speech: that is, so he sent to the cities gatherers, and the sorcerers came to Pharaoh.

His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed for us there is surely a reward"﴾, meaning: when they came to Pharaoh they said to him, "Indeed for us there is surely a reward." The sentence is a resumption (isti'nāfiyya), an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say to him when they came to him?" The "ajr" is a gift and a wage. They obliged Pharaoh to give them a reward if they overcame Moses with their magic.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "inna lanā" as a declarative statement. The rest read "a-inna lanā" as an interrogative, asking Pharaoh about the reward he would give them upon victory. The meaning of the interrogative here is confirmation (taqrīr). As for the first reading, it is as if they were certain of the reward and that they must receive it.

Pharaoh answered them with his saying: ﴿"Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near"﴾, meaning: indeed there is a reward for you, and indeed you, along with this reward sought from you, will be among those brought near to us.

His saying: ﴿They said: "O Moses, either you throw, or we will be the throwers"﴾. This sentence is a resumption, an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say to Moses after Pharaoh said to them: ﴿Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near﴾?"

The meaning is that they gave Moses the choice between beginning with the throwing of what he would throw upon them, or they would begin it, out of courtesy toward him, and out of confidence in themselves that they would prevail even if they delayed. "An" is in the accusative position. This was said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra': meaning, either you do the throwing or we do it.

Moses answered them with his saying: ﴿"Throw"﴾. He chose that they be the ones who go first in throwing what they would throw, not caring about them, nor fearing what they had come with.

Al-Farra' said: there is an omission in the speech; the meaning is: Moses said to them, "You will certainly not overcome your Lord, nor will you nullify His signs." It was also said that it is a threat, meaning: begin the throwing, and you will see what disgrace will befall you. What necessitated these two interpretations, according to those who held them, is that it is not permissible for Moses to command them to do magic.

﴿So when they threw﴾, meaning: their ropes and their staffs, ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, meaning: they turned them and altered them from the soundness of their perception through what they brought of deception, imagination, and illusion, which is what conjurers, charlatans and practitioners of sleight of hand do; ﴿and they struck terror into them﴾, meaning: they put dread into their hearts with a severe infusion; ﴿and they brought a great magic﴾ in the eyes of the onlookers regarding what they brought, even though it had no reality in fact.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw your staff"﴾. God, glorified is He, commanded him, when the sorcerers came with what they had brought of magic, to throw his staff, ﴿and behold, it﴾, that is the staff, ﴿swallowed up what they had fabricated﴾.

Hafs read "talqafu" with the lam sukun and the qaf light, from laqifa yalqafu. The rest read it with lam fatha and qaf shadda, from talaqqafa yatalaqqafu. It is said: laqiftu al-shay' and talaqqaftuhu, when I took it or reached it.

Abu Hatim said: it reached me that in some readings it is "talaqqamu" with mim and shadda.

The poet said:
"You are the staff of Moses which never ceased
to swallow up what the sorcerer fabricates."

"Mā" in ﴿what they fabricate﴾ is either verbal (maṣdariyya) or relative (mawṣūla): that is, their fabrication, or what they fabricate. He called it "ifk" (fabrication) because it has no reality in fact; rather it is falsehood, lies, deception and charlatanry.

﴿So the truth took place﴾, meaning: it became manifest and clear regarding what Moses had brought; ﴿and what they had been doing was nullified﴾, meaning: their magic was shown to be void.

119. ﴿So they were overcome there﴾, that is, the sorcerers were overcome in that place, the place where they displayed their magic, and they returned from that place humbled, abased, and subdued.

120. ﴿And the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾, that is, they fell down prostrating, as if someone had cast them down in the posture of prostration, or they could not restrain themselves from what they had seen, so it was as if they had cast themselves down.

The clause ﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron"﴾ is a resumption, an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say at their prostration, or during their prostration?" They said this statement and declared that they had believed in the Lord of the worlds; then they did not suffice with that, until they said: ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾, lest some interpreter from among the people of Pharaoh, who acknowledged his divinity, should suppose that the prostration was to him.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding his saying: ﴿Then We sent Moses﴾: He said: Moses was only named Moses because he was thrown between water and a tree; the word for water in Coptic is "mu," and the word for tree is "si."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid: that Pharaoh was Persian, from the people of Istakhr.

He also related from Ibn Lahi'a: that he was from the sons of Egypt. He also related, and Abu al-Shaykh, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir who said: Pharaoh lived three hundred years.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, [p-492] that Pharaoh was a Copt, a bastard, whose height was seven spans.

He also related from al-Hasan who said: he was a foreign man (ʿilj) from Hamadhan.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibrahim ibn Muqsim al-Hudhali who said: Pharaoh remained four hundred years, and no headache ever afflicted him.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, regarding his saying: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾, he said: It was mentioned to us that this staff was the staff of Adam, which an angel gave him when he set out toward Madyan. It would shine at night, and he would strike the earth with it by day, and it would bring forth his provision, and he would herd his sheep with it. ﴿And behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾: he said, a serpent that nearly sprang upon him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: Moses entered upon Pharaoh wearing a woollen zarmaniqa (a garment) that did not reach beyond his elbows. He sought permission to enter upon Pharaoh, and he said: "Let him enter." So he entered and said: "My God has sent me to you." Pharaoh said to the people around him: "I know of no god for you other than me. Seize him!"

He said: "I have certainly brought you a sign." Pharaoh said: "Then bring it, if you are among the truthful." So Moses threw down his staff, and it became a serpent, plainly visible, between its jaws from the ceiling to the ground. He put his hand into his garment and drew it out, and it was white like lightning, dazzling the eyes. They fell prostrate on their faces. Moses took up his staff and went out, and no one among the people did not flee from him. When Pharaoh recovered and the terror had left him, he said to the chiefs around him: "What do you advise?" They said: ﴿Put him off, and his brother﴾, and do not bring them to us, and let them not approach us. ﴿And send heralds to the cities to gather [the sorcerers]﴾. The sorcerers used to fear Pharaoh, so when he sent for them, they said: "Has your god needed you?" He said: "This man did such-and-such." They said: "This man is a sorcerer who has practised sorcery." ﴿Surely we shall have a reward if we are the victors﴾. ﴿He said: "Yes, and you will certainly be among those brought near [to me]"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "The name of Moses' staff was Masha."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded through various chains from him concerning the words ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾ that he said: "The male serpent."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Suddi, concerning the words ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, that he said: "A male among the serpents, opening its mouth, placing its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned toward Pharaoh to seize him. When he saw it, he was terrified and leaped up, and he defecated, which he had not done before that. He cried out: 'O Moses, take it! I believe in your Lord, and I will send the Children of Israel with you.' Moses took it, and it became a staff again."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words ﴿arjihu﴾ (put him off), that he said: "Delay him."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Qatada, who said: "Detain him and his brother."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas through various chains concerning the words ﴿and send heralds to the cities to gather﴾ that he said: "The police (al-shurat)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from him (Ibn Abbas) concerning the words ﴿and the sorcerers came﴾ that he said: "They were seventy men. They became sorcerers in the morning and martyrs by evening."

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed over their number. It was said they were seventy, as Ibn Abbas said; it was said they were twelve; it was said fifteen thousand; it was said seventeen thousand; it was said nineteen thousand; it was said thirty thousand; it was said seventy thousand; it was said eighty thousand; it was said three hundred thousand; and it was said nine hundred thousand.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatada, concerning the words ﴿surely we shall have a reward﴾, that it means "a gift."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Abbas, concerning the words ﴿when they cast﴾, that he said: "They cast thick ropes and long sticks, and they came to seem to him, from their sorcery, to be moving."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Suddi, who said: "Moses cast his staff, and it devoured every serpent of theirs. When they saw that, they prostrated."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Qatada something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Mujahid concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "It gulps down their ropes and their staves."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: "Moses met the chief of the sorcerers, and Moses said to him: 'Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I have brought is true?' The sorcerer said: 'I will certainly come tomorrow with a sorcery that no sorcery can overcome. By God, if you defeat me, I will indeed believe in you and bear witness that it is true.' Pharaoh was watching both of them, and this is the statement of Pharaoh: ﴿Surely this is a plot you have plotted in the city﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Awza'i, who said: "When the sorcerers fell down prostrate, Paradise was displayed to them until they looked upon it."

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent Moses﴾, meaning: after Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb. That is, We sent Moses after We had sent these messengers. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿after them﴾ refers to the earlier nations, meaning: after their destruction. ﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾: Pharaoh (Fir'awn) is a title for everyone who ruled the land of Egypt after the Amalekites. The chiefs (mala') of Pharaoh are the nobles of his people. The mention of them specifically, despite the universality of the message, is because those other than them are like their followers.

His saying: ﴿So they wronged them﴾, meaning: they disbelieved in them. The word "wrong" (zulm) is applied to disbelief because their disbelief in the signs that Moses brought was extreme disbelief, given the presence of the great miracles that should have compelled faith. The signs here are the nine signs. Or the meaning of ﴿they wronged them﴾ is: they wronged people by means of them, when they barred them from believing in them, or they wronged themselves by means of them. ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾, meaning: those who denied the signs and disbelieved in them, and whom He made corrupters, because their denial and disbelief are among the worst kinds of corruption.

His saying: ﴿And Moses said: "O Pharaoh, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds"﴾. He informed him that he had been sent by God to him, and made this the heading of his speech with him, because whoever is sent on behalf of the One who is Lord of all the worlds is deserving of acceptance for what he brings, as when a king sends a man on a need to his subjects: "I am the messenger of the king to you," and then he recounts what he was sent with. In that there is a great cultivation of awe and an introduction of dread whose extent cannot be measured.

His saying: ﴿Bound to say nothing about God except the truth﴾. It was recited (qurri'a) as "ḥaqīqun 'alayya an lā aqūla" (I am bound to say nothing...), meaning: it is obligatory and necessary for me that I say nothing, in what I convey to you from God, except the true word. It was also recited as "ḥaqīqun 'alā an lā aqūla" without the pronoun in ʿalā. It was said regarding its explanation that ʿalā here has the meaning of bā’ (by/with): that is, "deserving that I should not say." This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy and al-A'mash, for they both read "ḥaqīqun bi-an lā aqūla." It was also said that ḥaqīq is implicitly containing the meaning of "eager" (ḥarīṣ). It was also said that since it is necessarily bound to the truth, the truth is necessarily bound to it, so saying the truth is binding upon him and he is bound to the saying of the truth. It was also said that he went to great lengths in describing himself in that situation, until he made himself a reality "upon" the saying of the truth, as if it were obligatory upon the truth that Moses be its speaker.

ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud read "ḥaqīqun an lā aqūla" with ʿalā dropped, and its meaning is clear. Then he said after this: ﴿I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord﴾, meaning: with that by which my truthfulness and that I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds become clear.

Here he omitted the mention of the dialogue that took place between them, as in another place where Pharaoh said: ﴿Who then is the Lord of you two, O Moses?﴾ (Ta-Ha 49), and then after Moses' answer he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, and the verses that recount what passed between them.

His saying: ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾. He commanded him to let the Children of Israel go with him, and return to their homelands, which is the Holy Land. They had remained with him enslaved and prevented from returning to their homeland. The fa' (so) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes.

When he said that, Pharaoh said to him: ﴿If you have come with a sign﴾ from God, as you claim, ﴿then bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ in this claim which you have brought.

His saying: ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, meaning: he placed it on the ground and it turned into a serpent, that is, a great serpent of the male serpents. The meaning of "manifest" (mubīn) is that its being a serpent in that state was an apparent, clear matter with no ambiguity.

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, that is, he brought it out and displayed it from his collar (jayb), or from under his armpit. In the Revelation: ﴿Insert your hand into your collar; it will come out white without harm﴾ (An-Naml 12).

His saying: ﴿And behold, it was white to the observers﴾, meaning: and behold, his hand which he brought out was white, shining with light that appears to every beholder.

The chiefs (al-mala', that is, the nobles) ﴿of the people of Pharaoh﴾ said, when they witnessed the staff turn into a serpent and his hand become white without harm: "Indeed this," that is Moses, ﴿is a skilled sorcerer﴾, meaning: one with much knowledge of magic. There is no contradiction between attributing this saying to the chiefs here and to Pharaoh in Surat ash-Shu'ara', for they all said it, so that made it valid to attribute it to them at times and to him at other times.

The clause ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ is a description of "sorcerer." The land attributed to them is the land of Egypt. This is from the speech of the chiefs. As for ﴿So what do you command?﴾, it was said that it is from the speech of Pharaoh, who said to the chiefs when they had said what preceded: "By what thing do you command me?" It was also said that it is from the speech of the chiefs: meaning, they said to Pharaoh, "So by what thing do you command us?" and they addressed him with what a group is addressed with, as a sign of honour to him, as followers address their leaders. The word "mā" is in the accusative position with the verb that follows it. It is permissible that "dhā" be in the sense of "alladhī" (which), as the grammarians mentioned for "mādhā ṣanaʿta?" (what did you do?).

That this is from the speech of Pharaoh is more preferable, based on what follows it, which is: ﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother"﴾. The chiefs answered Pharaoh's speech, since he consulted them and asked for their opinion. "Arjih" means: delay him and his brother. It is said: arjaʾtuhu and arjaytuhu, meaning: I delayed him.

ʿĀsim, al-Kisa'i, Hamza and the people of Madina read "arjih" without a hamza. The rest read it with a hamza. The people of Kufa, except al-Kisa'i, read "arjih" with the ha' pronounced with sukun.

Al-Farra' said: this is a dialect of the Arabs who pause on the ha' in connected speech, and the Basran grammarians denied this. It was said that the meaning of "arjih" is: detain him. It was also said: it is from rajā, yarjū, meaning: make him hope, and leave him hoping in you. This was related by al-Nahhas from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad.

﴿And send to the cities gatherers﴾, meaning: send a company of gatherers to the cities in which there are sorcerers. "Ḥāshirīn" (gatherers) is the object of "send." It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿And they will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾ is the answer to the imperative: that is, those whom you send will bring you ﴿every skilled sorcerer﴾, meaning: every adept one in magic, with much knowledge of its craft.

The people of Kufa except ʿĀsim read "sahhār" (sahhār is intensive form), and all others read "sāḥir."

His saying: ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾. There is an omission (ṭayy) in the speech: that is, so he sent to the cities gatherers, and the sorcerers came to Pharaoh.

His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed for us there is surely a reward"﴾, meaning: when they came to Pharaoh they said to him, "Indeed for us there is surely a reward." They obliged Pharaoh to give them a reward if they overcame Moses with their magic.

Pharaoh answered them with his saying: ﴿"Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near"﴾, meaning: indeed there is a reward for you, and indeed you, along with this reward sought from you, will be among those brought near to us.

I believe in your Lord, and I will send the Children of Israel with you.' Moses took it, and it became a staff again."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Qatada, who said: "Detain him and his brother."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas through various chains concerning the words ﴿and send heralds to the cities to gather﴾ that he said: "The police (al-shurat)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from him (Ibn Abbas) concerning the words ﴿and the sorcerers came﴾ that he said: "They were seventy men. They became sorcerers in the morning and martyrs by evening."

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed over their number. It was said they were seventy, as Ibn Abbas said; it was said they were twelve; it was said fifteen thousand; it was said seventeen thousand; it was said nineteen thousand; it was said thirty thousand; it was said seventy thousand; it was said eighty thousand; it was said three hundred thousand; and it was said nine hundred thousand.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatada, concerning the words ﴿surely we shall have a reward﴾, that it means "a gift."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Abbas, concerning the words ﴿when they cast﴾, that he said: "They cast thick ropes and long sticks, and they came to seem to him, from their sorcery, to be moving."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Suddi, who said: "Moses cast his staff, and it devoured every serpent of theirs. When they saw that, they prostrated."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Qatada something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Mujahid concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "It gulps down their ropes and their staves."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: "Moses met the chief of the sorcerers, and Moses said to him: 'Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I have brought is true?' The sorcerer said: 'I will certainly come tomorrow with a sorcery that no sorcery can overcome. By God, if you defeat me, I will indeed believe in you and bear witness that it is true.' Pharaoh was watching both of them, and this is the statement of Pharaoh: ﴿Surely this is a plot you have plotted in the city﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Awza'i, who said: "When the sorcerers fell down prostrate, Paradise was displayed to them until they looked upon it."

His saying: ﴿Then after them We sent Moses﴾, meaning: after Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb. That is, We sent Moses after We had sent these messengers. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿after them﴾ refers to the earlier nations, meaning: after their destruction. ﴿To Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾: Pharaoh (Fir'awn) is a title for everyone who ruled the land of Egypt after the Amalekites. The chiefs (mala') of Pharaoh are the nobles of his people. The mention of them specifically, despite the universality of the message, is because those other than them are like their followers.

His saying: ﴿So they wronged them﴾, meaning: they disbelieved in them. The word "wrong" (zulm) is applied to disbelief because their disbelief in the signs that Moses brought was extreme disbelief, given the presence of the great miracles that should have compelled faith. The signs here are the nine signs. Or the meaning of ﴿they wronged them﴾ is: they wronged people by means of them, when they barred them from believing in them, or they wronged themselves by means of them. ﴿So look how was the end of the corrupters﴾, meaning: those who denied the signs and disbelieved in them, and whom He made corrupters, because their denial and disbelief are among the worst kinds of corruption.

His saying: ﴿And Moses said: "O Pharaoh, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds"﴾. He informed him that he had been sent by God to him, and made this the heading of his speech with him, because whoever is sent on behalf of the One who is Lord of all the worlds is deserving of acceptance for what he brings, as when a king sends a man on a need to his subjects: "I am the messenger of the king to you," and then he recounts what he was sent with. In that there is a great cultivation of awe and an introduction of dread whose extent cannot be measured.

His saying: ﴿Bound to say nothing about God except the truth﴾. It was recited (qurri'a) as "ḥaqīqun 'alayya an lā aqūla" (I am bound to say nothing...), meaning: it is obligatory and necessary for me that I say nothing, in what I convey to you from God, except the true word. It was also recited as "ḥaqīqun 'alā an lā aqūla" without the pronoun in ʿalā. It was said regarding its explanation that ʿalā here has the meaning of bā’ (by/with): that is, "deserving that I should not say." This is supported by the recitation of Ubayy and al-A'mash, for they both read "ḥaqīqun bi-an lā aqūla." It was also said that ḥaqīq is implicitly containing the meaning of "eager" (ḥarīṣ). It was also said that since it is necessarily bound to the truth, the truth is necessarily bound to it, so saying the truth is binding upon him and he is bound to the saying of the truth. It was also said that he went to great lengths in describing himself in that situation, until he made himself a reality "upon" the saying of the truth, as if it were obligatory upon the truth that Moses be its speaker.

ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud read "ḥaqīqun an lā aqūla" with ʿalā dropped, and its meaning is clear. Then he said after this: ﴿I have come to you with a clear proof from your Lord﴾, meaning: with that by which my truthfulness and that I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds become clear.

Here he omitted the mention of the dialogue that took place between them, as in another place where Pharaoh said: ﴿Who then is the Lord of you two, O Moses?﴾ (Ta-Ha 49), and then after Moses' answer he said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, and the verses that recount what passed between them.

His saying: ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾. He commanded him to let the Children of Israel go with him, and return to their homelands, which is the Holy Land. They had remained with him enslaved and prevented from returning to their homeland. The fa' (so) is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes.

When he said that, Pharaoh said to him: ﴿If you have come with a sign﴾ from God, as you claim, ﴿then bring it, if you are of the truthful﴾ in this claim which you have brought.

His saying: ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, meaning: he placed it on the ground and it turned into a serpent, that is, a great serpent of the male serpents. The meaning of "manifest" (mubīn) is that its being a serpent in that state was an apparent, clear matter with no ambiguity.

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, that is, he brought it out and displayed it from his collar (jayb), or from under his armpit. In the Revelation: ﴿Insert your hand into your collar; it will come out white without harm﴾ (An-Naml 12).

His saying: ﴿And behold, it was white to the observers﴾, meaning: and behold, his hand which he brought out was white, shining with light that appears to every beholder.

The chiefs (al-mala', that is, the nobles) ﴿of the people of Pharaoh﴾ said, when they witnessed the staff turn into a serpent and his hand become white without harm: "Indeed this," that is Moses, ﴿is a skilled sorcerer﴾, meaning: one with much knowledge of magic. There is no contradiction between attributing this saying to the chiefs here and to Pharaoh in Surat ash-Shu'ara', for they all said it, so that made it valid to attribute it to them at times and to him at other times.

The clause ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ is a description of "sorcerer." The land attributed to them is the land of Egypt. This is from the speech of the chiefs. As for ﴿So what do you command?﴾, it was said that it is from the speech of Pharaoh, who said to the chiefs when they had said what preceded: "By what thing do you command me?" It was also said that it is from the speech of the chiefs: meaning, they said to Pharaoh, "So by what thing do you command us?" and they addressed him with what a group is addressed with, as a sign of honour to him, as followers address their leaders. The word "mā" is in the accusative position with the verb that follows it. It is permissible that "dhā" be in the sense of "alladhī" (which), as the grammarians mentioned for "mādhā ṣanaʿta?" (what did you do?).

That this is from the speech of Pharaoh is more preferable, based on what follows it, which is: ﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother"﴾. The chiefs answered Pharaoh's speech, since he consulted them and asked for their opinion. "Arjih" means: delay him and his brother. It is said: arjaʾtuhu and arjaytuhu, meaning: I delayed him.

ʿĀsim, al-Kisa'i, Hamza and the people of Madina read "arjih" without a hamza. The rest read it with a hamza. The people of Kufa, except al-Kisa'i, read "arjih" with the ha' pronounced with sukun.

Al-Farra' said: this is a dialect of the Arabs who pause on the ha' in connected speech, and the Basran grammarians denied this. It was said that the meaning of "arjih" is: detain him. It was also said: it is from rajā, yarjū, meaning: make him hope, and leave him hoping in you. This was related by al-Nahhas from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad.

﴿And send to the cities gatherers﴾, meaning: send a company of gatherers to the cities in which there are sorcerers. "Ḥāshirīn" (gatherers) is the object of "send." It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿And they will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾ is the answer to the imperative: that is, those whom you send will bring you ﴿every skilled sorcerer﴾, meaning: every adept one in magic, with much knowledge of its craft.

The people of Kufa except ʿĀsim read "sahhār" (sahhār is intensive form), and all others read "sāḥir."

His saying: ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾. There is an omission (ṭayy) in the speech: that is, so he sent to the cities gatherers, and the sorcerers came to Pharaoh.

His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed for us there is surely a reward"﴾, meaning: when they came to Pharaoh they said to him, "Indeed for us there is surely a reward." The sentence is a resumption (isti'nāfiyya), an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say to him when they came to him?" The "ajr" is a gift and a wage. They obliged Pharaoh to give them a reward if they overcame Moses with their magic.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "inna lanā" as a declarative statement. The rest read "a-inna lanā" as an interrogative, asking Pharaoh about the reward he would give them upon victory. The meaning of the interrogative here is confirmation (taqrīr). As for the first reading, it is as if they were certain of the reward and that they must receive it.

Pharaoh answered them with his saying: ﴿"Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near"﴾, meaning: indeed there is a reward for you, and indeed you, along with this reward sought from you, will be among those brought near to us.

His saying: ﴿They said: "O Moses, either you throw, or we will be the throwers"﴾. This sentence is a resumption, an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say to Moses after Pharaoh said to them: ﴿Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near﴾?"

The meaning is that they gave Moses the choice between beginning with the throwing of what he would throw upon them, or they would begin it, out of courtesy toward him, and out of confidence in themselves that they would prevail even if they delayed. "An" is in the accusative position. This was said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra': meaning, either you do the throwing or we do it.

Moses answered them with his saying: ﴿"Throw"﴾. He chose that they be the ones who go first in throwing what they would throw, not caring about them, nor fearing what they had come with.

Al-Farra' said: there is an omission in the speech; the meaning is: Moses said to them, "You will certainly not overcome your Lord, nor will you nullify His signs." It was also said that it is a threat, meaning: begin the throwing, and you will see what disgrace will befall you. What necessitated these two interpretations, according to those who held them, is that it is not permissible for Moses to command them to do magic.

﴿So when they threw﴾, meaning: their ropes and their staffs, ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, meaning: they turned them and altered them from the soundness of their perception through what they brought of deception, imagination, and illusion, which is what conjurers, charlatans and practitioners of sleight of hand do; ﴿and they struck terror into them﴾, meaning: they put dread into their hearts with a severe infusion; ﴿and they brought a great magic﴾ in the eyes of the onlookers regarding what they brought, even though it had no reality in fact.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw your staff"﴾. God, glorified is He, commanded him, when the sorcerers came with what they had brought of magic, to throw his staff, ﴿and behold, it﴾, that is the staff, ﴿swallowed up what they had fabricated﴾.

Hafs read "talqafu" with the lam sukun and the qaf light, from laqifa yalqafu. The rest read it with lam fatha and qaf shadda, from talaqqafa yatalaqqafu. It is said: laqiftu al-shay' and talaqqaftuhu, when I took it or reached it.

Abu Hatim said: it reached me that in some readings it is "talaqqamu" with mim and shadda.

The poet said:
"You are the staff of Moses which never ceased
to swallow up what the sorcerer fabricates."

"Mā" in ﴿what they fabricate﴾ is either verbal (maṣdariyya) or relative (mawṣūla): that is, their fabrication, or what they fabricate. He called it "ifk" (fabrication) because it has no reality in fact; rather it is falsehood, lies, deception and charlatanry.

﴿So the truth took place﴾, meaning: it became manifest and clear regarding what Moses had brought; ﴿and what they had been doing was nullified﴾, meaning: their magic was shown to be void.

119. ﴿So they were overcome there﴾, that is, the sorcerers were overcome in that place, the place where they displayed their magic, and they returned from that place humbled, abased, and subdued.

120. ﴿And the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾, that is, they fell down prostrating, as if someone had cast them down in the posture of prostration, or they could not restrain themselves from what they had seen, so it was as if they had cast themselves down.

The clause ﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron"﴾ is a resumption, an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say at their prostration, or during their prostration?" They said this statement and declared that they had believed in the Lord of the worlds; then they did not suffice with that, until they said: ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾, lest some interpreter from among the people of Pharaoh, who acknowledged his divinity, should suppose that the prostration was to him.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding his saying: ﴿Then We sent Moses﴾: He said: Moses was only named Moses because he was thrown between water and a tree; the word for water in Coptic is "mu," and the word for tree is "si."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid: that Pharaoh was Persian, from the people of Istakhr.

He also related from Ibn Lahi'a: that he was from the sons of Egypt. He also related, and Abu al-Shaykh, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir who said: Pharaoh lived three hundred years.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, [p-492] that Pharaoh was a Copt, a bastard, whose height was seven spans.

He also related from al-Hasan who said: he was a foreign man (ʿilj) from Hamadhan.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibrahim ibn Muqsim al-Hudhali who said: Pharaoh remained four hundred years, and no headache ever afflicted him.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, regarding his saying: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾, he said: It was mentioned to us that this staff was the staff of Adam, which an angel gave him when he set out toward Madyan. It would shine at night, and he would strike the earth with it by day, and it would bring forth his provision, and he would herd his sheep with it. ﴿And behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾: he said, a serpent that nearly sprang upon him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: Moses entered upon Pharaoh wearing a woollen zarmaniqa (a garment) that did not reach beyond his elbows. He sought permission to enter upon Pharaoh, and he said: "Let him enter." So he entered and said: "My God has sent me to you." Pharaoh said to the people around him: "I know of no god for you other than me. Seize him!"

He said: "I have certainly brought you a sign." Pharaoh said: "Then bring it, if you are among the truthful." So Moses threw down his staff, and it became a serpent, plainly visible, between its jaws from the ceiling to the ground. He put his hand into his garment and drew it out, and it was white like lightning, dazzling the eyes. They fell prostrate on their faces. Moses took up his staff and went out, and no one among the people did not flee from him. When Pharaoh recovered and the terror had left him, he said to the chiefs around him: "What do you advise?" They said: ﴿Put him off, and his brother﴾, and do not bring them to us, and let them not approach us. ﴿And send heralds to the cities to gather [the sorcerers]﴾. The sorcerers used to fear Pharaoh, so when he sent for them, they said: "Has your god needed you?" He said: "This man did such-and-such." They said: "This man is a sorcerer who has practised sorcery." ﴿Surely we shall have a reward if we are the victors﴾. ﴿He said: "Yes, and you will certainly be among those brought near [to me]"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "The name of Moses' staff was Masha."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded through various chains from him concerning the words ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾ that he said: "The male serpent."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Suddi, concerning the words ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, that he said: "A male among the serpents, opening its mouth, placing its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned toward Pharaoh to seize him. When he saw it, he was terrified and leaped up, and he defecated, which he had not done before that. He cried out: 'O Moses, take it! I believe in your Lord, and I will send the Children of Israel with you.' Moses took it, and it became a staff again."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words ﴿arjihu﴾ (put him off), that he said: "Delay him."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Qatada, who said: "Detain him and his brother."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

As for ﴿So what do you command?﴾, it was said that it is from the speech of Pharaoh, who said to the chiefs when they had said what preceded: "By what thing do you command me?" It was also said that it is from the speech of the chiefs: meaning, they said to Pharaoh, "So by what thing do you command us?" and they addressed him with what a group is addressed with, as a sign of honour to him, as followers address their leaders. The word "mā" is in the accusative position with the verb that follows it. It is permissible that "dhā" be in the sense of "alladhī" (which), as the grammarians mentioned for "mādhā ṣanaʿta?" (what did you do?).

That this is from the speech of Pharaoh is more preferable, based on what follows it, which is: ﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother"﴾. The chiefs answered Pharaoh's speech, since he consulted them and asked for their opinion. "Arjih" means: delay him and his brother. It is said: arjaʾtuhu and arjaytuhu, meaning: I delayed him.

ʿĀsim, al-Kisa'i, Hamza and the people of Madina read "arjih" without a hamza. The rest read it with a hamza. The people of Kufa, except al-Kisa'i, read "arjih" with the ha' pronounced with sukun.

Al-Farra' said: this is a dialect of the Arabs who pause on the ha' in connected speech, and the Basran grammarians denied this. It was said that the meaning of "arjih" is: detain him. It was also said: it is from rajā, yarjū, meaning: make him hope, and leave him hoping in you. This was related by al-Nahhas from Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad.

﴿And send to the cities gatherers﴾, meaning: send a company of gatherers to the cities in which there are sorcerers. "Ḥāshirīn" (gatherers) is the object of "send." It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿And they will bring you every skilled sorcerer﴾ is the answer to the imperative: that is, those whom you send will bring you ﴿every skilled sorcerer﴾, meaning: every adept one in magic, with much knowledge of its craft.

The people of Kufa except ʿĀsim read "sahhār" (sahhār is intensive form), and all others read "sāḥir."

His saying: ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾. There is an omission (ṭayy) in the speech: that is, so he sent to the cities gatherers, and the sorcerers came to Pharaoh.

His saying: ﴿They said: "Indeed for us there is surely a reward"﴾, meaning: when they came to Pharaoh they said to him, "Indeed for us there is surely a reward." The sentence is a resumption (isti'nāfiyya), an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say to him when they came to him?" The "ajr" is a gift and a wage. They obliged Pharaoh to give them a reward if they overcame Moses with their magic.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "inna lanā" as a declarative statement. The rest read "a-inna lanā" as an interrogative, asking Pharaoh about the reward he would give them upon victory. The meaning of the interrogative here is confirmation (taqrīr). As for the first reading, it is as if they were certain of the reward and that they must receive it.

Pharaoh answered them with his saying: ﴿"Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near"﴾, meaning: indeed there is a reward for you, and indeed you, along with this reward sought from you, will be among those brought near to us.

His saying: ﴿They said: "O Moses, either you throw, or we will be the throwers"﴾. This sentence is a resumption, an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say to Moses after Pharaoh said to them: ﴿Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near﴾?"

The meaning is that they gave Moses the choice between beginning with the throwing of what he would throw upon them, or they would begin it, out of courtesy toward him, and out of confidence in themselves that they would prevail even if they delayed. "An" is in the accusative position. This was said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra': meaning, either you do the throwing or we do it.

Moses answered them with his saying: ﴿"Throw"﴾. He chose that they be the ones who go first in throwing what they would throw, not caring about them, nor fearing what they had come with.

Al-Farra' said: there is an omission in the speech; the meaning is: Moses said to them, "You will certainly not overcome your Lord, nor will you nullify His signs." It was also said that it is a threat, meaning: begin the throwing, and you will see what disgrace will befall you. What necessitated these two interpretations, according to those who held them, is that it is not permissible for Moses to command them to do magic.

﴿So when they threw﴾, meaning: their ropes and their staffs, ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, meaning: they turned them and altered them from the soundness of their perception through what they brought of deception, imagination, and illusion, which is what conjurers, charlatans and practitioners of sleight of hand do; ﴿and they struck terror into them﴾, meaning: they put dread into their hearts with a severe infusion; ﴿and they brought a great magic﴾ in the eyes of the onlookers regarding what they brought, even though it had no reality in fact.

His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw your staff"﴾. God, glorified is He, commanded him, when the sorcerers came with what they had brought of magic, to throw his staff, ﴿and behold, it﴾, that is the staff, ﴿swallowed up what they had fabricated﴾.

Hafs read "talqafu" with the lam sukun and the qaf light, from laqifa yalqafu. The rest read it with lam fatha and qaf shadda, from talaqqafa yatalaqqafu. It is said: laqiftu al-shay' and talaqqaftuhu, when I took it or reached it.

Abu Hatim said: it reached me that in some readings it is "talaqqamu" with mim and shadda.

The poet said:
"You are the staff of Moses which never ceased
to swallow up what the sorcerer fabricates."

"Mā" in ﴿what they fabricate﴾ is either verbal (maṣdariyya) or relative (mawṣūla): that is, their fabrication, or what they fabricate. He called it "ifk" (fabrication) because it has no reality in fact; rather it is falsehood, lies, deception and charlatanry.

﴿So the truth took place﴾, meaning: it became manifest and clear regarding what Moses had brought; ﴿and what they had been doing was nullified﴾, meaning: their magic was shown to be void.

119. ﴿So they were overcome there﴾, that is, the sorcerers were overcome in that place, the place where they displayed their magic, and they returned from that place humbled, abased, and subdued.

120. ﴿And the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾, that is, they fell down prostrating, as if someone had cast them down in the posture of prostration, or they could not restrain themselves from what they had seen, so it was as if they had cast themselves down.

The clause ﴿They said: "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron"﴾ is a resumption, an answer to a presumed question, as if it were said: "What did they say at their prostration, or during their prostration?" They said this statement and declared that they had believed in the Lord of the worlds; then they did not suffice with that, until they said: ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾, lest some interpreter from among the people of Pharaoh, who acknowledged his divinity, should suppose that the prostration was to him.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding his saying: ﴿Then We sent Moses﴾: He said: Moses was only named Moses because he was thrown between water and a tree; the word for water in Coptic is "mu," and the word for tree is "si."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid: that Pharaoh was Persian, from the people of Istakhr.

He also related from Ibn Lahi'a: that he was from the sons of Egypt. He also related, and Abu al-Shaykh, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir who said: Pharaoh lived three hundred years.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, [p-492] that Pharaoh was a Copt, a bastard, whose height was seven spans.

He also related from al-Hasan who said: he was a foreign man (ʿilj) from Hamadhan.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibrahim ibn Muqsim al-Hudhali who said: Pharaoh remained four hundred years, and no headache ever afflicted him.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatada, regarding his saying: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾, he said: It was mentioned to us that this staff was the staff of Adam, which an angel gave him when he set out toward Madyan. It would shine at night, and he would strike the earth with it by day, and it would bring forth his provision, and he would herd his sheep with it. ﴿And behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾: he said, a serpent that nearly sprang upon him.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: Moses entered upon Pharaoh wearing a woollen zarmaniqa (a garment) that did not reach beyond his elbows. He sought permission to enter upon Pharaoh, and he said: "Let him enter." So he entered and said: "My God has sent me to you." Pharaoh said to the people around him: "I know of no god for you other than me. Seize him!"

He said: "I have certainly brought you a sign." Pharaoh said: "Then bring it, if you are among the truthful." So Moses threw down his staff, and it became a serpent, plainly visible, between its jaws from the ceiling to the ground. He put his hand into his garment and drew it out, and it was white like lightning, dazzling the eyes. They fell prostrate on their faces. Moses took up his staff and went out, and no one among the people did not flee from him. When Pharaoh recovered and the terror had left him, he said to the chiefs around him: "What do you advise?" They said: ﴿Put him off, and his brother﴾, and do not bring them to us, and let them not approach us. ﴿And send heralds to the cities to gather [the sorcerers]﴾. The sorcerers used to fear Pharaoh, so when he sent for them, they said: "Has your god needed you?" He said: "This man did such-and-such." They said: "This man is a sorcerer who has practised sorcery." ﴿Surely we shall have a reward if we are the victors﴾. ﴿He said: "Yes, and you will certainly be among those brought near [to me]"﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from him (Ibn Abbas) that he said: "The name of Moses' staff was Masha."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded through various chains from him concerning the words ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾ that he said: "The male serpent."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Suddi, concerning the words ﴿then behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, that he said: "A male among the serpents, opening its mouth, placing its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace. Then it turned toward Pharaoh to seize him. When he saw it, he was terrified and leaped up, and he defecated, which he had not done before that. He cried out: 'O Moses, take it! I believe in your Lord, and I will send the Children of Israel with you.' Moses took it, and it became a staff again."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas, concerning his words ﴿arjihu﴾ (put him off), that he said: "Delay him."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Qatada, who said: "Detain him and his brother."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Abbas through various chains concerning the words ﴿and send heralds to the cities to gather﴾ that he said: "The police (al-shurat)."

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from him (Ibn Abbas) concerning the words ﴿and the sorcerers came﴾ that he said: "They were seventy men. They became sorcerers in the morning and martyrs by evening."

The early scholars (al-salaf) differed over their number. It was said they were seventy, as Ibn Abbas said; it was said they were twelve; it was said fifteen thousand; it was said seventeen thousand; it was said nineteen thousand; it was said thirty thousand; it was said seventy thousand; it was said eighty thousand; it was said three hundred thousand; and it was said nine hundred thousand.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatada, concerning the words ﴿surely we shall have a reward﴾, that it means "a gift."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Abbas, concerning the words ﴿when they cast﴾, that he said: "They cast thick ropes and long sticks, and they came to seem to him, from their sorcery, to be moving."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Suddi, who said: "Moses cast his staff, and it devoured every serpent of theirs. When they saw that, they prostrated."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Qatada something similar.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Mujahid concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "What they lie about."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from al-Hasan concerning the words ﴿it swallows what they fabricate﴾, that he said: "It gulps down their ropes and their staves."

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh recorded from Ibn Mas'ud and some of the Companions, who said: "Moses met the chief of the sorcerers, and Moses said to him: 'Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I have brought is true?' The sorcerer said: 'I will certainly come tomorrow with a sorcery that no sorcery can overcome. By God, if you defeat me, I will indeed believe in you and bear witness that it is true.' Pharaoh was watching both of them, and this is the statement of Pharaoh: ﴿Surely this is a plot you have plotted in the city﴾."

Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from al-Awza'i, who said: "When the sorcerers fell down prostrate, Paradise was displayed to them until they looked upon it."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 7, verses 123–130:

﴿You believed in Him﴾. It is read with the hamzah dropped, as a statement, and also with the hamzah retained.

Pharaoh denounced the sorcerers for believing in Musa before he had given them permission to do so. Then, after denouncing them, he explained what in his claim had driven them to it, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city﴾. That is, a scheme you devised, you and Musa, by prior agreement among yourselves, so that you might drive out the people of the city of Egypt, who are Copts, take control of it, and settle in it, you and the Children of Israel.

The meaning of "in the city" is that this scheme and this agreement were made between you while you were in the city of Egypt, before you and Musa went out into this desert. Then he threatened them with his words: ﴿So you will soon know﴾ the consequence of this deed of yours and its evil outcome.

Then he was not content with this general threat but spelled it out, saying: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides﴾. That is, the right foot and the left hand, or the left foot and the right hand. Then the enemy of Allah was not content with this but went beyond it to something else, saying: ﴿Then I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾. That is, I will make you crucified upon them, as an increase in punishing them and an excess in torturing them.

The clause ﴿They said: Indeed we are to our Lord returning﴾ is a resumptive statement, an answer to a question as has already been mentioned. Its meaning is: even if you do this to us, and you consider it a deed for the Day of Requital, Allah will requite you for your action and will reward us well for what has befallen us in His cause. So they threatened him with the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter, since he had threatened them with worldly punishment.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "Indeed we are to our Lord returning through death", that is, death is inevitable for us, and its being caused by you does not harm us.

His words: ﴿And you do not resent us [for anything]﴾.

Al-Hasan read the qaf with a fatha (taqnamu-with-fatha form). Al-Akhfash said: it is a dialect. The rest read it with a kasra. It is said: naqimtu al-amr, meaning "I disapproved of the matter". That is: you do not blame us or disapprove of us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Yet this is the great honour and the complete good, and such a thing cannot be a cause for blame or a ground for denunciation; rather it deserves fine praise and abundant approval. Then they abandoned addressing him, cut off speech with him, and turned to addressing the Exalted Majesty, entrusting the matter to Him and asking of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, that He make them firm in this trial through patience, saying: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾. Ifraagh is pouring; that is, pour it upon us until it overflows and overwhelms us. They asked for the most complete kind of patience, preparing themselves for what punishment would come upon them from the enemy of Allah, and settling their souls to be steadfast in the truth and firm in faith. Then they said: ﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾. That is, take us to You in a state of steadfastness in Islam, not altering, not changing, and not being tempted. What they had of sorcery and skill in its knowledge, despite its being pure evil, was a cause of success in happiness, because they knew that what Musa had brought was beyond human capacity and was from the action of Allah, glorified is He. Thus they reached good through evil. Among the followers of Pharaoh who did not know this knowledge, nothing comparable to the submission, acknowledgment, and faith that came from them occurred. If the skill in the knowledge of evil can bring about such a benefit, then what of skill in the knowledge of good? O Allah, benefit us by what You have taught us, make our feet firm upon the truth, pour upon us a flood of patience, and cause us to die as Muslims.

His words: ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land?﴾. This interrogation from them is for denunciation of him; that is, will you leave him and his people to spread corruption in the land by causing division and scattering the unity?

The land here means the land of Egypt.

His words: ﴿And leave you and your gods?﴾. Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read "wa-yadhuraka" with a damma, as a predicate for an implied subject: that is, "and he leaves you", or as a conjunction with "Will you leave Musa": that is, "will you leave him and he leaves you". Al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli read "wa-yadhraka" with a jazm, either as a lightening by sukun because of the heaviness of the damma, or as what has been said about the jazm in "wa-akun min as-salihin" (﴿and I would be among the righteous﴾, Al-Munafiqun 63:10). Anas ibn Malik read "wa-nadhraka" with nun and damma, meaning that they reported about themselves that they would leave him and his gods. The rest read "wa-yadhraka" with a fatha, with an implied "an" (that), taking it as an answer to the interrogation, and the waw standing in for the fa'; or as a conjunction with "yufsidu": that is, "to spread corruption", and "to leave you", since they, in their claim, were in corruption, and that leads to Pharaoh and his gods being left.

The exegetes differed about the meaning of "and your gods", since Pharaoh claimed lordship, as in his words: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ (al-Qasas 28:38) and his words: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾ (al-Nazi'at 79:24). It was said: the meaning of "your gods" is "your obedience", and it was said: its meaning is "your worship". This is supported by the reading of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak: "wa-ilahataka". In the codex of Ubayy: "Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land, while they have left you, to worship you?" It was said that he used to worship a cow, and it was said he used to worship the stars, and it was said that he had idols which his people worshipped as a means of drawing near to him, so they were attributed to him, and for this reason he said: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾. This is what al-Zajjaj said. It was said that he used to worship the sun.

Pharaoh answered them, confirming their hearts in disbelief, saying: ﴿We will surely kill their sons﴾.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "sanaqtulu" with a lightened form (sa-naqtulu). The rest read it with the shadda: that is, "we will surely kill the sons and spare the women": that is, we will leave them alive. He did not say "we will kill Musa", because he knew he could not do that. ﴿And indeed we are above them, dominant﴾: that is, we are exalted over them by power and conquest, or they are under our domination and in our hands; whatever we wish to do to them, we do.

The clause: ﴿Musa said to his people﴾ is resumptive, an answer to an implied question.

When Musa heard what Pharaoh had said, he commanded his people to seek help from Allah and to be patient through the trial. Then he informed them that ﴿the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whom He wills of His servants﴾, meaning the land of Egypt, or the category of the land. This is a promise from Musa to his people of victory over Pharaoh and his people, and that Allah will make them inherit their land and their homes.

Then he gave them the good news that ﴿the outcome is for the righteous﴾, that is, the praiseworthy outcome in this world and the Hereafter is for the righteous among His servants, who are Musa and those with him.

The outcome of everything is its end.

It has been read "wal-'aqibata" with a fatha, as a conjunction with "the earth".

The clause: ﴿They said: We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾ is resumptive, an answer to an implied question like the one before it. That is: we were harmed before you came to us as a messenger, through Pharaoh's killing of our sons at your birth, when he was told that a boy would be born whose hand would bring an end to his kingdom; and after you came to us as a messenger, through the killing of our sons now. It was also said that the meaning is: we were harmed before you came by being used in hard labour without wages, and after you came by what we are now in, of fear for ourselves, our children, and our families. It was also said that the harm before and the harm after are one and the same, which is the exaction of the jizya from them.

The clause: ﴿He said: It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾ is resumptive like the one before it. He promised them that Allah would destroy their enemy, who are Pharaoh and his people.

His words: ﴿And make you successors in the land﴾ is an explicit statement of what was previously hinted at, namely that the land belongs to Allah.

Allah fulfilled his hope: they came to possess Egypt in the time of Dawud and Sulayman, and they conquered Bayt al-Maqdis together with Yusha' ibn Nun. Allah destroyed Pharaoh and his people by drowning, and saved them, so that He may see how you act: that is, after He bestows on you the destruction of your enemy and makes you successors in the land, He will requite you for what you did in it, of good and evil.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city, that you conspired together to drive out its people. I will surely cut off your hands…﴾ (the verse), that he said: so he killed them and cut them off as he had said.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the first person to crucify was Pharaoh, and he was the first to cut off the hands and feet on alternate sides.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words: "on alternate sides", that he said: a hand from here and a foot from here.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾, that he said: before Allah sent you and after He sent you.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, regarding the verse, that he said: the Children of Israel said to Musa: Pharaoh used to impose on us the making of bricks before you came; when you came, he imposed on us bricks together with straw as well. Musa said: O my Lord, destroy Pharaoh; how long will You leave him? Allah revealed to him: They have not committed the sin for which I destroyed them.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: a soothsayer told the enemy of Allah that a boy would be born in that year who would take away your kingdom. He said: so he hunted down their children in that year, slaughtering the males among them; then he slaughtered them again after Musa had come to them.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: indeed, we of the household (Ahl al-Bayt) are opened and closed (in fortune), and there must be a dynasty for the Banu Hashim. So look at which of the Banu Hashim it will be. And concerning them was revealed: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then see how you act﴾. The authenticity of this from Ibn 'Abbas needs to be examined. The verse is about the Children of Israel, not the Banu Hashim, and it occurs in this story which narrates what took place between Musa and Pharaoh.

Then the enemy of Allah was not content with this but went beyond it to something else, saying: ﴿Then I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾. Its meaning is: even if you do this to us, and you consider it a deed for the Day of Requital, Allah will requite you for your action and will reward us well for what has befallen us in His cause. So they threatened him with the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter, since he had threatened them with worldly punishment.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "Indeed we are to our Lord returning through death", that is, death is inevitable for us, and its being caused by you does not harm us.

His words: ﴿And you do not resent us [for anything]﴾.

Al-Hasan read the qaf with a fatha (taqnamu-with-fatha form). Al-Akhfash said: it is a dialect. The rest read it with a kasra. It is said: naqimtu al-amr, meaning "I disapproved of the matter". That is: you do not blame us or disapprove of us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Ifraagh is pouring; that is, pour it upon us until it overflows and overwhelms us. They asked for the most complete kind of patience, preparing themselves for what punishment would come upon them from the enemy of Allah, and settling their souls to be steadfast in the truth and firm in faith. Then they said: ﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾. That is, take us to You in a state of steadfastness in Islam, not altering, not changing, and not being tempted. What they had of sorcery and skill in its knowledge, despite its being pure evil, was a cause of success in happiness, because they knew that what Musa had brought was beyond human capacity and was from the action of Allah, glorified is He. Thus they reached good through evil. Among the followers of Pharaoh who did not know this knowledge, nothing comparable to the submission, acknowledgment, and faith that came from them occurred. If the skill in the knowledge of evil can bring about such a benefit, then what of skill in the knowledge of good? This interrogation from them is for denunciation of him; that is, will you leave him and his people to spread corruption in the land by causing division and scattering the unity?

The land here means the land of Egypt.

Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read "wa-yadhuraka" with a damma, as a predicate for an implied subject: that is, "and he leaves you", or as a conjunction with "Will you leave Musa": that is, "will you leave him and he leaves you". Nu'aym ibn Maysarah read "wa-yadhuraka" with a damma, as a predicate for an implied subject: that is, "and he leaves you", or as a conjunction with "Will you leave Musa": that is, "will you leave him and he leaves you". Al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli read "wa-yadhraka" with a jazm, either as a lightening by sukun because of the heaviness of the damma, or as what has been said about the jazm in "wa-akun min as-salihin" (﴿and I would be among the righteous﴾, Al-Munafiqun 63:10). Anas ibn Malik read "wa-nadhraka" with nun and damma, meaning that they reported about themselves that they would leave him and his gods. The rest read "wa-yadhraka" with a fatha, with an implied "an" (that), taking it as an answer to the interrogation, and the waw standing in for the fa'; or as a conjunction with "yufsidu": that is, "to spread corruption", and "to leave you", since they, in their claim, were in corruption, and that leads to Pharaoh and his gods being left.

The exegetes differed about the meaning of "and your gods", since Pharaoh claimed lordship, as in his words: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ (al-Qasas 28:38) and his words: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾ (al-Nazi'at 79:24). It was said: the meaning of "your gods" is "your obedience", and it was said: its meaning is "your worship". This is supported by the reading of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Dahhak: "wa-ilahataka". In the codex of Ubayy: "Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land, while they have left you, to worship you?" It was said that he used to worship a cow, and it was said he used to worship the stars, and it was said that he had idols which his people worshipped as a means of drawing near to him, so they were attributed to him, and for this reason he said: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾. This is what al-Zajjaj said. It was said that he used to worship the sun.

Pharaoh answered them, confirming their hearts in disbelief, saying: ﴿We will surely kill their sons﴾.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "sanaqtulu" with a lightened form (sa-naqtulu). The rest read it with the shadda: that is, "we will surely kill the sons and spare the women": that is, we will leave them alive. He did not say "we will kill Musa", because he knew he could not do that. ﴿And indeed we are above them, dominant﴾: that is, we are exalted over them by power and conquest, or they are under our domination and in our hands; whatever we wish to do to them, we do.

The clause: ﴿Musa said to his people﴾ is resumptive, an answer to an implied question.

When Musa heard what Pharaoh had said, he commanded his people to seek help from Allah and to be patient through the trial. Then he informed them that ﴿the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whom He wills of His servants﴾, meaning the land of Egypt, or the category of the land. This is a promise from Musa to his people of victory over Pharaoh and his people, and that Allah will make them inherit their land and their homes.

Then he gave them the good news that ﴿the outcome is for the righteous﴾, that is, the praiseworthy outcome in this world and the Hereafter is for the righteous among His servants, who are Musa and those with him.

The outcome of everything is its end.

It has been read "wal-'aqibata" with a fatha, as a conjunction with "the earth".

The clause: ﴿They said: We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾ is resumptive, an answer to an implied question like the one before it. That is: we were harmed before you came to us as a messenger, through Pharaoh's killing of our sons at your birth, when he was told that a boy would be born whose hand would bring an end to his kingdom; and after you came to us as a messenger, through the killing of our sons now. It was also said that the meaning is: we were harmed before you came by being used in hard labour without wages, and after you came by what we are now in, of fear for ourselves, our children, and our families. It was also said that the harm before and the harm after are one and the same, which is the exaction of the jizya from them.

The clause: ﴿He said: It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾ is resumptive like the one before it. He promised them that Allah would destroy their enemy, who are Pharaoh and his people.

His words: ﴿And make you successors in the land﴾ is an explicit statement of what was previously hinted at, namely that the land belongs to Allah.

Allah fulfilled his hope: they came to possess Egypt in the time of Dawud and Sulayman, and they conquered Bayt al-Maqdis together with Yusha' ibn Nun. Allah destroyed Pharaoh and his people by drowning, and saved them, so that He may see how you act: that is, after He bestows on you the destruction of your enemy and makes you successors in the land, He will requite you for what you did in it, of good and evil.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from al-Suddi, regarding His words: ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city, that you conspired together to drive out its people. I will surely cut off your hands…﴾ (the verse), that he said: so he killed them and cut them off as he had said.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: the first person to crucify was Pharaoh, and he was the first to cut off the hands and feet on alternate sides.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words: "on alternate sides", that he said: a hand from here and a foot from here.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us﴾, that he said: before Allah sent you and after He sent you.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Wahb ibn Munabbih, regarding the verse, that he said: the Children of Israel said to Musa: Pharaoh used to impose on us the making of bricks before you came; when you came, he imposed on us bricks together with straw as well. Musa said: O my Lord, destroy Pharaoh; how long will You leave him? Allah revealed to him: They have not committed the sin for which I destroyed them.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: a soothsayer told the enemy of Allah that a boy would be born in that year who would take away your kingdom. He said: so he hunted down their children in that year, slaughtering the males among them; then he slaughtered them again after Musa had come to them.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: indeed, we of the household (Ahl al-Bayt) are opened and closed (in fortune), and there must be a dynasty for the Banu Hashim. So look at which of the Banu Hashim it will be. And concerning them was revealed: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then see how you act﴾. The authenticity of this from Ibn 'Abbas needs to be examined. The verse is about the Children of Israel, not the Banu Hashim, and it occurs in this story which narrates what took place between Musa and Pharaoh.

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 7, verses 123–130:

﴿You believed in Him﴾. It is read with the hamzah dropped, as a statement, and also with the hamzah retained.

Pharaoh denounced the sorcerers for believing in Musa before he had given them permission to do so. Then, after denouncing them, he explained what in his claim had driven them to it, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city﴾. That is, a scheme you devised, you and Musa, by prior agreement among yourselves, so that you might drive out the people of the city of Egypt, who are Copts, take control of it, and settle in it, you and the Children of Israel.

The meaning of "in the city" is that this scheme and this agreement were made between you while you were in the city of Egypt, before you and Musa went out into this desert. Then he threatened them with his words: ﴿So you will soon know﴾ the consequence of this deed of yours and its evil outcome.

Then he was not content with this general threat but spelled it out, saying: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on alternate sides﴾. That is, the right foot and the left hand, or the left foot and the right hand. Then the enemy of Allah was not content with this but went beyond it to something else, saying: ﴿Then I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾. That is, I will make you crucified upon them, as an increase in punishing them and an excess in torturing them.

The clause ﴿They said: Indeed we are to our Lord returning﴾ is a resumptive statement, an answer to a question as has already been mentioned. Its meaning is: even if you do this to us, and you consider it a deed for the Day of Requital, Allah will requite you for your action and will reward us well for what has befallen us in His cause. So they threatened him with the punishment of Allah in the Hereafter, since he had threatened them with worldly punishment.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "Indeed we are to our Lord returning through death", that is, death is inevitable for us, and its being caused by you does not harm us.

His words: ﴿And you do not resent us [for anything]﴾.

Al-Hasan read the qaf with a fatha (taqnamu-with-fatha form). Al-Akhfash said: it is a dialect. The rest read it with a kasra. It is said: naqimtu al-amr, meaning "I disapproved of the matter". That is: you do not blame us or disapprove of us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Yet this is the great honour and the complete good, and such a thing cannot be a cause for blame or a ground for denunciation; rather it deserves fine praise and abundant approval. Then they abandoned addressing him, cut off speech with him, and turned to addressing the Exalted Majesty, entrusting the matter to Him and asking of Him, the Mighty and Majestic, that He make them firm in this trial through patience, saying: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾. Ifraagh is pouring; that is, pour it upon us until it overflows and overwhelms us. They asked for the most complete kind of patience, preparing themselves for what punishment would come upon them from the enemy of Allah, and settling their souls to be steadfast in the truth and firm in faith. Then they said: ﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾. That is, take us to You in a state of steadfastness in Islam, not altering, not changing, and not being tempted. What they had of sorcery and skill in its knowledge, despite its being pure evil, was a cause of success in happiness, because they knew that what Musa had brought was beyond human capacity and was from the action of Allah, glorified is He. Thus they reached good through evil. Among the followers of Pharaoh who did not know this knowledge, nothing comparable to the submission, acknowledgment, and faith that came from them occurred. If the skill in the knowledge of evil can bring about such a benefit, then what of skill in the knowledge of good? O Allah, benefit us by what You have taught us, make our feet firm upon the truth, pour upon us a flood of patience, and cause us to die as Muslims.

His words: ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land?﴾. This interrogation from them is for denunciation of him; that is, will you leave him and his people to spread corruption in the land by causing division and scattering the unity?
