Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 131–136 (part 1 of 2):

The meaning of "the people of Pharaoh" here is his people. The meaning of "years" (al-sinin) is drought. This is well known among the people of the language, who say "a year (sanah) befell them," meaning a year of drought. In a hadith: "O Allah, make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf." Most Arabs inflect al-sinin with the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of the sound masculine plural (jam' mudhakkar salim). Some Arabs inflect it with the inflection of the singular and let the vowel movements fall on the nun. Al-Farra' recited:

"I see the passing of years have taken from me, as the crescent loses its light from the moon."

with a kasra on the nun of al-sinin.

Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh recited this line with a fatha on the nun.

I say:

There has occurred what admits of no doubt, which is the saying of the poet:

"And what do the people belittle in me, when I have passed the limit of forty?"

And after it:

"The man of fifty, my strength gathered, and the turning of years pulls at me."

Indeed the verses before it and after it are in the same metre (broken with a kasra).

The first of these verses is:

"I am the son of Jala and the climber of the heights; when I put down the turban, you will know me."

Al-Farra' related from the Banu 'Amir that they say: "I stayed with him years (sinin) with tanwin (ending in -an)." He said: the Banu Tamim do not give it tanwin. It is said: "asnata al-qawm," meaning the people suffered drought. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Zib'ara:

"And the men of Makkah are suffering drought, emaciated."

And the diminishing of the fruits, because of the absence of rain and the abundance of blights, so that "la'allahum yadhdhakkarun" (perhaps they may take heed): so that they may be admonished, return, and turn back from their error.

His saying: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours by right."﴾ That is, the good aspect of fertility through abundant rain, good produce and cheap prices. "They said, 'This is ours'," meaning: we have been given it by right, and it belongs to us exclusively. ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, meaning an evil aspect of drought, famine, abundance of illness and the like of afflictions, ﴿they ascribe it as an omen to Musa and those with him﴾, meaning they consider Musa and those with him among the believers to be a bad omen. The original is "yatatayyaru," with the ta' assimilated into the ta' (of the verb form).

Talha recited "tatayyarna" as a past verb. The Arabs used to take omens from things such as birds and animals; then this was used for anyone who considered something a bad omen. A similar example is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "And if an evil befalls them, they say: 'This is from you (O Muhammad)'" (al-Nisa' 78). It is said: the reason the good is defined (with al-) is that it occurs frequently, and the reason the evil is indefinite is the rarity of its occurrence.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾, meaning the cause of their good and evil, and all that reaches them of fertility and drought, is from Allah, not because of Musa and those with him. This answer was in accordance with what they believed and what they understood. For this reason he expressed the good and evil that come about by the decree, wisdom and will of Allah by the word "omen" (ta'ir). But most of them do not know this; rather, they attribute good and evil to other than Allah, out of ignorance.

Al-Hasan recited "tayruhum."

His saying: ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will not believe you."﴾ Al-Khalil said: the original of mahma is the conditional "ma," to which the emphatic "ma" was added, as it is added to other particles such as haythuma, aynama, kayfama and matama. But they disliked the joining of two similar elements, so they changed the alif of the first into a ha'.

Al-Kisa'i said: its original is "mah," meaning "stop," (i.e., "stop whatever sign you bring us"), and the conditional "ma" was added to it. It is also said: it is a single word by which one conditions. The position of mahma is in the nominative case as a subject, or in the accusative case governed by a verb that is explained by what follows it. "Min ayah" (a sign) explains mahma. They called it a sign of mockery directed at Musa, as what follows it indicates. And "li-tasharanā bihā" means "to turn us away from what we are upon, as the magicians do with their magic." The pronoun in "bihi" refers to mahma, and the pronoun in "bihā" refers to "ayah." It is also said that both pronouns refer to mahma: the first is masculine in view of the wording, and the second feminine in view of the meaning. ﴿Then we will not believe you﴾ is the answer of the condition, meaning: "we will not believe you as truthful." They informed about themselves that they would not believe in anything that he brings of the signs, which in their assumption are magic.

At that moment, the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, descended upon them, as explained by His saying: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾, which is heavy rain.

Al-Akhfash said: its singular is "tufanah." It is also said: it is a verbal noun like "rujhan" and "nuqsan," so it has no singular. It is also said: al-tufan is death.

Al-Nahhas said: in the language, al-tufan is whatever destroys, whether death or flood, that is, what surrounds them and destroys them. Al-jarad is the well-known creature that Allah sent to eat their crops, and it ate them. As for al-qummal, it is said: it is the "da'ba'" (a kind of locust), and the da'ba' is the locust before it flies. It is also said: it is the weevil, and it is said: the lice (bara'ith), and it is said: small black creatures, and it is said: a kind of tick, and it is said: beetles.

Al-Nahhas said: it is possible that all of these things were sent upon them.

Al-Hasan recited "al-qaml" with a fatha on the qaf and sukun on the mim.

The rest recited with a damma on the qaf and a fatha on the mim, with shadda.

'Ata' al-Khurasani explained al-qummal as "al-qaml" (lice) and "al-difda'" (frogs), the plural of difdi', which is the well-known creature that lives in water; and "al-dam" (blood). It is narrated that the Nile flowed with blood upon them. It is also said: it is nosebleed.

His saying: ﴿clear signs (ayat mufassalat)﴾, meaning clear and manifest.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

The meaning is: We sent these things upon them while they were clear and manifest signs. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they rose above faith in Allah, and they were a criminal people who did not follow guidance to the truth nor desist from falsehood.

His saying: ﴿And when the plague (rijz) fell upon them﴾, meaning the punishment by these matters that Allah sent upon them. It is recited with a damma on the ra', and both are dialects. It is also said: this rijz was a plague by which seventy thousand Copts died in a single day. ﴿They said, "O Musa, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you"﴾, meaning by what He has entrusted to you of knowledge, or by what He has singled you out with of prophethood, or by what He has covenanted with you that you should supplicate with, and He will answer you. The "ba'" is connected to "ud'u" (invoke) in the sense of: "help us to what we seek of supplication, by the right of what you have of Allah's covenant." Or: "invoke for us, seeking a means to Him by His covenant with you." It is also said: the "ba'" is for an oath, and its answer is "la-nu'minanna" (we will surely believe), meaning: "we swear by Allah's covenant with you that if you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe you," with the answer of the condition standing in place of the answer of the oath. And on the view that the "ba'" is not for an oath, the "lam" in "la-in kashafta 'anna al-rijz" is the answer of an implied oath, and "la-nu'minanna" is the answer of the condition standing in place of the answer of the oath. "Wa-la-nursilanna ma'aka Bani Isra'il" (and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you) is coordinated with "la-nu'minanna."

They had been holding the Children of Israel back with them, humiliating them in work, so they promised him to send them with him.

﴿So when We removed the plague from them until a term which they were to reach﴾, meaning: We lifted the punishment from them when they returned to Musa and asked him what they asked. But not an absolute lifting; rather a lifting limited by an end, which is the appointed term for their destruction by drowning. The answer of "lamma" is ﴿when they broke their word﴾, meaning they violated what they had pledged for themselves.

"Idha" here is the sudden one (idha al-fuja'iyyah): that is, they were suddenly upon the breaking and hastened to it.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾, meaning We wanted to take vengeance upon them when they broke their word, because of the many sins that preceded them. ﴿And We drowned them in the sea (al-yamm)﴾, meaning in the sea. It is said: it is that whose bottom cannot be reached. It is also said: it is its deep and middle part. The clause ﴿because they denied Our signs﴾ is the cause of the drowning, and ﴿and they were heedless of them﴾ is coordinated with "kadhdhabu" (they denied): that is, they were heedless of the vengeance indicated by "intaqamna" (We took vengeance), or heedless of the signs which they did not believe in but rather denied, and in their denial they were like those heedless of them. The second is better, because both clauses are the cause of the drowning.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years﴾ that he said: "al-sinin" is hunger.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Mujahid who said: "al-sinin" are calamities (jawa'ih), and a decrease in fruits short of that.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, in Nawadir al-Usul, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: When Allah seized the people of Pharaoh with years, everything for them dried up, and their livestock perished, until the Nile of Egypt dried up. with a kasra on the nun of al-sinin.

"And the men of Makkah are suffering drought, emaciated."

The original is "yatatayyaru," with the ta' assimilated into the ta' (of the verb form).

Talha recited "tatayyarna" as a past verb. The Arabs used to take omens from things such as birds and animals; then this was used for anyone who considered something a bad omen. It is said: the reason the good is defined (with al-) is that it occurs frequently, and the reason the evil is indefinite is the rarity of its occurrence.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾, meaning the cause of their good and evil, and all that reaches them of fertility and drought, is from Allah, not because of Musa and those with him. Al-Hasan recited "tayruhum."

His saying: ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will not believe you."﴾ Al-Khalil said: the original of mahma is the conditional "ma," to which the emphatic "ma" was added, as it is added to other particles such as haythuma, aynama, kayfama and matama. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to mahma, and the pronoun in "bihā" refers to "ayah." At that moment, the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, descended upon them, as explained by His saying: ﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾, which is heavy rain.

Al-Akhfash said: its singular is "tufanah." It is also said: it is a verbal noun like "rujhan" and "nuqsan," so it has no singular. It is also said: al-tufan is death.

Al-Nahhas said: in the language, al-tufan is whatever destroys, whether death or flood, that is, what surrounds them and destroys them. Or: "invoke for us, seeking a means to Him by His covenant with you." It is also said: the "ba'" is for an oath, and its answer is "la-nu'minanna" (we will surely believe), meaning: "we swear by Allah's covenant with you that if you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe you," with the answer of the condition standing in place of the answer of the oath. They had been holding the Children of Israel back with them, humiliating them in work, so they promised him to send them with him.

﴿So when We removed the plague from them until a term which they were to reach﴾, meaning: We lifted the punishment from them when they returned to Musa and asked him what they asked. The answer of "lamma" is ﴿when they broke their word﴾, meaning they violated what they had pledged for themselves.

"Idha" here is the sudden one (idha al-fuja'iyyah): that is, they were suddenly upon the breaking and hastened to it.

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾, meaning We wanted to take vengeance upon them when they broke their word, because of the many sins that preceded them. ﴿And We drowned them in the sea (al-yamm)﴾, meaning in the sea. It is said: it is that whose bottom cannot be reached. It is also said: it is its deep and middle part. The clause ﴿because they denied Our signs﴾ is the cause of the drowning, and ﴿and they were heedless of them﴾ is coordinated with "kadhdhabu" (they denied): that is, they were heedless of the vengeance indicated by "intaqamna" (We took vengeance), or heedless of the signs which they did not believe in but rather denied, and in their denial they were like those heedless of them. The second is better, because both clauses are the cause of the drowning.

This is well known among the people of the language, who say "a year (sanah) befell them," meaning a year of drought. In a hadith: "O Allah, make it upon them as years like the years of Yusuf." Most Arabs inflect al-sinin with the i'rab (grammatical inflection) of the sound masculine plural (jam' mudhakkar salim). Some Arabs inflect it with the inflection of the singular and let the vowel movements fall on the nun. Al-Farra' recited:

"I see the passing of years have taken from me, as the crescent loses its light from the moon."

with a kasra on the nun of al-sinin.

Al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh recited this line with a fatha on the nun.

I say:

There has occurred what admits of no doubt, which is the saying of the poet:

"And what do the people belittle in me, when I have passed the limit of forty?"

And after it:

"The man of fifty, my strength gathered, and the turning of years pulls at me."

Indeed the verses before it and after it are in the same metre (broken with a kasra).

The first of these verses is:

"I am the son of Jala and the climber of the heights; when I put down the turban, you will know me."

Al-Farra' related from the Banu 'Amir that they say: "I stayed with him years (sinin) with tanwin (ending in -an)." He said: the Banu Tamim do not give it tanwin. It is said: "asnata al-qawm," meaning the people suffered drought. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Zib'ara:

"And the men of Makkah are suffering drought, emaciated."

And the diminishing of the fruits, because of the absence of rain and the abundance of blights, so that "la'allahum yadhdhakkarun" (perhaps they may take heed): so that they may be admonished, return, and turn back from their error.

His saying: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours by right."﴾ That is, the good aspect of fertility through abundant rain, good produce and cheap prices. "They said, 'This is ours'," meaning: we have been given it by right, and it belongs to us exclusively. ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, meaning an evil aspect of drought, famine, abundance of illness and the like of afflictions, ﴿they ascribe it as an omen to Musa and those with him﴾, meaning they consider Musa and those with him among the believers to be a bad omen. The original is "yatatayyaru," with the ta' assimilated into the ta' (of the verb form).

Talha recited "tatayyarna" as a past verb. The Arabs used to take omens from things such as birds and animals; then this was used for anyone who considered something a bad omen. A similar example is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: "And if an evil befalls them, they say: 'This is from you (O Muhammad)'" (al-Nisa' 78). It is said: the reason the good is defined (with al-) is that it occurs frequently, and the reason the evil is indefinite is the rarity of its occurrence.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, their omen is with Allah﴾, meaning the cause of their good and evil, and all that reaches them of fertility and drought, is from Allah, not because of Musa and those with him. This answer was in accordance with what they believed and what they understood. For this reason he expressed the good and evil that come about by the decree, wisdom and will of Allah by the word "omen" (ta'ir). But most of them do not know this; rather, they attribute good and evil to other than Allah, out of ignorance.

Al-Hasan recited "tayruhum."

The Lord's Words: ﴿And We caused the people who were oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾, meaning the Children of Israel, who were being oppressed, that is, humiliated and degraded by being made to serve Pharaoh and his people. ﴿The eastern and western parts of the land﴾ is in the accusative because it is the object of ﴿We caused to inherit﴾ (manṣūbān bi-awrathnā, meaning they are in the accusative as the object of the verb).

Al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' said: the original was "fī mashāriqi al-arḍi wa-maghāribihā", then the preposition was dropped, so the two words became accusative. The first view is more apparent, because one says "I made him inherit the wealth" (awrathtuhu al-māl). The land is Egypt and Syria. Its eastern parts (mashāriquhā) are the eastern regions, and its western parts (maghāribuhā) are the western regions. These are the lands that belonged to Pharaoh and his people from among the Copts. It has also been said that the meaning is the whole earth, since Dawud and Sulayman were from the Children of Israel, and they ruled the earth.

The Lord's Words: ﴿which We blessed﴾ is a description (ṣifah) of the eastern and western parts. It has also been said that it describes the land. Its being blessed means that crops and fruits are brought forth from it in their most complete form and most beneficial abundance.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾, meaning it came to pass and continued to be fulfilled completely. The word is ﴿And We wish to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and make them the inheritors﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ: 5).

This is a promise from God, glory be to Him, of victory and triumph over the enemies and of taking possession of their kingdoms. ﴿al-ḥusnā﴾ (the good) is a description of ﴿the word﴾, and it is the feminine form of al-aḥsan (the best). The completion of this word for the Children of Israel was due to their patience with what they suffered from Pharaoh and his people.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been building﴾. Tadmīr means destruction, that is, We destroyed by ruin what they had been constructing of buildings. ﴿And what they had been erecting﴾: Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, read ﴿yaʿrishūn﴾ with a ḍammah on the rāʾ.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿and what they had been erecting﴾, that he said: they were building.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Qatādah, regarding His words ﴿they came upon a people devoted to their idols﴾, that he said: Lakhm and Judhām.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī something similar.

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse, that he said: they were images of cows made of copper. When the calf of al-Sāmirī came, it was made to appear to them that it was from those cows. That was the first beginning of the affair of the calf, so that God would have the proof against them, and then He would take vengeance upon them afterward.

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it sound, al-Nasā'ī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, Abū al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abū Wāqid al-Laythī, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before Ḥunayn, and we passed by a lote tree, so I said: O Messenger of God, make for us this one a dhāt anwāṭ, as the disbelievers have a dhāt anwāṭ. The disbelievers used to hang their weapons on a lote tree and sit devoted around it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: God is greatest! This is just as the Children of Israel said to Mūsā: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾. Indeed, you are following the ways of those before you."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Ṭabarānī and Ibn Mardawayh reported something similar through the chain of Kathīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAwf, from his father, from his grandfather, as a marfūʿ report, and Kathīr is extremely weak.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His words ﴿mutabbar﴾, that he said: it is loss.

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Abū al-Shaykh reported from him that he said: it is destruction.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And We caused the people who were oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾, meaning the Children of Israel, who were being oppressed, that is, humiliated and degraded by being made to serve Pharaoh and his people. ﴿The eastern and western parts of the land﴾ is in the accusative because it is the object of ﴿We caused to inherit﴾ (manṣūbān bi-awrathnā, meaning they are in the accusative as the object of the verb).

Al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' said: the original was "fī mashāriqi al-arḍi wa-maghāribihā", then the preposition was dropped, so the two words became accusative. The first view is more apparent, because one says "I made him inherit the wealth" (awrathtuhu al-māl). The land is Egypt and Syria. Its eastern parts (mashāriquhā) are the eastern regions, and its western parts (maghāribuhā) are the western regions. These are the lands that belonged to Pharaoh and his people from among the Copts. It has also been said that the meaning is the whole earth, since Dawud and Sulayman were from the Children of Israel, and they ruled the earth.

The Lord's Words: ﴿which We blessed﴾ is a description (ṣifah) of the eastern and western parts. It has also been said that it describes the land. Its being blessed means that crops and fruits are brought forth from it in their most complete form and most beneficial abundance.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾, meaning it came to pass and continued to be fulfilled completely. The word is ﴿And We wish to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and make them the inheritors﴾ (al-Qaṣaṣ: 5).

This is a promise from God, glory be to Him, of victory and triumph over the enemies and of taking possession of their kingdoms. ﴿al-ḥusnā﴾ (the good) is a description of ﴿the word﴾, and it is the feminine form of al-aḥsan (the best). The completion of this word for the Children of Israel was due to their patience with what they suffered from Pharaoh and his people.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been building﴾. Tadmīr means destruction, that is, We destroyed by ruin what they had been constructing of buildings. ﴿And what they had been erecting﴾: Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, read ﴿yaʿrishūn﴾ with a ḍammah on the rāʾ.

Al-Kisā'ī said: this is the dialect of Tamīm.

Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbalah read ﴿yuʿarrishūn﴾ with a shaddah on the rāʾ and a ḍammah on the letter of the present tense.

The rest of the readers read it with a kasrah on the rāʾ and no shaddah, meaning what they had been trellising of gardens. From this is the Lord's saying: ﴿And it is He who produced gardens, trellised and untrellised﴾. It has also been said that the meaning of yaʿrishūn is they build, as one says ʿarasha yaʿrishu, meaning he built, yabnī.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾, meaning We passed it with them and crossed it.

It was read as ﴿jawwazanā﴾ with shaddah, which has the same meaning as the reading of the majority.

The Lord's Words: ﴿Then they came upon a people devoted to their idols﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿yaʿkufūn﴾ with a kasrah on the kāf, and the rest read it with a ḍammah. One says ʿakafa yaʿkufu and yaʿkifu, meaning he stayed with the thing and adhered to it. The verbal noun from both is ʿukūf.

It has been said that these people whom the Children of Israel came upon were from Lakhm, who were dwelling in al-Raqqah. Their idols were images of cows. It has also been said they were from the Canaanites. The Children of Israel said, when they saw those images: ﴿O Mūsā, make for us a god﴾, meaning an idol that we may worship, like that which these people have. The kāf is connected to a deleted element that functions as a description of ﴿a god﴾. Then Mūsā answered them and said: ﴿Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant﴾. He described them as ignorant because they had witnessed from God's signs what would deter anyone with even slight knowledge from seeking the worship of other than God. But these people, meaning the Children of Israel, were the most stubborn, most ignorant and most inconsistent of God's creation. What occurred from them in this regard has already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah.

Then Mūsā said to them: ﴿Indeed, these, meaning the people devoted to the idols, are doomed in what they are in﴾. Tabbār means destruction. Every broken vessel is mutabbar, meaning these people are ruined in what they are doing, shattered and broken. What they are engaged in is the worship of idols. He informed them that this religion which these people follow is doomed and destroyed, and nothing of it will be completed.

The Lord's Words: ﴿And null is what they were doing﴾, meaning everything they were doing of deeds together with their worship of idols is gone and vanished.

In al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī's commentary) it is said: in placing ﴿these﴾ as the subject of inna, and in placing the predicate of the subject first from the clause that is the predicate of inna, and the subject being for the worshippers of idols, there is the indication that they are the ones exposed to destruction, that it will certainly overtake them, and that it is a binding decree for them, so as to warn them of the consequence of what they sought and to make hateful to them what they loved.

The Lord's Words: ﴿Shall I seek for you a god other than God?﴾ The interrogative is for denial and reproach, meaning: how could I seek for you other than God as a god for you to worship, when you have witnessed from His mighty signs what a part of them is sufficient for? The meaning is that what you have sought will never happen. The placing of the hamzah before ghayr is to indicate that what is denied is that the one sought other than Him, glory be to Him, would be a god. Ghayr is an object of the verb that follows it, and ilāhan is a tamyīz (specification) or a ḥāl (circumstantial description). The clause ﴿while He has favoured you over the worlds﴾ is in a place of accusative as a ḥāl, meaning while the state is that He has favoured you over the worlds of your time, by what He bestowed upon you of destroying your enemy, making you successors on the earth, and bringing you out of humiliation and disgrace to honour and elevation. So how will you repay these blessings by seeking the worship of other than Him?

The Lord's Words: ﴿And when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾, meaning remember the time when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh, after they had been your masters, enslaving you in what they wanted from you and humiliating you with all kinds of humiliation. This is according to the view that this speech is reported from Mūsā. But if it is in the sense of address to the Jews present in the age of Muhammad, then it means: remember when We saved your forefathers from the people of Pharaoh. The clause ﴿they inflicted upon you the worst torment﴾ is in a place of accusative as a ḥāl, meaning We saved you from the people of Pharaoh while they were inflicting upon you the worst torment. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence explaining what they were in of which He saved you. The clause ﴿they killed your sons and spared your women﴾ explains the clause before it, or is a substitute for it, and its explanation has already passed.

The reference in the Lord's words ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾ is to the torment: meaning in this torment you were in there was a great trial from your Lord. It has also been said that the reference is to the salvation, and that the trial means blessing. The first view is preferable.

This is one of the blessings with which God honoured Moses, peace be upon him, and exalted him.

The thirty and the ten are the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. God set this period as an appointed time for Moses to converse privately with Him and to be addressed by Him. It was said that the speaking took place on the Day of Sacrifice (يوم النحر). The purpose of the statement ﴿So the appointed time with his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾, despite the knowledge that the thirty and the ten make forty nights, is to prevent the assumption that the meaning is "We completed the thirty with ten of them." So He clarified that the ten are other than the thirty. The phrase "arba'ina laylatan" (forty nights) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (الحال), meaning: "So the appointed time was completed while it was forty nights."

His saying: ﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron, "Take my place among my people"﴾, that is, be my successor among them. Moses said this when he intended to set out for the private conversation, and [he said]: "Set right the affairs of the Children of Israel by good governance, by gentleness toward them, and by attending to their conditions." ﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾, that is, do not take the path of the disobedient, and do not be a helper to the wrongdoers.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related, through several chains, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "And We appointed for Moses thirty nights" (the verse), that he said: "Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten [days] of Dhu al-Hijjah."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid something similar to this.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: Moses said to his people, "My Lord promised me thirty nights, in which I would meet Him, and I would appoint Aaron over you." When Moses departed to his Lord, Allah added ten to them. So their trial occurred during the ten that Allah added. When thirty nights had passed, al-Samiri had seen Gabriel, so he took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of the horse. Then he mentioned the story of al-Samiri.

This is one of the blessings with which God honoured Moses, peace be upon him, and exalted him.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related, through several chains, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "And We appointed for Moses thirty nights" (the verse), that he said: "Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten [days] of Dhu al-Hijjah."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid something similar to this.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: Moses said to his people, "My Lord promised me thirty nights, in which I would meet Him, and I would appoint Aaron over you." When Moses departed to his Lord, Allah added ten to them. So their trial occurred during the ten that Allah added. When thirty nights had passed, al-Samiri had seen Gabriel, so he took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of the horse. Then he mentioned the story of al-Samiri.

This is one of the blessings with which God honoured Moses, peace be upon him, and exalted him.

The thirty and the ten are the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. God set this period as an appointed time for Moses to converse privately with Him and to be addressed by Him. It was said that the speaking took place on the Day of Sacrifice (يوم النحر). The purpose of the statement ﴿So the appointed time with his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾, despite the knowledge that the thirty and the ten make forty nights, is to prevent the assumption that the meaning is "We completed the thirty with ten of them." So He clarified that the ten are other than the thirty. The phrase "arba'ina laylatan" (forty nights) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (الحال), meaning: "So the appointed time was completed while it was forty nights."

His saying: ﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron, "Take my place among my people"﴾, that is, be my successor among them. Moses said this when he intended to set out for the private conversation, and [he said]: "Set right the affairs of the Children of Israel by good governance, by gentleness toward them, and by attending to their conditions." ﴿And do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾, that is, do not take the path of the disobedient, and do not be a helper to the wrongdoers.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related, through several chains, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "And We appointed for Moses thirty nights" (the verse), that he said: "Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten [days] of Dhu al-Hijjah."

Abd al-Razzaq and Abd ibn Humayd related from Mujahid something similar to this.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse, that he said: Moses said to his people, "My Lord promised me thirty nights, in which I would meet Him, and I would appoint Aaron over you." When Moses departed to his Lord, Allah added ten to them. So their trial occurred during the ten that Allah added. When thirty nights had passed, al-Samiri had seen Gabriel, so he took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of the horse. Then he mentioned the story of al-Samiri.

The lam in ﴿لِمِيقاتِنا﴾ (*li-miqatina*, "for Our appointed time") indicates specificity: his coming was specifically at the appointed time mentioned, meaning that he came at the promised time, and his Lord spoke to him, that is, made him hear His speech without an intermediary.

Regarding His words ﴿Show me Yourself that I may look at You﴾: the meaning is "Show me Yourself so that I may look at You." He asked to see Him out of longing for the vision, after He had made him hear His speech.

Moses' request to see Allah indicates that the vision is permissible in principle in his view. Had it been impossible in his view, he would not have asked for it. The answer, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, indicates either that he will not see Him at this time for which he asked, or that Allah is not seen as long as the seer is alive in this worldly abode.

As for the vision in the Hereafter, it has been established by mutawatir (widely transmitted, certain) hadiths, a mutawatir that is not hidden from anyone who knows the pure Sunnah. Dispute over such matters and evasion bring no benefit. The path of truth is clear. However, adherence to a school of thought in which a person has been raised, and in which he found his forefathers and the people of his land, together with a lack of attention to what Allah requires of His servants under this pure law, leads to partisanship (ta'assub). The partisan, even if his sight is sound, his insight is blind and his ear is deaf to hearing the truth. He rejects the truth while thinking that he rejects only falsehood, and he supposes that what he was raised upon is the truth, out of heedlessness and ignorance of the correct reflection (nazar) that Allah has made obligatory upon him and of receiving what the Book and the Sunnah have brought with acceptance and submission.

How few are the fair-minded after the emergence of these schools in the fundamentals (usul) and the branches (furu')! The door of truth has become closed by them, and the way of fairness has become rugged. The matter belongs to Allah, the Glorified, and guidance comes from Him. As a poet said:

*The youth refuses except to follow his desire, though the path of truth is clear to him.*

The clause ﴿He said: You will not see Me﴾ is resumptive (mustanafah), since it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" The istidrak (corrective exception) in His words ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me﴾ means that you cannot withstand My vision, and nor can what is greater than you in bulk, firmness and strength withstand it, namely the mountain. So look at it: if it remains firm in its place and does not shake when it sees Me, then you will see Me; and if it is weak in that respect, you are weaker than it. This statement is in the position of setting forth a parable for Moses, peace be upon him, through the mountain. It has also been said that it is of the type of conditioning upon the impossible (ta'liq bil-muhal). On the assumption of this, it concerns the vision in this world, for the reason we have mentioned.

Both the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) and the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari) have clung to this verse. The Mu'tazila argued from His words ﴿You will not see Me﴾ and from His command to look at the mountain. The Ash'ariyya said that making the vision dependent on the mountain's remaining firm indicates that it is permissible and not impossible. You are not unaware that the vision in the Hereafter is entirely outside all of this, and the disagreement between them concerns it, not the vision in this world. The disagreement over it existed in the time of the Companions, and their statements on it are well known.

His words ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾: *tajalla* means "appeared," from your saying *jalawtu al-'arus* ("I unveiled the bride," that is, I displayed her); *jalawtu al-sayf* ("I polished the sword," that is, I cleared it of rust); and *tajalla al-shay'* ("the thing became manifest," that is, it was uncovered).

The meaning is: when His Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it crumble. It has also been said that the one who manifested was His command and His power; this was stated by Qutrub and others. *Dakk* is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, meaning He made it crushed and ground, so it became dust. This is according to the reading of those who read *dakkan* as a verbal noun, namely the people of Medina and the people of Basra. As for the reading of the people of Kufa, *ja'alahu dakka'* (in the feminine), the plural is *dakka'at*, like *hamra'* and *hamra'at*. It denotes a rising hillock of earth or level ground. So the meaning is that the mountain became small like a hillock or a level plain.

al-Kisa'i said: *al-dakk* means broad mountains, whose singular is *adak*. *Al-dakka'at* is the plural of *dakka'*, which means soft hills of clay, not thick ones. *Al-dakadik* is what has become flattened in the earth and has not risen. A *naqa dakka'* is a she-camel without a hump.

﴿And Moses fell down unconscious (*sa'iqan*)﴾: meaning he fell into a swoon, taken from *al-sa'iqa* (the thunderbolt). The meaning is that his state, when he fainted, became like the state of one who is struck senseless when the thunderbolt strikes him. It is said: *sa'iqa al-rajul* ("the man was struck"), so he is *sa'iq* or *mas'uq*, when the thunderbolt has struck him.

When he recovered from his swoon, he said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning I declare You far above that I should ask anything for which You have not given me permission. ﴿I have repented to You﴾, meaning I turn back from returning to the like of this question.

al-Qurtubi said: The community has agreed that this repentance was not from a sin, since the prophets are infallible (ma'sum). It has been said that it was repentance from his killing of the Copt; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri, but there is no basis for it in this context. ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾, before my people who exist in this age, who acknowledge Your greatness and majesty.

His words ﴿He said: O Moses﴾ form a resumptive clause like the one before it, containing the honouring of Moses and the special favour Allah bestowed on him.

*Al-istifa'* means choosing and selecting, that is: I have chosen you above the people of your time, ﴿by My messages﴾. Thus Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *bi-risalati* in the singular, while the rest read it in the plural.

*Al-risala* is a verbal noun, and its original form is singular. Whoever reads it in the plural seems to consider that the messages are of various kinds, so it is pluralized for the variety of types. The word *kalam* here means *taklim* (speaking/making to hear).

Allah, the Glorified, bestowed upon him favour through these two great kinds of honour: the messages, and the speaking without an intermediary. Then He commanded him to take what He had given him, that is, what He had bestowed of this noble honour, and commanded him to be among the thankful for this great gift and this sublime honour.

His words ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾: *min kulli shay'* means of all that the Children of Israel need in their religion and their worldly affairs. These tablets are the Torah. It has been said they were of green emerald; it has been said of red ruby; it has been said of chrysolite; and it has been said of solid rock.

There is disagreement about the number of the tablets and about their length and width. *Al-alwah* is the plural of *lawh*, and it was called *lawh* because the meanings shine (talawwuh) in it. Allah, the Glorified, ascribed the writing to Himself to honour what was written on the tablets, and they were written by His command, the Glorified. It has also been said that it is writing that Allah created on the tablets.

*Min kulli shay'* is in the accusative position, as the object of *kataba*. *Mau'izatan wa tafsilan* is in apposition to the position of *kulli shay'*, that is: an admonition for whoever among the Children of Israel and others takes heed, and a detailed explanation of the rulings that require detailing. ﴿So take it with strength﴾, that is, take the tablets with strength: with earnestness and vigour.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the messages, or to everything, or to the Torah. It has been said that this command is on the presumption of an implied speech, that is: "So We said to him: take it." It has also been said that *fakhudha-ha* is a substitution for His words ﴿So take what I have given you﴾. ﴿And command your people; they will take the best of it﴾, that is, the best of what is in it, that which has greater reward than other things. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ (al-Zumar: 55), and His words: ﴿who follow the best of it﴾ (al-Zumar: 18). Among the best is patience in the face of others, pardoning them, acting upon the stronger course (*'azima*) rather than the concession (*rukhsa*), acting on the obligation rather than the supererogatory, doing what is commanded, and abstaining from what is forbidden.

His words ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾: it has been said that it is the land of Egypt, which belonged to Pharaoh and his people. It has been said it is the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud. It has been said it is Hell. It has been said it is the dwellings of the disbelievers, the tyrants and the Amalekites, so that they may take warning from them. It has been said that *al-dar* means destruction.

The meaning is: I will show you the destruction of the defiantly disobedient. The reality of the meaning of *fisq* has already been explained earlier.

His words ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾: it has been said the meaning of "I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant" is "I will prevent them from understanding My Book." It has been said: "I will turn them away from belief in them." It has been said: "I will turn them away from benefiting from them, as recompense for their arrogance, as in His words: ﴿When they swerved, Allah caused their hearts to swerve﴾ (al-Saff: 5)." It has been said: "I will seal their hearts so that they do not reflect upon them nor take warning from them."

The interpretation of *ayat* has been disputed. It has been said they are the miracles. It has been said they are the revealed Books. It has been said they are the creation of the heavens and the earth. Turning them away from these means not taking warning from them. There is no barrier to carrying the word "signs" upon all of that, and carrying "turning away" upon all the meanings mentioned. As for *bi-ghayri al-haqq* ("without right"), it is either connected with *yatakabbaruna* ("they are arrogant"), meaning they are arrogant with what is not true, or it is connected with an implied element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they are arrogant while clothed in what is without right.

His words ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ are conjoined to *yatakabbaruna* and included with it in the same governing relation to the relative clause (silah).

The meaning is: I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant, who abandon belief in what they see of the signs. Under the term "every sign" fall the revealed verses, the cosmic signs, and the miracles. That is: they do not believe in any sign whatsoever.

Malik ibn Dinar read *yarawa* with a *damma* on the *ya'* in both places. The clause ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it and falls within its ruling. Likewise the clause ﴿And if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾. The meaning is that when they find a path of the paths of right guidance, they abandon and avoid it, and when they see a path of the paths of error, they follow it and choose it for themselves.

The people of Medina and the people of Basra read *al-rushd* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and sukun on the *shin*. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and the *shin*.

Abu 'Ubayda said: Abu 'Amr distinguished between *al-rashad* and *al-rushd*, saying: *al-rashad* is righteousness, and *al-rushd* is in religion.

al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh holds that *al-rushd* and *al-rashad* are like *al-sukht* and *al-sakhat* (both meaning anger).

al-Kisa'i said: What is correct from Abu 'Amr and others is what Abu 'Ubayda said.

The root meaning of *rushd* in the language is that a person attains what he desires; it is the opposite of failure.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the turning away: that is, that turning away is due to their denial. Or the demonstrative refers to arrogance, non-belief in the signs, avoiding the way of right guidance, and following the way of error. The demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is the clause ﴿that they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, that is, because of their denial of the signs and their heedlessness of them.

The relative pronoun in ﴿Those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿their deeds have become void﴾. By "the meeting of the Hereafter" is meant the meeting of the Hereafter abode: that is, their meeting with it, or their meeting with what they were promised in it, on the basis that the annexation is to a time-place (*zarf*).

*Huba't al-a'mal* (the nullification of deeds) is their becoming void: that is, the voiding of what they did which had the form of obedience, such as charity and kinship ties, even though in their state of disbelief they had no acts of obedience. It may also be intended that they become void after having been hoped to benefit them, on the supposition that they would become Muslims, in accordance with the authentic hadith: "You have embraced Islam with whatever good you had previously done."

﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾: of disbelief in Allah, denial of His signs, avoidance of the way of truth, and following the way of error.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related in *Nawadir al-Usul* from Ka'b, who said: When Allah spoke to Moses, he said: "O my Lord, is Your speech like this?" He said: "O Moses, I speak to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and I have the power of all tongues. Had I spoken to you with the full reality of My speech, you would not have been anything."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related from the hadith of Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah spoke to Moses on the day of Tur, He spoke to him with other than the speech with which He had spoken to him on the day He called to him. Moses said to Him: 'O my Lord, is this Your speech with which You spoke to me?' He said: 'O Moses, I spoke to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and I have the power of all tongues and more than that.' When Moses returned to the Children of Israel, they said: 'O Moses, describe for us the speech of the Most Merciful.' He said: 'You cannot bear it. Have you not seen the sounds of the thunderbolts that kill? In the sweetest sweetness that you heard, that is near to it but is not it.'"

(p-500) Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, related from Abu al-Huwayrith Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya that he said: Allah only spoke to Musa (Moses) to the extent of what he could bear of His speech. Had He spoken to him with all of His speech, nothing could have endured it. Musa remained forty nights, and no one who saw Him died except from the light of the Lord of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," that it means: give me [the ability to] look at You.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: When he heard the speech, he desired to see [Allah].

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: When Musa said to his Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, "(p-500) My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," Allah said, "O Musa, you will not see Me." He said: That is, "You will not see Me, and that will never happen." "O Musa, no one will see Me and live." Musa said, "My Lord, I see You and then die; that is dearer to me than not seeing You and then living." Then Allah said to Musa, "O Musa, look at the great, tall, firm mountain. If it remains in its place," meaning: if it stays firm in its place and does not collapse before some of what it sees of My greatness, "then you will see Me," [meaning] you, because of your weakness and humiliation. But if the mountain collapses under its strength, firmness and greatness, then you are weaker and more humble.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi in al-Kamil, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related by several chains from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust," and said, "Like this," and he gestured with his two fingers, placing his thumbs on the joint of the little finger. In another wording: on the upper joint of the little finger. The mountain then sank, and Musa fell down unconscious.

In another wording: the mountain sank into the earth and keeps sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection.

This hadith is sound according to the conditions of Muslim.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: The mountain that Allah commanded him to look at was Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related from Ibn Abbas: "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain." He said: Only the size of the little finger of Him manifested itself. "He made it crumble," he said: into dust. "And Musa fell down unconscious," he said: he was overcome, insensible.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Daylami related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to the mountain, six mountains flew off from awe of His greatness. Three fell in Medina and three in Mecca. In Medina: Uhud, Warqan and Radwa. In Mecca: Hira, Thabir and Thawr."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to Musa, seven mountains scattered. Five of them were in the Hijaz and two in Yemen. In the Hijaz: Uhud, Thabir, Hira, Thawr and Warqan. In Yemen: Hudur and Sabr."

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that when his Lord spoke to Musa, he desired to look at Him, so he asked. [Allah] said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain." He said: The angels surrounded the mountain, and angels surrounded the angels with fire, and fire surrounded them, and angels surrounded the fire. Then his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, and of Him there manifested only the size of a little finger. He made the mountain crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious. He remained unconscious for as long as Allah willed. Then he recovered and said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers among the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: Allah wrote the tablets for Musa while he heard the scratching of the pens on a tablet.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The tablets that were sent down to Musa were of the lote tree of Paradise, and the length of the tablet was twelve cubits."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: They used to say the tablets were of ruby, but I say they were of emerald, and their writing was gold. Allah wrote them with His own hand, and the people of the heavens heard the scratching of the pens.

I say: May Allah have mercy on Sa'id; how much he could have dispensed with what he said on his own account. Such a matter is not said by personal opinion or conjecture. What is most likely is that many of the salaf (the early generations) used to ask the Jews about these matters, which is why the reports differed and became confused. This one says [they were] of wood, another says of ruby, another says of emerald, another says of chrysolite, another says of silk brocade, and another says of stone.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, regarding "And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything, every thing": they were commanded with it and forbidden from it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar.

The salaf differed greatly about what was written on the tablets. There is no objection to understanding what was written as including all of that, since there is no contradiction.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding "So take it with strength": with diligence and resolve. "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": he said, the abode of the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding "And order your people to take the best of it": Musa was commanded to take it with more strictness than his people were commanded.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding "So take it with strength": with obedience.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "So take it with strength": meaning with diligence and striving. "And order your people to take the best of it": [he said] with the best of what they find in it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": their destination in the Hereafter.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah that he said: Their dwellings in this world.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan that he said: Hell.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah that he said: Egypt (Misr).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "I will turn away from My signs": from reflecting upon My signs.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj regarding "My signs," that he said: [They are] the creation of the heavens and the earth and the signs within them. "I will turn them away from reflecting upon them or taking lessons from them."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sufyan ibn Uyayna regarding the verse that he said: "I will strip from them the understanding of the Qur'an."
