On the assumption of this, it concerns the vision in this world, for the reason we have mentioned.

Both the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) and the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari) have clung to this verse. The Mu'tazila argued from His words ﴿You will not see Me﴾ and from His command to look at the mountain. The Ash'ariyya said that making the vision dependent on the mountain's remaining firm indicates that it is permissible and not impossible. You are not unaware that the vision in the Hereafter is entirely outside all of this, and the disagreement between them concerns it, not the vision in this world. The disagreement over it existed in the time of the Companions, and their statements on it are well known.

His words ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾: *tajalla* means "appeared," from your saying *jalawtu al-'arus* ("I unveiled the bride," that is, I displayed her); *jalawtu al-sayf* ("I polished the sword," that is, I cleared it of rust); and *tajalla al-shay'* ("the thing became manifest," that is, it was uncovered).

The meaning is: when His Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it crumble. It has also been said that the one who manifested was His command and His power; this was stated by Qutrub and others. *Dakk* is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, meaning He made it crushed and ground, so it became dust. This is according to the reading of those who read *dakkan* as a verbal noun, namely the people of Medina and the people of Basra. As for the reading of the people of Kufa, *ja'alahu dakka'* (in the feminine), the plural is *dakka'at*, like *hamra'* and *hamra'at*. It denotes a rising hillock of earth or level ground. So the meaning is that the mountain became small like a hillock or a level plain.

al-Kisa'i said: *al-dakk* means broad mountains, whose singular is *adak*. *Al-dakka'at* is the plural of *dakka'*, which means soft hills of clay, not thick ones. *Al-dakadik* is what has become flattened in the earth and has not risen. A *naqa dakka'* is a she-camel without a hump.

﴿And Moses fell down unconscious (*sa'iqan*)﴾: meaning he fell into a swoon, taken from *al-sa'iqa* (the thunderbolt). The meaning is that his state, when he fainted, became like the state of one who is struck senseless when the thunderbolt strikes him. It is said: *sa'iqa al-rajul* ("the man was struck"), so he is *sa'iq* or *mas'uq*, when the thunderbolt has struck him.

When he recovered from his swoon, he said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning I declare You far above that I should ask anything for which You have not given me permission. ﴿I have repented to You﴾, meaning I turn back from returning to the like of this question.

al-Qurtubi said: The community has agreed that this repentance was not from a sin, since the prophets are infallible (ma'sum). It has been said that it was repentance from his killing of the Copt; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri, but there is no basis for it in this context. ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾, before my people who exist in this age, who acknowledge Your greatness and majesty.

His words ﴿He said: O Moses﴾ form a resumptive clause like the one before it, containing the honouring of Moses and the special favour Allah bestowed on him.

*Al-istifa'* means choosing and selecting, that is: I have chosen you above the people of your time, ﴿by My messages﴾. Thus Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *bi-risalati* in the singular, while the rest read it in the plural.

*Al-risala* is a verbal noun, and its original form is singular. Whoever reads it in the plural seems to consider that the messages are of various kinds, so it is pluralized for the variety of types. The word *kalam* here means *taklim* (speaking/making to hear).

Allah, the Glorified, bestowed upon him favour through these two great kinds of honour: the messages, and the speaking without an intermediary. Then He commanded him to take what He had given him, that is, what He had bestowed of this noble honour, and commanded him to be among the thankful for this great gift and this sublime honour.

His words ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾: *min kulli shay'* means of all that the Children of Israel need in their religion and their worldly affairs. These tablets are the Torah. It has been said they were of green emerald; it has been said of red ruby; it has been said of chrysolite; and it has been said of solid rock.

There is disagreement about the number of the tablets and about their length and width. *Al-alwah* is the plural of *lawh*, and it was called *lawh* because the meanings shine (talawwuh) in it. Allah, the Glorified, ascribed the writing to Himself to honour what was written on the tablets, and they were written by His command, the Glorified. It has also been said that it is writing that Allah created on the tablets.

*Min kulli shay'* is in the accusative position, as the object of *kataba*. *Mau'izatan wa tafsilan* is in apposition to the position of *kulli shay'*, that is: an admonition for whoever among the Children of Israel and others takes heed, and a detailed explanation of the rulings that require detailing. ﴿So take it with strength﴾, that is, take the tablets with strength: with earnestness and vigour.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the messages, or to everything, or to the Torah. It has been said that this command is on the presumption of an implied speech, that is: "So We said to him: take it." It has also been said that *fakhudha-ha* is a substitution for His words ﴿So take what I have given you﴾. ﴿And command your people; they will take the best of it﴾, that is, the best of what is in it, that which has greater reward than other things. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ (al-Zumar: 55), and His words: ﴿who follow the best of it﴾ (al-Zumar: 18). Among the best is patience in the face of others, pardoning them, acting upon the stronger course (*'azima*) rather than the concession (*rukhsa*), acting on the obligation rather than the supererogatory, doing what is commanded, and abstaining from what is forbidden.

His words ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾: it has been said that it is the land of Egypt, which belonged to Pharaoh and his people. It has been said it is the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud. It has been said it is Hell. It has been said it is the dwellings of the disbelievers, the tyrants and the Amalekites, so that they may take warning from them. It has been said that *al-dar* means destruction.

The meaning is: I will show you the destruction of the defiantly disobedient. The reality of the meaning of *fisq* has already been explained earlier.

His words ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾: it has been said the meaning of "I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant" is "I will prevent them from understanding My Book." It has been said: "I will turn them away from belief in them." It has been said: "I will turn them away from benefiting from them, as recompense for their arrogance, as in His words: ﴿When they swerved, Allah caused their hearts to swerve﴾ (al-Saff: 5)." It has been said: "I will seal their hearts so that they do not reflect upon them nor take warning from them."

The interpretation of *ayat* has been disputed. It has been said they are the miracles. It has been said they are the revealed Books. It has been said they are the creation of the heavens and the earth. Turning them away from these means not taking warning from them. There is no barrier to carrying the word "signs" upon all of that, and carrying "turning away" upon all the meanings mentioned. As for *bi-ghayri al-haqq* ("without right"), it is either connected with *yatakabbaruna* ("they are arrogant"), meaning they are arrogant with what is not true, or it is connected with an implied element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they are arrogant while clothed in what is without right.

His words ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ are conjoined to *yatakabbaruna* and included with it in the same governing relation to the relative clause (silah).

The meaning is: I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant, who abandon belief in what they see of the signs. Under the term "every sign" fall the revealed verses, the cosmic signs, and the miracles. That is: they do not believe in any sign whatsoever.

Malik ibn Dinar read *yarawa* with a *damma* on the *ya'* in both places. The clause ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it and falls within its ruling. Likewise the clause ﴿And if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾. The meaning is that when they find a path of the paths of right guidance, they abandon and avoid it, and when they see a path of the paths of error, they follow it and choose it for themselves.

The people of Medina and the people of Basra read *al-rushd* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and sukun on the *shin*. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and the *shin*.

Abu 'Ubayda said: Abu 'Amr distinguished between *al-rashad* and *al-rushd*, saying: *al-rashad* is righteousness, and *al-rushd* is in religion.

al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh holds that *al-rushd* and *al-rashad* are like *al-sukht* and *al-sakhat* (both meaning anger).

al-Kisa'i said: What is correct from Abu 'Amr and others is what Abu 'Ubayda said.

The root meaning of *rushd* in the language is that a person attains what he desires; it is the opposite of failure.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the turning away: that is, that turning away is due to their denial. Or the demonstrative refers to arrogance, non-belief in the signs, avoiding the way of right guidance, and following the way of error. The demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is the clause ﴿that they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, that is, because of their denial of the signs and their heedlessness of them.

The relative pronoun in ﴿Those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿their deeds have become void﴾. By "the meeting of the Hereafter" is meant the meeting of the Hereafter abode: that is, their meeting with it, or their meeting with what they were promised in it, on the basis that the annexation is to a time-place (*zarf*).

*Huba't al-a'mal* (the nullification of deeds) is their becoming void: that is, the voiding of what they did which had the form of obedience, such as charity and kinship ties, even though in their state of disbelief they had no acts of obedience. It may also be intended that they become void after having been hoped to benefit them, on the supposition that they would become Muslims, in accordance with the authentic hadith: "You have embraced Islam with whatever good you had previously done."

﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾: of disbelief in Allah, denial of His signs, avoidance of the way of truth, and following the way of error.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related in *Nawadir al-Usul* from Ka'b, who said: When Allah spoke to Moses, he said: "O my Lord, is Your speech like this?" He said: "O Moses, I speak to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and I have the power of all tongues. Had I spoken to you with the full reality of My speech, you would not have been anything."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related from the hadith of Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah spoke to Moses on the day of Tur, He spoke to him with other than the speech with which He had spoken to him on the day He called to him. Moses said to Him: 'O my Lord, is this Your speech with which You spoke to me?' He said: 'O Moses, I spoke to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and I have the power of all tongues and more than that.' When Moses returned to the Children of Israel, they said: 'O Moses, describe for us the speech of the Most Merciful.' He said: 'You cannot bear it. Have you not seen the sounds of the thunderbolts that kill? In the sweetest sweetness that you heard, that is near to it but is not it.'"

(p-500) Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, related from Abu al-Huwayrith Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya that he said: Allah only spoke to Musa (Moses) to the extent of what he could bear of His speech. Had He spoken to him with all of His speech, nothing could have endured it. Musa remained forty nights, and no one who saw Him died except from the light of the Lord of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," that it means: give me [the ability to] look at You.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: When he heard the speech, he desired to see [Allah].

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: When Musa said to his Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, "(p-500) My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," Allah said, "O Musa, you will not see Me." He said: That is, "You will not see Me, and that will never happen." "O Musa, no one will see Me and live." Musa said, "My Lord, I see You and then die; that is dearer to me than not seeing You and then living." Then Allah said to Musa, "O Musa, look at the great, tall, firm mountain. If it remains in its place," meaning: if it stays firm in its place and does not collapse before some of what it sees of My greatness, "then you will see Me," [meaning] you, because of your weakness and humiliation. But if the mountain collapses under its strength, firmness and greatness, then you are weaker and more humble.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi in al-Kamil, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related by several chains from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust," and said, "Like this," and he gestured with his two fingers, placing his thumbs on the joint of the little finger. In another wording: on the upper joint of the little finger. The mountain then sank, and Musa fell down unconscious.

In another wording: the mountain sank into the earth and keeps sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection.

This hadith is sound according to the conditions of Muslim.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: The mountain that Allah commanded him to look at was Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related from Ibn Abbas: "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain." He said: Only the size of the little finger of Him manifested itself. "He made it crumble," he said: into dust. "And Musa fell down unconscious," he said: he was overcome, insensible.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Daylami related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to the mountain, six mountains flew off from awe of His greatness. Three fell in Medina and three in Mecca. In Medina: Uhud, Warqan and Radwa. In Mecca: Hira, Thabir and Thawr."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to Musa, seven mountains scattered. Five of them were in the Hijaz and two in Yemen. In the Hijaz: Uhud, Thabir, Hira, Thawr and Warqan. In Yemen: Hudur and Sabr."

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that when his Lord spoke to Musa, he desired to look at Him, so he asked. [Allah] said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain." He said: The angels surrounded the mountain, and angels surrounded the angels with fire, and fire surrounded them, and angels surrounded the fire. Then his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, and of Him there manifested only the size of a little finger. He made the mountain crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious. He remained unconscious for as long as Allah willed. Then he recovered and said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers among the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: Allah wrote the tablets for Musa while he heard the scratching of the pens on a tablet.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The tablets that were sent down to Musa were of the lote tree of Paradise, and the length of the tablet was twelve cubits."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: They used to say the tablets were of ruby, but I say they were of emerald, and their writing was gold. Allah wrote them with His own hand, and the people of the heavens heard the scratching of the pens.

I say: May Allah have mercy on Sa'id; how much he could have dispensed with what he said on his own account. Such a matter is not said by personal opinion or conjecture. What is most likely is that many of the salaf (the early generations) used to ask the Jews about these matters, which is why the reports differed and became confused. This one says [they were] of wood, another says of ruby, another says of emerald, another says of chrysolite, another says of silk brocade, and another says of stone.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, regarding "And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything, every thing": they were commanded with it and forbidden from it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar.

The salaf differed greatly about what was written on the tablets. There is no objection to understanding what was written as including all of that, since there is no contradiction.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding "So take it with strength": with diligence and resolve. "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": he said, the abode of the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding "And order your people to take the best of it": Musa was commanded to take it with more strictness than his people were commanded.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding "So take it with strength": with obedience.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "So take it with strength": meaning with diligence and striving. "And order your people to take the best of it": [he said] with the best of what they find in it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": their destination in the Hereafter.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah that he said: Their dwellings in this world.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan that he said: Hell.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah that he said: Egypt (Misr).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "I will turn away from My signs": from reflecting upon My signs.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj regarding "My signs," that he said: [They are] the creation of the heavens and the earth and the signs within them. "I will turn them away from reflecting upon them or taking lessons from them."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sufyan ibn Uyayna regarding the verse that he said: "I will strip from them the understanding of the Qur'an."

The lam in ﴿لِمِيقاتِنا﴾ (*li-miqatina*, "for Our appointed time") indicates specificity: his coming was specifically at the appointed time mentioned, meaning that he came at the promised time, and his Lord spoke to him, that is, made him hear His speech without an intermediary.

Regarding His words ﴿Show me Yourself that I may look at You﴾: the meaning is "Show me Yourself so that I may look at You." He asked to see Him out of longing for the vision, after He had made him hear His speech.

Moses' request to see Allah indicates that the vision is permissible in principle in his view. Had it been impossible in his view, he would not have asked for it. The answer, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, indicates either that he will not see Him at this time for which he asked, or that Allah is not seen as long as the seer is alive in this worldly abode.

As for the vision in the Hereafter, it has been established by mutawatir (widely transmitted, certain) hadiths, a mutawatir that is not hidden from anyone who knows the pure Sunnah. Dispute over such matters and evasion bring no benefit. The path of truth is clear. However, adherence to a school of thought in which a person has been raised, and in which he found his forefathers and the people of his land, together with a lack of attention to what Allah requires of His servants under this pure law, leads to partisanship (ta'assub). The partisan, even if his sight is sound, his insight is blind and his ear is deaf to hearing the truth. He rejects the truth while thinking that he rejects only falsehood, and he supposes that what he was raised upon is the truth, out of heedlessness and ignorance of the correct reflection (nazar) that Allah has made obligatory upon him and of receiving what the Book and the Sunnah have brought with acceptance and submission.

How few are the fair-minded after the emergence of these schools in the fundamentals (usul) and the branches (furu')! The door of truth has become closed by them, and the way of fairness has become rugged. The matter belongs to Allah, the Glorified, and guidance comes from Him. As a poet said:

*The youth refuses except to follow his desire, though the path of truth is clear to him.*

The clause ﴿He said: You will not see Me﴾ is resumptive (mustanafah), since it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" The istidrak (corrective exception) in His words ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me﴾ means that you cannot withstand My vision, and nor can what is greater than you in bulk, firmness and strength withstand it, namely the mountain. So look at it: if it remains firm in its place and does not shake when it sees Me, then you will see Me; and if it is weak in that respect, you are weaker than it. This statement is in the position of setting forth a parable for Moses, peace be upon him, through the mountain. It has also been said that it is of the type of conditioning upon the impossible (ta'liq bil-muhal). On the assumption of this, it concerns the vision in this world, for the reason we have mentioned.

Both the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) and the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari) have clung to this verse. The Mu'tazila argued from His words ﴿You will not see Me﴾ and from His command to look at the mountain. The Ash'ariyya said that making the vision dependent on the mountain's remaining firm indicates that it is permissible and not impossible. You are not unaware that the vision in the Hereafter is entirely outside all of this, and the disagreement between them concerns it, not the vision in this world. The disagreement over it existed in the time of the Companions, and their statements on it are well known.

His words ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾: it has been said that it is the land of Egypt, which belonged to Pharaoh and his people. It has been said it is the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud. It has been said it is Hell. It has been said it is the dwellings of the disbelievers, the tyrants and the Amalekites, so that they may take warning from them. It has been said that *al-dar* means destruction.

The meaning is: I will show you the destruction of the defiantly disobedient. The reality of the meaning of *fisq* has already been explained earlier.

His words ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾: it has been said the meaning of "I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant" is "I will prevent them from understanding My Book." It has been said: "I will turn them away from belief in them." It has been said: "I will turn them away from benefiting from them, as recompense for their arrogance, as in His words: ﴿When they swerved, Allah caused their hearts to swerve﴾ (al-Saff: 5)." It has been said: "I will seal their hearts so that they do not reflect upon them nor take warning from them."

The interpretation of *ayat* has been disputed. It has been said they are the miracles. It has been said they are the revealed Books. It has been said they are the creation of the heavens and the earth. Turning them away from these means not taking warning from them. There is no barrier to carrying the word "signs" upon all of that, and carrying "turning away" upon all the meanings mentioned. As for *bi-ghayri al-haqq* ("without right"), it is either connected with *yatakabbaruna* ("they are arrogant"), meaning they are arrogant with what is not true, or it is connected with an implied element that stands as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they are arrogant while clothed in what is without right.

His words ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ are conjoined to *yatakabbaruna* and included with it in the same governing relation to the relative clause (silah).

The meaning is: I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant, who abandon belief in what they see of the signs. Under the term "every sign" fall the revealed verses, the cosmic signs, and the miracles. That is: they do not believe in any sign whatsoever.

Malik ibn Dinar read *yarawa* with a *damma* on the *ya'* in both places. The clause ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾ is conjoined to what precedes it and falls within its ruling. Likewise the clause ﴿And if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾. The meaning is that when they find a path of the paths of right guidance, they abandon and avoid it, and when they see a path of the paths of error, they follow it and choose it for themselves.

The people of Medina and the people of Basra read *al-rushd* with a *damma* on the *ra'* and sukun on the *shin*. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a *fatha* on the *ra'* and the *shin*.

Abu 'Ubayda said: Abu 'Amr distinguished between *al-rashad* and *al-rushd*, saying: *al-rashad* is righteousness, and *al-rushd* is in religion.

al-Nahhas said: Sibawayh holds that *al-rushd* and *al-rashad* are like *al-sukht* and *al-sakhat* (both meaning anger).

al-Kisa'i said: What is correct from Abu 'Amr and others is what Abu 'Ubayda said.

The root meaning of *rushd* in the language is that a person attains what he desires; it is the opposite of failure.

The demonstrative in His words ﴿that﴾ refers to the turning away: that is, that turning away is due to their denial. Or the demonstrative refers to arrogance, non-belief in the signs, avoiding the way of right guidance, and following the way of error. The demonstrative is the subject, and its predicate is the clause ﴿that they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, that is, because of their denial of the signs and their heedlessness of them.

The relative pronoun in ﴿Those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿their deeds have become void﴾. By "the meeting of the Hereafter" is meant the meeting of the Hereafter abode: that is, their meeting with it, or their meeting with what they were promised in it, on the basis that the annexation is to a time-place (*zarf*).

*Huba't al-a'mal* (the nullification of deeds) is their becoming void: that is, the voiding of what they did which had the form of obedience, such as charity and kinship ties, even though in their state of disbelief they had no acts of obedience. It may also be intended that they become void after having been hoped to benefit them, on the supposition that they would become Muslims, in accordance with the authentic hadith: "You have embraced Islam with whatever good you had previously done."

﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾: of disbelief in Allah, denial of His signs, avoidance of the way of truth, and following the way of error.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi related in *Nawadir al-Usul* from Ka'b, who said: When Allah spoke to Moses, he said: "O my Lord, is Your speech like this?" He said: "O Moses, I speak to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and I have the power of all tongues. Had I spoken to you with the full reality of My speech, you would not have been anything."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related from the hadith of Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah spoke to Moses on the day of Tur, He spoke to him with other than the speech with which He had spoken to him on the day He called to him. Moses said to Him: 'O my Lord, is this Your speech with which You spoke to me?' He said: 'O Moses, I spoke to you with the power of ten thousand tongues, and I have the power of all tongues and more than that.' When Moses returned to the Children of Israel, they said: 'O Moses, describe for us the speech of the Most Merciful.' He said: 'You cannot bear it. Have you not seen the sounds of the thunderbolts that kill? In the sweetest sweetness that you heard, that is near to it but is not it.'"

(p-500) Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, related from Abu al-Huwayrith Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya that he said: Allah only spoke to Musa (Moses) to the extent of what he could bear of His speech. Had He spoken to him with all of His speech, nothing could have endured it. Musa remained forty nights, and no one who saw Him died except from the light of the Lord of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," that it means: give me [the ability to] look at You.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: When he heard the speech, he desired to see [Allah].

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: When Musa said to his Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, "(p-500) My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," Allah said, "O Musa, you will not see Me." He said: That is, "You will not see Me, and that will never happen." "O Musa, no one will see Me and live." Musa said, "My Lord, I see You and then die; that is dearer to me than not seeing You and then living." Then Allah said to Musa, "O Musa, look at the great, tall, firm mountain. If it remains in its place," meaning: if it stays firm in its place and does not collapse before some of what it sees of My greatness, "then you will see Me," [meaning] you, because of your weakness and humiliation. But if the mountain collapses under its strength, firmness and greatness, then you are weaker and more humble.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi in al-Kamil, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related by several chains from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust," and said, "Like this," and he gestured with his two fingers, placing his thumbs on the joint of the little finger. In another wording: on the upper joint of the little finger. The mountain then sank, and Musa fell down unconscious.

In another wording: the mountain sank into the earth and keeps sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection.

This hadith is sound according to the conditions of Muslim.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: The mountain that Allah commanded him to look at was Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related from Ibn Abbas: "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain." He said: Only the size of the little finger of Him manifested itself. "He made it crumble," he said: into dust. "And Musa fell down unconscious," he said: he was overcome, insensible.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Daylami related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to the mountain, six mountains flew off from awe of His greatness. Three fell in Medina and three in Mecca. In Medina: Uhud, Warqan and Radwa. In Mecca: Hira, Thabir and Thawr."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to Musa, seven mountains scattered. Five of them were in the Hijaz and two in Yemen. In the Hijaz: Uhud, Thabir, Hira, Thawr and Warqan. In Yemen: Hudur and Sabr."

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that when his Lord spoke to Musa, he desired to look at Him, so he asked. [Allah] said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain." He said: The angels surrounded the mountain, and angels surrounded the angels with fire, and fire surrounded them, and angels surrounded the fire. Then his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, and of Him there manifested only the size of a little finger. He made the mountain crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious. He remained unconscious for as long as Allah willed. Then he recovered and said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers among the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: Allah wrote the tablets for Musa while he heard the scratching of the pens on a tablet.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The tablets that were sent down to Musa were of the lote tree of Paradise, and the length of the tablet was twelve cubits."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: They used to say the tablets were of ruby, but I say they were of emerald, and their writing was gold. Allah wrote them with His own hand, and the people of the heavens heard the scratching of the pens.

I say: May Allah have mercy on Sa'id; how much he could have dispensed with what he said on his own account. Such a matter is not said by personal opinion or conjecture. What is most likely is that many of the salaf (the early generations) used to ask the Jews about these matters, which is why the reports differed and became confused. This one says [they were] of wood, another says of ruby, another says of emerald, another says of chrysolite, another says of silk brocade, and another says of stone.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, regarding "And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything, every thing": they were commanded with it and forbidden from it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar.

The salaf differed greatly about what was written on the tablets. There is no objection to understanding what was written as including all of that, since there is no contradiction.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding "So take it with strength": with diligence and resolve. "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": he said, the abode of the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding "And order your people to take the best of it": Musa was commanded to take it with more strictness than his people were commanded.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding "So take it with strength": with obedience.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "So take it with strength": meaning with diligence and striving. "And order your people to take the best of it": [he said] with the best of what they find in it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": their destination in the Hereafter.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah that he said: Their dwellings in this world.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan that he said: Hell.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah that he said: Egypt (Misr).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "I will turn away from My signs": from reflecting upon My signs.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj regarding "My signs," that he said: [They are] the creation of the heavens and the earth and the signs within them. "I will turn them away from reflecting upon them or taking lessons from them."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sufyan ibn Uyayna regarding the verse that he said: "I will strip from them the understanding of the Qur'an."

The lam in ﴿لِمِيقاتِنا﴾ (*li-miqatina*, "for Our appointed time") indicates specificity: his coming was specifically at the appointed time mentioned, meaning that he came at the promised time, and his Lord spoke to him, that is, made him hear His speech without an intermediary.

Regarding His words ﴿Show me Yourself that I may look at You﴾: the meaning is "Show me Yourself so that I may look at You." He asked to see Him out of longing for the vision, after He had made him hear His speech.

Moses' request to see Allah indicates that the vision is permissible in principle in his view. Had it been impossible in his view, he would not have asked for it. The answer, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, indicates either that he will not see Him at this time for which he asked, or that Allah is not seen as long as the seer is alive in this worldly abode.

As for the vision in the Hereafter, it has been established by mutawatir (widely transmitted, certain) hadiths, a mutawatir that is not hidden from anyone who knows the pure Sunnah. Dispute over such matters and evasion bring no benefit. The path of truth is clear. However, adherence to a school of thought in which a person has been raised, and in which he found his forefathers and the people of his land, together with a lack of attention to what Allah requires of His servants under this pure law, leads to partisanship (ta'assub). The partisan, even if his sight is sound, his insight is blind and his ear is deaf to hearing the truth. He rejects the truth while thinking that he rejects only falsehood, and he supposes that what he was raised upon is the truth, out of heedlessness and ignorance of the correct reflection (nazar) that Allah has made obligatory upon him and of receiving what the Book and the Sunnah have brought with acceptance and submission.

How few are the fair-minded after the emergence of these schools in the fundamentals (usul) and the branches (furu')! The door of truth has become closed by them, and the way of fairness has become rugged. The matter belongs to Allah, the Glorified, and guidance comes from Him. As a poet said:

*The youth refuses except to follow his desire, though the path of truth is clear to him.*

The clause ﴿He said: You will not see Me﴾ is resumptive (mustanafah), since it is an answer to an implied question, as if it were said: "What did Allah say to him?" The istidrak (corrective exception) in His words ﴿But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me﴾ means that you cannot withstand My vision, and nor can what is greater than you in bulk, firmness and strength withstand it, namely the mountain. So look at it: if it remains firm in its place and does not shake when it sees Me, then you will see Me; and if it is weak in that respect, you are weaker than it. This statement is in the position of setting forth a parable for Moses, peace be upon him, through the mountain. It has also been said that it is of the type of conditioning upon the impossible (ta'liq bil-muhal). On the assumption of this, it concerns the vision in this world, for the reason we have mentioned.

Both the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) and the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari) have clung to this verse. The Mu'tazila argued from His words ﴿You will not see Me﴾ and from His command to look at the mountain. The Ash'ariyya said that making the vision dependent on the mountain's remaining firm indicates that it is permissible and not impossible. You are not unaware that the vision in the Hereafter is entirely outside all of this, and the disagreement between them concerns it, not the vision in this world. The disagreement over it existed in the time of the Companions, and their statements on it are well known.

His words ﴿When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾: *tajalla* means "appeared," from your saying *jalawtu al-'arus* ("I unveiled the bride," that is, I displayed her); *jalawtu al-sayf* ("I polished the sword," that is, I cleared it of rust); and *tajalla al-shay'* ("the thing became manifest," that is, it was uncovered).

The meaning is: when His Lord appeared to the mountain, He made it crumble. It has also been said that the one who manifested was His command and His power; this was stated by Qutrub and others. *Dakk* is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, meaning He made it crushed and ground, so it became dust. This is according to the reading of those who read *dakkan* as a verbal noun, namely the people of Medina and the people of Basra. As for the reading of the people of Kufa, *ja'alahu dakka'* (in the feminine), the plural is *dakka'at*, like *hamra'* and *hamra'at*. It denotes a rising hillock of earth or level ground. So the meaning is that the mountain became small like a hillock or a level plain.

al-Kisa'i said: *al-dakk* means broad mountains, whose singular is *adak*. *Al-dakka'at* is the plural of *dakka'*, which means soft hills of clay, not thick ones. *Al-dakadik* is what has become flattened in the earth and has not risen. A *naqa dakka'* is a she-camel without a hump.

﴿And Moses fell down unconscious (*sa'iqan*)﴾: meaning he fell into a swoon, taken from *al-sa'iqa* (the thunderbolt). The meaning is that his state, when he fainted, became like the state of one who is struck senseless when the thunderbolt strikes him. It is said: *sa'iqa al-rajul* ("the man was struck"), so he is *sa'iq* or *mas'uq*, when the thunderbolt has struck him.

When he recovered from his swoon, he said: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, meaning I declare You far above that I should ask anything for which You have not given me permission. ﴿I have repented to You﴾, meaning I turn back from returning to the like of this question.

al-Qurtubi said: The community has agreed that this repentance was not from a sin, since the prophets are infallible (ma'sum). It has been said that it was repentance from his killing of the Copt; this was mentioned by al-Qushayri, but there is no basis for it in this context. ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾, before my people who exist in this age, who acknowledge Your greatness and majesty.

His words ﴿He said: O Moses﴾ form a resumptive clause like the one before it, containing the honouring of Moses and the special favour Allah bestowed on him.

*Al-istifa'* means choosing and selecting, that is: I have chosen you above the people of your time, ﴿by My messages﴾. Thus Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read *bi-risalati* in the singular, while the rest read it in the plural.

*Al-risala* is a verbal noun, and its original form is singular. Whoever reads it in the plural seems to consider that the messages are of various kinds, so it is pluralized for the variety of types. The word *kalam* here means *taklim* (speaking/making to hear).

Allah, the Glorified, bestowed upon him favour through these two great kinds of honour: the messages, and the speaking without an intermediary. Then He commanded him to take what He had given him, that is, what He had bestowed of this noble honour, and commanded him to be among the thankful for this great gift and this sublime honour.

His words ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾: *min kulli shay'* means of all that the Children of Israel need in their religion and their worldly affairs. These tablets are the Torah. It has been said they were of green emerald; it has been said of red ruby; it has been said of chrysolite; and it has been said of solid rock.

There is disagreement about the number of the tablets and about their length and width. *Al-alwah* is the plural of *lawh*, and it was called *lawh* because the meanings shine (talawwuh) in it. Allah, the Glorified, ascribed the writing to Himself to honour what was written on the tablets, and they were written by His command, the Glorified. It has also been said that it is writing that Allah created on the tablets.

*Min kulli shay'* is in the accusative position, as the object of *kataba*. *Mau'izatan wa tafsilan* is in apposition to the position of *kulli shay'*, that is: an admonition for whoever among the Children of Israel and others takes heed, and a detailed explanation of the rulings that require detailing. ﴿So take it with strength﴾, that is, take the tablets with strength: with earnestness and vigour.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to the messages, or to everything, or to the Torah. It has been said that this command is on the presumption of an implied speech, that is: "So We said to him: take it." It has also been said that *fakhudha-ha* is a substitution for His words ﴿So take what I have given you﴾. ﴿And command your people; they will take the best of it﴾, that is, the best of what is in it, that which has greater reward than other things. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Follow the best of what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ (al-Zumar: 55), and His words: ﴿who follow the best of it﴾ (al-Zumar: 18). Among the best is patience in the face of others, pardoning them, acting upon the stronger course (*'azima*) rather than the concession (*rukhsa*), acting on the obligation rather than the supererogatory, doing what is commanded, and abstaining from what is forbidden.

His words ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾: it has been said that it is the land of Egypt, which belonged to Pharaoh and his people. It has been said it is the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud. It has been said it is Hell. It has been said it is the dwellings of the disbelievers, the tyrants and the Amalekites, so that they may take warning from them. It has been said that *al-dar* means destruction.

The meaning is: I will show you the destruction of the defiantly disobedient. The reality of the meaning of *fisq* has already been explained earlier.

Have you not seen the sounds of the thunderbolts that kill? In the sweetest sweetness that you heard, that is near to it but is not it.'"

(p-500) Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, related from Abu al-Huwayrith Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya that he said: Allah only spoke to Musa (Moses) to the extent of what he could bear of His speech. Had He spoken to him with all of His speech, nothing could have endured it. Musa remained forty nights, and no one who saw Him died except from the light of the Lord of the worlds.

Ibn Jarir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," that it means: give me [the ability to] look at You.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Qatadah, regarding the verse, that he said: When he heard the speech, he desired to see [Allah].

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: When Musa said to his Lord, may He be blessed and exalted, "(p-500) My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You," Allah said, "O Musa, you will not see Me." He said: That is, "You will not see Me, and that will never happen." "O Musa, no one will see Me and live." Musa said, "My Lord, I see You and then die; that is dearer to me than not seeing You and then living." Then Allah said to Musa, "O Musa, look at the great, tall, firm mountain. If it remains in its place," meaning: if it stays firm in its place and does not collapse before some of what it sees of My greatness, "then you will see Me," [meaning] you, because of your weakness and humiliation. But if the mountain collapses under its strength, firmness and greatness, then you are weaker and more humble.

Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Adi in al-Kamil, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related by several chains from Anas ibn Malik that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse, "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust," and said, "Like this," and he gestured with his two fingers, placing his thumbs on the joint of the little finger. In another wording: on the upper joint of the little finger. The mountain then sank, and Musa fell down unconscious.

In another wording: the mountain sank into the earth and keeps sinking into it until the Day of Resurrection.

This hadith is sound according to the conditions of Muslim.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas that he said: The mountain that Allah commanded him to look at was Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and al-Bayhaqi in Kitab al-Ru'ya related from Ibn Abbas: "When his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain." He said: Only the size of the little finger of Him manifested itself. "He made it crumble," he said: into dust. "And Musa fell down unconscious," he said: he was overcome, insensible.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, and al-Daylami related from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to the mountain, six mountains flew off from awe of His greatness. Three fell in Medina and three in Mecca. In Medina: Uhud, Warqan and Radwa. In Mecca: Hira, Thabir and Thawr."

Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related from Anas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah manifested Himself to Musa, seven mountains scattered. Five of them were in the Hijaz and two in Yemen. In the Hijaz: Uhud, Thabir, Hira, Thawr and Warqan. In Yemen: Hudur and Sabr."

Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas that when his Lord spoke to Musa, he desired to look at Him, so he asked. [Allah] said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain." He said: The angels surrounded the mountain, and angels surrounded the angels with fire, and fire surrounded them, and angels surrounded the fire. Then his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, and of Him there manifested only the size of a little finger. He made the mountain crumble, and Musa fell down unconscious. He remained unconscious for as long as Allah willed. Then he recovered and said, "Glory be to You! I repent to You, and I am the first of the believers among the Children of Israel."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ali ibn Abi Talib that he said: Allah wrote the tablets for Musa while he heard the scratching of the pens on a tablet.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The tablets that were sent down to Musa were of the lote tree of Paradise, and the length of the tablet was twelve cubits."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said: They used to say the tablets were of ruby, but I say they were of emerald, and their writing was gold. Allah wrote them with His own hand, and the people of the heavens heard the scratching of the pens.

I say: May Allah have mercy on Sa'id; how much he could have dispensed with what he said on his own account. Such a matter is not said by personal opinion or conjecture. What is most likely is that many of the salaf (the early generations) used to ask the Jews about these matters, which is why the reports differed and became confused. This one says [they were] of wood, another says of ruby, another says of emerald, another says of chrysolite, another says of silk brocade, and another says of stone.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, regarding "And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything, every thing": they were commanded with it and forbidden from it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid something similar.

The salaf differed greatly about what was written on the tablets. There is no objection to understanding what was written as including all of that, since there is no contradiction.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas regarding "So take it with strength": with diligence and resolve. "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": he said, the abode of the disbelievers.

Ibn Jarir related from him regarding "And order your people to take the best of it": Musa was commanded to take it with more strictness than his people were commanded.

Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas regarding "So take it with strength": with obedience.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "So take it with strength": meaning with diligence and striving. "And order your people to take the best of it": [he said] with the best of what they find in it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid regarding "I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient": their destination in the Hereafter.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah that he said: Their dwellings in this world.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan that he said: Hell.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah that he said: Egypt (Misr).

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi regarding His words, "I will turn away from My signs": from reflecting upon My signs.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj regarding "My signs," that he said: [They are] the creation of the heavens and the earth and the signs within them. "I will turn them away from reflecting upon them or taking lessons from them."

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Sufyan ibn Uyayna regarding the verse that he said: "I will strip from them the understanding of the Qur'an."

(p-501) His words: ﴿And the people of Musa took, after him,﴾ meaning after his departure to the Mount, ﴿from their ornaments﴾ a calf. The phrase ﴿from their ornaments﴾ is connected to *ittakhadha* (took), or to an omitted word functioning as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The *min* may be partitive (*lil-tab'id*), of origin (*lil-ibtida'*), or explanatory (*lil-bayan*). *Hulii* is the plural of *hulyun* (ornament).

The people of Madina and the people of Basra read *min hulyihim* with a *damma* on the *ha'* and a shadda on the *ya'*. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a *kasra* on the *ha'*. Ya'qub read it with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and without a shadda on the *ya'*.

Al-Nahhas said: The plural of *hulyun* is *huliyyun* and *hiliyyun*, like *thadyun* becoming *thadiyyun* and *thidiyyun*. The original form is *hulwiyy*; the *waw* was assimilated into the *ya'*, so the *lam* took a *kasra* because it is adjacent to the *ya'*. The *ha'* may take a *kasra* because of the *kasra* on the *lam*, or a *damma* in keeping with the original form. The ornaments are attributed to them although they belonged to others, because attribution is permitted on the slightest connection. *'Ijlan* is the object of *ittakhadha*. It was said that it has the meaning of "making," so it takes two objects, the second of which is omitted: that is, they took a calf as a god. *Jasadan* is a substitute (*badal*) for *'ijlan*. It was said that it is a qualifier of it. *Al-khuwar* is the lowing. It is said: *khara yakhuru khawran* when it lows, and likewise *khara yukharu khuwaran*.

The taking of the calf is attributed to the whole people, although it was made by al-Samiri alone, because he was one of them and they approved of his action.

It is narrated that when Musa promised his people thirty nights and then delayed among them for the additional ten, al-Samiri, who was obeyed among the Children of Israel, said to them: "With you are ornaments from the ornaments of the family of Pharaoh, which you borrowed from them to adorn yourselves for the festival, and you went out with them while they are still with you. Allah has drowned their people, the Copts, so bring them here." They handed them over to him, and he made from them the calf mentioned.

His words: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾. The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach; that is: did they not take heed that this which they took as a god cannot speak to them, let alone have the power to bring them benefit or repel harm from them, and ﴿nor guide them to a way﴾, meaning a clear path they could follow. ﴿They took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾, meaning they took it as a god and were wrongdoers, either to themselves in taking it or in everything, of which this taking is one part.

His words: ﴿And when they were stricken with remorse﴾, meaning they regretted and were bewildered after Musa returned from the appointed meeting. It is said of a regretful and bewildered person: *qad sugita fi yadihi* (he has been struck in his hand).

Al-Akhfash said: it is said *suqita fi yadihi* and *usqita*. Whoever says *saqata fi aydihim* in the active form, the meaning according to him is: remorse fell. The origin of this is that whoever's regret and grief become intense bites his hand in sorrow, so his hand becomes a thing that has fallen into, because his mouth has fallen upon it.

Al-Azhari, al-Zajjaj, al-Nahhas and others said: the meaning of *suqita fi aydihim* is: in their hearts and souls, just as one says that something disliked has occurred in his hand. Although it is impossible for it to be in the hand, this is a metaphor for what occurs in the heart and soul by comparison with what occurs in the hand, because dealing with things is generally done by the hand. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ (al-Hajj: 10). Also, remorse, though it settles in the heart, its effect appears in the body, because the remorseful person bites his hand and strikes one hand against the other. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he began to turn over his palms over what he had spent upon it﴾ (al-Kahf: 42). And from this: ﴿And the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾ (al-Furqan: 27), meaning from remorse. Also, the remorseful person places his chin on his hand.

﴿And they saw that they had gone astray﴾ is conjoined to *suqita* (was struck): that is, they realized that they had gone astray by taking the calf, and that they had been tested with disobedience to Allah, glorified is He. They said: ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verbs in both places with the second-person (*ta'*) form, while the rest read them with the third-person (*ya'*) form. The *lam* is for oath, and its answer is *la-nakunanna min al-khasirin*.

In these words of theirs there is what conveys seeking refuge in Allah, humble supplication, and earnest entreaty in asking. What is reported of them here took place after Musa's return, as will be shown in Surat Ta-Ha, if Allah wills. He placed it here before his return for the purpose of narrating what proceeded from them of speech and action in one place.

His words: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾. This is an explanation of what happened from Musa after his return. *Ghadbana* and *asifan* are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*hal*). *Al-Asif* is intense anger. It was said: it is a station beyond anger, more intense than it. It has the forms *asif*, *asif*, *asfan*, *asuf*. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: Allah had informed him before his return that they had been tested, so for that reason he returned angry and grieved. He said: ﴿Wretched is what you did after me﴾. This is a reproach from Musa to his people, meaning: wretched is the deed you did after me, that is, after my absence from you. It is said: *khalafahu bi-khayr* and *khalafahu bi-sharr*. He denounced what they had done and reproached them, because they had witnessed signs which, some of them, require restraint and faith in Allah alone. But this is the way of the Children of Israel: changing states and unstable deeds. Then he said, rebuking them: ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ *Al-'ajalah* is to advance something before its time. It is said: *'ajiltu al-shay'* meaning I preceded it, and *a'jaltu al-rajul* meaning I made him act hastily. The meaning is: you hastened ahead of waiting for the command of your Lord, that is, His appointed time that He promised me, which was forty nights, and so you did what you did. It was also said: its meaning is: you hastened the wrath of your Lord. It was also said: its meaning is: you hastened to worship the calf before the command of your Lord came to you. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, that is, he cast them down because of the intense anger and grief that overcame him when he came upon his people while they were devoted to worshipping the calf.

His words: ﴿And he seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward him﴾, that is, he seized his brother Harun by the head or by the hair of his head, while dragging him toward himself. He did this to him because he had not denounced al-Samiri or anyone else for what he saw of the Children of Israel's worship of the calf. Harun said, excusing himself to him: ﴿Son of my mother, indeed the people oppressed me and nearly killed me﴾, that is, I was unable to change what they did because of these two matters: their oppression of me and their approaching to kill me. He said "son of my mother" although he was his brother from both father and mother, because it is a word of gentleness and tenderness, and because she was, as it is said, a believer.

Al-Zajjaj said: It was said that Harun was the brother of Musa from his mother only, not from his father.

It was read *ibna umma* with a *fatha* on the *mim*, likening him to *khamsata 'ashara* (fifteen), so it became like your saying: *ya khamsata 'ashara aqbilu* (O fifteen, come forward).

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd said: the *fatha* is on the presumption of *ya ibna umma* (O son of my mother) with the *alif* omitted.

The Basrans said this view is erroneous, because the *alif* is light and is not omitted. Rather, making the two nouns one noun like *khamsata 'ashara* is the correct analysis. This was preferred by al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas.

As for the one who reads with a *kasra* on the *mim*, it is on the presumption of *ibna ummi* (son of my mother), then the *ya'* was omitted and the *kasra* was kept to indicate it.

Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim said: *ibna umm* with a *kasra* is like your saying *ya ghulamu aqbil* (O boy, come). It is an irregular dialect, and reading with it is far-fetched; this applies only to what is a construct (*mudaf*) to you.

It was read *ibna ummi* with the *ya'* retained.

His words: ﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾. *Al-shamatah* is the joy of enemies at the calamities that befall those they oppose. From this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the evil of decree, from the descent of misery, from the severity of calamity, and from the gloating of enemies," and it is in the Sahih. From this is the saying of the poet:

When time drags its chest over a people, it makes others kneel down.

So say to those who gloat over us: "Be aware, the gloaters will meet what we met."

The meaning is: do not do to me what would be a cause of gloating from them.

Mujahid and Malik ibn Dinar read *fa-la tashmat bi al-a'da'* with a *fatha* on the initial letter of the imperfect and on the *mim*, and a *raf'* on *al-a'da'*, on the basis that the verb is attributed to them: that is, that would not come from them because of an action you take against me.

It was narrated from Mujahid that he read *tushmit* as mentioned before, with *nasb* (accusative) on *al-a'da'*.

Ibn Jinni said: the meaning is: do not let them gloat over me, you, O Lord. This is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ (al-Baqarah: 15) and similar, then he returned to the intended meaning and supposed a verb which he used to put *al-a'da'* in the accusative, as if he had said: O Lord, do not let the enemies gloat over me. How far this reading is from correctness, and how far its interpretation is from the aspects of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

His words: ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning do not place me, by Your anger at me, among the number of the wrongdoing people, that is, those who worshipped the calf; or do not believe that I am among them.

His words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother"﴾. This is a new sentence answering an assumed question, as if it was said: what did Musa say after Harun's words? So it was said: he said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother." He first sought forgiveness for himself, and then for his brother, to remove from his brother what he feared of gloating. He thus apologized for what he had done to his brother and showed that there was no justification for it, and he sought forgiveness from Allah for what had proceeded from him toward him. Then he sought forgiveness for his brother in case there had been any shortcoming on his part in what he was obliged to do by denouncing them and changing what they had done. Then he asked that both of them be admitted into the mercy of Allah, which encompasses all things, for He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿And the people of Musa took...﴾, the verse: when they buried it, al-Samiri threw upon it a handful of dust from the hoofprint of the horse of Jibril, peace be upon him.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning the verse: he said: they borrowed ornaments from the family of Pharaoh, and al-Samiri gathered them and fashioned from them a calf, and made it a body of flesh and blood that had a lowing.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning His words: *khuwar*, he said: it is the sound.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: the calf lowed once, without moaning. Do you not see that Allah said: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾?

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿Was struck in their hands﴾, he said: they regretted.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated through various chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning *asifan*: he said: grieved.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: *al-asaf* is a station beyond anger, more intense than that.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: *al-asaf* is intense anger.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Musa threw down the tablets, they broke, and they were lifted up except for a sixth of them.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, who said: Allah lifted up six-sevenths of them and one-seventh remained.

Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from Mujahid or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: When Musa threw them, the detailed explanation departed and the guidance remained.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: they were nine, of which two tablets were lifted and seven remained.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, he said: with the companions of the calf.
