It was also said: its meaning is: you hastened to worship the calf before the command of your Lord came to you. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, that is, he cast them down because of the intense anger and grief that overcame him when he came upon his people while they were devoted to worshipping the calf.

His words: ﴿And he seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward him﴾, that is, he seized his brother Harun by the head or by the hair of his head, while dragging him toward himself. He did this to him because he had not denounced al-Samiri or anyone else for what he saw of the Children of Israel's worship of the calf. Harun said, excusing himself to him: ﴿Son of my mother, indeed the people oppressed me and nearly killed me﴾, that is, I was unable to change what they did because of these two matters: their oppression of me and their approaching to kill me. He said "son of my mother" although he was his brother from both father and mother, because it is a word of gentleness and tenderness, and because she was, as it is said, a believer.

Al-Zajjaj said: It was said that Harun was the brother of Musa from his mother only, not from his father.

It was read *ibna umma* with a *fatha* on the *mim*, likening him to *khamsata 'ashara* (fifteen), so it became like your saying: *ya khamsata 'ashara aqbilu* (O fifteen, come forward).

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayd said: the *fatha* is on the presumption of *ya ibna umma* (O son of my mother) with the *alif* omitted.

The Basrans said this view is erroneous, because the *alif* is light and is not omitted. Rather, making the two nouns one noun like *khamsata 'ashara* is the correct analysis. This was preferred by al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas.

As for the one who reads with a *kasra* on the *mim*, it is on the presumption of *ibna ummi* (son of my mother), then the *ya'* was omitted and the *kasra* was kept to indicate it.

Al-Akhfash and Abu Hatim said: *ibna umm* with a *kasra* is like your saying *ya ghulamu aqbil* (O boy, come). It is an irregular dialect, and reading with it is far-fetched; this applies only to what is a construct (*mudaf*) to you.

It was read *ibna ummi* with the *ya'* retained.

His words: ﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾. *Al-shamatah* is the joy of enemies at the calamities that befall those they oppose. From this is the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the evil of decree, from the descent of misery, from the severity of calamity, and from the gloating of enemies," and it is in the Sahih. From this is the saying of the poet:

When time drags its chest over a people, it makes others kneel down.

So say to those who gloat over us: "Be aware, the gloaters will meet what we met."

The meaning is: do not do to me what would be a cause of gloating from them.

Mujahid and Malik ibn Dinar read *fa-la tashmat bi al-a'da'* with a *fatha* on the initial letter of the imperfect and on the *mim*, and a *raf'* on *al-a'da'*, on the basis that the verb is attributed to them: that is, that would not come from them because of an action you take against me.

It was narrated from Mujahid that he read *tushmit* as mentioned before, with *nasb* (accusative) on *al-a'da'*.

Ibn Jinni said: the meaning is: do not let them gloat over me, you, O Lord. This is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ (al-Baqarah: 15) and similar, then he returned to the intended meaning and supposed a verb which he used to put *al-a'da'* in the accusative, as if he had said: O Lord, do not let the enemies gloat over me. How far this reading is from correctness, and how far its interpretation is from the aspects of *i'rab* (grammatical inflection).

His words: ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning do not place me, by Your anger at me, among the number of the wrongdoing people, that is, those who worshipped the calf; or do not believe that I am among them.

His words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, forgive me and my brother"﴾. This is a new sentence answering an assumed question, as if it was said: what did Musa say after Harun's words? So it was said: he said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother." He first sought forgiveness for himself, and then for his brother, to remove from his brother what he feared of gloating. He thus apologized for what he had done to his brother and showed that there was no justification for it, and he sought forgiveness from Allah for what had proceeded from him toward him. Then he sought forgiveness for his brother in case there had been any shortcoming on his part in what he was obliged to do by denouncing them and changing what they had done. Then he asked that both of them be admitted into the mercy of Allah, which encompasses all things, for He is the Most Merciful of the merciful.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿And the people of Musa took...﴾, the verse: when they buried it, al-Samiri threw upon it a handful of dust from the hoofprint of the horse of Jibril, peace be upon him.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Qatadah concerning the verse: he said: they borrowed ornaments from the family of Pharaoh, and al-Samiri gathered them and fashioned from them a calf, and made it a body of flesh and blood that had a lowing.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning His words: *khuwar*, he said: it is the sound.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Dahhak, who said: the calf lowed once, without moaning. Do you not see that Allah said: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾?

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿Was struck in their hands﴾, he said: they regretted.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated through various chains from Ibn 'Abbas concerning *asifan*: he said: grieved.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Abu al-Darda', who said: *al-asaf* is a station beyond anger, more intense than that.

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: *al-asaf* is intense anger.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When Musa threw down the tablets, they broke, and they were lifted up except for a sixth of them.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him, who said: Allah lifted up six-sevenths of them and one-seventh remained.

Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated from Mujahid or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: When Musa threw them, the detailed explanation departed and the guidance remained.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: they were nine, of which two tablets were lifted and seven remained.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His words: ﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾, he said: with the companions of the calf.

(p-501) His words: ﴿And the people of Musa took, after him,﴾ meaning after his departure to the Mount, ﴿from their ornaments﴾ a calf. The phrase ﴿from their ornaments﴾ is connected to *ittakhadha* (took), or to an omitted word functioning as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The *min* may be partitive (*lil-tab'id*), of origin (*lil-ibtida'*), or explanatory (*lil-bayan*). *Hulii* is the plural of *hulyun* (ornament).

The people of Madina and the people of Basra read *min hulyihim* with a *damma* on the *ha'* and a shadda on the *ya'*. The people of Kufa, except 'Asim, read it with a *kasra* on the *ha'*. Ya'qub read it with a *fatha* on the *ha'* and without a shadda on the *ya'*.

Al-Nahhas said: The plural of *hulyun* is *huliyyun* and *hiliyyun*, like *thadyun* becoming *thadiyyun* and *thidiyyun*. The original form is *hulwiyy*; the *waw* was assimilated into the *ya'*, so the *lam* took a *kasra* because it is adjacent to the *ya'*. The *ha'* may take a *kasra* because of the *kasra* on the *lam*, or a *damma* in keeping with the original form. The ornaments are attributed to them although they belonged to others, because attribution is permitted on the slightest connection. *'Ijlan* is the object of *ittakhadha*. It was said that it has the meaning of "making," so it takes two objects, the second of which is omitted: that is, they took a calf as a god. *Jasadan* is a substitute (*badal*) for *'ijlan*. It was said that it is a qualifier of it. *Al-khuwar* is the lowing. It is said: *khara yakhuru khawran* when it lows, and likewise *khara yukharu khuwaran*.

The taking of the calf is attributed to the whole people, although it was made by al-Samiri alone, because he was one of them and they approved of his action.

It is narrated that when Musa promised his people thirty nights and then delayed among them for the additional ten, al-Samiri, who was obeyed among the Children of Israel, said to them: "With you are ornaments from the ornaments of the family of Pharaoh, which you borrowed from them to adorn yourselves for the festival, and you went out with them while they are still with you. Allah has drowned their people, the Copts, so bring them here." They handed them over to him, and he made from them the calf mentioned.

His words: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them﴾. The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach; that is: did they not take heed that this which they took as a god cannot speak to them, let alone have the power to bring them benefit or repel harm from them, and ﴿nor guide them to a way﴾, meaning a clear path they could follow. ﴿They took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾, meaning they took it as a god and were wrongdoers, either to themselves in taking it or in everything, of which this taking is one part.

His words: ﴿And when they were stricken with remorse﴾, meaning they regretted and were bewildered after Musa returned from the appointed meeting. It is said of a regretful and bewildered person: *qad sugita fi yadihi* (he has been struck in his hand).

Al-Akhfash said: it is said *suqita fi yadihi* and *usqita*. Whoever says *saqata fi aydihim* in the active form, the meaning according to him is: remorse fell. The origin of this is that whoever's regret and grief become intense bites his hand in sorrow, so his hand becomes a thing that has fallen into, because his mouth has fallen upon it.

Al-Azhari, al-Zajjaj, al-Nahhas and others said: the meaning of *suqita fi aydihim* is: in their hearts and souls, just as one says that something disliked has occurred in his hand. Although it is impossible for it to be in the hand, this is a metaphor for what occurs in the heart and soul by comparison with what occurs in the hand, because dealing with things is generally done by the hand. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ (al-Hajj: 10). Also, remorse, though it settles in the heart, its effect appears in the body, because the remorseful person bites his hand and strikes one hand against the other. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So he began to turn over his palms over what he had spent upon it﴾ (al-Kahf: 42). And from this: ﴿And the wrongdoer will bite his hands﴾ (al-Furqan: 27), meaning from remorse. Also, the remorseful person places his chin on his hand.

﴿And they saw that they had gone astray﴾ is conjoined to *suqita* (was struck): that is, they realized that they had gone astray by taking the calf, and that they had been tested with disobedience to Allah, glorified is He. They said: ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy upon us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verbs in both places with the second-person (*ta'*) form, while the rest read them with the third-person (*ya'*) form. The *lam* is for oath, and its answer is *la-nakunanna min al-khasirin*.

In these words of theirs there is what conveys seeking refuge in Allah, humble supplication, and earnest entreaty in asking. What is reported of them here took place after Musa's return, as will be shown in Surat Ta-Ha, if Allah wills. He placed it here before his return for the purpose of narrating what proceeded from them of speech and action in one place.

His words: ﴿And when Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾. This is an explanation of what happened from Musa after his return. *Ghadbana* and *asifan* are in the accusative as circumstantial clauses (*hal*). *Al-Asif* is intense anger. It was said: it is a station beyond anger, more intense than it. It has the forms *asif*, *asif*, *asfan*, *asuf*. Ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: Allah had informed him before his return that they had been tested, so for that reason he returned angry and grieved. He said: ﴿Wretched is what you did after me﴾. This is a reproach from Musa to his people, meaning: wretched is the deed you did after me, that is, after my absence from you. It is said: *khalafahu bi-khayr* and *khalafahu bi-sharr*. He denounced what they had done and reproached them, because they had witnessed signs which, some of them, require restraint and faith in Allah alone. But this is the way of the Children of Israel: changing states and unstable deeds. Then he said, rebuking them: ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ *Al-'ajalah* is to advance something before its time. It is said: *'ajiltu al-shay'* meaning I preceded it, and *a'jaltu al-rajul* meaning I made him act hastily. The meaning is: you hastened ahead of waiting for the command of your Lord, that is, His appointed time that He promised me, which was forty nights, and so you did what you did. It was also said: its meaning is: you hastened the wrath of your Lord. It was also said: its meaning is: you hastened to worship the calf before the command of your Lord came to you. ﴿And he threw down the tablets﴾, that is, he cast them down because of the intense anger and grief that overcame him when he came upon his people while they were devoted to worshipping the calf.

The wrath (al-ghadab) is the punishment that befell them in this world through the killing of themselves, and the punishment that will befall them in the Hereafter. The humiliation (al-dhilla) is what God decreed upon them by His saying: ﴿Humiliation was decreed upon them﴾ (al-Baqara: 61). It was said that it is their expulsion from their homes. It was also said that it is the jizya (poll tax). But there is a problem with this view, because it was not taken from them; it was taken from their descendants.

The more appropriate view is that the wrath and the humiliation are restricted to this world, because of His saying: ﴿in the life of this world﴾. This applies specifically to those who took the calf as a god, not to those who came after them among their descendants. The mere command they received to kill themselves was itself a wrath from God upon them, and by it they became humbled. Likewise, their departure from their homes was from the wrath of God upon them, and by it they became humbled. As for the humiliation that reached their descendants, it is not valid to interpret what is in the verse as referring to it, unless it is impossible to carry the verse on its literal meaning, and that is not impossible here. ﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾, meaning: as We did to these, so We do to the fabricators. Al-iftira' (fabrication) is lying. Whoever fabricates against God will receive from God wrath and humiliation in the life of this world, even if it is not the very same thing with which these were punished. Rather, what is intended is whatever truly counts as being from the wrath of God, the Glorified, and that in it there is humiliation of some kind.

﴿And those who do evil deeds﴾, whatever evil deed it may be, ﴿and then repent﴾ of them after doing them, and believe in God, ﴿indeed your Lord, after them﴾, meaning after this repentance, or after the doing of these evil deeds from which their doer has repented and believed in God, ﴿is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning He is greatly forgiving of the sins of His servants and greatly merciful to them.

His saying: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses﴾. The original meaning of sukut (subsiding) is calm and cessation. It is said: "The valley flowed for three days, then calmed," meaning it stopped flowing. It was said: this is a figure of speech, as if the wrath had been urging him on to what he did and saying to him: "Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and drag your brother by the head." So he abandoned that urging and fell silent. It was also said: this sentence contains an inversion (qalb), and the original order is "Moses fell silent from the wrath," like their saying: "I inserted the finger into the ring" and "the ring into the finger," and "I put the skullcap on my head" and "my head into the skullcap."

Mu'awiya ibn Qurra recited: "And when the wrath calmed from Moses" (sakana). It was also read as "sakata" and as "asktata" (caused to subside). [He] took up the tablets that he had thrown down in his anger, and in their copy (nuskhatiha) was guidance and mercy. Naskh (copying) is the transfer of what is in one book into another book. The original from which the transfer is made is also called a nuskha, and the copied version is likewise called a nuskha.

Al-Qushayri said:

The meaning of "and in their nuskha" is: in what was copied from the broken tablets and transferred onto the new tablets, there is guidance and mercy. It was said: the meaning is: and in what was copied for him from them, that is, from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). It was also said: the meaning is: and in what was written for him in them there is guidance and mercy, so there is no need for an original from which it is copied. This is like saying: "Copy what so-and-so says," meaning: "record it in your book." The word nuskha is of the form fu'la, in the sense of maf'ula (the thing copied), like khutba.

Al-huda (guidance) is what they are guided by of the rulings, and al-rahma (mercy) is what comes to them from God when they act by what is in it of the vast mercy. The lam in ﴿for those who﴾ (li-lladhina) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: existing for them, or for their sake. The lam in ﴿for their Lord they fear﴾ (li-rabbihim yarhabun) serves to strengthen the verb, because when its object is placed before it, the verb is weakened to some extent by that.

Al-Kisa'i explicitly stated that it is extra (za'ida).

Al-Akhfash said: it is the lam of purpose, meaning: for the sake of their Lord they fear.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: it is connected to the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb mentioned, and the implied sense is: "for those whose fear is for their Lord they fear."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ayyub who said: Abu Qilaba recited this verse, ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ up to His saying ﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾, and said: it is the recompense of every fabricator until the Day of Resurrection, that God humiliates him.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Moses was given the Torah on seven tablets of emerald (zabarjad), in which there was an explanation of everything and an admonition. When he came and saw the Children of Israel devoted to the calf, he threw the Torah from his hand and it shattered. He turned to Harun and seized him by the head. God then lifted six-sevenths of it and one-seventh remained. [The verse says]: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their copy was guidance and mercy﴾. He said: [this refers to] what remained of them.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the tablets were of emerald (zumurrud). When Moses threw them, the detailed explanation (al-tafsil) went away, and guidance and mercy remained. He recited ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ (al-A'raf: 145), and he recited ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their copy was guidance and mercy﴾, and said: [the verse] did not mention the detailed explanation here.

Al-iftira' (fabrication) is lying. Whoever fabricates against God will receive from God wrath and humiliation in the life of this world, even if it is not the very same thing with which these were punished. Rather, what is intended is whatever truly counts as being from the wrath of God, the Glorified, and that in it there is humiliation of some kind.

﴿And those who do evil deeds﴾, whatever evil deed it may be, ﴿and then repent﴾ of them after doing them, and believe in God, ﴿indeed your Lord, after them﴾, meaning after this repentance, or after the doing of these evil deeds from which their doer has repented and believed in God, ﴿is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning He is greatly forgiving of the sins of His servants and greatly merciful to them.

His saying: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses﴾. The original meaning of sukut (subsiding) is calm and cessation. It is said: "The valley flowed for three days, then calmed," meaning it stopped flowing. It was said: this is a figure of speech, as if the wrath had been urging him on to what he did and saying to him: "Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and drag your brother by the head." So he abandoned that urging and fell silent. It was also said: this sentence contains an inversion (qalb), and the original order is "Moses fell silent from the wrath," like their saying: "I inserted the finger into the ring" and "the ring into the finger," and "I put the skullcap on my head" and "my head into the skullcap."

Mu'awiya ibn Qurra recited: "And when the wrath calmed from Moses" (sakana). It was also read as "sakata" and as "asktata" (caused to subside). [He] took up the tablets that he had thrown down in his anger, and in their copy (nuskhatiha) was guidance and mercy. Naskh (copying) is the transfer of what is in one book into another book. The original from which the transfer is made is also called a nuskha, and the copied version is likewise called a nuskha.

Al-Qushayri said:

The meaning of "and in their nuskha" is: in what was copied from the broken tablets and transferred onto the new tablets, there is guidance and mercy. It was said: the meaning is: and in what was copied for him from them, that is, from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). It was also said: the meaning is: and in what was written for him in them there is guidance and mercy, so there is no need for an original from which it is copied. This is like saying: "Copy what so-and-so says," meaning: "record it in your book." The word nuskha is of the form fu'la, in the sense of maf'ula (the thing copied), like khutba.

Al-huda (guidance) is what they are guided by of the rulings, and al-rahma (mercy) is what comes to them from God when they act by what is in it of the vast mercy. The lam in ﴿for those who﴾ (li-lladhina) is connected to an omitted element, meaning: existing for them, or for their sake. The lam in ﴿for their Lord they fear﴾ (li-rabbihim yarhabun) serves to strengthen the verb, because when its object is placed before it, the verb is weakened to some extent by that.

Al-Kisa'i explicitly stated that it is extra (za'ida).

Al-Akhfash said: it is the lam of purpose, meaning: for the sake of their Lord they fear.

Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: it is connected to the verbal noun (masdar) of the verb mentioned, and the implied sense is: "for those whose fear is for their Lord they fear."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ayyub who said: Abu Qilaba recited this verse, ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾ up to His saying ﴿And thus We recompense the fabricators﴾, and said: it is the recompense of every fabricator until the Day of Resurrection, that God humiliates him.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Abbas, who said: Moses was given the Torah on seven tablets of emerald (zabarjad), in which there was an explanation of everything and an admonition. When he came and saw the Children of Israel devoted to the calf, he threw the Torah from his hand and it shattered. He turned to Harun and seized him by the head. God then lifted six-sevenths of it and one-seventh remained. [The verse says]: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their copy was guidance and mercy﴾. He said: [this refers to] what remained of them.

Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Mujahid or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: the tablets were of emerald (zumurrud). When Moses threw them, the detailed explanation (al-tafsil) went away, and guidance and mercy remained. He recited ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ (al-A'raf: 145), and he recited ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their copy was guidance and mercy﴾, and said: [the verse] did not mention the detailed explanation here.

The wrath (al-ghadab) is the punishment that befell them in this world through the killing of themselves, and the punishment that will befall them in the Hereafter. The humiliation (al-dhilla) is what God decreed upon them by His saying: ﴿Humiliation was decreed upon them﴾ (al-Baqara: 61). It was said that it is their expulsion from their homes. It was also said that it is the jizya (poll tax). But there is a problem with this view, because it was not taken from them; it was taken from their descendants.

The more appropriate view is that the wrath and the humiliation are restricted to this world, because of His saying: ﴿in the life of this world﴾. This applies specifically to those who took the calf as a god, not to those who came after them among their descendants. The mere command they received to kill themselves was itself a wrath from God upon them, and by it they became humbled. Likewise, their departure from their homes was from the wrath of God upon them, and by it they became humbled. Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 7, verses 155–157 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾. This begins the account of what happened between Musa and the people he chose. "Seventy" is the object of *ikhtara* (chose), and "his people" (*qawmahu*) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "from his people," by elision and transitive extension. A similar usage is the verse of al-Ra'i:

*"I chose you from among the people when their characters had decayed, and he in whom hope was placed had become ill, and the* sul *(a kind of tree) …"*

He means "I chose you from among the people." The meaning of *li-mīqātinā* ("for Our appointed time") is: for the time We had set for him after what had happened among his people. *Al-mīqāt* (the appointed time) is the matter previously mentioned, because Allah commanded him to come to Mount Sinai with some of the Children of Israel, who would apologize to Him, glory be to Him, for worshipping the calf. This is what has been said.

*Al-rajfa* (the violent quake), linguistically, is a severe earthquake. It is said that they were shaken until they died. When Musa saw the quake seize them, he said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾. He, peace be upon him, said this in grief and distress, because the cause of the quake that seized them was what Allah related about their saying: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not believe you until we see Allah openly," the thunderbolt seized you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 55), as was explained in al-Baqarah.

It is also said that these seventy were other than those who said ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ (al-Nisa': 153), but that the quake seized them because they did not desist from worshipping the calf. It is also said that they were a people who did not approve of worshipping the calf, nor did they forbid al-Samiri and those with him from worshipping it, so the quake seized them because of their silence. The meaning is: If You had willed to destroy us, You would have destroyed us for our sins before this time. This is an acknowledgment from him, peace be upon him, of the sin, and a lament over what his people had neglected.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ is for denial: that is, you are not one who does such a thing. He said this out of confidence in Allah's mercy, and its intent is to seek compassion and to entreat. It is also said that its meaning is supplication and request, that is: do not destroy us.

Al-Mubarrad said: The intent of the interrogative is the interrogative of magnification, as if he were saying: Musa knew that no one is destroyed for the sin of another, but he said it like the saying of Jesus: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 118). It is also said that the "foolish" refers to the seventy, and the meaning is: Will You destroy the Children of Israel for what these foolish ones did in saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ (al-Nisa': 153)? It is also said that the intent is al-Samiri and his companions.

His saying: ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that is: what the trial in which these foolish ones fell into is nothing but Your trial, by which You test whom You will and examine whom You desire. It is likely that he, peace be upon him, derived this from His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿We have indeed tried your people after you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 85), ﴿You mislead thereby whom You will, and You guide whom You will﴾, that is, You mislead by this trial whom You will of Your servants, and You guide thereby whom You will of them. Similar is His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ (Hud: 7).

Then he returned to entreaty and supplication, and said: ﴿You are our Protector﴾, that is, the one who manages our affairs. ﴿So forgive us﴾ for what we have committed, ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ with Your mercy which encompasses all things, ﴿and You are the best of the forgivers﴾ of sins.

﴿And ordain for us in this world good﴾ by granting us success in righteous deeds, or bestow upon us favor by pouring out blessings in this world, such as well-being and abundance of provision; and in the Hereafter, that is: ordain for us in the Hereafter Paradise, by what You reward us with, or by the bounty You bestow upon us (p. 504) of delight in the Hereafter. The clause ﴿Indeed, we have returned to You﴾ is a cause for what precedes it, namely the request for forgiveness, mercy, and good in this world and the Hereafter. That is: indeed we have repented to You and turned back from the error that occurred among the Children of Israel.

*Al-hawd* means repentance, and it has been explained in al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾ is a fresh statement, like its counterparts previously mentioned. It has been said that the punishment here means the quake. It has also been said that His command to them to kill themselves is meant: that is, this is not up to you, O Musa; rather, whatever I will comes to be, and whatever I do not will does not come to be.

The apparent meaning is that the punishment here includes every punishment, and the punishment of these people enters it as a primary inclusion. It has been said that the intent is "whom I will" among those deserving punishment, or "whom I will" to let go astray and deprive of success. ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ among things, among the responsible and others. Then He, glory be to Him, informed that He will prescribe this vast mercy ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾ (i.e., avoid sins), ﴿and give zakat﴾ which is obligatory upon them, ﴿and those who believe in Our signs﴾, that is, they affirm them and submit to them.

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified who those are for whom He prescribed this mercy, with a clarification more evident and explicit than what preceded, and said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾, and he is Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace. Thus the Jews, the Christians, and all other religions are excluded.

*Al-ummi* (unlettered) is either a relative form of *al-ummah al-ummiyyah*, which does not write or calculate, namely the Arabs, or a relative form of *al-umm* (mother). The meaning is that he remained in the state in which he was born, not writing nor reading what is written. It has also been said that it is a relative form of *Umm al-Qura*, which is Makkah.

﴿Whom they find﴾, meaning the Jews and Christians, that is: they find his description ﴿written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾, which are their reference in religion. This statement from Him, glory be to Him, with Musa, was before the revelation of the Gospel, so it is of the category of informing about what will be. Then He described this prophet whom they find thus as one who ﴿enjoins what is right﴾, that is, everything that the hearts recognize and do not deny, among the things that are noble characteristics; ﴿and forbids them from what is wrong﴾, that is, what the hearts deny and do not recognize, which is what is among the bad characteristics. It has been said that His saying ﴿He enjoins them what is right﴾ up to His saying ﴿those are the successful﴾ is a statement comprising the detailed rulings of the mercy He promised. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. It has also been said that it occupies a place of accusative as a state (*hal*) of the Prophet, and it has been said that it explains His saying "written."

His saying: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things﴾, that is, the delicious ones. It has been said: He makes lawful for them what was forbidden for them, among the things that were prohibited for them because of their sins; and He forbids them the *khaba'ith* (foul things), that is, the loathsome ones, such as insects and swine; and ﴿He relieves them of their burden﴾. *Al-isr* means the heavy weight, that is: He relieves them of the hard and heavy obligations.

Its explanation has been given in al-Baqarah. ﴿And the shackles that were upon them﴾, that is, He relieves them of the shackles that were upon them. The shackles are a metaphor for the hard obligations with which they had been charged. ﴿So those who believed in him﴾, that is, in Muhammad (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), ﴿and honored him﴾ and followed him in what he brought of the laws, and ﴿honored him﴾, that is, glorified and revered him, as al-Akhfash said. It has been said that the meaning is: they protected him from his enemy. The root of *al-'azr* is prevention. Al-Jahdari read *wa-'azzarūhu* with light emphasis, and ﴿supported him﴾, that is, they stood in supporting him against whoever opposed him, ﴿and followed the light which was sent down with him﴾, that is, they followed the Qur'an which was sent down upon him along with his prophethood. It has been said: the meaning is: they followed the Qur'an sent down to him, along with following it by acting upon his Sunnah in what he commands and forbids; or they followed the Qur'an, being companions to it in following it. The reference of "those" (*ulā'ika*) to those characterized by these attributes is: ﴿they are the successful﴾, the ones who attain good and success, not others among the nations.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Allah had commanded him to choose seventy men from among his people. So he chose seventy men and went out with them to supplicate their Lord. Among what they asked of Allah was that they said: O Allah, give us what You have not given anyone before us, and do not give it to anyone after us. Allah disliked this supplication of theirs, so the quake seized them. Musa said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? It is nothing but Your trial﴾. He means: it is nothing but Your punishment; You afflict with it whom You will and turn it away from whom You will.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, concerning ﴿for Our appointed time﴾, that he said: for the completion of the promise. And concerning His saying: ﴿So when the quake seized them﴾, he said: they died, then He brought them back to life.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His saying ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that he said: Your affliction.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that he said: Your will.

Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, that he said: The seventy whom Musa chose from his people were only seized by the quake because they did not approve of the deed, nor did they forbid it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from him, concerning His saying: ﴿And ordain for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter﴾, that Musa did not give it. ﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾ up to His saying ﴿the successful﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah, concerning His saying ﴿And ordain for us in this world good and in the Hereafter﴾, that he said: So He wrote mercy that day for this nation.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through various chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, we have returned (*hudna*) to You﴾, that he said: we have repented to You. Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Wajza al-Sa'di, who was among the most knowledgeable people in Arabic, that he said: No, by Allah, I do not know *hudna* in the speech of the Arabs. It was said: Then how did he say *hidna* with a kasra on the ha'? He says: *milna* (we turned).

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan and Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾, that he said: His mercy encompassed in this world the righteous and the wicked; and on the Day of Resurrection it is for those who feared Allah specifically.

Muslim and others related from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed Allah has one hundred mercies. Of them is one mercy with which creation shows mercy to one another, and with which wild animals show tenderness to their young; and He delayed the other ninety-nine until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Diya al-Maqdisi related something similar from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: When the verse ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ was revealed, Iblis said: "And I am among things." So Allah abrogated (*nasakha*, i.e., replaced by a later ruling) it, and the verse was revealed: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When the verse ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ was revealed, Iblis said: "I am among things." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah and give zakat﴾. The Jews said: "We fear Allah and give zakat." Allah said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾. So Allah removed it from Iblis and from the Jews, and made it for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar from Qatadah.

Al-Bazzar in his *Musnad*, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Musa asked his Lord a request, and He gave it to Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And Musa chose﴾ to His saying ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾: He gave Muhammad everything that Musa asked his Lord for in this verse.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, concerning His saying ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾, that he said: Allah ordained it for this nation.

Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "Those who fear Allah" means those who fear shirk.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Nakha'i concerning His saying ﴿the unlettered Prophet﴾, that he said: He did not read nor write.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning the verse, that he said: He is your Prophet (ﷺ); he was unlettered, not writing.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verse 155–157 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿those whom they find written down with them﴾: they find his description, his command and his prophethood written down with them.

Ibn Sa'd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: I met Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As and I said to him: "Tell me about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, he is described in the Torah with some of his description in the Qur'an: 'O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My Messenger. I have named you al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies upon Allah). He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets, and he does not repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks. Allah will not take him until He has set straight through him the crooked community, by their saying: there is no god but Allah, and through him He will open blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts.'"

Ibn Sa'id, al-Darimi in his Musnad, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn Asakir related from Abdullah ibn Salam something similar to this.

Something similar to this has been related with variation in some wording, addition in some, and omission in some, from a group of narrators.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things﴾: "the lawful." ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: "the harshness that was in their religion."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾: "such as the flesh of swine, usury, and what they used to deem lawful of the forbidden foods which Allah had prohibited." And concerning His saying ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: "it is what Allah had taken from them of covenant regarding what He had made unlawful for them."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His saying ﴿and relieves them of their burden﴾: "what was made severe upon the Children of Israel, such as cutting off the parts of their skins affected by urine when it struck them, and the like."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and honoured him﴾: "that is, they exalted him and showed him reverence."

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 7, verses 155–157 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾. This begins the account of what happened between Musa and the people he chose. "Seventy" is the object of *ikhtara* (chose), and "his people" (*qawmahu*) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "from his people," by elision and transitive extension. A similar usage is the verse of al-Ra'i:

*"I chose you from among the people when their characters had decayed, and he in whom hope was placed had become ill, and the* sul *(a kind of tree) …"*

He means "I chose you from among the people." The meaning of *li-mīqātinā* ("for Our appointed time") is: for the time We had set for him after what had happened among his people. *Al-mīqāt* (the appointed time) is the matter previously mentioned, because Allah commanded him to come to Mount Sinai with some of the Children of Israel, who would apologize to Him, glory be to Him, for worshipping the calf. This is what has been said.

*Al-rajfa* (the violent quake), linguistically, is a severe earthquake. It is said that they were shaken until they died. When Musa saw the quake seize them, he said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾. He, peace be upon him, said this in grief and distress, because the cause of the quake that seized them was what Allah related about their saying: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not believe you until we see Allah openly," the thunderbolt seized you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 55), as was explained in al-Baqarah.

It is also said that these seventy were other than those who said ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ (al-Nisa': 153), but that the quake seized them because they did not desist from worshipping the calf. It is also said that they were a people who did not approve of worshipping the calf, nor did they forbid al-Samiri and those with him from worshipping it, so the quake seized them because of their silence. The meaning is: If You had willed to destroy us, You would have destroyed us for our sins before this time. This is an acknowledgment from him, peace be upon him, of the sin, and a lament over what his people had neglected.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ is for denial: that is, you are not one who does such a thing. He said this out of confidence in Allah's mercy, and its intent is to seek compassion and to entreat. It is also said that its meaning is supplication and request, that is: do not destroy us.

Al-Mubarrad said: The intent of the interrogative is the interrogative of magnification, as if he were saying: Musa knew that no one is destroyed for the sin of another, but he said it like the saying of Jesus: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 118). It is also said that the "foolish" refers to the seventy, and the meaning is: Will You destroy the Children of Israel for what these foolish ones did in saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ (al-Nisa': 153)? It is also said that the intent is al-Samiri and his companions.

His saying: ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that is: what the trial in which these foolish ones fell into is nothing but Your trial, by which You test whom You will and examine whom You desire. It is likely that he, peace be upon him, derived this from His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿We have indeed tried your people after you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 85), ﴿You mislead thereby whom You will, and You guide whom You will﴾, that is, You mislead by this trial whom You will of Your servants, and You guide thereby whom You will of them. Similar is His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ (Hud: 7).

Then he returned to entreaty and supplication, and said: ﴿You are our Protector﴾, that is, the one who manages our affairs. ﴿So forgive us﴾ for what we have committed, ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ with Your mercy which encompasses all things, ﴿and You are the best of the forgivers﴾ of sins.

﴿And ordain for us in this world good﴾ by granting us success in righteous deeds, or bestow upon us favor by pouring out blessings in this world, such as well-being and abundance of provision; and in the Hereafter, that is: ordain for us in the Hereafter Paradise, by what You reward us with, or by the bounty You bestow upon us (p. 504) of delight in the Hereafter. The clause ﴿Indeed, we have returned to You﴾ is a cause for what precedes it, namely the request for forgiveness, mercy, and good in this world and the Hereafter. That is: indeed we have repented to You and turned back from the error that occurred among the Children of Israel.

*Al-hawd* means repentance, and it has been explained in al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾ is a fresh statement, like its counterparts previously mentioned. It has been said that the punishment here means the quake. It has also been said that His command to them to kill themselves is meant: that is, this is not up to you, O Musa; rather, whatever I will comes to be, and whatever I do not will does not come to be.

The apparent meaning is that the punishment here includes every punishment, and the punishment of these people enters it as a primary inclusion. It has been said that the intent is "whom I will" among those deserving punishment, or "whom I will" to let go astray and deprive of success. ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ among things, among the responsible and others. Then He, glory be to Him, informed that He will prescribe this vast mercy ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾ (i.e., avoid sins), ﴿and give zakat﴾ which is obligatory upon them, ﴿and those who believe in Our signs﴾, that is, they affirm them and submit to them.

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified who those are for whom He prescribed this mercy, with a clarification more evident and explicit than what preceded, and said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾, and he is Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace. Thus the Jews, the Christians, and all other religions are excluded.

*Al-ummi* (unlettered) is either a relative form of *al-ummah al-ummiyyah*, which does not write or calculate, namely the Arabs, or a relative form of *al-umm* (mother). The meaning is that he remained in the state in which he was born, not writing nor reading what is written. It has also been said that it is a relative form of *Umm al-Qura*, which is Makkah.

﴿Whom they find﴾, meaning the Jews and Christians, that is: they find his description ﴿written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾, which are their reference in religion. This statement from Him, glory be to Him, with Musa, was before the revelation of the Gospel, so it is of the category of informing about what will be. Then He described this prophet whom they find thus as one who ﴿enjoins what is right﴾, that is, everything that the hearts recognize and do not deny, among the things that are noble characteristics; ﴿and forbids them from what is wrong﴾, that is, what the hearts deny and do not recognize, which is what is among the bad characteristics. It has been said that His saying ﴿He enjoins them what is right﴾ up to His saying ﴿those are the successful﴾ is a statement comprising the detailed rulings of the mercy He promised. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. It has also been said that it occupies a place of accusative as a state (*hal*) of the Prophet, and it has been said that it explains His saying "written."

His saying: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things﴾, that is, the delicious ones. It has been said: He makes lawful for them what was forbidden for them, among the things that were prohibited for them because of their sins; and He forbids them the *khaba'ith* (foul things), that is, the loathsome ones, such as insects and swine; and ﴿He relieves them of their burden﴾. *Al-isr* means the heavy weight, that is: He relieves them of the hard and heavy obligations.

Its explanation has been given in al-Baqarah. ﴿And the shackles that were upon them﴾, that is, He relieves them of the shackles that were upon them. The shackles are a metaphor for the hard obligations with which they had been charged. ﴿So those who believed in him﴾, that is, in Muhammad (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), ﴿and honored him﴾ and followed him in what he brought of the laws, and ﴿honored him﴾, that is, glorified and revered him, as al-Akhfash said. It has been said that the meaning is: they protected him from his enemy. The root of *al-'azr* is prevention. Al-Jahdari read *wa-'azzarūhu* with light emphasis, and ﴿supported him﴾, that is, they stood in supporting him against whoever opposed him, ﴿and followed the light which was sent down with him﴾, that is, they followed the Qur'an which was sent down upon him along with his prophethood. It has been said: the meaning is: they followed the Qur'an sent down to him, along with following it by acting upon his Sunnah in what he commands and forbids; or they followed the Qur'an, being companions to it in following it. The reference of "those" (*ulā'ika*) to those characterized by these attributes is: ﴿they are the successful﴾, the ones who attain good and success, not others among the nations.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Allah had commanded him to choose seventy men from among his people. So he chose seventy men and went out with them to supplicate their Lord. Among what they asked of Allah was that they said: O Allah, give us what You have not given anyone before us, and do not give it to anyone after us. Allah disliked this supplication of theirs, so the quake seized them. Musa said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? It is nothing but Your trial﴾. He means: it is nothing but Your punishment; You afflict with it whom You will and turn it away from whom You will.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, concerning ﴿for Our appointed time﴾, that he said: for the completion of the promise. And concerning His saying: ﴿So when the quake seized them﴾, he said: they died, then He brought them back to life.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His saying ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that he said: Your affliction.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that he said: Your will.

Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, that he said: The seventy whom Musa chose from his people were only seized by the quake because they did not approve of the deed, nor did they forbid it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from him, concerning His saying: ﴿And ordain for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter﴾, that Musa did not give it. ﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾ up to His saying ﴿the successful﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah, concerning His saying ﴿And ordain for us in this world good and in the Hereafter﴾, that he said: So He wrote mercy that day for this nation.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through various chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, we have returned (*hudna*) to You﴾, that he said: we have repented to You. Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Wajza al-Sa'di, who was among the most knowledgeable people in Arabic, that he said: No, by Allah, I do not know *hudna* in the speech of the Arabs. It was said: Then how did he say *hidna* with a kasra on the ha'? He says: *milna* (we turned).

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan and Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾, that he said: His mercy encompassed in this world the righteous and the wicked; and on the Day of Resurrection it is for those who feared Allah specifically.

Muslim and others related from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed Allah has one hundred mercies. Of them is one mercy with which creation shows mercy to one another, and with which wild animals show tenderness to their young; and He delayed the other ninety-nine until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Diya al-Maqdisi related something similar from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: When the verse ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ was revealed, Iblis said: "And I am among things." So Allah abrogated (*nasakha*, i.e., replaced by a later ruling) it, and the verse was revealed: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When the verse ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ was revealed, Iblis said: "I am among things." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah and give zakat﴾. The Jews said: "We fear Allah and give zakat." Allah said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾. So Allah removed it from Iblis and from the Jews, and made it for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar from Qatadah.

Al-Bazzar in his *Musnad*, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Musa asked his Lord a request, and He gave it to Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And Musa chose﴾ to His saying ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾: He gave Muhammad everything that Musa asked his Lord for in this verse.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, concerning His saying ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾, that he said: Allah ordained it for this nation.

Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "Those who fear Allah" means those who fear shirk.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Nakha'i concerning His saying ﴿the unlettered Prophet﴾, that he said: He did not read nor write.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning the verse, that he said: He is your Prophet (ﷺ); he was unlettered, not writing.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verse 155–157 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿those whom they find written down with them﴾: they find his description, his command and his prophethood written down with them.

Ibn Sa'd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: I met Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As and I said to him: "Tell me about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, he is described in the Torah with some of his description in the Qur'an: 'O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My Messenger. I have named you al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies upon Allah). He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets, and he does not repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks. Allah will not take him until He has set straight through him the crooked community, by their saying: there is no god but Allah, and through him He will open blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts.'"

Ibn Sa'id, al-Darimi in his Musnad, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn Asakir related from Abdullah ibn Salam something similar to this.

Something similar to this has been related with variation in some wording, addition in some, and omission in some, from a group of narrators.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things﴾: "the lawful." ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: "the harshness that was in their religion."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾: "such as the flesh of swine, usury, and what they used to deem lawful of the forbidden foods which Allah had prohibited." And concerning His saying ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: "it is what Allah had taken from them of covenant regarding what He had made unlawful for them."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His saying ﴿and relieves them of their burden﴾: "what was made severe upon the Children of Israel, such as cutting off the parts of their skins affected by urine when it struck them, and the like."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and honoured him﴾: "that is, they exalted him and showed him reverence."

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, on Surah 7, verses 155–157 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time﴾. This begins the account of what happened between Musa and the people he chose. "Seventy" is the object of *ikhtara* (chose), and "his people" (*qawmahu*) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning "from his people," by elision and transitive extension. A similar usage is the verse of al-Ra'i:

*"I chose you from among the people when their characters had decayed, and he in whom hope was placed had become ill, and the* sul *(a kind of tree) …"*

He means "I chose you from among the people." The meaning of *li-mīqātinā* ("for Our appointed time") is: for the time We had set for him after what had happened among his people. *Al-mīqāt* (the appointed time) is the matter previously mentioned, because Allah commanded him to come to Mount Sinai with some of the Children of Israel, who would apologize to Him, glory be to Him, for worshipping the calf. This is what has been said.

*Al-rajfa* (the violent quake), linguistically, is a severe earthquake. It is said that they were shaken until they died. When Musa saw the quake seize them, he said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾. He, peace be upon him, said this in grief and distress, because the cause of the quake that seized them was what Allah related about their saying: ﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not believe you until we see Allah openly," the thunderbolt seized you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 55), as was explained in al-Baqarah.

It is also said that these seventy were other than those who said ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ (al-Nisa': 153), but that the quake seized them because they did not desist from worshipping the calf. It is also said that they were a people who did not approve of worshipping the calf, nor did they forbid al-Samiri and those with him from worshipping it, so the quake seized them because of their silence. The meaning is: If You had willed to destroy us, You would have destroyed us for our sins before this time. This is an acknowledgment from him, peace be upon him, of the sin, and a lament over what his people had neglected.

The interrogative in His saying ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ is for denial: that is, you are not one who does such a thing. He said this out of confidence in Allah's mercy, and its intent is to seek compassion and to entreat. It is also said that its meaning is supplication and request, that is: do not destroy us.

Al-Mubarrad said: The intent of the interrogative is the interrogative of magnification, as if he were saying: Musa knew that no one is destroyed for the sin of another, but he said it like the saying of Jesus: ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 118). It is also said that the "foolish" refers to the seventy, and the meaning is: Will You destroy the Children of Israel for what these foolish ones did in saying ﴿Show us Allah openly﴾ (al-Nisa': 153)? It is also said that the intent is al-Samiri and his companions.

His saying: ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that is: what the trial in which these foolish ones fell into is nothing but Your trial, by which You test whom You will and examine whom You desire. It is likely that he, peace be upon him, derived this from His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿We have indeed tried your people after you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 85), ﴿You mislead thereby whom You will, and You guide whom You will﴾, that is, You mislead by this trial whom You will of Your servants, and You guide thereby whom You will of them. Similar is His saying: ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ (Hud: 7).

Then he returned to entreaty and supplication, and said: ﴿You are our Protector﴾, that is, the one who manages our affairs. ﴿So forgive us﴾ for what we have committed, ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ with Your mercy which encompasses all things, ﴿and You are the best of the forgivers﴾ of sins.

﴿And ordain for us in this world good﴾ by granting us success in righteous deeds, or bestow upon us favor by pouring out blessings in this world, such as well-being and abundance of provision; and in the Hereafter, that is: ordain for us in the Hereafter Paradise, by what You reward us with, or by the bounty You bestow upon us (p. 504) of delight in the Hereafter. The clause ﴿Indeed, we have returned to You﴾ is a cause for what precedes it, namely the request for forgiveness, mercy, and good in this world and the Hereafter. That is: indeed we have repented to You and turned back from the error that occurred among the Children of Israel.

*Al-hawd* means repentance, and it has been explained in al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾ is a fresh statement, like its counterparts previously mentioned. It has been said that the punishment here means the quake. It has also been said that His command to them to kill themselves is meant: that is, this is not up to you, O Musa; rather, whatever I will comes to be, and whatever I do not will does not come to be.

The apparent meaning is that the punishment here includes every punishment, and the punishment of these people enters it as a primary inclusion. It has been said that the intent is "whom I will" among those deserving punishment, or "whom I will" to let go astray and deprive of success. ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ among things, among the responsible and others. Then He, glory be to Him, informed that He will prescribe this vast mercy ﴿for those who fear Allah﴾ (i.e., avoid sins), ﴿and give zakat﴾ which is obligatory upon them, ﴿and those who believe in Our signs﴾, that is, they affirm them and submit to them.

Then He, glory be to Him, clarified who those are for whom He prescribed this mercy, with a clarification more evident and explicit than what preceded, and said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾, and he is Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace. Thus the Jews, the Christians, and all other religions are excluded.

*Al-ummi* (unlettered) is either a relative form of *al-ummah al-ummiyyah*, which does not write or calculate, namely the Arabs, or a relative form of *al-umm* (mother). The meaning is that he remained in the state in which he was born, not writing nor reading what is written. It has also been said that it is a relative form of *Umm al-Qura*, which is Makkah.

﴿Whom they find﴾, meaning the Jews and Christians, that is: they find his description ﴿written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾, which are their reference in religion. This statement from Him, glory be to Him, with Musa, was before the revelation of the Gospel, so it is of the category of informing about what will be. Then He described this prophet whom they find thus as one who ﴿enjoins what is right﴾, that is, everything that the hearts recognize and do not deny, among the things that are noble characteristics; ﴿and forbids them from what is wrong﴾, that is, what the hearts deny and do not recognize, which is what is among the bad characteristics. It has been said that His saying ﴿He enjoins them what is right﴾ up to His saying ﴿those are the successful﴾ is a statement comprising the detailed rulings of the mercy He promised. This was mentioned by al-Zajjaj. It has also been said that it occupies a place of accusative as a state (*hal*) of the Prophet, and it has been said that it explains His saying "written."

His saying: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things﴾, that is, the delicious ones. It has been said: He makes lawful for them what was forbidden for them, among the things that were prohibited for them because of their sins; and He forbids them the *khaba'ith* (foul things), that is, the loathsome ones, such as insects and swine; and ﴿He relieves them of their burden﴾. *Al-isr* means the heavy weight, that is: He relieves them of the hard and heavy obligations.

Its explanation has been given in al-Baqarah. ﴿And the shackles that were upon them﴾, that is, He relieves them of the shackles that were upon them. The shackles are a metaphor for the hard obligations with which they had been charged. ﴿So those who believed in him﴾, that is, in Muhammad (may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace), ﴿and honored him﴾ and followed him in what he brought of the laws, and ﴿honored him﴾, that is, glorified and revered him, as al-Akhfash said. It has been said that the meaning is: they protected him from his enemy. The root of *al-'azr* is prevention. Al-Jahdari read *wa-'azzarūhu* with light emphasis, and ﴿supported him﴾, that is, they stood in supporting him against whoever opposed him, ﴿and followed the light which was sent down with him﴾, that is, they followed the Qur'an which was sent down upon him along with his prophethood. It has been said: the meaning is: they followed the Qur'an sent down to him, along with following it by acting upon his Sunnah in what he commands and forbids; or they followed the Qur'an, being companions to it in following it. The reference of "those" (*ulā'ika*) to those characterized by these attributes is: ﴿they are the successful﴾, the ones who attain good and success, not others among the nations.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿And Musa chose from his people﴾ to the end of the verse, that he said: Allah had commanded him to choose seventy men from among his people. So he chose seventy men and went out with them to supplicate their Lord. Among what they asked of Allah was that they said: O Allah, give us what You have not given anyone before us, and do not give it to anyone after us. Allah disliked this supplication of theirs, so the quake seized them. Musa said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? It is nothing but Your trial﴾. He means: it is nothing but Your punishment; You afflict with it whom You will and turn it away from whom You will.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Mujahid, concerning ﴿for Our appointed time﴾, that he said: for the completion of the promise. And concerning His saying: ﴿So when the quake seized them﴾, he said: they died, then He brought them back to life.

Ibn Abi Shayba and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His saying ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that he said: Your affliction.

Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿It is nothing but Your trial﴾, that he said: Your will.

Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Abbas, that he said: The seventy whom Musa chose from his people were only seized by the quake because they did not approve of the deed, nor did they forbid it.

Sa'id ibn Mansur related from him, concerning His saying: ﴿And ordain for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter﴾, that Musa did not give it. ﴿He said: My punishment — I afflict with it whom I will﴾ up to His saying ﴿the successful﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ikrimah, concerning His saying ﴿And ordain for us in this world good and in the Hereafter﴾, that he said: So He wrote mercy that day for this nation.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim related through various chains from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿Indeed, we have returned (*hudna*) to You﴾, that he said: we have repented to You. Ibn Abi Hatim related the same from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Abu Wajza al-Sa'di, who was among the most knowledgeable people in Arabic, that he said: No, by Allah, I do not know *hudna* in the speech of the Arabs. It was said: Then how did he say *hidna* with a kasra on the ha'? He says: *milna* (we turned).

Abd al-Razzaq, Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Hasan and Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾, that he said: His mercy encompassed in this world the righteous and the wicked; and on the Day of Resurrection it is for those who feared Allah specifically.

Muslim and others related from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed Allah has one hundred mercies. Of them is one mercy with which creation shows mercy to one another, and with which wild animals show tenderness to their young; and He delayed the other ninety-nine until the Day of Resurrection."

Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and al-Diya al-Maqdisi related something similar from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abd Allah al-Bajali.

Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Suddi, who said: When the verse ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ was revealed, Iblis said: "And I am among things." So Allah abrogated (*nasakha*, i.e., replaced by a later ruling) it, and the verse was revealed: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When the verse ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ was revealed, Iblis said: "I am among things." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah and give zakat﴾. The Jews said: "We fear Allah and give zakat." Allah said: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet﴾. So Allah removed it from Iblis and from the Jews, and made it for the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Abu al-Shaykh related something similar from Qatadah.

Al-Bazzar in his *Musnad*, and Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Musa asked his Lord a request, and He gave it to Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿And Musa chose﴾ to His saying ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾: He gave Muhammad everything that Musa asked his Lord for in this verse.

Ibn Abi Shayba, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh related from him, concerning His saying ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Allah﴾, that he said: Allah ordained it for this nation.

Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, that he said: "Those who fear Allah" means those who fear shirk.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from al-Nakha'i concerning His saying ﴿the unlettered Prophet﴾, that he said: He did not read nor write.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah concerning the verse, that he said: He is your Prophet (ﷺ); he was unlettered, not writing.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verse 155–157 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, concerning His saying ﴿those whom they find written down with them﴾: they find his description, his command and his prophethood written down with them.

Ibn Sa'd, al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il related from Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: I met Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As and I said to him: "Tell me about the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." He said: "Indeed, by Allah, he is described in the Torah with some of his description in the Qur'an: 'O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and a guardian for the unlettered. You are My servant and My Messenger. I have named you al-Mutawakkil (the one who relies upon Allah). He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets, and he does not repay evil with evil, but he pardons and overlooks. Allah will not take him until He has set straight through him the crooked community, by their saying: there is no god but Allah, and through him He will open blind eyes, deaf ears and veiled hearts.'"

Ibn Sa'id, al-Darimi in his Musnad, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn Asakir related from Abdullah ibn Salam something similar to this.

Something similar to this has been related with variation in some wording, addition in some, and omission in some, from a group of narrators.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj concerning His saying ﴿and He makes lawful for them the good things﴾: "the lawful." ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: "the harshness that was in their religion."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and He makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾: "such as the flesh of swine, usury, and what they used to deem lawful of the forbidden foods which Allah had prohibited." And concerning His saying ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾: "it is what Allah had taken from them of covenant regarding what He had made unlawful for them."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, concerning His saying ﴿and relieves them of their burden﴾: "what was made severe upon the Children of Israel, such as cutting off the parts of their skins affected by urine when it struck them, and the like."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying ﴿and honoured him﴾: "that is, they exalted him and showed him reverence."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verse 158:

When the description of the attributes of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) written in the Torah and the Gospel had preceded, Allah (glory be to Him) commanded him to say this statement, which implies the universality of his message to mankind all together, unlike the other messengers (peace be upon them), for they were sent only to their own people. The word jami'an (all together) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: while you are all together. The phrase ﴿Alladhi lahu mulku as-samawati wa al-ard﴾ (﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾) is either in the genitive position as an attribute of the noble name, or in the accusative by way of praise, or in the nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject. The clause ﴿la ilaha illa huwa﴾ (﴿there is no deity except Him﴾) is a substitute (badal) for the relative clause, confirming its content and clarifying it, because whoever owns the heavens and the earth and what is in them is truly the God. Likewise, whoever gives life and causes death is the one deserving of sole lordship and of the negation of partners from Him. The command to believe in Allah and His Messenger follows from what precedes it. The interpretation of ﴿an-Nabiyy al-ummiyy﴾ (﴿the unlettered Prophet﴾) has already been given, and these are two attributes of His Messenger. Likewise ﴿Alladhi yu'minu billahi wa kalimatihi﴾ (﴿who believes in Allah and His words﴾) is an attribute of him. By "the words" is meant what Allah revealed to him and to the prophets before him, or the Qur'an alone. The clause ﴿wa-ttabi'uhu﴾ (﴿and follow him﴾) confirms the clause ﴿fa-amminu billah﴾ (﴿so believe in Allah﴾). The clause ﴿wa la'allakum tahtadun﴾ (﴿that you may be guided﴾) is the reason for the command to believe and to follow.

Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to the red and the black, and he said: 'O people, I am the Messenger of Allah to you all.'" The many sound hadiths with this meaning are well known, so we will not lengthen the discussion by mentioning them.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿yu'minu billahi wa kalimatihi﴾, that he said: "His signs (ayatihi)."

Abu 'Ubayd and Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, regarding ﴿wa kalimatihi﴾, that he said: "Jesus."

(p. 506) His words: ﴿And among the people of Moses﴾.
