Ummah means a group: that is, a group of the righteous people of the town said to others among those who used to strive to admonish the transgressors on the Sabbath, when they had despaired of their accepting admonition and giving up disobedience: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy﴾, meaning who are destined for punishment ﴿or punish them with a severe punishment﴾ for the sacred things they violated and the disobedience they committed. It was said that the group saying "why do you admonish a people" were the disobedient who hunted on the Sabbath; they said this to those who admonished them when they admonished them.

The meaning: if you know that Allah is going to destroy us, as you claim, then why do you admonish us? They said: ﴿An excuse to your Lord﴾, meaning the admonishers said to the group who said to them "why do you admonish": they are a group of the righteous people of the town according to the first interpretation, or the doers (of the sin) according to the second. ﴿An excuse to your Lord﴾: ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar and Talhah ibn Musarrif recited "ma'dhiratan" in the accusative, which is the recitation of Hafs from ʿAsim; the rest recited it in the nominative.

Al-Kisa'i said: its accusative has two possibilities: one of them is as a verbal noun (masdar), and the second is by the implied meaning "we did that as an excuse," that is, for the sake of the excuse.

The nominative is by an implied subject: that is, our admonition is an excuse to Allah, so that He will not hold us accountable for abandoning the commanding of good and forbidding of evil which He made obligatory upon us, and in hope that they might take heed, fear Allah, and give up what they are engaged in of disobedience.

The majority of the commentators said: the Children of Israel split into three groups. One group disobeyed and hunted, and they were about seventy thousand. One group withdrew and did not admonish and did not disobey. And one group withdrew and admonished and did not disobey. The group that did not admonish and did not disobey said to the admonishing group: ﴿Why do you admonish a people﴾, meaning the disobedient group, ﴿whom Allah is going to destroy or punish?﴾ They said this based on the strong presumption according to Allah's custom of destroying or punishing the disobedient without total annihilation. The admonishing group said: our admonition is an excuse to Allah, ﴿and perhaps they will fear Allah﴾. If they had been only two groups, the admonishing non-disobedient group and the disobedient group, he would have said: "perhaps you will fear Allah."

His words: ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, meaning when the disobedient people of the town left what the righteous who forbid evil had reminded them of, leaving like one who forgets a thing and turns away from it completely. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil﴾, meaning those who performed the forbidding and did not abandon it. ﴿And We seized those who did wrong﴾, and they were the transgressors who exceeded the limits on the Sabbath, ﴿with a grievous punishment (bi'sin)﴾, meaning a severe one, from ba'usa (to be severe) when a thing is harsh. There are eleven recitations of this word by the Seven and others. ﴿Because they were defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning because of their defiance. The prepositional phrase is connected to "akhadhna" (We seized).

﴿So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden﴾, meaning they exceeded the limit in disobedience to Allah, glory be to Him, out of rebelliousness and arrogance. ﴿We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾, meaning We commanded them with a creational command, not a verbal command: that is, We transformed them into apes. It was said: He, glory be to Him, first punished them for their disobedience, and when they did not give up, He transformed them into apes. It was also said: His words "So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden" are a repetition of His words "So when they forgot what they had been reminded of," for emphasis and affirmation, and that the transformation is the grievous punishment. "Khasi'in" means abject, humiliated, or distanced and expelled. It is said: "khasa'tuhu fakhusi'a," meaning I pushed him away and he withdrew.

Know that the apparent meaning of the Qur'anic text is that none were saved from the punishment except the forbidding group which did not disobey, according to His words: ﴿We saved those who forbade evil﴾, and that none were punished by transformation except the disobedient group, according to His words: ﴿So when they insolently persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them: Be apes, despised﴾. If the groups among them were three as previously mentioned, then the group that did not forbid and did not disobey may possibly have been transformed along with the disobedient group, because they wronged themselves by staying silent about the prohibition and were insolent toward what Allah had forbidden them, namely abandoning the forbidding of evil. And it is possible that they were not transformed, because although they wronged themselves and were insolent toward their Lord's command and prohibition, they did not wrong themselves by this specific sin, which is hunting the fish on the Sabbath day, nor were they insolent toward His prohibition to them against hunting. As for when the third group was forbidding like the second group, and was only made a separate group because a discussion took place between it and the other group of forbidders who withdrew, then in reality they are one group, since they are united in forbidding, withdrawing, and salvation from transformation.

Among the reports from al-Firyabi and Ibn Abi Hatim, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Moses said, "My Lord, I find a community whose Gospels are in their hearts." He said, "That is a community that will come after you: the community of Ahmad (ﷺ)." He said, "My Lord, I find a community who pray the five (prayers), which are expiations for what lies between them." He said, "That is a community that will come after you: the community of Ahmad (ﷺ)." He said, "My Lord, I find a community who give the charity of their wealth, then it returns to them and they eat it." He said, "That is [a community] after you: the community of Ahmad (ﷺ)." He said, "My Lord, make me one of the community of Ahmad (ﷺ)." So Allah revealed, in a manner that pleased Moses, ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice﴾.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community﴾ and the rest of the verse, that he said: "It has reached me that the Children of Israel, when they killed their prophets and disbelieved, and they were twelve tribes (asbat), one tribe disassociated itself from what they had done, made an excuse, and asked Allah to separate them from them. So Allah opened for them a tunnel (nafaq) in the earth, and they travelled through it until they emerged from beyond China. There they are upright (hunafa') Muslims, facing our qibla."

Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "That is His saying: ﴿And We said after him to the Children of Israel, 'Dwell in the land, and when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you together as a mixed multitude﴾ [al-Isra' 17:104]. And the promise of the Hereafter is 'Isa ibn Maryam."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "They travelled in the tunnel (sarb) for a year and a half."

I say: A report as strange and remarkable as this needs verification of its transmission.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "After Moses, the Children of Israel split into seventy-one sects, all of them in the Fire except one sect. The Christians split after 'Isa into seventy-two sects, all of them in the Fire except one sect. This community will certainly split into seventy-three sects, all of them in the Fire except one sect. As for the Jews, Allah says: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice﴾, so this is the one that will be saved. As for the Christians, Allah says: ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:66], so this is the one that will be saved. As for us, He says: ﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it do justice﴾ [al-A'raf 7:181], so this is the one that will be saved from this community."

We have already mentioned that the addition "all of them in the Fire" is not authentically established, neither as a marfu' (attributed to the Prophet) nor as a mawquf (attributed to a Companion).

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿fanbajasat﴾ [gushed forth], that he said: "﴿fanfajarat﴾ [burst forth]."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from 'Ikrimah, who said: "I entered upon Ibn 'Abbas while he was reciting this verse: ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea﴾. He said: 'O 'Ikrimah, do you know what town this is?' I said: 'No.' He said: 'It is Aylah.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Zuhri, who said: "It is Tiberias."

Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿when they transgressed in the Sabbath﴾, that he said: "They wronged."

Ibn Jarir reported from him regarding His saying ﴿shurra'an﴾ [appearing in abundance], he said: "He means from every place."

Ibn Jarir also reported from him, who said: "Floating upon the water."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him, who said: "Coming in."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from him regarding the verse, who said: "It is a town on the shore of the sea between Egypt and Madinah, called Aylah. Allah forbade them the fish on their Sabbath day, and they would come to them on their Sabbath day, appearing in abundance on the shore of the sea. But when the Sabbath day had passed, they could not catch them. They remained like this for as long as Allah willed. Then a group of them took the fish on their Sabbath day. A group admonished them, but they only increased in misguidance. A group of those who forbade said, knowing that these were a people upon whom the punishment was due: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾ They were more angry than the other group, and all of them had been forbidding. When the wrath of Allah befell them, the two groups who said ﴿Why do you admonish?﴾ and those who said ﴿as an excuse before your Lord﴾ were saved, and Allah destroyed the people of His disobedience who had taken the fish, and He transformed them into apes."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him that they were three groups: the group of the sinners, the group of those who forbade, and the group who said ﴿Why do you admonish?﴾. "Only those who forbade were saved, and the rest perished. Then one morning those who had forbidden found themselves in their gatherings searching for the people and not seeing them. They had spent the night and locked their houses behind them. So they began to say: 'Surely something has happened to the people. Look into their affairs.' They looked into their houses, and behold, the people had been transformed: they recognised the man by his eye, and he was an ape, and the woman by her eye, and she was an ape."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, and he mentioned the story, and at its end he said: "I see that those who forbade were saved, and I do not see that the others were mentioned. And we see things that we disapprove of, but we do not say anything about them."

'Ikrimah said: "I said: 'May Allah make me your ransom, do you not see that they disliked what they were upon and opposed them, and said: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾'" He said: "He then ordered that I be clothed in two thick garments."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, also, who said: "Those who forbade evil were saved, and those who committed it perished, and I do not know what was done to those who remained silent."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Abu al-Shaykh reported from him, who said: "By Allah, if I knew that the people who said ﴿Why do you admonish a people?﴾ were saved along with those who forbade evil, it would be dearer to me than what I would exchange it for."

In another wording: "than red camels. But I fear that the punishment descended upon them all."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from 'Ikrimah, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "I do not know whether those who said ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾ were saved or not." He said: "I kept looking at him until he realised that they had been saved, and he clothed me in a robe."

'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, who said: "Those who said ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy?﴾ were transformed into stones."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿with a severe punishment (bi-'adhabin ba'is)﴾, that he said: "Painful and grievous."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 167–170:

His statement ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it: that is, ask them about the time when your Lord proclaimed. *Ta'adhdhana* is of the form *tafa''ala* from *al-iydhan*, which means informing.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: *adhana* with the long vowel means "informed," and *adhdhana* with the doubled letter means "called out."

Some people said: both mean "informed," as one says *ayqana* and *tayaqqana* (both meaning "became certain").

The meaning of the verse is: ask them about the time when the proclamation from your Lord reached them, that He would surely send against them. It has been said that this verb carries the sense of an oath, like "Allah knows" and "Allah bears witness." For this reason, its response takes the form that an oath takes, when He says ﴿He would surely send against them﴾, that is, He would surely dispatch and empower against them, as in His words ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours of great might﴾ (al-Isra: 5), until the Day of Resurrection, as an end-point for their being subjected to the worst torment by whoever Allah sends against them. They had been, by Allah's decree, humiliated, oppressed and tormented at the hands of the people of other religions. Likewise, in this Islamic community they remain, in every region of the earth, in the abasement imposed upon them, in torment and in lowliness. They pay the *jizya* (poll tax, a tax levied on non-Muslim subjects in exchange for protection) to preserve their lives, and Muslims degrade them in matters that involve humiliation, in works that other groups of disbelievers would disdain.

The meaning of *yasumuhum* (p. 509) is "makes them taste." The basic sense of this has already been explained. Then He gave the reason for this in His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾, hastening it in this world, as happened to these people, ﴿and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ after it, that is, abundant in forgiveness and mercy.

168. ﴿And We divided them upon the earth﴾, that is, We scattered them throughout its regions, or We dispersed their affair so that no unified word would gather for them. *Umaman* is in the accusative either as a circumstantial state (*hal*) or as a second object of *qatta'na*, with the verb taken to include the sense of *sayyarna* ("made them"). The clause ﴿among them are the righteous﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for *umaman*. It has been said: they are those who believed in Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family) and those who died before the Muhammadan mission without altering their religion. It has also been said: they are those who settled beyond China, as its explanation was given earlier. ﴿And among them are others below that﴾, that is, below this quality that the first group possessed, which is righteousness. The position of *dun dhalika* ("below that") is nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject; the full sense is "and among them are people below that." What is meant by these is those who did not believe, but immersed themselves in opposition to what Allah had commanded them.

Al-Nahhas said: *dun* is in the accusative as an adverb of place, and we know of no one who put it in the nominative.

﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾, that is, We put them to trial with good and evil, hoping that they would return from their disbelief and sins.

﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾. What is meant by them are the descendants of those whom Allah scattered upon the earth.

Abu Hatim said: *khalf* with the letter *lam* unvocalized means "descendants," singular and plural alike. *Khalaf* with the *lam* vocalized means "replacement," whether a son or otherwise.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: *khalaf* with the vowel means the righteous, and with the sukun it means the wicked.

Labid said:

"Those by whose flanks one lived have gone, and I remain among a successor like the mangy camel's skin."

From this, it is said that *khalf* with the sukun denotes poor speech, and each of the two may be used in place of the other. From this is the statement of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"For us is the first step toward You, and behind us follows our first in obedience to Allah."

﴿They inherited the Book﴾, that is, the Torah from their predecessors, reciting it but not acting by it. ﴿They take the goods of this lower life﴾. Allah informed about them that they take whatever worldly goods come their way, because of the intensity of their greed and the strength of their desire. *Al-adna* ("lower") is derived from *al-dunuww*, which means nearness; that is, they take the goods of this lower thing, which is the world, seeking its benefits quickly through bribery, and what is allotted to them of unlawful gain, in exchange for their distorting the words of Allah, belittling the practice of the rulings of the Torah, and concealing what they conceal of it. It has also been said that *al-adna* is derived from baseness and lowliness, meaning that they take the goods of a base, fallen thing. ﴿And they say, "It will be forgiven us"﴾, that is, they console themselves with forgiveness despite their persistence in error and their failure to return to the truth. The clause ﴿they take﴾ may be either a new sentence explaining their condition or in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, and the clause "they say" is coordinated with it. The purpose of this speech is rebuke and reproach directed at them. The clause ﴿and if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state: that is, they console themselves with forgiveness, while the situation is that if goods like those they used to take come to them, they take them, unconcerned about punishment and not fearful of consequences. It has also been said: the pronoun in *ya'tihim* refers to the Jews of Medina; that is, if goods like those their predecessors used to take come to these Jews who live in the time of Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family), they take them just as their predecessors did. ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them﴾, that is, of the Torah, that they should not say about Allah except the truth? The interrogative is for rebuke and reproach. The clause ﴿and they studied what is in it﴾ is coordinated with "is taken," in meaning, and it has been said that it is coordinated with "they inherited the Book." The better view is that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state, with *qad* implied.

The meaning is: they abandoned acting upon the covenant taken from them in the Book, while in fact they had studied what is in the Book and known it. Thus their abandonment was from knowledge, not from ignorance, and that is a greater sin and a more serious crime.

It has also been said that the meaning of *darasu ma fihi* is that they erased it, by abandoning acting upon it and by not understanding it, from the expression "the wind effaced the traces" when it wipes them out. ﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Allah and avoid His disobedience. Do you not then reason?﴾, so that you may know this and understand it. In this there is a rebuke and reproach beyond measure.

His statement: ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾. The majority read *yumassikuna* with the doubled letter, from *massaka* and *tamassaka*, that is, they firmly hold to the Book, which is the Torah.

Abu al-Aliyah and Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read it with the single letter, from *amsaka yumsiku*.

It is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that he read *masakū*. The meaning is that a group of the People of the Book do not hold fast to the Book and do not act by what is in it, although they have studied it and known it, and they are the ones previously mentioned. And a group hold fast to the Book, that is, the Torah, and act by what is in it and refer to it in matters of their religion. These are the good-doers whose reward Allah does not waste. The relative pronoun is the subject, and ﴿Indeed We do not waste the reward of the reformers﴾ is its predicate, that is, We do not waste the reward of the reformers among them. The explicit mention of prayer occurred even though it is included among the other acts of worship practiced by those who hold to the Torah, because it is the head of acts of worship and the greatest of them. This was the reason for singling it out for mention. It has also been said that it is because it is performed at specific times, while holding fast to the Book is continuous, so it was mentioned for this reason. But this is open to question, since in general every act of worship is bound to a specific time. It is also possible that the relative clause is coordinated with the relative clause preceding it, which is "for those who fear Allah," and that ﴿Do you not then reason?﴾ is a parenthetical clause.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿who will subject them to the worst torment﴾: He said: Muhammad and his community until the Day of Resurrection. The worst torment is the *jizya*.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him that he said: the worst torment is the *kharaj* (land tax). Concerning His words ﴿and We divided them﴾, he said: they are the Jews, whom Allah spread upon the earth, so there is no region of it without a band or group of them in it.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted, concerning His words ﴿He would surely send against them﴾, that he said: against the Jews and the Christians, ﴿until the Day of Resurrection, those who will subject them to the worst torment﴾. So Allah sent against them the community of Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family), who take the *jizya* from them while they are humbled. ﴿And We divided them upon the earth into nations﴾: he said, Jews. ﴿Among them are the righteous﴾: they are the Muslims of the People of the Book. ﴿And among them are others below that﴾: he said, the Jews. ﴿And We tested them with good things﴾: he said, ease and well-being. ﴿And bad things﴾: he said, calamity and punishment.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning ﴿We tested them with good things and bad things﴾, that it means with fertility and drought.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him that he was asked about this verse, ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life﴾, and he said: they are peoples who turn to the world, consuming it and following the easy concessions of the Qur'an, and saying, "It will be forgiven us," and whatever worldly thing comes their way they take.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾: he said, the Christians. ﴿Taking the goods of this lower life﴾: he said, whatever worldly thing of theirs is noble, whether lawful or unlawful, that they desire, they take, and they wish for forgiveness. And if they find the next day something like it, they take it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾: he says, they take whatever they obtain and leave whatever they wish, whether lawful or unlawful, and they say, "It will be forgiven us."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them that they should not say about Allah except the truth﴾: regarding what they require of Allah concerning the forgiveness of their sins, which they continue to return to and do not repent of.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Zayd concerning His words ﴿and they studied what is in it﴾: he said, they knew what is in the Book and did not commit it out of ignorance.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾: he said, it is for the people of faith among them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾: he said, from the Jews and the Christians.

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him that he was asked about this verse, ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life﴾, and he said: they are peoples who turn to the world, consuming it and following the easy concessions of the Qur'an, and saying, "It will be forgiven us," and whatever worldly thing comes their way they take.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾: he said, the Christians. ﴿Taking the goods of this lower life﴾: he said, whatever worldly thing of theirs is noble, whether lawful or unlawful, that they desire, they take, and they wish for forgiveness. And if they find the next day something like it, they take it.

Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning the verse ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor﴾: he says, they take whatever they obtain and leave whatever they wish, whether lawful or unlawful, and they say, "It will be forgiven us."

Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them that they should not say about Allah except the truth﴾: regarding what they require of Allah concerning the forgiveness of their sins, which they continue to return to and do not repent of.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu Zayd concerning His words ﴿and they studied what is in it﴾: he said, they knew what is in the Book and did not commit it out of ignorance.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from al-Hasan concerning His words ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾: he said, it is for the people of faith among them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Mujahid concerning His words ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾: he said, from the Jews and the Christians.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verse 171:

His saying "wa-idh" (and when) is in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, coordinated with what precedes it: that is, "and ask them when We lifted up the mountain" — i.e., We raised the mountain above them. "As though it were a canopy" means that, because of its height, it was as though it were a cloud shading them. The ẓullah (canopy) is the name for anything that provides shade. It has also been read as ṭullah with the ṭā', from aṭalla ʿalayhi, meaning he looked down upon him. "And they thought that it was about to fall upon them," i.e., that it was about to drop down on them.

It is said: the ẓann (thought) here means ʿilm (knowledge). It is also said: it retains its original meaning. "Take what We have given you with strength" — this is under the assumption of an implied saying: that is, "And We said to them: Take," and quwwah (strength) is earnestness and resolve; that is, take it with a strength that is real. "And remember what is in it of the rulings which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not forget it, so that you may be God-fearing" — in hope that you will refrain from what you have been forbidden and act upon what you have been commanded. The explanation of this in al-Baqarah has already been given in full, so we will not repeat it here.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His saying "And when We lifted up the mountain" (7:171), that he said: "We raised it," and this is His saying: "And We raised over them the Mount" (4:154). Then He said: "Take what We have given you with strength, or else I will send it down upon you."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning the verse that he said: "The angels lifted it above their heads, and it was said to them: 'Take what We have given you with strength.' So whenever they looked at the mountain they said: 'We hear and we obey,' and whenever they looked at the Book they said: 'We hear and we disobey.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh also related from him, likewise, that he said: "Indeed I know why the Jews prostrate on one side (ḥarf). Allah said: 'And when We lifted up the mountain over them,' and he said: 'You shall certainly take My command, or I will hurl it upon you.' So they prostrated while looking at it, fearing that it would fall upon them. And it was a prostration that Allah, glorified is He, was pleased with, and they made it a sunnah."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh related from Qatadah, regarding "And when We lifted up the mountain," that he said: "Allah uprooted it from its base, then placed it above their heads, then said: 'You shall certainly take My command, or I will hurl it upon you.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 7, verses 172–174:

His saying: *wa-idh* (and when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that is coordinated with what precedes it, as has already been explained.

His saying: *min Banī Ādam* (from the children of Adam). From this, some have argued that the ones taken (*al-ma'khūdhīn*) here are the descendants of the children of Adam, whom Allah brought forth from their loins generation after generation.

A group of exegetes (*mufassirūn*) held this view. They said: the meaning of *ashhadahum 'alā anfusihim* (He made them testify against themselves) is that He showed them, through His creation, that He is their Creator, so this indication (*dalāla*) took the place of testimony. This verse is then a case of figurative expression (*tamthīl*), as in His saying, ﴿So He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ (Fussilat: 11).

It has also been said: the meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, brought forth the souls (*arwāh*) before creating the bodies, and placed in them the knowledge by which they understood His address, may He be exalted. It has also been said: the "children of Adam" here means Adam himself, as occurs in other places in the Qur'an.

The meaning, according to this view, is that when Allah, glory be to Him, created Adam, He passed His hand over his back, drew out his offspring, and took from them a covenant. These are the people of the world of atoms (*'ālam al-dharr*). This is the truth from which one should not turn aside or go over to anything else, because it is established as *marfū'* (traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)) and as *mawqūf* (traced back to a Companion) from other Companions, and there is no compulsion to resort to figurative interpretation. When the river of Allah comes, the stream of Ma'qil is nullified (*a proverbial expression: the clear truth overrides lesser claims*). At the end of this discussion, if Allah wills, we shall mention some of what has been transmitted on this matter.

His saying: ﴿min ẓuhūrihim﴾ (from their backs) is a substitute (*badal*) for "from the children of Adam," a partial substitution (*badal ba'ḍ min kull*). It has been said that *dhurriyyātihim* (their offspring) is a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*). The Kufans and Ibn Kathir read *dhurriyyatahum* (their offspring) in the singular, which can refer to one or to many. The rest read *dhurriyyātihim* in the plural.

*Wa-ashhadahum 'alā anfusihim* means: He made each one of them testify, saying, *"Am I not your Lord?"* — that is, saying, "Am I not your Lord?" This is by way of the implied saying (*'alā irādat al-qawl*). They said, *"Yes, we testify"*, that is, against ourselves, that You are our Lord.

His saying: *an taqūlū* (that you should not say). Abu 'Amr read it with the *yā'* (third person, "they say") here and in His saying *an yaqūlū* (that they should say), in keeping with the third person used before it. The rest read it with the *tā'* (second person, addressing them directly).

The meaning is: lest they say, or so that they would not say — that is, We did this taking and making them testify, lest they say on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿"Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾, that is, unaware of the fact that Allah is our Lord alone, with no partner. (p-511)

His saying: ﴿or [lest] you say, "Indeed, our fathers associated [others with Allah] before, and we were [only] descendants after them"﴾ is coordinated with the first "lest you say". That is, We did this lest you excuse yourselves through heedlessness, or attribute the association to your fathers rather than to yourselves. The particle *aw* (or) here is for preventing the absence of both (*li-man'i al-khuluw*), not for preventing their combination. They might offer an excuse by combining both matters: "from before" (that is, before our time), and "we were descendants after them, not guided to the truth and not knowing what is right. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers among our fathers did, when we bear no blame, due to our ignorance, our inability to reflect, and our following the footsteps of our predecessors?"

Allah, glory be to Him, has made clear in this wisdom, for which He brought them forth from the back of Adam and made them testify against themselves, that He did this so that they would not say this statement on the Day of Resurrection, and would not plead this false cause or offer this worthless excuse.

*Wa-kadhālika* (and thus), that is, and in like manner to this detailed explanation, *nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt* (We detail the signs), *wa-la'allahum yarji'ūn* (so that perhaps they may return to the truth and abandon what they are upon of falsehood).

Malik in *al-Muwatta'*, Ahmad in *al-Musnad*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih*, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* transmitted that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about this verse, ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾, the verse. He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being asked about it, and he said: 'Allah created Adam, then passed His right hand over his back and drew out from it offspring. He said, "I have created these for Paradise, and they will act with the deeds of the people of Paradise." Then He passed His hand over his back and drew out from it offspring, and said, "I have created these for the Fire, and they will act with the deeds of the people of the Fire."' A man said, 'O Messenger of Allah, then what is the point of action?' He said: 'When Allah creates a servant for Paradise, He makes him act with the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of Paradise, and so He admits him to Paradise by it. And when He creates a servant for the Fire, He makes him act with the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of the Fire, and so He admits him to the Fire.'"

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who graded it *sahih*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah took the covenant from the back of Adam at Nu'man on the Day of 'Arafa. He brought forth from his loins every offspring He had created, scattered them before Himself, then spoke to them and said, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes, we testify...'" up to His saying, "the falsifiers." Its chain (*isnad*) is free of any flaw.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted it, *mawqūf* on Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mandah, in *Kitab al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyya*, transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Wa-idh akhadha rabbuka min Banī Ādam min ẓuhūrihim dhurriyyātihim* (And when your Lord took from the children of Adam from their backs their offspring)." He said: "He took them from his back as a comb is drawn through hair. Then He said to them, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes.' The angels said, 'We testify, lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this."'" In its chain is Ahmad ibn Abi Zayba, Abu Muhammad al-Jurjani, judge of Qumis, who was one of the ascetics (*zuhhād*). al-Nasa'i included him in his *Sunan*.

Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "His hadith is written down." Ibn 'Adi said: "He narrated many strange (*gharā'ib*) hadiths."

This hadith was also narrated by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and these are trustworthy imams.

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama*, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Umama that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the creation, decreed the decree, and took the covenant of the prophets, and His Throne was upon the water, He took the people of the right hand with His right hand, and He took the people of the left with His other hand, and both hands of the Merciful are right. He said, 'O companions of the right hand!' They responded to Him and said, 'Here we are, our Lord, at Your service.' He said, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes...'" to the end of the hadith.

The narrations on this subject are numerous. Some are specifically tied to the explanation of this verse, and others are general, including the bringing forth of the offspring of Adam from his back and the taking of the covenant from them, as in the hadith of Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), in the *Two Sahihs* and elsewhere.

As for what has been transmitted from the Companions in explaining this verse as the bringing forth of Adam's offspring from his loins in the world of atoms, the taking of the covenant from them, and their being made to testify against themselves, these are numerous. Among them is what 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, the verse. He said: "Allah created Adam and took his covenant that He is his Lord, and wrote his term and his provision. Then He brought forth his offspring from his back like particles of dust (*dharr*), and took their covenants that He is their Lord, and wrote their terms, their provisions, and their afflictions."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also transmitted something similar from him.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir also transmitted something similar from him.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mandah transmitted something similar from him. This meaning is reported from him through many other chains, as a statement of his own (*mawqūf*).

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, concerning His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, the verse: "He took them as a comb takes from the head."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and several Companions something similar in explaining the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal in the narration of *al-Musnad*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mandah, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara*, and Ibn 'Asakir in his *Tarikh* transmitted from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, concerning His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, the verse: "He gathered them all together, made them spirits in their forms, then made them speak, and they spoke. Then He took from them the covenant and the pact, and then He made them testify against themselves."

It has also been transmitted from a group of those after the Companions that this verse refers to the bringing forth of Adam's offspring from his back. What the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in explaining it, which we have already mentioned, is sufficient and makes further lengthy discussion unnecessary.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (*Fath al-Qadir*) on surah 7, verses 172–174:

His saying: *wa-idh* (and when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that is coordinated with what precedes it, as has already been explained.

His saying: *min Banī Ādam* (from the children of Adam). From this, some have argued that the ones taken (*al-ma'khūdhīn*) here are the descendants of the children of Adam, whom Allah brought forth from their loins generation after generation.

A group of exegetes (*mufassirūn*) held this view. They said: the meaning of *ashhadahum 'alā anfusihim* (He made them testify against themselves) is that He showed them, through His creation, that He is their Creator, so this indication (*dalāla*) took the place of testimony. This verse is then a case of figurative expression (*tamthīl*), as in His saying, ﴿So He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ (Fussilat: 11).

It has also been said: the meaning is that Allah, glory be to Him, brought forth the souls (*arwāh*) before creating the bodies, and placed in them the knowledge by which they understood His address, may He be exalted. It has also been said: the "children of Adam" here means Adam himself, as occurs in other places in the Qur'an.

The meaning, according to this view, is that when Allah, glory be to Him, created Adam, He passed His hand over his back, drew out his offspring, and took from them a covenant. These are the people of the world of atoms (*'ālam al-dharr*). This is the truth from which one should not turn aside or go over to anything else, because it is established as *marfū'* (traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ)) and as *mawqūf* (traced back to a Companion) from other Companions, and there is no compulsion to resort to figurative interpretation. When the river of Allah comes, the stream of Ma'qil is nullified (*a proverbial expression: the clear truth overrides lesser claims*). At the end of this discussion, if Allah wills, we shall mention some of what has been transmitted on this matter.

His saying: ﴿min ẓuhūrihim﴾ (from their backs) is a substitute (*badal*) for "from the children of Adam," a partial substitution (*badal ba'ḍ min kull*). It has been said that *dhurriyyātihim* (their offspring) is a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimāl*). The Kufans and Ibn Kathir read *dhurriyyatahum* (their offspring) in the singular, which can refer to one or to many. The rest read *dhurriyyātihim* in the plural.

*Wa-ashhadahum 'alā anfusihim* means: He made each one of them testify, saying, *"Am I not your Lord?"* — that is, saying, "Am I not your Lord?" This is by way of the implied saying (*'alā irādat al-qawl*). They said, *"Yes, we testify"*, that is, against ourselves, that You are our Lord.

His saying: *an taqūlū* (that you should not say). Abu 'Amr read it with the *yā'* (third person, "they say") here and in His saying *an yaqūlū* (that they should say), in keeping with the third person used before it. The rest read it with the *tā'* (second person, addressing them directly).

The meaning is: lest they say, or so that they would not say — that is, We did this taking and making them testify, lest they say on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿"Indeed, we were unaware of this"﴾, that is, unaware of the fact that Allah is our Lord alone, with no partner. (p-511)

His saying: ﴿or [lest] you say, "Indeed, our fathers associated [others with Allah] before, and we were [only] descendants after them"﴾ is coordinated with the first "lest you say". That is, We did this lest you excuse yourselves through heedlessness, or attribute the association to your fathers rather than to yourselves. The particle *aw* (or) here is for preventing the absence of both (*li-man'i al-khuluw*), not for preventing their combination. They might offer an excuse by combining both matters: "from before" (that is, before our time), and "we were descendants after them, not guided to the truth and not knowing what is right. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers among our fathers did, when we bear no blame, due to our ignorance, our inability to reflect, and our following the footsteps of our predecessors?"

Allah, glory be to Him, has made clear in this wisdom, for which He brought them forth from the back of Adam and made them testify against themselves, that He did this so that they would not say this statement on the Day of Resurrection, and would not plead this false cause or offer this worthless excuse.

*Wa-kadhālika* (and thus), that is, and in like manner to this detailed explanation, *nufaṣṣilu al-āyāt* (We detail the signs), *wa-la'allahum yarji'ūn* (so that perhaps they may return to the truth and abandon what they are upon of falsehood).

Malik in *al-Muwatta'*, Ahmad in *al-Musnad*, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it *hasan*, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban in his *Sahih*, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara* transmitted that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about this verse, ﴿And when your Lord took...﴾, the verse. He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being asked about it, and he said: 'Allah created Adam, then passed His right hand over his back and drew out from it offspring. He said, "I have created these for Paradise, and they will act with the deeds of the people of Paradise." Then He passed His hand over his back and drew out from it offspring, and said, "I have created these for the Fire, and they will act with the deeds of the people of the Fire."' A man said, 'O Messenger of Allah, then what is the point of action?' He said: 'When Allah creates a servant for Paradise, He makes him act with the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of Paradise, and so He admits him to Paradise by it. And when He creates a servant for the Fire, He makes him act with the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of the Fire, and so He admits him to the Fire.'"

Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, al-Hakim, who graded it *sahih*, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat* transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Allah took the covenant from the back of Adam at Nu'man on the Day of 'Arafa. He brought forth from his loins every offspring He had created, scattered them before Himself, then spoke to them and said, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes, we testify...'" up to His saying, "the falsifiers." Its chain (*isnad*) is free of any flaw.

Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted it, *mawqūf* on Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mandah, in *Kitab al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyya*, transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "*Wa-idh akhadha rabbuka min Banī Ādam min ẓuhūrihim dhurriyyātihim* (And when your Lord took from the children of Adam from their backs their offspring)." He said: "He took them from his back as a comb is drawn through hair. Then He said to them, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes.' The angels said, 'We testify, lest you say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this."'" In its chain is Ahmad ibn Abi Zayba, Abu Muhammad al-Jurjani, judge of Qumis, who was one of the ascetics (*zuhhād*). al-Nasa'i included him in his *Sunan*.

Abu Hatim al-Razi said: "His hadith is written down." Ibn 'Adi said: "He narrated many strange (*gharā'ib*) hadiths."

This hadith was also narrated by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and these are trustworthy imams.

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul*, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh in *al-'Azama*, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu Umama that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created the creation, decreed the decree, and took the covenant of the prophets, and His Throne was upon the water, He took the people of the right hand with His right hand, and He took the people of the left with His other hand, and both hands of the Merciful are right. He said, 'O companions of the right hand!' They responded to Him and said, 'Here we are, our Lord, at Your service.' He said, 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes...'" to the end of the hadith.

The narrations on this subject are numerous. Some are specifically tied to the explanation of this verse, and others are general, including the bringing forth of the offspring of Adam from his back and the taking of the covenant from them, as in the hadith of Anas, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), in the *Two Sahihs* and elsewhere.

As for what has been transmitted from the Companions in explaining this verse as the bringing forth of Adam's offspring from his loins in the world of atoms, the taking of the covenant from them, and their being made to testify against themselves, these are numerous. Among them is what 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, the verse. He said: "Allah created Adam and took his covenant that He is his Lord, and wrote his term and his provision. Then He brought forth his offspring from his back like particles of dust (*dharr*), and took their covenants that He is their Lord, and wrote their terms, their provisions, and their afflictions."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar from him.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also transmitted something similar from him.

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir also transmitted something similar from him.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, and Ibn Mandah transmitted something similar from him. This meaning is reported from him through many other chains, as a statement of his own (*mawqūf*).

Ibn Abi Shayba, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, concerning His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, the verse: "He took them as a comb takes from the head."

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr in *al-Tamhid* transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and several Companions something similar in explaining the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad ibn Hanbal in the narration of *al-Musnad*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mandah, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-al-Sifat*, al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtara*, and Ibn 'Asakir in his *Tarikh* transmitted from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, concerning His saying, ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam...﴾, the verse: "He gathered them all together, made them spirits in their forms, then made them speak, and they spoke. Then He took from them the covenant and the pact, and then He made them testify against themselves."

It has also been transmitted from a group of those after the Companions that this verse refers to the bringing forth of Adam's offspring from his back. What the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said in explaining it, which we have already mentioned, is sufficient and makes further lengthy discussion unnecessary.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 7, verses 175–178:**

His saying: *wa-tlu* ("and recite") is coordinated with the verbs implied in the earlier narratives. He, glorified is He, mentioned this story and reminded the People of the Book of it because it was recorded among them in the Torah.

Scholars have differed about this one "to whom We gave Our signs, but he cast them off." It was said that he was Bal'am ibn Ba'ura' (Bal'am son of Ba'ura'). He had memorized some of the revealed books. It was also said that he had been given prophethood and that his supplications were answered. God sent him to Madyan to call them to faith, but they gave him generous gifts, so he followed their religion and abandoned what he had been sent with. When Musa (Moses) came with the Children of Israel to fight the tyrants (al-jabbarin), the tyrants asked Bal'am ibn Ba'ura' to invoke a curse on Musa. He stood up to curse him, but his tongue turned to cursing his own companions. He was asked about this, and he said: "I cannot do more than what you hear." His tongue then hung out over his chest, and he said: "Now both this world and the Hereafter have gone from me, and nothing is left but deceit, trickery and stratagem. I will scheme for you. I think you should send your young women out to them, for God hates fornication. If they fall into it, they will perish." So the Children of Israel fell into fornication, and God sent the plague upon them, and seventy thousand of them died. It was also said that this man's name was Ba'im and that he was from the Children of Israel. It was said that the intended person is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi, who had read the books and knew that God would send a messenger in that time. When God sent Muhammad (ﷺ), he envied him and disbelieved in him. It was said that he is Abu 'Amir ibn Sayfi, who used to wear wool garments (al-musuh) in the pre-Islamic period, and he disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said that the verse was revealed about Quraysh, to whom God gave His signs that He revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), but they rejected them. It was also said that it was revealed about the Jews and Christians, who awaited the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ) and then disbelieved in him.

His saying: *fa-nsalakha minha* means: from these signs that were given to him, just as a sheep strips off its skin (tansalikh al-shatu 'an jildiha), so that no connection with them remained for him. *Fa-atba'ahu al-shaytan* ("Then Satan followed him") means: when he stripped away from the signs, Satan overtook him, reached him and became his companion. Or it means that he followed in his footsteps. It is also read *fa-ttaba'ahu* with a doubled *ta'* (shaddah), meaning "he followed him." *Fa-kana min al-ghawin* ("So he became one of the misguided") means: those firmly established in error, who are the disbelievers.

His saying: *Wa-law shi'na larafa'nahu biha* ("Had We willed, We would have elevated him by them"): the pronoun refers to the one who was given the signs. The meaning is: had We willed to raise him by means of the signs We had given him, We would have raised him by them, i.e., by their means. But We did not will that, because he stripped away from them and abandoned acting upon them. It was also said that the meaning is: had We willed, We would have caused him to die before he disobeyed, and raised him to Paradise by them, i.e., by acting upon them. "But he clung to the earth" (*akhlada ila al-ardi*): the root of *ikhlad* is adherence. It is said: "So-and-so clung to the place" when he stayed in it and remained attached to it. The meaning here is that he inclined toward this world, desired it, and preferred it over the Hereafter. *Wa-ttaba'a hawahu* ("and followed his desire") means: he followed what he desired and abandoned acting upon what the knowledge God had taught him required, which was the trash of this world. It was also said that his desire was with the disbelievers. It was said that he followed the pleasure of his wife, and she was the one who drove him to strip away from the signs of God.

His saying: *Fa-mathaluhu ka-mathali al-kalb* ("So his likeness is the likeness of a dog"): meaning, when he stripped away from the signs and did not act upon them, he sank to the lowest rank, resembling the most base of animals in lowliness, and matching it in its worst attributes. The dog pants in both states, whether a person approaches it or leaves it. It pants whether it is driven off or not, whether it is pursued or not. Nothing is lower or baser than this. The clause *in tahmil 'alayhi yalhath aw tatrukhu yalhath* ("whether you attack it, it pants, or you leave it, it pants") is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal): i.e., his likeness is the likeness of the dog, in a state of having this attribute. The meaning is that this one who has stripped away from the signs does not desist from disobedience in any of his circumstances, whether a preacher admonishes him, a reminder reminds him, or a restrainer restrains him, or none of that happens to him.

Al-Qutaybi said: Everything that pants does so from exhaustion or thirst, except the dog, which pants in a state of fatigue, in a state of rest, in a state of illness, in a state of health, in a state of satiety, and in a state of thirst. So God struck this as a parable for the one who denied His signs, saying: "If you admonish him, he goes astray, and if you leave him, he goes astray." He is like the dog: if you leave it, it pants, and if you drive it away, it pants, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you; it is the same for you whether you call them or you remain silent﴾ (al-A'raf 7:193). *Al-lahth* is letting the tongue hang out due to fatigue, thirst, or other things.

Al-Jawhari said: *lahatha al-kalbu* (with a fatha) *yalhathu lahthan wa-luhaan* (with a damma) means the dog let its tongue hang out from exhaustion or thirst. Likewise a man does so when he is exhausted.

It was said: the meaning of the verse is that if you pursue the dog, it barks and runs away, and if you leave it, it attacks you and barks. It exhausts itself, approaching you and turning away from you. So it experiences at that moment what it experiences when thirsty, namely letting its tongue hang out. The reference in His saying *dhalika* ("that") is to the preceding parable with that base condition.

*Huwa* is the subject, and its predicate is *mathalu al-qawm alladhina kadhdhabu bi-ayatina* ("the likeness of the people who denied Our signs"). That is: that base parable is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, from among the Jews, after they had come to know them and recognized them, yet they distorted, altered and concealed the description of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and denied them. *Fa-qsusi al-qasas* ("So relate the stories") means: relate to them this story, which describes the man who stripped away from the signs. His aforementioned likeness is like the likeness of these denying people from among the Jews, to whom you relate it, so that perhaps they will reflect upon it, apply their understanding to it, and thereby restrain themselves from error and turn toward what is right.

His saying: *sa'a mathalan al-qawmu alladhina kadhdhabu bi-ayatina* ("Evil is the example of the people who denied Our signs"): this sentence contains an explanation of the state of these people, extremely ugly. It is said: *sa'a al-shay'u* means it became ugly; this is intransitive. *Sa'ahu yasu'uhu mas'ah* is transitive, and it is one of the verbs of blame, like *bi'sa*. Its agent is a hidden pronoun within it, and *mathalan* is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) explaining it. The one to whom the blame applies is "the people who denied Our signs." It is necessary to assume an omitted genitive phrase for agreement, i.e., *sa'a mathalan* "the likeness of the people who denied" is evil.

Al-Akhfash said: The word *mathal* was made to refer to the people by way of metaphor. The people are in the nominative case as the subject, or by assuming an implied subject. The construction is: "The likeness is evil, a likeness that is the likeness of the people." So he said.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi estimated it as: *sa'a mathalan mathalu al-qawm*, as we have already mentioned.

Al-Jahdari and al-A'mash read: *wa-sa'a mathalan al-qawmu* ("and evil is the example, the people").

His saying: *wa-anfusahum kanu yazlimun* ("and they were wronging themselves"): meaning, they wronged no one by denying except themselves; their wrongdoing did not extend beyond them to others and did not exceed them. The clause is coordinated with the one before it, in the sense that they combined denying the signs of God with wronging themselves.

*Man yahdi Allahu fa-huwa al-muhtadi* ("Whomever God guides, he is the one guided"), by what He prescribed and legislated for His servants. *Wa-man yudlil fa-ulaika hum al-khasirun* ("and whomever He leads astray, those are the losers"), those who are complete in loss. Whomever He guides, there is no misleader for him, and whomever He misleads, there is no guide for him: what He wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur.

Al-Firyabi, 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, regarding His saying: ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾, that he said: "He is a man from the Children of Israel called Bal'am ibn Ba'ura'."

Ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "He is Bal'am ibn Ba'ura'." In another wording: "Bal'am ibn Ba'ir, the one who was given the Name, was among the Children of Israel."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾, that he said: "He is a man from the city of the tyrants called Bal'am. He had learned the Greatest Name of God. When Musa came down upon them, his kinsmen and people came to him and said: 'Musa is a fierce man, and with him are many troops, and if he prevails over us, he will destroy us. So invoke God to turn Musa and those with him away from us.' He said: 'If I invoke God to turn Musa and those with him away, my worldly life and my Hereafter will be lost.' They kept at him until he invoked God, and so He stripped from him what was in him."

Regarding His saying: ﴿If you attack him, he pants, or if you leave him, he pants﴾, he said: "If he is burdened with wisdom, he does not carry it; and if he is left alone, he does not become guided to goodness, like the dog: if it is lying down, it pants, and if it is driven away, it pants."

Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him regarding the verse, that he said: "He is a man who was given three supplications, which would be answered for him. He had a wife, and he had a child by her. She said: 'Make one of them for me.' He said: 'Then you will have one. What is it that you want?' She said: 'Invoke God to make me the most beautiful woman among the Children of Israel.' He invoked God, and He made her the most beautiful woman among the Children of Israel. When she knew that there was none like her among them, she became averse to him and wanted something else. So he invoked God to make her a female dog, and she became a female dog. Two supplications were gone. Then her sons came and said: 'We cannot bear this. Our mother has become a female dog, and people taunt us with her. Invoke God to return her to the state she was in.' So he invoked God, and she returned as she had been. The three supplications were gone, and she was named al-Basus."

'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr regarding the verse, that he said: "He is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi." In another wording: "It was revealed about your companion Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir transmitted from him something similar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from al-Sha'bi, regarding this verse, that he said: "Ibn 'Abbas said: 'He is a man from the Children of Israel called Bal'am ibn Ba'ura'.' The Ansar used to say: 'He is the son of the monk for whom the Mosque of Discord (masjid al-shiqaq) was built.' The Thaqif used to say: 'He is Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "He is Sayfi ibn al-Rahib."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu al-Shaykh transmitted from him regarding His saying: *fa-nsalakha minha*, that he said: "Knowledge was removed from him."

Regarding His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them﴾, he said: "God raised him by His knowledge."

Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa-l-Sifat* transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ), in his sermon, would praise God and extol Him with what is fitting for Him. Then he would say: 'Whomever God guides, there is none to mislead him, and whomever He leads astray, there is none to guide him. The truest speech is the Book of God, the best guidance is the guidance of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the worst of affairs are their novelties. Every novelty is an innovation (bid'ah), every innovation is misguidance, and every misguidance is in the Fire.' Then he would say: 'I and the Hour have been sent like these two.'"
